case_title: Parag Sheth vs Mr. Sunil Kumar Agarwal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Parag Sheth (erstwhile IRP), Respondent 1 is Sunil Kumar Agarwal (RP), R2/R3 are banks[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying CIRP of Digjam Ltd. initiated by an Operational Creditor[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not detailed as the issue concerns IRP fees[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IRP was replaced by RP on 01.01.2020[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The IRP renewed insurance at a higher premium without CoC approval and appointed professionals without authorization, leading the CoC to deduct Rs. 4,19,719 from his fees[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT dismissed the IRP's application for payment of the deducted fees and professional costs, which was appealed[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether Section 20(2)(b) of the IBC authorizes an IRP to enter into a new contract (renewing insurance at a higher premium) and appoint professionals without the approval of the Committee of Creditors[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Interim Resolution Professional cannot make new financial commitments, such as renewing insurance at a higher rate or appointing legal/financial professionals, without the explicit approval of the Committee of Creditors[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 20(2)(b) of the IBC only authorizes the IRP to enter into or modify contracts that were entered into before the commencement of CIRP, not to create entirely new contracts post-commencement[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found the IRP was aware of his limitations as he circulated quotations, yet proceeded without CoC approval[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC lawfully deducted the unauthorized premium from the IRP's fees, and the IRP is not entitled to claim fees for unauthorized professionals[cite: 11].
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 11].
summary: An erstwhile IRP appealed the NCLT's dismissal of his claim for deducted fees and unpaid professional costs[cite: 11]. The NCLAT held that under Section 20(2)(b) of the IBC, an IRP cannot enter into new contracts or appoint professionals without CoC approval[cite: 11]. Thus, the CoC's deduction of the unauthorized excess insurance premium from his fees was justified[cite: 11].

case_title: STCI Finance Limited vs Parinee Developers Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are STCI Finance Ltd (Financial Creditor) and Vipul Dilip Shah & Ors (Promoters); Respondent is Parinee Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial debt leading to CIRP initiation[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt repayment, settled via a settlement deed covering principal, interest, and expenses[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 09.06.2020; Settlement proposal sent on 08.12.2020; CoC approved withdrawal on 08.02.2021[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC approved the settlement deed and withdrawal under Section 12A with a 99.91% voting share[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the Section 12A withdrawal application citing procedural delays and conditional settlement terms, prompting this appeal[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can reject a Section 12A withdrawal application that has been approved by 99.91% of the CoC on grounds of procedural delays and the conditional nature of the settlement[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the CoC in approving a settlement and withdrawing CIRP under Section 12A is paramount and should not be interfered with on hyper-technical or procedural delay grounds if the terms do not violate the law[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A and Regulation 30A provide a clear mechanism for withdrawal; procedural timelines under IBC are directory for settlements, and conditions allowing for revival of CIRP upon default are legally permissible[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the settlement was overwhelmingly approved (99.91%) and found none of its conditions violated the IBC[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the withdrawal application; the CoC's commercial decision to settle must be respected and implemented[cite: 13].
operative_order: The appeals were allowed, the NCLT order was set aside, the Section 12A application was allowed, and the Corporate Debtor was released from the rigour of CIRP with immediate effect[cite: 13].
summary: The NCLT rejected a Section 12A withdrawal application despite 99.91% CoC approval, citing procedural delays and uncertainties in the settlement deed[cite: 13]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, ruling that the CoC's commercial wisdom is paramount and the Adjudicating Authority cannot reject a valid, overwhelmingly approved settlement on hyper-technical grounds[cite: 13].

case_title: The State Of Telangana & Anr vs Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ranjit Kapoor (Promoter/Suspended Director of White Metals Ltd.), Respondent 1 is ARCIL, Respondent 2 is Hemant Sharma (RP)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying CIRP of White Metals Ltd[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not detailed[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 13.06.2018; 330 days expired on 09.05.2019; total 1091 days passed[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Successful Resolution Applicant itself went into CIRP, causing massive delays[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT directed the RP to invite fresh Expression of Interest on 01.07.2021 due to the original applicant's CIRP; the Promoter appealed because the CIRP period was never formally extended[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether fresh Expressions of Interest can be invited without a formal extension of the CIRP period under Section 12 of the IBC when the original 330-day timeline has massively expired[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While an Adjudicating Authority has the power to order fresh EOIs if the previous successful applicant fails, it must concurrently address and decide upon the mandatory extension of the CIRP period under Section 12 of the IBC[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 prescribes statutory timelines that must be judicially managed; massive lapses (1091 days) require a formal extension order to legitimize ongoing CIRP steps[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Acknowledged the Appellant's intent to submit a resolution plan and the fact that no formal extension under Section 12 had been passed despite 1091 days elapsing[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal declined to set aside the order calling for fresh EOIs but remanded the matter specifically for the Adjudicating Authority to pass an order regarding the extension of the CIRP period[cite: 15].
operative_order: The appeal was disposed of by remitting the matter back to the Adjudicating Authority solely to consider and decide on the extension of the CIRP period under Section 12[cite: 15].
summary: After 1091 days of CIRP, the NCLT ordered fresh EOIs because the successful resolution applicant entered CIRP itself[cite: 15]. The Corporate Debtor's promoter appealed, noting the CIRP period had never been formally extended[cite: 15]. The NCLAT kept the EOI process intact but remanded the case for the NCLT to explicitly rule on extending the CIRP period under Section 12 of the IBC[cite: 15].

case_title: M/s Bindu Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. vs M/s Sonu Jain, Liquidator of Falcon Consultancy Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Bindu Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. (Bidder), Respondent 1 is Sonu Jain (Liquidator of Falcon Consultancy)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Auction sale of the Corporate Debtor's property during liquidation[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (Liquidation phase)[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Re-auction took place on 23.08.2021[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant bid Rs. 1 Crore, but another bidder who paid the EMD was locked out due to technical glitches and offered Rs. 1.20 Crore; the Financial Creditor insisted on re-auction[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT allowed the Liquidator's application to cancel the initial auction and hold a re-auction to maximize value; the Appellant appealed[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether a liquidator can cancel an auction where the highest bidder has deposited the bid amount and conduct a re-auction if another eligible bidder was prevented from participating due to technical glitches[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A liquidator is justified in conducting multiple rounds of auctions to maximize the value of the assets in the interest of the creditors, especially when technical glitches prevent fair participation[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Clause 11 of Schedule I read with Regulation 33 of the Liquidation Process Regulations expressly permits the liquidator to conduct multiple rounds of auctions[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the re-auction successfully yielded a significantly higher bid (Rs. 2.17 Crores compared to Rs. 1 Crore), validating the commercial logic of the re-auction[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: There was no material irregularity in the Adjudicating Authority's order permitting the re-auction to maximize creditor returns[cite: 17].
operative_order: The appeal was summarily dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 17].
summary: An auction bidder appealed the NCLT's decision allowing the liquidator to hold a re-auction after the appellant had deposited the Rs. 1 Crore bid amount[cite: 17]. The liquidator argued another bidder was excluded due to technical glitches, and a re-auction maximized value[cite: 17]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Regulation 33 permits multiple auction rounds to maximize creditor returns, which was vindicated by the new Rs. 2.17 Crore bid[cite: 17].

case_title: Anuj Tejpal vs Rakesh Yadav & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Anuj Tejpal (Ex-Director of Corporate Debtor); Corporate Debtor: OYO Hotels and Homes Private Limited; Operational Creditor: Rakesh Yadav; Intervenors: Various third-party hoteliers. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management Service Agreement (MSA) dated 16.11.2018 to manage and operate Hotel Yellow White Residency, Gurgaon. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default amount was Rs. 16,02,000 for the period July 2019 to November 2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notices were issued on 13.09.2019 (demanding Rs. 7,02,000) and 11.11.2019 (demanding Rs. 16,02,000). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence showed that MSA rights were transferred to a sister concern MTH, which made payments; a demand draft of Rs. 16,02,000 was paid by MTH on 03.04.2021 resulting in full and final settlement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition was filed in NCLT Ahmedabad which admitted it on 30.03.2021; Appellant filed IA 815/2021 in NCLAT seeking withdrawal under Rule 11 due to pre-CoC settlement.
legal_issues: Whether NCLAT can exercise inherent powers under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules to allow withdrawal of an admitted CIRP application prior to the constitution of CoC, notwithstanding the procedure under Regulation 30-A(1)(a).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Appellate Tribunal possesses inherent powers under Rule 11 to allow withdrawal of an admitted CIRP application prior to the constitution of the Committee of Creditors upon a settlement, regardless of procedural regulations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12-A of IBC applies post-CoC constitution; Regulation 30-A(1)(a) is directory, not mandatory, and cannot curtail inherent powers under Rule 11 as substantive law takes precedence over regulations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mere filing of claims by third-party operational creditors with the IRP prior to CoC constitution does not constitute default per se nor grant them locus standi to block a valid settlement between the primary parties. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the operational debt was satisfied in full prior to CoC formation and third-party interventions were untenable, the withdrawal application under Rule 11 was allowed and the admission order set aside.
operative_order: IA 815 of 2021 is allowed. Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) 298 of 2021 is allowed and the Impugned Order dated 30.03.2021 admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP is set aside. The Corporate Debtor is released from the rigours of CIRP and allowed to function independently. Proposed Intervention Applications are dismissed.
summary: The Appellant challenged the admission of a Section 9 petition against OYO Hotels. During the appeal, the parties reached a settlement before the CoC was constituted, and the Appellant sought withdrawal under Rule 11. Third-party intervenors objected, citing Regulation 30-A. The NCLAT held that Rule 11 inherent powers can be exercised for withdrawal pre-CoC and that Regulation 30-A is directory. The appeal was allowed, and the CIRP admission was set aside.

case_title: Fourth Dimension Solution Limited vs Ricoh India Limited & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Fourth Dimension Solution Ltd (FDSL, Operational Creditor); Corporate Debtor: Ricoh India Ltd; Successful Resolution Applicants: Kalpraj Dharamshi & Rekha Jhunjhunwala. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Over 90 contracts for various projects worth Rs. 2400 Crores between Appellant and Corporate Debtor since 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant filed six claims totaling Rs. 511,58,39,247/- in Form-A before IRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 10 on 14.05.2018; claim submitted on 05.06.2018; updated lists of creditors issued marking claim as 'Nil' and disputed on 29.11.2018 and 24.01.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP found claims disputed in pending arbitrations; forensic audit by A&M and SEBI interim order dated 16.08.2018 showed transactions between FDSL and Corporate Debtor were fraudulent and extortionate. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the resolution plan on 28.11.2019 despite FDSL's pending avoidance application and 'Nil' claim status; Appellant challenged the plan's approval.
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional committed a material irregularity by keeping the operational creditor's disputed claim at 'Nil' value and whether a resolution plan can extinguish pending/undecided claims upon approval.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A successful resolution applicant takes over the business of the corporate debtor on a clean slate; all claims not included in the approved resolution plan stand permanently extinguished. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 of the IBC renders the approved resolution plan binding on all stakeholders, extinguishing pre-CIRP claims not accounted for in the plan, even if previously disputed or subject to arbitration. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Findings of fraudulent and extortionate transactions by a forensic auditor (A&M) and regulatory authority (SEBI) justify the Resolution Professional's determination to not admit a claim and mark it as disputed/Nil. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP acted bonafide in not admitting the Appellant's claims due to evidence of fraud; following Supreme Court precedents (Essar Steel, Ghanshyam Mishra), the unadmitted claims were rightly extinguished by the approved resolution plan.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs. The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority approving the Resolution Plan is upheld.
summary: The Operational Creditor appealed against the approval of a Resolution Plan, arguing its Rs. 511 Crore claim was wrongly marked as 'Nil' by the RP. The NCLAT found that the RP acted correctly based on a forensic audit and SEBI orders indicating the transactions were fraudulent. Applying the 'clean slate' doctrine from Supreme Court precedents, the NCLAT held that claims not part of the approved plan stand extinguished, dismissing the appeal.

case_title: S. Irudaya Nathan vs G. V. Ravikumar
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: S. Irudaya Nathan (Promoter/Director of Corporate Debtor); Corporate Debtor: M/s Air Carnival Pvt Ltd; Respondent: G.V. Ravikumar (Liquidator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not applicable; matter involves submission of a compromise scheme during liquidation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The account was declared NPA on 29.06.2017 prior to CIRP commencement. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 02.11.2017; Liquidation ordered on 20.12.2018; Compromise proposal submitted by Promoter on 24.05.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Promoter submitted a compromise scheme under Sec 230 Companies Act; Liquidator sought direction for CoC meeting but also obtained an affidavit of eligibility under Sec 29A; Promoter obtained an MSME Registration Certificate clandestinely on 03.10.2020 during liquidation without Liquidator's knowledge. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai dismissed Liquidator's MA 32/2020 on 12.01.2021, holding the scheme proponent disqualified under Section 29A of IBC and the MSME certificate obtained illegally.
legal_issues: Whether a promoter/director, ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC, can submit a scheme of compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 during liquidation, and whether an MSME certificate obtained without the liquidator's consent can cure this ineligibility.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A person who is ineligible to submit a resolution plan under Section 29A of the IBC is also disqualified from proposing a scheme of compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act during the liquidation process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A applies retrospectively to promoters, and Regulation 2B(1) of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations explicitly bars ineligible persons from being a party to any compromise or arrangement. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Obtaining an MSME Registration Certificate by an ex-promoter during the liquidation period without the knowledge or involvement of the Liquidator is illegal, void ab initio, and cannot be used as a backdoor entry to bypass Section 29A ineligibility. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed that the Appellant was disqualified under Section 29A and could not propose a compromise scheme, dismissing the appeal.
operative_order: The Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 07 of 2021 is dismissed. No costs. IA/22/2021 (Stay) is closed.
summary: The Promoter of the Corporate Debtor in liquidation challenged the NCLT's refusal to consider his compromise scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT order, ruling that the promoter was ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC and that his act of obtaining an MSME certificate during liquidation without the liquidator's consent to circumvent this ineligibility was illegal. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Anil Kumar vs Allahabad Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Anil Kumar (Ex-IRP); Corporate Debtor: M/s. KSL & Industries Limited; Respondent 1: Allahabad Bank (Secured Financial Creditor); Respondent 2: Kiran Shah (New RP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Unsecured and secured lending to Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not specific to default; involves voting share disputes in CoC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 06.09.2019; first CoC meeting on 16.10.2019; CIRP 180-day period expired 04.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: IRP constituted CoC with 37 creditors (7 financial institutions with 36.53% vote share, 30 non-financial institutions with 63.47% vote share); secured creditors raised objections regarding verification of non-financial institutions causing a stalemate in appointing an RP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Allahabad Bank filed IA 691/2019 under Sec 60(5) in NCLT Ahmedabad, which removed the IRP and appointed a new RP under Rule 11 of NCLT Rules on 28.07.2020 due to the CoC stalemate; Appellant challenged his removal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can invoke its inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to replace an IRP/RP when a deadlock between secured and unsecured financial creditors prevents the CoC from reaching the required 66% majority under Section 22 or 27 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority may exercise its inherent powers under Rule 11 to replace an Interim Resolution Professional to break a stalemate in the Committee of Creditors and ensure the timely completion of the CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Sections 22 and 27 of the IBC provide the statutory mechanism for appointing and replacing an RP via a 66% CoC vote, if these ingredients cannot be met due to an insurmountable conflict between creditor classes jeopardizing statutory timelines, Rule 11 can be invoked to meet the ends of justice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evidence of a continued deadlock between secured and unsecured creditors, the inability of the IRP to provide leadership or complete verification, and the expiry of the 180-day CIRP period justified judicial intervention. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT correctly exercised its inherent jurisdiction under Rule 11 to appoint a new RP to prevent the frustration of the CIRP object, dismissing the ex-IRP's appeal.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed without costs. The period spent in pursuing the appeal shall be excluded from the CIRP process. The appointment of the new RP is upheld.
summary: The Appellant, an ex-IRP, challenged his removal by the NCLT under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules. A stalemate had occurred in the CoC between secured and unsecured creditors regarding voting shares, preventing the appointment of an RP under Sections 22 or 27 of the IBC. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's use of inherent powers to replace the IRP to break the deadlock and ensure the CIRP proceeded within timelines, dismissing the appeal.

case_title: NTPC Limited vs Ram Ratan Modi, Liquidator of DC Industrial Plant Services Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: NTPC Limited; Corporate Debtor: DC Industrial Plant Services Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent: Ram Ratan Modi (Liquidator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Two contracts awarded to Corporate Debtor in 2006 for Ash Water Re-circulation System package at BARH super thermal power project. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant claimed Rs. 1,08,03,28,286/- as the difference between liquidation expenditure incurred to complete balance work through third party (MELCO) and what would have been incurred had Corporate Debtor completed it. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Contracts terminated on 22.06.2015; CIRP admitted 30.07.2018; Liquidation ordered 19.06.2019; Liquidator rejected claim on 04.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Adjudicator award dated 03.01.2017 rejected Corporate Debtor's counterclaims and upheld NTPC's termination, stating exact amount at risk and cost to be assessed; Expert Settlement Council (ESC) later recommended closure due to wide divergence. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata partly allowed the appeal under Sec 42 on 02.02.2021 classifying Appellant as 'Other Creditor', but Appellant appealed to NCLAT against the Liquidator's rejection of the unquantified claim amount.
legal_issues: Whether a liquidator can reject a claim simply because the corporate debtor disputed it and it is not reflected in the corporate debtor's books, without exercising statutory duties to estimate the quantum of an imprecise claim.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A liquidator has a statutory duty to verify claims and make the best estimate of imprecise claims due to contingencies, rather than outright rejecting them based solely on the corporate debtor's internal records or disputes. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 39 of the IBC and Regulations 20, 23, and 25 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, the liquidator holds the power and duty to call for evidence and determine the quantum of claim where the amount is not precise. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An award by a contractual adjudicator upholding termination and dismissing counterclaims constitutes sufficient basis for the liquidator to assess and estimate the creditor's risk and cost claim, overriding mere ledger discrepancies. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Liquidator avoided performing his statutory duty to estimate the claim amount based on the Adjudicator's award, and thus directed the Liquidator to process the claim properly.
operative_order: The Liquidator is directed to process the claim of the Appellant as 'other creditor', arrive at the best estimate of the claim amount based on available documents, and give necessary benefit. The Liquidator's communication dated 04.09.2019 rejecting the claim is quashed and set aside. The Appeal is disposed of.
summary: NTPC appealed the Liquidator's rejection of its Rs. 108 Crore claim for costs incurred completing a terminated contract. The Liquidator rejected the claim because the Corporate Debtor disputed it and it wasn't in their books. The NCLAT held that under IBBI Liquidation Regulations, the Liquidator has a duty to verify evidence and make a 'best estimate' of imprecise claims, especially given a prior Adjudicator's award in NTPC's favor. The Liquidator's rejection was quashed.

case_title: Shri Digambar Anandrao Pingle vs Shrikant Madanlal Zawar & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Digambar Anandrao Pingle (Ex-Director/Promoter of Corporate Debtor); Corporate Debtor: M/s Pingle Builders Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent 1: Shrikant Madanlal Zawar (Erstwhile RP); Respondent 5: M/s Soorajmull Baijnath Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed; relates to underlying operational debt leading to CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details not elaborated, focuses on post-CIRP resolution attempts. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 CIRP initiated on 19.07.2018; Liquidation ordered on 11.12.2020; Appellant applied for MSME certificate on 05.03.2019 during CIRP. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant claimed Corporate Debtor was an MSME to bid in liquidation, presenting an MSME certificate obtained during CIRP without the RP's consent; an avoidance application under Sec 43/66 (MA 3020/2019) remained pending against the Appellant. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai ordered liquidation on 11.12.2020 and observed in Para 4 that the Appellant was ineligible under Section 29A; Appellant challenged this specific observation seeking to bid as an MSME.
legal_issues: Whether an ex-promoter can obtain an MSME certificate for the corporate debtor during the CIRP without the Resolution Professional's consent to bypass Section 29A ineligibility, and whether Section 29A(g) ineligibility observations can stand while the underlying avoidance application remains pending.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An ex-promoter cannot unilaterally obtain an MSME certificate for the corporate debtor during the CIRP period without the authority of the Resolution Professional in order to circumvent ineligibility under Section 29A. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A(g) requires an explicit order from the Adjudicating Authority establishing a preferential or fraudulent transaction; mere pendency of an avoidance application under Sections 43, 65, or 66 does not automatically trigger this specific clause, rendering premature observations ignorable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An MSME application made by a suspended management while the entity is under the legal control of an IRP/RP is unauthorized and cannot be relied upon to confer benefits or cure Section 29A disqualifications, preventing backdoor entries. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT declined to recognize the Corporate Debtor as an MSME due to the unauthorized certificate but ignored the NCLT's premature Section 29A observations, directing the NCLT to formally decide the pending avoidance application.
operative_order: The NCLAT ignored the observations made in Para 4 of the impugned order regarding Section 29A and requested the Adjudicating Authority to formally decide the pending MA 3020/2019. The NCLAT declined to accept the claim that the Corporate Debtor is an MSME or give directions to the Liquidator regarding the Appellant's bid. The appeal is disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary: The ex-promoter appealed against a liquidation order, specifically challenging a finding that he was ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC. The NCLAT held that the ex-promoter's act of obtaining an MSME certificate during CIRP without the RP's consent was unauthorized and could not cure his ineligibility. However, since the avoidance application under Sec 43/66 was still pending, the NCLAT ignored the NCLT's premature Section 29A observations, directing the NCLT to decide the pending application first.

case_title: Manoj Kunwar vs Punjab National Bank Erstwhile
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Manoj Kunwar (Promoter/Ex-Director); Corporate Debtor: M/s SSMP Industries Ltd.; Respondent 1: Punjab National Bank (Financial Creditor); Respondent 2: Yogesh Sethi (Liquidator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facilities provided by Financial Creditors (PNB and Kotak Prime Ltd) to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted debt of Financial Creditors stood at Rs. 15.93 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 27.08.2018; Liquidation ordered on 31.07.2019; OTS proposals submitted on 09.11.2020 and 22.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant submitted multiple One Time Settlement (OTS) proposals under Sec 230 of the Companies Act during liquidation (offering Rs. 5.5 Crores, then Rs. 1.5 Crores); both were rejected by the CoC with 100% voting due to being non-viable and lower than security enforcement options. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Delhi dismissed IA 346/2021 on 04.02.2021 as infructuous due to CoC's rejection of the OTS; Appellant appealed to NCLAT seeking directions to the liquidator to consider settlement.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal has the jurisdiction to review or overturn the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in rejecting a One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The acceptance or rejection of a settlement proposal or resolution plan falls exclusively within the domain of the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors, which is not amenable to judicial review. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory framework of the IBC does not empower the NCLT or NCLAT to evaluate the quantitative viability of a settlement offer; as long as there is no procedural violation, the CoC's decision prevails over any qualitative assessment by the tribunals. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A unanimous 100% vote by the CoC rejecting an OTS proposal on the grounds that it is financially non-viable or lower than alternative enforcement options is sufficient and conclusive evidence of a valid commercial decision. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Relying on Supreme Court precedents (Essar Steel, K. Sashidhar), the NCLAT concluded that it cannot trespass upon the business decision of the CoC to reject the OTS proposals, and dismissed the appeal.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed. The NCLAT found no ground to interfere with the impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority dismissing the Appellant's application. No order as to costs.
summary: The Promoter of a Corporate Debtor in liquidation appealed the NCLT's dismissal of his application seeking to force the consideration of OTS proposals under Section 230 of the Companies Act. The NCLAT held that the CoC had already rejected the OTS proposals via a 100% vote based on commercial non-viability. Citing Supreme Court precedents, the NCLAT affirmed that it cannot review the commercial wisdom of the CoC, dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Anand Natrvalal Khant vs Kush Structure Pvt. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Anand Natvarlal Khant (Operational Creditor); Corporate Debtor: Kush Structure Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Construction Agreement dated 27.10.2017 (or 17.11.2017) to construct a Government School at Dang Ahwa, where the Corporate Debtor agreed to pay the Appellant 20% of amounts received from the Government. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed principal amount of INR 29,00,000/- plus 18% interest per annum; date of default was unclear due to absence of invoices. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 was issued claiming the debt, but precise dates of invoices/default were missing. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant relied on the Construction Agreement and a Police Statement dated 17.06.2021 where the respondent allegedly admitted receiving funds; however, no invoices, bills, or debit notes were annexed to prove actual provision of goods or services. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application (CP (IB) No. 605/NCLT/AHM/2018) was dismissed by NCLT Ahmedabad on 05.04.2021 for failure to prove the debt qualified as an operational debt; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a contractual claim for a percentage of funds received, unsupported by invoices or proof of actual services rendered, constitutes an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) for the purpose of maintaining a Section 9 petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To qualify as an Operational Creditor and maintain a petition under Section 9, the claimant must definitively prove the provision of goods or services through concrete material such as invoices or bills. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) of the IBC restricts the definition of 'operational debt' strictly to claims arising in respect of the provision of goods, services, or employment; a mere contractual agreement to share received funds without evidentiary backing of services rendered does not meet this threshold. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The absence of annexed invoices, bills, or debit notes in the Section 8 demand notice and the Section 9 application is fatal, as it prevents the establishment of a clear date of default and proof of service delivery. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concurred with the Adjudicating Authority that the vital ingredients of an operational debt were missing, declining to admit the appeal and upholding the dismissal.
operative_order: The NCLAT declined to interfere with the impugned order or admit the Appeal. The Appeal is disposed of with no order as to costs. The Appellant was granted liberty to approach the appropriate forum or file another Section 9 application with proper procedure if advised.
summary: The Appellant challenged the dismissal of his Section 9 petition based on a claim for 20% of funds received by the Corporate Debtor under a construction agreement. The NCLAT upheld the dismissal, ruling that the claim did not qualify as an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC because the Appellant failed to produce any invoices or evidence showing actual goods or services were provided.

case_title: Concast Steel And Power Limited vs MSTC Limited[cite: 21]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Concast Steel and Power Limited (Corporate Debtor through Liquidator); Respondent: MSTC Limited (Operational Creditor/Secured Creditor)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: MSTC supplied goods (coal, steel billets) to the Corporate Debtor, storing them in the debtor's premises under a pledge agreement with a custodian (FSNL)[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding dues claimed were Rs. 300.71 Crores[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 07.11.2017[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: First inspection on 29.03.2018 found 63,124 MT coal and 40,489 MT billets; second inspection on 03.05.2018 found billets missing and coal reduced[cite: 21]. The liquidator admitted the claim amount but refused to classify MSTC as a secured creditor because the charge was not registered under the Companies Act[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata ordered the RP to recognize MSTC as a secured creditor. The Liquidator appealed to NCLAT[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether an operational creditor holding a pledge over goods can be classified as a secured creditor under the IBC even if the charge is not registered with the Registrar of Companies under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor with a valid pledge agreement holds a security interest and qualifies as a secured creditor regardless of non-registration of the charge[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(31) of the IBC defining 'security interest' includes pledges[cite: 21]. Section 77(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that non-registration does not prejudice the contract or obligation for repayment[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Joint inspection reports confirming the existence of pledged goods before their disappearance while under the RP's control establish the secured nature of the creditor's claim[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority correctly recognized MSTC as a Secured Operational Creditor based on the pledge agreements and the loss of goods during the RP's management, dismissing the liquidator's appeal[cite: 21].
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed. No order as to costs[cite: 21].
summary: The Liquidator of Concast Steel appealed the NCLT's order recognizing MSTC as a secured operational creditor[cite: 21]. MSTC had pledged goods at the debtor's premises which disappeared during CIRP[cite: 21]. The liquidator argued the charge wasn't registered[cite: 21]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that a valid pledge creates a security interest under the IBC, making MSTC a secured creditor regardless of registration, especially since the goods vanished while under the RP's control[cite: 21].

case_title: J.M. Financial Asset Reconstruction vs Anil Kumar Tandon & Ors[cite: 22]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants: J.M. Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd (Financial Creditor) and Dr. Anil Kumar Tandon & Ors (Real Estate Allottees); Corporate Debtor: Sandhya Prakash Ltd.; Respondent: Devendra Padamchand Jain (Liquidator)[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dr. Tandon & Ors paid Rs. 2.17 Crores under an Agreement to Sell dated 31.03.2012 for a commercial unit in AURA Mall with an assured return plan[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Assured returns stopped after February 2015[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 14.09.2017; Liquidation ordered 20.09.2019[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's audited balance sheets reflected the receipt of Rs. 2.17 Crores as application money for space booking[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected Dr. Tandon's claim as Financial Creditors because the ATS was unregistered and the project was supposedly complete, but ordered a refund outside the waterfall mechanism. Both J.M. Financial and Dr. Tandon appealed[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether allottees holding an unregistered Agreement to Sell in a real estate project qualify as Financial Creditors under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, and whether the NCLT can direct a refund of their advance outside the Section 53 waterfall mechanism[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Real estate allottees who advanced money for commercial space with assured returns fall within the definition of Financial Creditors, even if their Agreement to Sell is unregistered[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) and its Explanation broadly define 'financial debt' to include amounts raised from an allottee under a real estate project, superseding evidentiary bars of the Registration Act for establishing creditor status under the IBC[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unregistered Agreements to Sell, corroborated by bank entries and the corporate debtor's audited financial statements acknowledging receipts as advances, are sufficient to establish the status of a Financial Creditor[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held the NCLT erred in rejecting the allottees' status as Financial Creditors and incorrectly ordered a refund outside the IBC provisions[cite: 22]. The Liquidator was directed to admit their claims as Financial Creditors[cite: 22].
operative_order: The Impugned Order dated 18.09.2019 is quashed and set aside[cite: 22]. The Liquidator is directed to treat Dr. Tandon and others as Financial Creditors[cite: 22]. Appeals 1219 and 1327 of 2019 are disposed of[cite: 22]. Appeals 1203 and 1176 of 2019 are dismissed[cite: 22].
summary: The NCLAT heard multiple appeals arising from the liquidation of Sandhya Prakash Ltd[cite: 22]. The NCLT had ruled that commercial space allottees with unregistered agreements were not financial creditors but ordered a refund of their advance[cite: 22]. The NCLAT reversed this, holding that under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, such allottees are Financial Creditors based on the agreement, bank entries, and audited balance sheets, regardless of non-registration, and directed the Liquidator to admit their claims[cite: 22].

case_title: Deccan Value Investors L.P. vs Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian & Ors.[cite: 23]
appeal_number: I.A No. 915 of 2021 In Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 654 of 2020[cite: 23]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicant: Vistra ITCL (India) Limited (Mortgagee/Secured Creditor); Respondent 1: Deccan Value Investors L.P. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent 2: Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian (RP for Amtek Auto Ltd)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Vistra held a valid mortgage over 21.11 acres of Ace Complex Land leased to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Vistra issued a SARFAESI notice on 21.01.2020 for possession[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Judgment in main appeal passed on 16.04.2021; IA 915/2021 filed on 29.04.2021[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP executed a 20-year lease on 28.01.2020 without Vistra's consent[cite: 23]. NCLAT's earlier judgment contained an observation that the 2020 lease was 'entered into in accordance with law'[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Vistra filed an Interlocutory Application seeking clarification or modification of the NCLAT's prior judgment, arguing the observation was incongruous and affected its SARFAESI rights[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal possesses the jurisdiction under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to entertain an application for 'clarification' that effectively seeks a substantive review or modification of a final judgment[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Appellate Tribunal has no statutory power of review under the IBC; inherent powers under Rule 11 cannot be invoked to revisit, review, or revise findings on merits under the guise of an application for clarification[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules is declaratory of inherent powers to prevent abuse of process but does not override the absence of a statutory provision for substantive review in the IBC[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An application labeled as one for 'clarification' that seeks to delete or modify a factual/legal finding (e.g., the validity of a lease execution) is fundamentally a review application and must be rejected straightaway[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Concluding that the IBC does not permit reviewing judgments, the Tribunal dismissed the application, holding it was an impermissible attempt to obtain a review of the previous order[cite: 23].
operative_order: I.A. No. 915 of 2021 is dismissed. No order as to costs[cite: 23].
summary: Vistra ITCL filed an application seeking clarification of an observation made in a prior NCLAT judgment regarding the validity of a lease executed by the RP, claiming it affected its mortgage rights[cite: 23]. The NCLAT dismissed the application, ruling that the IBC does not contain provisions for reviewing a judgment[cite: 23]. Invoking inherent powers under Rule 11 to effectively review or modify substantive findings under the guise of a clarification is impermissible[cite: 23].

case_title: 9M Corporation vs Naresh Verma[cite: 24]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: 9M Corporation (Financial Creditor); Respondent 1: Naresh Verma (RP of Bohra Pratisthan Pvt Ltd); Respondent 2: STCI Finance Limited (Creditor)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: STCI Finance disbursed a loan of Rs. 24 crores to Bohra Industries Limited (BIL). The Corporate Debtor (BPPL) provided an unconditional and irrevocable corporate guarantee for this loan[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the principal borrower led the creditor to invoke the corporate guarantee[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against BPPL admitted on 05.08.2019; first CoC meeting held on 04.09.2019[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A Deed of Guarantee was executed on 21.12.2017 between BPPL and STCI. The RP admitted STCI's claim and assigned it a 75.90% voting share in the CoC[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Jaipur dismissed the Appellant's IA seeking reconstitution of the CoC to exclude STCI. The Appellant appealed, arguing a third-party security provider is not a financial debtor[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether a creditor holding an unconditional corporate guarantee from the corporate debtor for a loan disbursed to a third party qualifies as a 'financial creditor' under Section 5(8)(i) of the IBC[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate guarantee provided to secure a loan disbursed to a third party constitutes a financial debt, conferring the status of a financial creditor upon the guarantee holder[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(i) explicitly includes the amount of any liability in respect of a guarantee for any items referred to in sub-clauses (a) to (h) within the definition of 'financial debt'[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An unconditional and irrevocable Deed of Guarantee executed by the corporate debtor, backing a disbursed term loan to a principal borrower, satisfies the threshold of disbursement against the consideration for the time value of money[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that STCI Finance Ltd is a financial creditor of the Corporate Debtor based on the corporate guarantee, distinguishing it from a mere third-party security/mortgage holder as clarified in the Supreme Court's Anuj Jain judgment, and dismissed the appeal[cite: 24].
operative_order: Finding no error in the Impugned Order we dismiss the Appeal. There is no order as to costs[cite: 24].
summary: The Appellant challenged the inclusion of STCI Finance in the CoC as a financial creditor[cite: 24]. STCI had advanced a loan to a third party, for which the Corporate Debtor provided a corporate guarantee[cite: 24]. Relying on Section 5(8)(i) of the IBC and distinguishing the Supreme Court's ruling in Anuj Jain, the NCLAT affirmed that a liability arising from a corporate guarantee for a disbursed loan constitutes a financial debt, confirming STCI's status as a financial creditor[cite: 24].

case_title: Rajpal Singh Solanki vs Quazar Infrastructure Pvt Ltd & Anr[cite: 29]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Rajpal Singh Solanki (Ex-Director of Minarch Overseas Pvt Ltd); Corporate Debtor: Minarch Overseas Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent 1: Quazar Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Works contract awarded on 18.01.2013 for civil work and construction of an office building for Rs. 5,32,74,331[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid operational debt balance outstanding claimed at Rs. 2,91,00,770 after deducting alleged alternative payments[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice issued on 23.02.2018; Corporate Debtor replied on 23.03.2018[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor alleged sub-standard work and abandonment using letters dated 14.10.2014 and 18.01.2016, but these were absent from its Section 8 and Section 9 replies[cite: 29]. Running Account (RA) bills were certified by the architect's representative, but the Corporate Debtor failed to conduct mandatory joint measurements per the contract[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 9 application on 25.02.2020, rejecting the claim of a pre-existing dispute. The Ex-Director appealed[cite: 29].
legal_issues: Whether uncorroborated letters produced only during final arguments, alleging sub-standard work, constitute a genuine pre-existing dispute sufficient to reject an application under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A defense of a pre-existing dispute must be genuine, plausible, and not a spurious or patently feeble legal argument unsupported by credible evidence[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2)(a) requires the corporate debtor to bring the existence of a dispute to the operational creditor's notice; failure to mention alleged dispute communications in the statutory reply renders them highly suspect as an afterthought[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Letters indicating disputes that are completely omitted from the formal reply to a Section 8 demand notice and the reply to a Section 9 application lack evidentiary value and establish that the dispute is illusory and spurious[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded there was no real pre-existing dispute since the alleged letters were an afterthought and the Corporate Debtor had failed to fulfill its own contractual obligation to jointly measure RA bills, upholding the admission of the CIRP[cite: 29].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. Interim orders, if any, do not survive. The Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) shall proceed as required under law. No order as to costs[cite: 29].
summary: The Ex-Director of the Corporate Debtor appealed a Section 9 CIRP admission, alleging a pre-existing dispute over construction quality[cite: 29]. The NCLAT found that the letters purportedly raising the dispute were an afterthought, as they were not cited in the Corporate Debtor's reply to the Section 8 demand notice or its formal Section 9 reply[cite: 29]. Ruling the defense as spurious and lacking evidence, the NCLAT affirmed the admission order and dismissed the appeal[cite: 29].

case_title: Shibaankur Roychowdhury & Ors. vs. Pralayankur Roychowdhury & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pralayankur and Rudrankur Roychowdhury are the Original Petitioners (40% shareholders). The Appellants and other respondents are brothers holding the remaining 60% shares in M.P. Jewellers Co. (1945) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Memorandum of Understanding was executed in 2009 regarding the use of the company's trademark by different partnership firms run by the brothers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (Oppression and Mismanagement dispute). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The MoU expired on 31.07.2011. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: There was a deadlock in the company due to Article 53 of the Articles of Association requiring a 2/3rd quorum, which could not be met without the petitioners. A Special Officer appointed by NCLT had a valuer assess the shares after the respondents failed to cooperate. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CP No. 492/KB/2017 was filed for oppression and mismanagement. The NCLT allowed an interlocutory application, fixing a reserve price based on the valuation report and ordering an open bidding for a buyout/sellout among the brothers. The appellants challenged this order.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in directing a buyout/sellout of shares through open bidding based on a valuation report to resolve a family deadlock without fully adjudicating the main oppression and mismanagement petition?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In closely-held family companies where the relationship between groups is irretrievably broken and a complete deadlock exists, the tribunal may order a buyout/sellout of shares as a just and equitable remedy. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The NCLT has broad, equitable powers under Sections 241 and 242 to bring an end to the matters complained of and resolve deadlocks efficiently. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the admitted quorum requirements blocking board meetings, the multitude of pending litigations, and the appellants' lack of cooperation in naming a valuer as clear evidence of a deadlock. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT correctly adopted a judicious approach to end the family dispute by allowing competitive bidding for an exit, and dismissed the appeals as the appellants were merely employing delaying tactics.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 141, 132, and 123 of 2020 were dismissed. No orders as to costs.
summary: The NCLAT upheld an NCLT order directing the litigating brothers of M.P. Jewellers to engage in open bidding to buy out or sell out their shares. Acknowledging an irretrievable breakdown and a structural deadlock in the family company, the Tribunal found the NCLT's equitable intervention justified to bring peace and save the company from continuous litigation.

case_title: Mukul Kumar vs. M/s RPS Infrastructure Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: KST Infrastructure Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. Mukul Kumar is the Resolution Professional (Appellant). M/s RPS Infrastructure Ltd. is the claimant/creditor (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: RPS Infrastructure had an arbitral award dated 01.08.2016 against the Corporate Debtor arising from a real estate development agreement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: RPS claimed Rs. 35,67,05,337 based on the arbitral award. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CIRP commenced on 27.03.2019. RPS filed its claim via email on 19.08.2020, which was 287 days after the extended 90-day period expired. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Committee of Creditors (CoC) had already approved the resolution plan on 17.07.2020. The RP rejected the belated claim on 25.08.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RPS filed an application before the NCLT, which directed the RP to consider the claim on merits on 03.11.2020. The RP appealed to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional can be directed to entertain a claim filed after a massive delay of 287 days when the Committee of Creditors has already approved the Resolution Plan?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A belated claim submitted long after the extended statutory period and post-approval of the Resolution Plan by the CoC cannot be entertained, as it would jeopardize the time-bound nature of the CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 12(2) provides a 90-day extended period for claims, beyond which the RP has no statutory discretion to admit claims. Public announcement under Regulation 6 is deemed valid service. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal rejected the creditor's defense of ignorance, noting they had issued a power of attorney to the Corporate Debtor post the arbitral award confirmation, proving they were aware of the proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the NCLT erred in directing the RP to consider the delayed claim, as it would open floodgates to undecided claims and derail the time-bound resolution process. The NCLT order was set aside.
operative_order: The NCLT order dated 03.11.2020 was set aside and the appeal was allowed. No order as to costs.
summary: The NCLAT ruled that a creditor cannot file a claim after a massive delay of 287 days once the CoC has already approved the resolution plan. Reversing the NCLT's direction to the RP to consider the delayed claim, the NCLAT emphasized the strict, time-bound nature of the IBC and stated that entertaining such belated claims would create endless delays and jeopardize the insolvency resolution process.

case_title: Shree Ambica Rice Mill vs. M/s Kaneri Agro Industries Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shree Ambica Rice Mill is the Financial Creditor. M/s Kaneri Agro Industries Limited is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Financial Creditor alleged it advanced a loan of Rs. 10 lakhs to the Corporate Debtor on 20.04.2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The claimed default amount was Rs. 10 lakhs, with an alleged default date of 21.04.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application was filed on 19.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor had a paid-up capital of Rs. 7.30 crores and a cash credit limit of Rs. 24 crores from Bank of Baroda. There was no board resolution, loan agreement, or fixed repayment period. Bank of Baroda had declared the Corporate Debtor's account an NPA on 02.08.2019 and initiated SARFAESI proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT dismissed the Section 7 application on 07.10.2020 as collusive and directed a Section 65 notice to be issued. The Financial Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 7 of the IBC by investigating the real nature of the transaction and concluding it was collusive rather than a genuine financial debt?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority must investigate the real nature of a transaction to prevent parties from misusing the IBC to defraud legitimate creditors through sham or collusive petitions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) requires disbursement against consideration for the time value of money, which was absent in this running account transaction. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the absurdity of a company with a Rs. 24 crore credit limit defaulting on a Rs. 10 lakh loan the very next day, combined with the Corporate Debtor's immediate concession to CIRP to thwart SARFAESI proceedings by its main bank. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed that the transaction lacked the essential ingredients of a financial debt and was a collusive attempt to misuse the IBC moratorium against legitimate recovery proceedings.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed for lack of merit. The interim stay on the Section 65 show-cause notice against the Appellant was vacated. No order as to costs.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed an appeal by a purported financial creditor whose Section 7 application was rejected by the NCLT for being collusive. The Tribunal found no genuine financial debt, noting the absence of a loan agreement or time value of money. The Corporate Debtor's immediate consent to CIRP for a minor Rs. 10 lakh default, while facing a Rs. 24 crore NPA recovery action by a bank, proved the petition was a sham to misuse the IBC moratorium.

case_title: P J Mathews & Ors. vs. C Mohanan Pillai & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants (P.J. Mathews & Ors.) are the original petitioners alleging oppression and mismanagement. The 1st Respondent (C Mohanan Pillai) is the applicant seeking impleadment. The 2nd Respondent (Jatayupara Tourism Pvt. Ltd.) is the primary company involved. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The matter pertains to the management and affairs of the Jatayu Earth's Center tourism project. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The 1st Respondent holds 1,00,000 preference shares in the 9th Respondent Company (Jatayupara Sculpture and Museum Pvt. Ltd., the 1st Respondent in the main petition). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The 1st Respondent filed an application for impleadment in the main company petition (CP 21/KOB/2020) alleging oppression. The NCLT allowed the impleadment on 15.03.2021, and the original petitioners appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a shareholder of a respondent company is a proper and necessary party to be impleaded in a petition alleging oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any person concerned with the affairs of the company, especially a shareholder, is a proper and necessary party to proceedings alleging oppression and mismanagement, and their impleadment facilitates a fair adjudication. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates that the Tribunal be guided by principles of natural justice, which requires hearing all interested parties whose rights might be affected by an order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found it undisputed that the applicant was a shareholder in the company against which allegations of mismanagement were leveled, making him vitally interested in the outcome. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT rightly exercised its discretion to implead the shareholder, as a complete, comprehensive, and satisfactory order could not be passed without hearing him.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed without costs. The stay application (IA No. 238 of 2021) was closed.
summary: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision to implead a shareholder in an ongoing oppression and mismanagement petition. Rejecting the original petitioners' argument that the shareholder had no role in management and no relief was sought against him, the Tribunal emphasized that principles of natural justice require hearing parties whose interests could be affected by the outcome.

case_title: Anoop Kumar Chhawchharia vs. M/s Emgreen Impex Ltd & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Emgreen Impex Ltd. is the Operational Creditor. M/s ANR International Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. Anoop Kumar Chhawchharia is the suspended director (Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Operational Creditor supplied goods to the Corporate Debtor between July and September 2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor claimed Rs. 1,12,99,101 as the principal default amount. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor replied to the Section 8 demand notice raising a counter-claim. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor claimed it was owed Rs. 85,067 based on alleged counter-supplies made in June 2018. However, this claim was unsupported by purchase orders, delivery challans, or account confirmations. Discrepancies existed, such as manual invoices and incorrect transport details. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT admitted the Section 9 application on 19.04.2021, finding the Corporate Debtor's defense fraudulent. The suspended director appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a counter-claim raised by the Corporate Debtor in response to a Section 8 demand notice constitutes a genuine pre-existing dispute if it lacks supporting evidentiary documentation?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A defense of a pre-existing dispute or counter-claim must be genuine, substantial, and supported by prima facie evidence; mere spurious or unsupported claims raised as an afterthought do not bar the initiation of CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: For a dispute under Section 8 to hold, it must exist prior to the demand notice and cannot be a fabricated defense to evade insolvency. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the Corporate Debtor's counter-claim was raised without prior communication and was entirely unsupported by valid invoices, delivery proofs, or balance confirmations, rendering it a spurious defense. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the debt was legally due, default had occurred, and the alleged dispute was unsubstantiated. The admission of CIRP was justified.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. Interim orders were vacated. No orders as to costs.
summary: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's admission of a Section 9 petition against ANR International Pvt. Ltd. The Corporate Debtor attempted to avoid insolvency by alleging a pre-existing dispute through a counter-claim. However, the Tribunal found the counter-claim was a spurious afterthought completely unsupported by evidence such as delivery challans or prior communication, justifying the initiation of CIRP.

case_title: C & C Construction Ltd. vs. Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: C & C Construction Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor represented by its RP (Appellant). Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. is the Respondent. Axis Bank Ltd. is the guarantee issuer. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor and the Respondent entered into multiple EPC contracts. The Corporate Debtor provided performance and mobilization bank guarantees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor allegedly failed to complete contracts and return materials, leading the Respondent to seek encashment of the bank guarantees. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against the Corporate Debtor on 14.02.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The bank guarantees were unconditional. Axis Bank sought clarity on encashment due to the IBC moratorium. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT vacated an ad-interim injunction and allowed the invocation of the bank guarantees on 22.07.2019. The RP appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a bank guarantee issued on behalf of the Corporate Debtor can be encashed by the beneficiary during the moratorium period under Section 14 of the IBC, and whether such encashment affects the Corporate Debtor's assets?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Bank guarantees provided by a surety are outside the scope of the IBC moratorium, and the beneficiary can encash them. However, to protect the Corporate Debtor's assets during CIRP, the encashment must be restricted to the guarantee value minus the margin money provided by the Corporate Debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(3)(b) explicitly exempts a surety in a contract of guarantee from the moratorium. However, under Section 14(1)(c), the Corporate Debtor's own security interest (margin money) remains protected. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the Supreme Court's precedent (SBI v. Rama Krishnan) clarifying that a surety's assets are distinct from the Corporate Debtor's, meaning bank funds can be paid out, but the Corporate Debtor's margin money cannot be touched. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT modified the NCLT order, permitting the encashment of the bank guarantees but directing the banks to restrict the release of funds to the full value of the guarantee minus the margin money provided by the Corporate Debtor.
operative_order: The NCLT order dated 22.07.2019 was modified. The banks were directed to release the funds to the extent of the full value of the bank guarantee minus the margin money provided by the Corporate Debtor. Interim orders were vacated. No order as to costs.
summary: The NCLAT clarified the scope of the IBC moratorium regarding the encashment of bank guarantees. While upholding the beneficiary's right to invoke guarantees under Section 14(3)(b), the Tribunal modified the NCLT order to protect the Corporate Debtor's assets. It directed that banks can honor the guarantees using their own funds but cannot touch the margin money provided by the Corporate Debtor, which remains protected under the moratorium.

case_title: Bhaskar Biswas vs. Avaani Oxford Owners' Association
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Avaani Oxford Owners' Association is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1). Oxford Facilities Management is the Corporate Debtor. Bhaskar Biswas is the suspended director (Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Flat owners deposited maintenance and sinking funds with the Developer, which were transferred to the Corporate Debtor (a subsidiary maintenance company) to hold until an owners' association was formed. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Financial Creditor claimed a default of Rs. 5,64,72,615.80, with the date of default being 21.03.2016 (completion of the project's second phase). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application was filed on 21.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The amounts were acknowledged in the Corporate Debtor's balance sheets from 2016 to 2018. The association was formed, but the funds were not handed over. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT admitted the Section 7 application on 13.03.2020. The suspended director appealed, arguing the debt was not financial and was time-barred.
legal_issues: Whether maintenance and sinking funds collected from allottees in a real estate project and held by a maintenance company constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any amount raised from an allottee under a real estate project is deemed to have the commercial effect of a borrowing and qualifies as a financial debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) Explanation explicitly classifies amounts raised from real estate allottees as financial debt, bringing the unrefunded sinking and maintenance funds within the IBC's purview. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the debt was acknowledged in the Corporate Debtor's balance sheets and the flat owners had continuously pursued their remedies before consumer forums, meaning the claim was not time-barred. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the unrefunded deposits constituted a financial debt due and in default, and upheld the NCLT's admission of the CIRP.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. No costs.
summary: The NCLAT upheld the initiation of CIRP against a maintenance company that failed to hand over maintenance and sinking funds to a flat owners' association. Rejecting the appellant's defense, the Tribunal affirmed that funds collected from real estate allottees qualify as 'financial debt' under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, and continuous litigation by the owners ensured the claim was not time-barred.

case_title: M/s Gopalpur Ports Ltd. vs. M/s Sri Avantika Contractors Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Sri Avantika Contractors Ltd. is the Operational Creditor. M/s Gopalpur Ports Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Pre-existing contractual disputes pending since 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 9 application was filed in December 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: At the pre-admission stage, the NCLT verbally directed the Corporate Debtor to file its profit and loss account and balance sheets. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT issued an interlocutory order on 02.03.2020 requiring the production of the balance sheets. The Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing the order lacked reasons and bypassed CPC procedures for discovery.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses the inherent power to direct the production of documents, such as balance sheets, at the pre-admission stage of an IBC petition without strictly following CPC discovery procedures?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority is not strictly bound by the Code of Civil Procedure but is guided by principles of natural justice and has the inherent power to regulate its own procedure, including directing the production of relevant documents. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424(1) and (2) of the Companies Act, 2013 grant the Tribunal the power to require the discovery and production of documents without being shackled by formal CPC rules. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the requested documents were public documents and were necessary for the NCLT to evaluate the merits of the pending application, making the appeal an unnecessary delaying tactic. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the NCLT acted within its powers under the Companies Act and Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to seek documents necessary for adjudication, and dismissed the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. Interim orders were withdrawn.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed a Corporate Debtor's appeal challenging an NCLT interlocutory order that directed the production of balance sheets during a Section 9 hearing. The Tribunal affirmed that under Section 424 of the Companies Act, the NCLT is not bound by strict CPC procedures and possesses the inherent power to demand relevant documents to regulate its own procedure and facilitate adjudication.

case_title: Dr. Anees Ahmad & Ors. vs. Amit Jain RP Neesa Leisure Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Neesa Leisure Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. Amit Jain is the Resolution Professional. Dr. Anees Ahmad & Ors. are Fixed Deposit Holders (Appellants). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants held fixed deposits in the Corporate Debtor company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Committee of Creditors (CoC) approved a Resolution Plan that allegedly reduced the amounts payable to Fixed Deposit Holders. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed interlocutory applications objecting to the plan before the NCLT had formally approved it under Section 31. The NCLT rejected the applications on 10.02.2021, citing the primacy of the CoC's commercial wisdom. The FD holders appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal challenging the treatment of Fixed Deposit Holders in a CoC-approved Resolution Plan is maintainable before the Adjudicating Authority has formally accepted or rejected the plan under Section 31?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Objections to a Resolution Plan are premature if filed and appealed before the Adjudicating Authority has formally adjudicated upon the plan's approval or rejection under Section 31. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 vests the Adjudicating Authority with the final power to approve or reject a plan; piecemeal challenges to the CoC's commercial wisdom before this final order are not ripe for appellate review. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed that the NCLT had not yet passed a final order accepting or rejecting the Resolution Plan, rendering the FD holders' present agitation premature. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT declined to admit the appeal, stating the appellants must wait until the NCLT formally decides on the Resolution Plan, at which point they would be at liberty to challenge it on merits.
operative_order: The admission of the appeal was declined (dismissed as premature).
summary: The NCLAT declined to entertain an appeal by Fixed Deposit Holders who challenged a CoC-approved resolution plan that reduced their claims. The Tribunal ruled the appeal was premature because the NCLT had not yet formally accepted or rejected the plan under Section 31 of the IBC, preserving the appellants' right to challenge the plan once a final order is passed.

case_title: Om Prakash Agrawal vs UPL Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Om Prakash Agrawal is the Liquidator of S Kumars Nationwide Ltd (Corporate Debtor) / Appellant. UPL Ltd. is the Successful Bidder / Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale of CD's assets (leasehold and freehold land) as a going concern through E-auction. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent delayed payment of balance sale consideration; Liquidator demanded interest of Rs. 1,57,46,696. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: E-auction on Jan 16, 2020. LOI issued on Jan 18, 2020. Payment due within 30 days (by Feb 17, 2020). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: E-auction memo clauses, email dated Jan 9, 2020 waiving interest for delay due to leasehold land subdivision by GIDC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai) waived the entire interest on Feb 12, 2021. Liquidator appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Successful Bidder is liable to pay interest on the delayed payment of the balance sale consideration when the delay is partially attributed to the subdivision of leasehold land by a statutory authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A successful bidder is only exempt from paying interest on delayed payments to the extent the delay is not attributable to them, as governed by the auction terms. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: E-auction terms strictly dictate the liability. The Liquidator's clarification waived interest only for the leasehold land portion delayed by GIDC subdivision. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the explicit clauses of the E-auction Sale Process Memorandum and the Liquidator's email clarification. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the Respondent was not liable for interest on the leasehold land portion but was responsible for the delay concerning the freehold land, setting aside the NCLT's blanket waiver.
operative_order: The NCLAT directed the Appellant to refund the excess interest deducted from the Respondent only to the extent of the leasehold land, setting aside the NCLT's order dated 12.02.2021.
summary: The Liquidator appealed against an NCLT order directing the refund of interest charged on a delayed auction payment by the successful bidder. The NCLAT analyzed the auction terms and found the bidder exempt from interest on the leasehold land due to subdivision delays but liable for the freehold land delay. The NCLT order was set aside with directions to refund only the interest portion related to the leasehold land[cite: 10].

case_title: M.P. Industrial Development Corporation vs Mr. Jagdish Parulkar & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M.P. Industrial Development Corporation is the Appellant/Creditor. Jagdish Parulkar is the Resolution Professional (R1). Madhya Bharat Phosphates Pvt. Ltd is the Corporate Debtor (R2). Shree Pushkar Chemicals is the Resolution Applicant (R3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of lease land, maintenance, and water services to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid lease/maintenance bill of Rs. 5,41,142 and water bill of Rs. 11,52,646 for the year 2019-2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 09.09.2018. Resolution plan approved on 05.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease Agreement dated 18.07.2007. Bills generated during the CIRP period. The approved Resolution Plan stated that if actual CIRP cost is higher, the Resolution Applicant will pay it. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad approved the Resolution Plan on 05.03.2020 which allocated NIL for statutory dues based on liquidation value. Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether lease rent and utility bills (water) incurred during the CIRP period should be classified as CIRP costs payable in full rather than operational debt treated at liquidation value.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Essential supplies provided to a corporate debtor during the CIRP period must be treated as part of the CIRP costs and cannot be settled at nil or reduced value as operational debt in a resolution plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(2) read with Section 5(13)(e) of the IBC and Regulations 31 & 32 of CIRP Regulations mandate that essential services during moratorium form part of CIRP costs. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the bills were for the CIRP period and the Resolution Plan explicitly included a clause (6.2) committing the Resolution Applicant to pay any higher actual CIRP costs. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench modified the NCLT order, classifying the principal due for the CIRP period as CIRP cost, mandating the Resolution Applicant to pay it.
operative_order: The NCLAT partially allowed the appeal, modifying the NCLT's order by directing the Resolution Applicant to pay the principal amount due for the specified period of the bills (CIRP period) as CIRP costs.
summary: M.P. Industrial Development Corporation appealed against the NCLT's approval of a resolution plan that did not pay its lease and water dues incurred during the CIRP.
