The NCLAT held that essential services supplied during the moratorium period must be classified as CIRP costs under Section 14(2) and Section 5(13)(e) of the IBC, and thus the Resolution Applicant must pay the principal amounts due[cite: 11].

case_title: Venugopal Dhoot & Anr. vs Pravin R. Navandar & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Venugopal Dhoot and Deepak Anant Pednekar are the Suspended Directors/Appellants. Pravin R. Navandar is the Resolution Professional of VOVL Ltd (Corporate Debtor) / Respondent No. 1. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor (a subsidiary of Videocon Industries) participated in oil and gas blocks in Brazil through overseas step-down subsidiaries. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total financial debt involved is Rs. 30,654 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 08.11.2019. RP appointed on 20.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP sought details and documents pertaining to foreign subsidiaries of the Corporate Debtor to investigate avoidance transactions. The Appellants argued they had handed over available documents and CD was merely an SPV. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai directed the Appellants to cooperate and hand over documents under threat of Section 70 on 15.12.2020. Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Professional can compel suspended directors to provide documents and asset details of foreign subsidiaries of the Corporate Debtor under Sections 18 and 19 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Resolution Professional's power to take control and custody of assets does not extend to the assets of any Indian or foreign subsidiary of the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Explanation to Section 18 of the IBC explicitly states that the term 'assets' shall not include assets of any Indian or foreign subsidiary of the corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the RP was seeking information that could be reconstructed from the holding company (VIL) or MCA/bank records, rather than coercing the promoters for subsidiary assets. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench found the NCLT's order was passed in haste without appreciating the limits of Section 18 and remanded the matter.
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the impugned order dated 15.12.2020 and remanded the application back to the Adjudicating Authority for fresh consideration in light of the Tribunal's observations.
summary: Suspended directors appealed an NCLT order compelling them to hand over documents relating to foreign subsidiaries of the Corporate Debtor. The NCLAT set aside the order, holding that under the Explanation to Section 18 of the IBC, the term 'assets' explicitly excludes assets of the corporate debtor's subsidiaries, and the RP should obtain necessary information through alternative professional means[cite: 12].

case_title: State Bank of India vs Afco Energy Pte Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India is the Appellant/Financial Creditor. Afco Energy Pte Ltd is the Operational Creditor (R1). Kiran Global Chem Limited is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim by Operational Creditor against the Corporate Debtor which was settled post-admission. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly quantified for OC; Appellant had a separate Section 7 claim. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 CIRP initiated on 05.03.2021. Form FA for withdrawal received on 10.03.2021. Withdrawal allowed on 19.03.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement between OC and CD occurred before the constitution of the Committee of Creditors (CoC). Form FA submitted with a cheque for expenses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai permitted withdrawal under Section 12A. SBI appealed, arguing it should have been heard. Later, SBI's own Section 7 petition was admitted on 27.04.2021, initiating CIRP against the CD again.
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor must be heard before the Adjudicating Authority allows a withdrawal of CIRP under Section 12A if the withdrawal application is filed before the constitution of the Committee of Creditors (CoC).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for withdrawal of CIRP under Section 12A filed prior to the constitution of the CoC can be allowed based on a settlement between the initiating creditor and the corporate debtor without mandatorily requiring the consent or hearing of other creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A read with Regulation 30A(1)(a) allows for withdrawal before CoC constitution. The Tribunal distinguished the scenario from post-CoC withdrawals where collective consent is required. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed that the Operational Creditor submitted Form FA complying with Regulation 30A prior to the CoC formation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the NCLT's exercise of discretion to allow the withdrawal, rendering the appeal meritless, especially since the Corporate Debtor was already back in CIRP via the Appellant's separate petition.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the Company Appeal, holding that the Adjudicating Authority's exercise of judicial discretion to allow the withdrawal of the main petition prior to the constitution of the CoC was free from legal flaws.
summary: State Bank of India appealed an NCLT order that permitted an Operational Creditor to withdraw its Section 9 CIRP petition against the Corporate Debtor following a settlement. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that since the withdrawal application was filed prior to the constitution of the Committee of Creditors, the NCLT correctly exercised its discretion under Section 12A and Regulation 30A without needing to hear other creditors[cite: 13].

case_title: The Asst. Commissioner of CGST & Central Excise vs Kuresh Hatim Khambati (Resolution Professional) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Asst. Commissioner of CGST & Central Excise is the Appellant/Operational Creditor. Kuresh Hatim Khambati is the Resolution Professional (R1). MCPI Pvt Ltd is the Successful Resolution Applicant (R2). Garden Silk Mills Ltd is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim for unpaid government statutory dues (penalty and duty). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Revised claim filed for Rs. 73.76 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 24.06.2020. Claim filed on 04.09.2020 and revised on 16.09.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Plan allocated NIL to statutory dues. The liquidation value of the Corporate Debtor was Rs. 694.18 Crores, while admitted financial creditor claims were over Rs. 2,090 Crores, meaning operational creditors' liquidation value was zero. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad approved the Resolution Plan on 01.01.2021. The Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Plan can allocate a NIL amount to statutory dues of the Government if the liquidation value of the corporate debtor is insufficient to cover secured financial creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Operational creditors, including government authorities, are bound by a CoC-approved Resolution Plan that allocates them nil value, provided the amount is not less than what they would receive in the event of liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC, operational creditors must receive at least the liquidation value under Section 53. Since the liquidation value for operational creditors was zero, a nil allocation is legally valid. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the valuation report (Liquidation Value: Rs. 694.18 Crores; Secured Debt: Rs. 2090 Crores) clearly established that operational creditors would receive nil in liquidation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Applying the Supreme Court's decision in Ghanashyam Mishra, the bench upheld the approved resolution plan, confirming that the nil allocation to statutory dues was lawful and binding.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal without costs, finding no fault in the approved Resolution Plan that allocated nil value to the Appellant's statutory dues.
summary: The Assistant Commissioner of CGST appealed an NCLT order approving a Resolution Plan that allocated nil value to its statutory dues claim of Rs. 73.76 Crores. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that since the liquidation value of the corporate debtor was insufficient to even pay the secured financial creditors, the operational creditors were legally entitled to nil under Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC, making the plan valid and binding[cite: 14].

case_title: Orbit Electro Equipments Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs Kapil Dev Taneja (Ex Resolution Professional) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Orbit Electro Equipments Pvt. Ltd and Siddharth Shah are the Appellants/Successful Resolution Applicants. Kapil Dev Taneja is the Ex-Resolution Professional (R1). Apex Drugs Ltd is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Implementation of an approved Resolution Plan for the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants paid Rs. 6,35,90,000 towards the plan's first tranche, plus delay interest of Rs. 15,67,625. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved by CoC in its 10th meeting and approved by NCLT on 18.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants paid substantial sums but claimed they did not receive control of the Corporate Debtor. NCLT observed the Appellants were dragging the matter without fully implementing the plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad, while hearing an application by the Appellants for handover of control, suo moto remitted the Resolution Plan back to the CoC for fresh consideration and ordered forfeiture of the amounts paid on 20.04.2021. Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to suo moto remit an already approved Resolution Plan back to the Committee of Creditors for fresh consideration and order forfeiture of payments due to implementation delays.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a Resolution Plan is approved by the Adjudicating Authority, the Committee of Creditors becomes functus officio, and the Adjudicating Authority cannot suo moto direct reconsideration of the plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(3) and (4) of the IBC prescribe that the only statutory course of action available upon the failure or contravention of an approved resolution plan is to pass an order of liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction by inventing a remedy (remand to CoC) not prescribed within the four corners of the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the Adjudicating Authority acted illegally by directing the defunct CoC to reconsider the plan and forfeit the significant amounts already paid by the Appellants.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, setting aside the impugned order dated 20.04.2021, and remitted the matter back to the Adjudicating Authority for passing de novo reasoned orders in accordance with the law.
summary: The Successful Resolution Applicants appealed an NCLT order that suo moto remitted an already approved Resolution Plan back to the CoC for reconsideration and forfeited their part-payments due to implementation delays. The NCLAT set aside the order, holding that the CoC becomes functus officio after plan approval, and the IBC mandates liquidation under Section 33—not a remand to the CoC—in the event of a plan's failure[cite: 15].

case_title: D.R. Corporation (Proprietorship Firm) vs Ravi Kapoor (Liquidator)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: D.R Corporation is the Appellant/Highest Bidder. Ravi Kapoor is the Liquidator (R1). Seazone Granito Pvt. Ltd is the Unsuccessful Bidder (R2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale of Corporate Debtor's plant and machinery via E-auction. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: E-auction held on 12.04.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant was declared the highest bidder and paid a 25% deposit. R2 claimed technical snags prevented their bid and offered a higher amount. The Liquidator informed the NCLT of a decision to conduct a fresh public announcement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Ahmedabad merely recorded the Liquidator's submission for a fresh auction and adjourned the matter to 16.06.2021. The Appellant appealed this adjournment to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal can be maintained under Section 61(1) of the IBC against a daily proceeding record of the Adjudicating Authority that merely notes a submission and adjourns the matter without passing a formal order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal under Section 61(1) of the IBC lies only against an 'order' passed by the Adjudicating Authority, not against an adjournment or a mere recording of submissions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(1) strictly requires an adjudication or direction by the NCLT to trigger appellate jurisdiction. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the NCLT had not approved or disapproved the Liquidator's decision but merely listed the matter for a future date. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench dismissed the appeal as premature and non-maintainable since no formal order had been passed by the NCLT.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal as non-maintainable and devoid of merit, vacating the interim order and directing the Appellant to first seek redressal before the Adjudicating Authority.
summary: A successful bidder appealed against an NCLT daily record that noted the Liquidator's decision to conduct a fresh auction and adjourned the matter. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal as non-maintainable, ruling that Section 61(1) of the IBC only permits appeals against formal orders of the Adjudicating Authority, not mere adjournments[cite: 16].

case_title: Lotus City Plot Buyers Welfare Association vs Three C Homes Pvt. Ltd & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Lotus City Plot Buyers Welfare Association is the Appellant/Homebuyers. Three C Homes Pvt. Ltd is the Corporate Debtor. Gaurav Katiyar is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development project involving homebuyers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Homebuyers owed Rs. 211 Crores; Liquidation value of CD assessed at Rs. 480.70 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC voting commenced on 08.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Applicant proposed to infuse Rs. 95 Crores. NCLT found the plan value (19.77% of liquidation value) inadequate and noted it assumed farmers would forgo a Rs. 71.66 Crore claim for a Rs. 15 Crore village development promise. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi rejected the CoC-approved Resolution Plan on 08.02.2021 and directed liquidation. Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in rejecting a CoC-approved Resolution Plan and ordering liquidation primarily because the resolution value was significantly below the liquidation value and the CoC comprised solely of homebuyers.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Liquidation is a last resort, particularly in real estate projects where homebuyers seek possession of their homes rather than financial realization, requiring a distinct evaluative approach. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A CoC composed of homebuyers lacks the financial expertise of institutional lenders, meaning their commercial wisdom in accepting a plan below liquidation value must be calibrated carefully rather than summarily rejected. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the NCLT failed to consider certain monetary values (like satisfied debt of allottees) that increased the real value of the plan beyond the upfront Rs. 95 Crores. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench set aside the liquidation order, remanding the matter for a holistic review, including impleading the statutory authority (YEIDA) to ascertain the actual impact of farmers' disputes.
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's liquidation order and remanded the matter back to the Adjudicating Authority to review the resolution programme in full, including impleading YEIDA, and to pass appropriate orders in accordance with the law.
summary: Homebuyers appealed an NCLT order that rejected their CoC-approved Resolution Plan and ordered the liquidation of the real estate Corporate Debtor. The NCLAT set aside the liquidation order and remanded the case, holding that real estate resolutions require a different perspective since homebuyers seek possession of homes, not just financial recovery, and directed a fresh holistic evaluation of the plan's true value[cite: 17].

case_title: Chalasani Udaya Sankar & Ors. vs Lexus Technologies Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Chalasani Udaya Sankar and others are the Appellants/Petitioners. Lexus Technologies Pvt. Ltd is the Respondent Company. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate dispute under Section 241 of the Companies Act. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (Oppression and Mismanagement petition). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Final arguments heard by NCLT on 26.04.2021. Appeal filed on 28.04.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT Amaravati Bench passed an order on 22.04.2021 containing harsh and disparaging remarks against the Appellants and their counsel for allegedly dragging the matter for 10 months and instructing them to make alternate arrangements if the counsel was unwell. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Aggrieved by the unparliamentary language and prejudicial remarks in the NCLT's interim order, the Appellants filed an appeal before the NCLAT seeking to expunge the remarks.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority acted appropriately in recording harsh, disparaging, and unparliamentary remarks against the parties and their counsel in a judicial order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Judicial officers must exercise judicial restraint and discipline, maintaining sobriety and avoiding harsh, vituperative, or disparaging remarks against parties or their counsel in orders. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A (Focus on judicial conduct). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the specific excerpts of the impugned order and found the comments to be unpalatable, unnecessary for the conclusion, and prejudicial to the counsel's career. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the unwarranted remarks in the NCLT's order must be expunged as they violated the principles of judicial restraint.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal by setting aside and expunging the specific unsavoury observations and comments made against the Appellants and their counsel in the NCLT's order dated 22.04.2021.
summary: The Appellants challenged an interim NCLT order that contained harsh and disparaging remarks against them and their counsel regarding alleged delays. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and expunged the remarks, emphasizing that tribunals must exercise judicial restraint and avoid vituperative comments that prejudice a counsel's career or violate judicial discipline[cite: 19].

case_title: Emerald Realtors Pvt. Ltd. vs Suraksha Asset Reconstruction Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Emerald Realtors Pvt. Ltd. (Shareholder of Principal Borrower Sapphire Land Development) is the Appellant. Suraksha Asset Reconstruction Ltd. is the Financial Creditor (R1). Ankur Kumar is the IRP (R2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan provided by the Financial Creditor to the Principal Borrower, secured by a corporate guarantee from HDIL. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted claim of Rs. 150 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against Corporate Guarantor (HDIL) initiated on 20.08.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Financial Creditor's claim of Rs. 150 crores had already been admitted in the CIRP of the Corporate Guarantor. The Financial Creditor subsequently filed a Section 7 application against the Principal Borrower. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 7 petition against the Principal Borrower on 30.04.2021. The Appellant appealed, claiming parallel CIRPs are impermissible.
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor can initiate parallel Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) proceedings against both the Principal Borrower and the Corporate Guarantor for the exact same debt.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Parallel insolvency proceedings against a principal borrower and a corporate guarantor for the same debt are legally maintainable under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(2) of the IBC explicitly contemplates and permits applications relating to the insolvency of a corporate guarantor to be filed before the same NCLT where the CIRP of the principal borrower is pending. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on its prior judgment in 'State Bank of India v. Athena Energy Ventures' which held parallel proceedings are permissible, establishing it as the correct position of law. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that simultaneous CIRPs against both entities are maintainable, and the appeal lacked legal substance, thus dismissing it at the admission stage.
operative_order: The NCLAT declined to admit the appeal and disposed of it accordingly, thereby upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order initiating CIRP against the Principal Borrower.
summary: A shareholder of the Principal Borrower appealed against an NCLT order admitting a Section 7 CIRP petition, arguing that parallel proceedings were impermissible since the creditor's claim was already admitted in the Corporate Guarantor's CIRP. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 60(2) of the IBC and recent precedents permit simultaneous CIRPs against both a principal borrower and a corporate guarantor for the same debt[cite: 20].

case_title: Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd. vs The Administrator, Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd. is the Appellant/Successful Resolution Applicant. The Administrator of Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Ltd. is Respondent No. 1. The Committee of Creditors is Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Ltd (DHFL). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned NCLT order approving the resolution plan was passed on 07.06.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT order directed that the approval of the plan shall not be construed as a waiver of statutory obligations and that any waiver must be individually approved by concerned authorities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the resolution plan but included a conditional paragraph regarding statutory waivers. The Successful Resolution Applicant appealed to the NCLAT to modify this specific direction.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in directing the Successful Resolution Applicant to seek individual approvals from statutory authorities for waivers of statutory dues not part of the approved Resolution Plan, contrary to the Supreme Court's ruling in Ghanshyam Mishra.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is approved under Section 31 of the IBC, all statutory dues owed to any government authority that are not part of the resolution plan stand automatically extinguished. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 of the IBC (as amended in 2019) is declaratory and clarificatory, meaning the approved plan is binding on all stakeholders, including the Central and State Governments. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found the NCLT's direction to be contradictory to the explicit mandate set out in Para 95 of the Supreme Court's 'Ghanshyam Mishra' judgment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench substituted the NCLT's order to correctly reflect the law that no person or authority is entitled to initiate or continue any proceedings in respect to a claim for a prior period if it is not part of the approved resolution plan.
operative_order: The NCLAT substituted the impugned direction (Para ii) with a clear declaration that all statutory dues owed to government authorities not part of the resolution plan stand extinguished, and no proceedings for prior dues can be continued.
summary: The Successful Resolution Applicant for DHFL appealed a specific direction in the NCLT's plan approval order that required it to seek individual waivers from statutory authorities for prior dues. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and substituted the direction to align with the Supreme Court's 'Ghanshyam Mishra' ruling, confirming that all prior statutory dues not included in the approved resolution plan are automatically extinguished[cite: 23].

case_title: Deputy Commissioner, CGST Kalol, Gujrat vs M/s Gopala Polyplast Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Deputy Commissioner, CGST Kalol is the Appellant/Operational Creditor. M/s Gopala Polyplast Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Outstanding GST statutory dues owed by the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant's admitted claim was Rs. 2,36,67,282. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Claim dated 30.05.2019. NCLT approved the plan on 07.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC-approved Resolution Plan allocated only Rs. 1,18,336 as a full and final settlement of the Appellant's GST dues. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad approved the Resolution Plan on 07.08.2020. The Appellant challenged the approval before NCLAT, arguing the allocation was highly insufficient.
legal_issues: Whether an operational creditor representing statutory tax dues can challenge a CoC-approved Resolution Plan on the ground that the payment allocation provided for its admitted claim is insufficient.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The approval of a resolution plan by the Adjudicating Authority makes it binding on all stakeholders, including government authorities, and prior claims not fully paid stand extinguished. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: As clarified by the Supreme Court in 'Ghanshyam Mishra' and the 2019 amendment to Section 31 of the IBC, statutory authorities are strictly bound by the provisions of an approved resolution plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the amount approved for the Appellant, whether sufficient or insufficient, is a matter of the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench declined to interfere with the NCLT's approval order, ruling that the sufficiency of the allocation is a commercial decision of the CoC that cannot be subject to judicial review on merits.
operative_order: The NCLAT declined to admit the appeal and disposed of it as not admitted with no order as to costs, upholding the NCLT's approval of the Resolution Plan.
summary: The CGST Department appealed an NCLT order approving a Resolution Plan for Gopala Polyplast Ltd, protesting that only Rs. 1.18 Lakh was allocated against its admitted claim of Rs. 2.36 Crores. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that per the Supreme Court's 'Ghanshyam Mishra' judgment, an approved plan binds government authorities and the sufficiency of payment is a non-justiciable commercial decision of the CoC[cite: 25].

case_title: Convergytics Solutions Private Limited vs Randhir Hebbar
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: First Appellant is the Corporate Entity (Employer); First Respondent is the former Employee. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment agreement dated 02.07.2013 for personal service containing a termination-at-will clause. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute relates to the termination of the First Respondent's employment on 25.11.2020, not a debt default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original company petition was filed on 07.12.2020. The Appellants subsequently filed a Section 8 Arbitration application. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Employment agreement explicitly barring specific performance; internal communications allegedly containing defamation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru passed an ex-parte interim order on 10.03.2021 staying the termination and directing the payment of remuneration without deciding the pending Section 8 arbitration application or assigning reasoned grounds.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in granting a mandatory interim injunction staying the termination of a determinable employment contract without recording specific reasons and prior to deciding the pending Section 8 arbitration application?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interim mandatory injunction cannot be granted to specifically enforce a determinable contract of personal service, and all judicial orders must be supported by cogent reasons. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(c) read with Section 41(e) of the Specific Relief Act explicitly bars the specific performance of a contract that is determinable in nature. Section 8 of the Arbitration Act mandates that the judicial authority must first address the jurisdiction ouster before deciding interim relief. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority failed the test of judicial reasoning by passing a laconic order that lacked discussion on the prima facie case, balance of convenience, or irreparable injury. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT's unreasoned interim order enforcing a private employment contract was legally unsustainable, requiring a remand for fresh adjudication.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed, and the impugned NCLT order dated 10.03.2021 was set aside. The matter was remitted to the NCLT Bengaluru to decide the interim relief afresh on merits after providing due opportunities to the parties and deciding the Section 8 arbitration applications.
summary: The Appellants challenged the NCLT's interim order which stayed the termination of the First Respondent's employment and directed continued remuneration. The Appellants argued that the employment contract was determinable and its specific performance was barred by the Specific Relief Act. They also contended that the NCLT failed to provide reasons for the mandatory injunction and ignored a pending Section 8 arbitration application. The NCLAT Chennai agreed, holding that judicial orders must contain cogent reasons and that determinable contracts of personal service cannot be specifically enforced. The impugned order was set aside and remanded for a fresh, reasoned hearing.

case_title: Yogesh Kundra vs Sew And Prasad-Joint Venture
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor (Gati Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent is the Operational Creditor (SEW & Prasad Joint Venture). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement dated 12.08.2006 for civil and hydro-mechanical works, leading to a Settlement Agreement dated 14.12.2013 due to delays. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt default of Rs. 31,40,57,776. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued on 03.08.2017; Corporate Debtor invoked arbitration on 10.08.2017; Section 9 petition filed on 26.09.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Settlement Agreement capped the Corporate Debtor's liability at Rs. 10 Crores, shifting the balance burden to its holding company. An email dated 21.01.2015 from a holding company director allegedly acknowledged the debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad admitted the Section 9 petition on 26.04.2021, leading to this appeal which resulted in a split verdict among the NCLAT bench regarding the maintainability and existence of a pre-existing dispute.
legal_issues: Whether a pre-existing dispute regarding project delays and defective works, coupled with a Settlement Agreement capping the Corporate Debtor's liability, rendered the Section 9 IBC petition non-maintainable?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a split verdict, differing interpretations arise regarding whether an email acknowledgment by a related entity binds the Corporate Debtor, and whether breach of a settlement agreement constitutes an operational debt devoid of a pre-existing dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 requires the Adjudicating Authority to reject a Section 9 petition if there is a plausible pre-existing dispute. Section 18 of the Limitation Act allows extension of limitation via written acknowledgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Member (Judicial) evaluated the 2015 email as a valid acknowledgment extending limitation and defeating the dispute defense. Member (Technical) evaluated the pre-demand notice correspondence and settlement terms to conclude that a genuine, non-spurious dispute existed regarding defective works and assigned liability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Due to the divergent opinions—one dismissing the appeal and the other allowing it—the matter was referred to the Chairperson to nominate a third member for a final decision.
operative_order: The Member (Judicial) ordered the dismissal of the appeal, while the Member (Technical) opined the appeal should be allowed. Consequently, the Registry was directed to place the matter before the Officiating Chairperson to nominate a Third Member to render a final decision.
summary: The Appellant challenged the initiation of CIRP against the Corporate Debtor by an Operational Creditor, arguing that the underlying debt arose from a breached settlement agreement meant to be discharged by a holding company, and that a pre-existing dispute regarding defective works existed. The NCLAT bench delivered a split verdict. The Judicial Member found the debt admitted via email and not time-barred, upholding the CIRP admission. The Technical Member dissented, noting the debt had been assigned, liability capped, and a genuine pre-existing dispute existed, warranting the appeal's allowance. The case was referred to a third member.

case_title: Jayanta Banerjee vs Sashi Agarwal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is an Operational Creditor (employee); Respondent 1 is the Liquidator/RP (Sashi Agarwal); Respondent 2 is the Committee of Creditors (CoC) including Kamla Mills Ltd and Fasqua Investment. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment dues owed to the Appellant; underlying corporate loans held by the Financial Creditors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding operational and financial debts leading to the insolvency of INCAB Industries Ltd. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 07.08.2019; CoC voted for liquidation on 05.12.2019 without issuing an Information Memorandum. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MCA Master Data established that the majority shareholder of the Financial Creditors was a Director of the Corporate Debtor until he strategically resigned on 20.11.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kolkata ordered liquidation on 07.02.2020 based on the CoC's resolution. The Appellant appealed, challenging the validity of the CoC's constitution.
legal_issues: Whether Financial Creditors holding a majority voting share were 'related parties' under Section 5(24) of the IBC and thereby barred from participating in the CoC under the proviso to Section 21(2)?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A related party Financial Creditor cannot circumvent the prohibition against participating in the CoC by strategically resigning from the Corporate Debtor's board post the insolvency commencement date. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Section 21(2) read with Section 5(24)(f) strictly bars related parties from voting to prevent them from sabotaging the CIRP. Resignation after the commencement of CIRP does not cure the related-party taint. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized MCA Master Data and Annual Reports, rejecting the NCLT's reliance on Section 260 of the Companies Act to presume a 'deemed vacation' of directorship, confirming the director held office until his post-CIRP resignation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC was invalidly constituted by including related parties and was formed by the RP without properly verifying and admitting claims, rendering the resolution to liquidate the Corporate Debtor null and void in law.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed. The NCLT's liquidation order dated 07.02.2020 was quashed. The Adjudicating Authority was directed to replace the current RP/Liquidator within seven days. The new RP was instructed to verify all claims, exclude the related party Financial Creditors from the CoC, and restart the CIRP. Time spent in litigation was excluded from the CIRP timeline.
summary: An employee (Operational Creditor) challenged the NCLT's order sending the Corporate Debtor into liquidation, alleging that the CoC was illegally dominated by related-party Financial Creditors holding 77.20% voting rights. The NCLAT found that the majority shareholder of these creditors was a Director of the Corporate Debtor who strategically resigned after the CIRP commenced. Relying on Supreme Court precedent, the NCLAT held that such entities remain related parties and are barred from the CoC. Furthermore, the RP had unlawfully constituted the CoC without verifying claims and pushed for liquidation without preparing an Information Memorandum. The liquidation order was quashed, and a fresh CIRP with a new RP was ordered.

case_title: Hytone Merchants Private Limited vs Satabadi Investment Consultants
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Financial Creditor (Hytone Merchants); Respondent is the Corporate Debtor (Satabadi Investment). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An unsecured short-term loan of Rs. 3 Lakhs given for 6 months at 15% interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repaying the principal amount of Rs. 3 Lakhs plus interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan disbursed on 15.02.2019; Demand notice issued on 16.10.2019; Section 7 petition filed in December 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor readily admitted the default in its reply affidavit. However, Master Data showed the Corporate Debtor had a net worth of Rs. 15.36 Crores and had extended massive corporate guarantees worth Rs. 482 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata dismissed the Section 7 petition on 02.02.2021, holding that despite the debt and default, the petition appeared to be filed in collusion to escape the corporate guarantees.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the discretion under Section 65 of the IBC to reject an otherwise complete Section 7 application if it suspects the proceedings are initiated collusively or with malicious intent?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority is not bound to admit a Section 7 petition merely because debt and default are established; it has the inherent discretion to reject the petition to prevent the malicious or fraudulent initiation of insolvency proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5) uses the word 'may', granting discretionary power. This must be read harmoniously with Section 65, which penalizes the fraudulent initiation of proceedings for purposes other than resolving insolvency. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal applied the doctrine of piercing the corporate veil, concluding that a company with Rs. 15 Crores in net worth claiming inability to pay a trivial Rs. 3 Lakhs loan presented a highly plausible case of collusion designed to trigger a moratorium and evade Rs. 482 Crores in corporate guarantee liabilities. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT rightly exercised its caution and discretion to reject the collusive petition, preventing the misuse of the IBC machinery.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's decision to reject the Section 7 application on the grounds of suspected collusion and malicious intent.
summary: The Financial Creditor appealed the NCLT's rejection of its Section 7 IBC petition. Despite acknowledging that the debt and default of Rs. 3 Lakhs were established, the NCLT dismissed the plea suspecting collusion, noting the Corporate Debtor had a net worth of Rs. 15.36 Crores and was seeking to use the IBC to escape massive corporate guarantees of Rs. 482 Crores. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, ruling that Section 7(5) grants the Adjudicating Authority discretion to reject an application. Read alongside Section 65, the Tribunal must pierce the corporate veil to prevent the fraudulent or malicious misuse of the insolvency process for ulterior motives.

case_title: Dwarkadhish Sakhar Karkhana Limited vs Pankaj Joshi & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant 1 is a Prospective Resolution Applicant (DSKL); Appellant 2 is the Resolution Professional (Pankaj Joshi); Respondent is a competing Resolution Applicant (GIACL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission of an Expression of Interest (EOI) for resolving the Corporate Debtor (KGS Sugar). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (Dispute pertains to CIRP procedural irregularities). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The deadline for submitting EOIs was 10.02.2020. DSKL submitted its EOI late on 12.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The 7th CoC meeting dated 03.04.2020 explicitly rejected DSKL's late EOI. The new RP (Pankaj Joshi) unilaterally emailed DSKL on 05.06.2020 inviting resubmission and subsequently guided the 9th CoC meeting to accept it. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai passed an order on 01.03.2021 excluding DSKL's late EOI from the CIRP and issued strong adverse remarks deprecating the RP's biased and manipulative conduct.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Professional and the CoC can bypass the mandatory timelines under Regulation 36-A(6) to accept a late Expression of Interest under the guise of 'commercial wisdom'?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The 'commercial wisdom' of the CoC is strictly limited to the evaluation and selection of Resolution Plans; it does not empower the CoC or the RP to arbitrarily bypass or violate mandatory procedural regulations governing the CIRP timeline. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 36-A(6) is mandatory and explicitly states that an EOI received after the specified time 'shall be rejected'. Section 60(5)(c) vests the Adjudicating Authority with the jurisdiction to intervene and correct procedural illegalities before final plan approval. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the RP's timeline and communications, finding that the RP suppressed material facts, independently overturned a prior CoC rejection, and actively misguided the CoC to favor a specific applicant, thereby destroying the transparency of the process. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that accepting the late EOI was a procedural breach, not a commercial decision, and upheld the Adjudicating Authority's intervention and the adverse remarks against the RP's mala fide conduct.
operative_order: The appeals filed by DSKL and the Resolution Professional were dismissed without costs. The NCLAT upheld the Adjudicating Authority's order setting aside the acceptance of the late EOI and maintained the adverse remarks against the RP.
summary: The Resolution Professional and a late-filing applicant (DSKL) challenged an NCLT order that excluded DSKL from the CIRP for missing the Expression of Interest (EOI) deadline. The Appellants argued that the CoC's decision to accept the late EOI was protected under 'commercial wisdom' to maximize asset value. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that 'commercial wisdom' applies to evaluating resolution plans, not to arbitrarily violating the mandatory procedural timelines of Regulation 36-A(6). The Tribunal found the RP had acted with bias, suppressed facts, and unlawfully overturned a previous CoC decision to favor DSKL, justifying the NCLT's intervention and adverse remarks against the RP.

case_title: Rakesh Kumar Agarwal & Ors vs Devendra P Jain Liquidator Of Asis
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are the Promoters of the Corporate Debtor (Asis Industries Ltd.); Respondent is the Liquidator. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A proposed scheme of arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act to revive the Corporate Debtor as a going concern during liquidation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor committed default, leading to voluntary insolvency initiation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 10 CIRP initiated on 11.01.2018; Liquidation ordered on 28.08.2019; MSME classification criteria revised by the Govt on 01.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Due to the revised MSME investment thresholds introduced by the 01.06.2020 notification, the Corporate Debtor qualified as an MSME. The 4th Stakeholders meeting favored the promoters' scheme over outright liquidation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad rejected the promoters' application on 15.10.2020, ruling that the MSME notification was prospective and the Corporate Debtor was not an MSME at the time the initial Section 10 application was filed, leaving the promoters barred by Section 29A.
legal_issues: Whether Promoters are eligible to submit a scheme of arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act during liquidation if the Corporate Debtor qualifies as an MSME due to a statutory notification issued during the pendency of the liquidation process?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The primary objective of the IBC is corporate revival; therefore, statutory benefits (such as MSME exemptions) enacted during the pendency of liquidation must be applied to allow promoters to propose a scheme of arrangement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 240A of the IBC exempts MSME promoters from the disqualifications of Section 29A. The notification amending Section 7 of the MSMED Act is applicable to pending liquidations, granting the Corporate Debtor MSME status. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that liquidation is a matter of last resort. Since the liquidation process was ongoing and the corporate entity now met the revised MSME criteria, the promoters immediately acquired eligibility to propose a revival scheme. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's strict chronological interpretation, concluding that the promoters were legally eligible to submit a Section 230 scheme to prevent the corporate death of the entity.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed and the NCLT Ahmedabad's order dated 15.10.2020 was set aside. The Appellants were granted one week to submit their scheme of arrangement to the liquidator, and the liquidator was directed to consider the scheme in accordance with the law.
summary: The Promoters appealed an NCLT order that rejected their attempt to submit a scheme of arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act during the Corporate Debtor's liquidation. The NCLT reasoned that the Corporate Debtor was not an MSME when insolvency commenced, barring the promoters under Section 29A. The NCLAT reversed this decision, highlighting that during the pending liquidation, a June 2020 government notification expanded MSME criteria, qualifying the Corporate Debtor. Emphasizing the IBC's objective of resolving insolvency and treating liquidation as a last resort, the NCLAT applied Section 240A of the IBC, declaring the promoters eligible to submit the revival scheme.

case_title: Vivek Malik vs Punjab National Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor (Amzen Machines Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent is the Financial Creditor (Punjab National Bank). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A term loan of Rs. 200 Crores and working capital consortium facilities disbursed in 2011 and 2014. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding financial debt claimed was Rs. 268,37,90,311/- with the date of NPA declared as 15.03.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice issued on 10.05.2016; Corporate Debtor acknowledged the debt in writing on 10.07.2018; Section 7 IBC application filed on 11.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A formal letter dated 10.07.2018 on the Corporate Debtor's letterhead explicitly admitted the outstanding debit balances to the Bank, corroborated by entries in the balance sheet. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 7 petition on 11.03.2021, rejecting the Corporate Debtor's defense that the 2019 application was time-barred since the NPA date was 2016.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 IBC application is barred by limitation when filed more than three years after the date of NPA, if the Corporate Debtor has provided a written acknowledgment of debt within the initial limitation period?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An explicit written acknowledgment of debt by the Corporate Debtor prior to the expiration of the original limitation period successfully restarts a fresh three-year period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238A of the IBC applies the provisions of the Limitation Act to IBC proceedings. Section 18 of the Limitation Act mandates that an acknowledgment of a present subsisting liability made in writing extends the limitation timeline. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the letter dated 10.07.2018 provided in Part V of the Section 7 format, confirming it constituted a valid, unequivocal acknowledgment of the exact debt amounts owed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the limitation period had been legally reset by the 2018 written acknowledgment, rendering the Section 7 application filed in September 2019 perfectly within time.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's decision to admit the Section 7 application and initiate the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process.
summary: The Appellant challenged the initiation of CIRP, arguing that the Bank's Section 7 petition was time-barred because it was filed in 2019, more than three years after the account was declared NPA in March 2016. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal relying on recent Supreme Court rulings confirming that Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to IBC proceedings. The Tribunal found that the Corporate Debtor had issued a letter on July 10, 2018, explicitly acknowledging its outstanding financial liability to the Bank. This written acknowledgment validly reset the limitation clock, making the 2019 petition timely and legally sustainable.

case_title: Mr Vikas Sureshbhai Patel vs The Registrar Of Companies
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are the Directors and Shareholders of the Company (Hiraj Hospitality Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent is the Registrar of Companies (ROC), Gujarat. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ongoing operations of a private hospitality business. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Company failed to file Annual Accounts and Returns for the consecutive financial years 2016-17, 2017-18, and 2018-19. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: ROC issued STK-1 notice on 17.07.2019 and subsequently published the STK-7 dissolution notice on 13.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Financial statements showing continuous operational revenue ranging from Rs. 93 Lakhs to Rs. 1.35 Crores across the missing years, ownership of tangible assets, and active employment of 22-25 staff members. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad rejected the Section 252 restoration application on 29.01.2020, reasoning that the company was running in accumulated losses and lacked a future business plan.
legal_issues: Whether the Registrar of Companies was justified in striking off a company's name for non-filing of statutory returns when overwhelming evidence demonstrated that the company was a continuously operating, going concern?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The failure to file annual returns, while a statutory default, should not result in the permanent striking off of a company if there is conclusive evidence that the company is actively operating and carrying on business. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 248(1)(c) of the Companies Act empowers the ROC to strike off a company if it is not carrying on business. However, Section 252(3) mandates the Tribunal to restore the company if it is satisfied that the company was actually carrying on business or in operation at the time it was struck off. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the submitted balance sheets showing continuous revenue generation, asset ownership, and active employee rosters, determining that the non-filing was due to inadvertence rather than the company being defunct. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the company was operational and a going concern; hence, striking it off was an disproportionate penalty for a curable compliance default.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's order and the ROC's STK strike-off notices. The ROC Gujarat was directed to restore the company's name to the Register, subject to the company filing all outstanding statutory returns and paying applicable penalties/interest for the defaults.
summary: The Appellants appealed the NCLT's refusal to restore their company to the ROC Register. The ROC had struck off the company under Section 248 for failing to file annual returns for three years. The NCLT upheld the strike-off because the company showed accumulated losses. The NCLAT overturned this, noting that Section 252 of the Companies Act mandates restoration if a company is operational. Financial statements and employee records proved the company generated over Rs. 1 Crore in revenue and was an active going concern. The NCLAT ordered the company's restoration, viewing the compliance failure as a curable defect subject to penalties.

case_title: Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority vs Pramod Agrawal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Land Lessor (Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority - GNIDA); Respondent 1 is the Ex-Director; Respondent 2 is the Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor (Primrose Infratech Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Registered Lease Deed executed on 29.09.2011, granting a 99-year land lease to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding lease premiums and dues claimed by GNIDA. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant originally submitted a claim in Form 'C' and was part of early CoC meetings, but was excluded from the CoC during the 6th meeting on 17.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The provisions of the 99-year Lease Deed evaluated against the Indian Accounting Standards to determine the transfer of ownership risks and rewards. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following an Ex-Director's application, the RP reclassified GNIDA from a Financial Creditor to an Operational Creditor, excluding them from the CoC. The NCLT New Delhi upheld this reclassification on 28.02.2020.
legal_issues: Whether a 99-year land lease deed granted by an Industrial Development Authority qualifies as a 'Financial Lease' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, thereby elevating the Authority to the status of a Financial Creditor?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A long-term lease deed does not automatically constitute a financial lease; it must substantially transfer all risks and rewards incidental to the ownership of the underlying asset to qualify as financial debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(d) defines financial debt to include the amount of any liability in respect of any lease or hire purchase contract which is deemed as a finance or capital lease under the Indian Accounting Standards. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on the precedent set in 'New Okhla Industrial Development Authority vs. Anand Sonbhadra', the Tribunal examined the specific recitals of the lease deed and determined that the rewards incidental to ultimate ownership of the land were not transferred to the Corporate Debtor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the 99-year lease agreement was merely an operational transaction and did not meet the rigorous threshold of a financial lease, thus justifying the Appellant's reclassification as an Operational Creditor.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs. The NCLAT affirmed the Adjudicating Authority's decision to treat the Appellant as an Operational Creditor, validating their exclusion from the Committee of Creditors.
summary: The Appellant (GNIDA) challenged the NCLT's order which reclassified its claim from a Financial Debt to an Operational Debt, effectively removing it from the Corporate Debtor's Committee of Creditors. GNIDA argued that its 99-year land lease deed transferred rights incidental to ownership, qualifying it as a financial lease under Indian Accounting Standards. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, relying on its precedent involving similar Noida Authority leases. The Tribunal held that the lease did not substantially transfer the rewards incidental to ownership of the underlying land. Consequently, the transaction did not meet the criteria for financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC.

case_title: Tottempudi Salalith vs State Bank Of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor (Totem Infrastructure Ltd); Respondent No.1 is the Financial Creditor (State Bank of India). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple loan facilities extended by SBI and its associate banks to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to DRT Recovery Certificates for an aggregate amount exceeding Rs. 613 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: DRT Recovery Certificates issued between 2015 and 2017. A One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal was submitted by the Corporate Debtor on 29.01.2020. Section 7 IBC application filed on 06.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor argued the debt was time-barred since NPA classification occurred in 2012-2013, and that the petition was invalidly filed under the ultra vires RBI Circular of 12.02.2018. However, an OTS letter dated 29.01.2020 acknowledged the debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad admitted the Section 7 petition on 12.01.2021, holding the debt was acknowledged via the OTS and within limitation based on the DRT Recovery Certificates.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 IBC application based on DRT Recovery Certificates is maintainable, and whether an OTS proposal extends the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Recovery Certificate issued by a competent tribunal (DRT) provides a fresh cause of action for initiating CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC. Furthermore, an OTS proposal acknowledging the liability within the limitation period triggers a fresh period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(10) of the IBC includes a 'decree holder' within the definition of a creditor. The limitation for filing under Section 7 can be validly extended by written acknowledgment (OTS) under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the Recovery Certificates established the debt and default conclusively. The OTS letter dated 29.01.2020 constituted a clear, unequivocal written acknowledgment of liability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed the admission of the Section 7 petition, concluding it was not time-barred and was properly supported by DRT Recovery Certificates and a valid OTS acknowledgment.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs. The NCLT's admission of the Section 7 application was upheld.
summary: The Appellant challenged the initiation of CIRP against the Corporate Debtor, arguing the Section 7 petition by SBI was time-barred since the NPA dates were 2012/2013 and was filed under an invalidated RBI circular. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the DRT Recovery Certificates (issued in 2015-2017) provided a fresh cause of action. Additionally, an OTS proposal by the Corporate Debtor on 29.01.2020 served as a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, effectively keeping the debt within the limitation period.

case_title: Mohit Agro Commodities Processing Pvt. Ltd. vs Gujarat Ambuja Exports Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant 1 is the Transferor Company (Mohit Agro); Appellant 2 is the Transferee Company (Gujarat Ambuja Exports Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Scheme of Amalgamation to merge the Wholly Owned Subsidiary (Transferor) into the Holding Company (Transferee). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (Merger/Amalgamation matter). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board resolutions approving the scheme passed on 20.10.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Transferor Company had zero creditors. The Transferee Company had a highly positive net worth (excess assets of Rs. 1436.62 Crores) and no new shares were being issued, thus not affecting shareholders' or creditors' rights. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad on 10.03.2021 dispensed with the meetings of the Transferor Company but refused to dispense with the meetings of the Equity Shareholders, Secured Creditors, and Unsecured Creditors of the Transferee Company.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can exercise its discretion to dispense with the meetings of shareholders and creditors of a Transferee Company when a Wholly Owned Subsidiary merges into it and the financial position remains highly positive without compromising creditors' rights?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In cases of amalgamation of a Wholly Owned Subsidiary into its parent company where no new shares are issued and the parent company's net worth is highly positive, convening meetings of the parent's shareholders and creditors is an empty formality and should be dispensed with. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 232(1) of the Companies Act uses the word 'may', granting the Tribunal discretionary power to dispense with meetings when it is established that the scheme does not prejudice the stakeholders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the financial statements showing a massive positive net worth of the Transferee Company and noted the absence of any compromise with creditors or reorganization of share capital, concluding that no prejudice would be caused. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Adjudicating Authority erred in mechanically directing the convening of meetings for the Transferee Company, which defeated the objective of expeditious corporate restructuring.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed. The NCLT's direction requiring the Transferee Company to convene meetings of its Equity Shareholders, Secured Creditors, and Unsecured Creditors was set aside.
summary: The Appellants appealed an NCLT order that mandated holding meetings for the Transferee Company's shareholders and creditors regarding an amalgamation scheme. The Transferor Company was a Wholly Owned Subsidiary of the Transferee. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, ruling that since the merger involved no new share issuance, no compromise with creditors, and the Transferee had a highly positive net worth, convening such meetings was an unnecessary formality. The NCLAT invoked the discretionary power under Section 232(1) to dispense with the meetings.

case_title: Trilok Chand Agarwal vs Punjab National Bank & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor (Megha Granules Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent 1 is the Financial Creditor (Punjab National Bank/United Bank of India). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loans, cash credit, and working capital limits granted by a consortium of banks. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total debt of Rs. 32,59,99,856.25 in default as of 31.03.2018 (UBI) and 06.04.2019 (PNB). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original Section 7 petition filed on 09.03.2020; Amended petition filed on 30.11.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor claimed the debts were time-barred since default dates were 2014/2016 and that the banks, having converted debt to 51% equity under Strategic Debt Restructuring (SDR), should have filed under Section 10 instead of Section 7. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati admitted the Section 7 petition on 05.05.2021 after multiple hearings where the Corporate Debtor failed to file a timely reply, relying instead on written submissions.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 application is maintainable if the consortium of banks previously invoked Strategic Debt Restructuring (SDR) to convert debt into equity, and whether the debt was barred by limitation?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The mere invocation of an SDR scheme resulting in the conversion of debt into equity, without actual takeover of the corporate debtor's management, does not strip the financial creditors of their right to invoke Section 7 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: As long as a financial debt is 'due' and 'payable' and a default is established, the Adjudicating Authority is bound to admit the Section 7 application regardless of ongoing SDR arrangements or other disputes. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found the debt was properly acknowledged via balance confirmations and letters extending limitation. The claim that the banks had taken over management was unsupported by material evidence. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the debt was established, in default, and within limitation, justifying the NCLT's admission of the Section 7 application.
operative_order: The appeals (including a connected unnumbered appeal) were dismissed with no orders as to costs. The NCLT's admission of the CIRP was upheld.
summary: The Appellant challenged the initiation of CIRP, arguing the debt was time-barred and that the Financial Creditors, having acquired 51% equity through an SDR scheme, were essentially management and thus barred from filing a Section 7 petition. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that limitation was continuously extended by written acknowledgments. Furthermore, the NCLAT held that converting debt to equity under SDR without actively taking over management does not preclude banks from enforcing their rights as Financial Creditors under Section 7 of the IBC.

case_title: Martin S.K. Golla vs Wig Associates Pvt. Ltd. & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Resolution Professional; Respondent 1 is the Corporate Debtor (Wig Associates); Respondent 2 is the Sole Financial Creditor (Bank of Baroda); Respondent 3 is the IBBI. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A 'One Time Settlement' (OTS) submitted by the Corporate Debtor's guarantor (Mr. Mahendra Wig) was presented and approved as a Resolution Plan. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding bank debt of Rs. 1067.39 Lakhs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 24.08.2017. Section 29A introduced via Ordinance on 23.11.2017. Resolution Plan approved by CoC on 20.04.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Resolution Applicant (Mr. Wig) was a related party/guarantor. The NCLT approved the plan, reasoning that since CIRP commenced before Section 29A was enacted, the amendment did not apply retrospectively. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The IBBI originally appealed the NCLT's approval. NCLAT ruled IBBI lacked locus and directed the RP to file the appeal. The NCLT Mumbai had approved the plan on 04.06.2018 despite recognizing Mr. Wig's related-party status.
legal_issues: Whether Section 29A of the IBC applies to a CIRP initiated prior to its enactment, thereby barring a related party/guarantor from submitting a Resolution Plan?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 29A applies to all resolution plans submitted after its enactment, regardless of when the CIRP commenced; a resolution applicant has no vested right to have their plan considered under pre-amendment laws. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A's opening words ('a person shall not be eligible to submit...') dictate that ineligibility attaches at the exact time the resolution plan is submitted to the RP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on 'ArcelorMittal India' and 'Swiss Ribbons', the Tribunal confirmed that since Mr. Wig submitted the OTS/Resolution Plan after 23.11.2017, he was barred under Section 29A. Furthermore, presenting an OTS directly as a Resolution Plan contravenes IBC norms. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded the Adjudicating Authority erred in law by interpreting Section 29A as prospective based on the CIRP admission date. The resolution plan submitted by a related party was invalid and had to be quashed.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed. The impugned NCLT order approving the Resolution Plan was quashed and set aside. The matter was remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to pass an order of liquidation under Section 33 of the IBC.
summary: The Resolution Professional appealed the NCLT's approval of a Resolution Plan submitted by a guarantor/related party. The NCLT had reasoned that Section 29A (which disqualifies related parties) did not apply because the CIRP began before the amendment was enacted. The NCLAT overturned this, relying on Supreme Court precedents which clarify that Section 29A applies at the time the plan is submitted, and applicants have no vested right to bypass it. The NCLAT quashed the plan approval and ordered the Corporate Debtor into liquidation.

case_title: Ms. Vidhya Achu Roy vs M/S Suraj Mani Engineers Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is a 50% shareholder/Director (Wife); Respondent 1 is the Company; Respondent 2 is the remaining 50% shareholder/Managing Director (Husband). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Running of an engineering/air-conditioning business amidst marital discord. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (Oppression and Mismanagement case). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Authorized share capital increased in a Board meeting on 10.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant claimed the Husband diverted business to a new entity, unlawfully transferred company funds to personal accounts, and increased share capital to dilute her holding. Evidence showed the fund transfer was approved variable pay, the new entity did no significant business, and the company was highly profitable. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the main O&M petition on 01.08.2019 but on compassionate grounds ordered the company to provide the Appellant with a residence, car, and monthly salary.
legal_issues: Whether marital disharmony leading to alleged administrative exclusions constitutes 'oppression and mismanagement' when the financial health of the company remains robust and shareholder proprietary rights are not unlawfully prejudiced?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Oppression must involve harsh, burdensome, and wrongful conduct that prejudices a person strictly in their capacity as a shareholder; marital or personal disputes that do not undermine corporate proprietary rights or financial health do not constitute oppression. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 241 and 242, the Tribunal must test directorial acts strictly to rule out ulterior motives, but resolutions passed via proper legal procedures (e.g., increasing authorized share capital or granting variable pay for good performance) do not inherently constitute mismanagement. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found the Appellant's claims pertained largely to preserving personal perks rather than protecting corporate interests. The company's revenues were growing, and the alleged 'diverted' business or 'unauthorized' transfers were legally sound commercial decisions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Appellant failed to prove oppression or mismanagement. The NCLT's equitable relief granting her maintenance benefits was deemed a reasonable and sufficient remedy for the deadlock.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed, affirming the NCLT Bengaluru's order. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, a 50% shareholder and wife of the Managing Director, appealed the dismissal of her Oppression and Mismanagement petition. She alleged her husband diverted business to a dummy company and increased share capital to dilute her stake amid marital strife. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that the company was financially thriving and the challenged actions (like variable pay bonuses and capital increases) were legal commercial decisions. The Tribunal affirmed that personal marital disharmony does not equate to corporate oppression unless proprietary shareholder rights are prejudiced.

case_title: M/s. Manipal Media Network Ltd. vs M/s. Vishwakshara Media Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Operational Creditor (Printer); Respondent is the Corporate Debtor (Publisher). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreements signed on 04.12.2015 for printing three newspaper editions. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid invoices for printing jobs between February 2018 and November 2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original agreements expired on 03.12.2017. Demand Notice issued on 23.04.2019; Section 9 petition filed on 07.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Despite contract expiry, the CD continued sending email print orders which were executed by the OC. The CD raised a defense of high newsprint wastage, but print orders were far below the 10,000 copy minimum threshold stipulated in the agreement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the Section 9 petition on 16.12.2019, ruling the contract had lapsed and a pre-existing dispute existed regarding newsprint wastage and interest calculations.
legal_issues: Whether continued email orders constitute an extension of a lapsed contract by conduct, and whether a defense of material wastage—raised inconsistently against specific invoices—qualifies as a genuine pre-existing dispute?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A contract may be extended by the continuous conduct of the parties (e.g., placing and executing orders via email) beyond its expiry date. A dispute raised as an afterthought or mere bluster, incompatible with the contractual terms or the party's own conduct, is a spurious defense and does not constitute a valid 'pre-existing dispute'. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2) requires a genuine, pre-existing dispute. If the dispute is spurious or hypothetically manufactured to evade debt, the Adjudicating Authority must admit the Section 9 petition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the 66 emails showing the CD repeatedly requested print jobs and promised to pay after the contract expired. The wastage defense was dismissed because the agreement's 4% wastage cap applied only if print orders met the 10,000 copy minimum, which they did not. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the debt was acknowledged, the contract was extended by conduct, and the alleged dispute was mere bluster, thereby validating the Section 9 application.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed. The NCLT's dismissal order was set aside. The matter was remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to admit the Section 9 application and pass consequential directions.
summary: The Operational Creditor appealed the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 9 petition. The NCLT had ruled the printing contract had lapsed and found a pre-existing dispute regarding newsprint wastage. The NCLAT overturned the decision, finding that the parties extended the contract by their continued conduct through email orders and promises to pay. The Tribunal declared the wastage dispute a 'spurious defense' because the Corporate Debtor consistently ordered far fewer copies than the contractual minimum, inherently causing higher wastage. The NCLAT ordered the NCLT to admit the CIRP petition.

case_title: Sangunity Exim India Ltd. vs Kapil Batra & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Company (Sangunity Exim India Ltd.); Respondent 1 is the Petitioner claiming oppression. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: N/A (Shareholder dispute regarding oppression and mismanagement). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT passed the impugned order issuing notices on 04.06.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Respondent 1 admitted in the pleadings that they held only 9.41% and 5.22% shares in the respective companies, falling short of the statutory 10% requirement to file a Section 241 petition. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent 1 filed a Section 241 petition with a generic prayer to waive the 10% requirement. The NCLT Principal Bench directly issued notices to the respondents on 04.06.2021 without first adjudicating the waiver request.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can entertain a Section 241 petition and issue notices to respondents when the petitioner holds less than 10% shares and the Tribunal has not yet granted a waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1)?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for oppression and mismanagement by a minority shareholder holding less than the 10% threshold cannot proceed to the merits (e.g., issuance of notices) unless the Tribunal first explicitly grants a waiver of the eligibility criteria. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 244(1) lays down mandatory eligibility criteria for filing a Section 241 petition. The proviso allows the Tribunal to waive these requirements upon a specific application, but this waiver is a strict precondition to maintaining the main petition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed that the petitioner self-admitted their ineligibility and filed a separate application (CA No. 259/2021) for waiver. Issuing notices on the main petition before deciding the waiver application violates procedural mandates. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT erred in taking cognizance of the main petition before resolving the threshold jurisdictional issue of waiver.
operative_order: The appeal was disposed of without costs. The NCLAT advised and directed the NCLT to first dispose of the Respondent's application seeking a waiver from the eligibility criteria under Section 244 before proceeding further with the Section 241 petition.
summary: The Appellant challenged the NCLT's order issuing notices in an Oppression and Mismanagement petition filed by a shareholder holding less than the mandatory 10% share capital. The NCLAT held that while the NCLT has the power to waive this requirement under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, it cannot proceed with the main petition or issue notices without first adjudicating the waiver application. The appeal was disposed of with directions for the NCLT to decide the waiver application before taking further steps in the case.

case_title: Vivekanand Jha vs Punjab National Bank And Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Suspended Management of the Corporate Debtor (Telstar Industries Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent 1 is the Financial Creditor (Punjab National Bank). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Cash credit and overdraft facilities disbursed in November 2010. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default date declared as 27.12.2014, with outstanding dues of Rs. 16,15,39,662.27. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NPA declared on 29.12.2014; OTS offers submitted by CD on 09.11.2015 and 29.03.2016; Section 7 petition filed on 14.02.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor claimed the petition was time-barred since the default was in 2014. The Bank relied on the OTS proposals submitted in 2015 and 2016 as written acknowledgments of debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the Section 7 petition on 15.04.2021, ruling the limitation period was extended by the OTS proposals.
legal_issues: Whether a One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal submitted by a Corporate Debtor constitutes a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act to extend the limitation period for filing a Section 7 IBC petition?
ratio_decidendi: 1.
