ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An OTS proposal submitted by a debtor before the expiration of the original limitation period constitutes a valid, written acknowledgment of liability, which triggers a fresh three-year limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act is applicable to proceedings under the IBC (via Section 238A). Acknowledgment in the form of an OTS extends the limitation clock starting from the date of the acknowledgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the OTS proposal dated 29.03.2016 was made within 3 years of the default date (27.12.2014). This acknowledgment legally reset the clock, making the Section 7 petition filed on 14.02.2019 perfectly within the newly extended 3-year limitation period. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded the Adjudicating Authority correctly applied the law of limitation, affirming that the debt was due, in default, and legally enforceable.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs. The NCLT's admission of the Corporate Debtor into CIRP was upheld.
summary: The Appellant challenged the initiation of CIRP, arguing that the Bank's Section 7 petition filed in 2019 was time-barred because the default date was December 2014. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the Corporate Debtor's submission of a One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal in March 2016 acted as a valid written acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. This acknowledgment successfully restarted the three-year limitation clock, making the 2019 petition timely and maintainable.

case_title: The Assistant Commissioner of Central Tax vs V. Shanker Resolution Professional
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the GST Department (Assistant Commissioner of Central Tax); Respondent 1 is the Resolution Professional; Respondents 2 & 3 are the Successful Resolution Applicants. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Unpaid statutory GST dues. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational dues amounting to Rs. 3,88,38,963/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 12.12.2018. Last date for claim submission was 03.01.2019. The maximum 90-day limit expired in early 2019. Appellant sent a letter regarding the claim on 16.08.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant filed the claim late using the incorrect Form (Form F instead of Form B for operational creditors) and merely sent a letter to the NCLT Registry rather than formally filing an application for condonation of delay. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad approved the Resolution Plan on 28.01.2020. The plan did not include the Appellant's statutory dues, prompting the GST department to appeal.
legal_issues: Whether statutory dues can be accommodated or recognized in an approved Resolution Plan if the claimant fails to file the claim in the prescribed format and strictly within the statutory timeline?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory dues that are not properly filed, verified, and integrated into a Resolution Plan prior to its approval by the Adjudicating Authority stand legally extinguished and cannot be claimed subsequently. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) makes the approved resolution plan binding on all stakeholders, including the Government for statutory dues. Regulation 12 of the CIRP Regulations strictly mandates a 90-day outer limit for claim submissions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on the Supreme Court's judgment in 'Ghanashyam Mishra', the Tribunal found the GST department utterly failed to comply with procedural mandates—submitting late, in the wrong format (Form F), and failing to file a proper condonation application. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the RP correctly rejected the unformatted, delayed claim. Since the dues were not part of the approved Resolution Plan, they were permanently extinguished.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs. The NCLAT upheld the Adjudicating Authority's approval of the Resolution Plan, confirming the extinguishment of the unfiled statutory dues.
summary: The GST Department appealed the NCLT's approval of a Resolution Plan, arguing their claim for Rs. 3.88 Crores in tax dues was ignored by the Resolution Professional. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting the Department failed to file its claim in the prescribed Form B within the 90-day statutory window. Furthermore, instead of filing a formal application for condonation of delay, the Department merely sent a letter to the NCLT Registry. Citing the Supreme Court's ruling in Ghanashyam Mishra, the NCLAT affirmed that statutory dues not included in an approved Resolution Plan are extinguished, and the RP was correct to exclude the improperly filed claim.

case_title: Earth Gracia Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. vs. Earth Infrastructure Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Earth Gracia Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor) and Earth Infrastructure Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), both undergoing CIRP, represented by their RPs. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged loan from the Financial Creditor to its parent company (Corporate Debtor) for maintaining financial health of five projects. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim amount of Rs. 20,78,13,695/- with an underlying ledger entry showing Rs. 16,82,17,052/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form C filed on 08.04.2019, rejected by RP on 25.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Relying solely on ledger and bank account statements; no loan agreement, board resolution, or interest clause. Common directors and promoters exist. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority dismissed the Section 60(5) application on 08.01.2020 holding the transactions were a sham and not financial debt.
legal_issues: Whether the claim made by the Appellant is a Financial Debt as defined under Section 5(8) of the IBC without any loan agreement or time value for money?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Disbursal against consideration for the time value of money is an essential ingredient of a financial debt, and sham or collusive transactions lacking commercial borrowing effect do not qualify. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) of IBC requires the 'commercial effect of a borrowing', which is absent in mere inter-company ledger entries devoid of loan agreements between related parties. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Ledger entries alone, without board resolutions, loan agreements, or stipulations for repayment period, establish only round-tripping of funds. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held the transactions were collusive and sham, dismissing the appeal and affirming they did not constitute a Financial Debt.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed. No costs.
summary: The Appellant (Financial Creditor's RP) appealed against the rejection of its claim by the Corporate Debtor's RP. Both companies are under CIRP with common promoters. The NCLAT affirmed the Adjudicating Authority's finding that the alleged inter-company loans lacked a loan agreement, interest clause, or commercial effect of a borrowing, rendering them sham transactions. Thus, the debt did not qualify as a Financial Debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC.

case_title: Navneet Jain vs. Manoj Sehgal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Navneet Jain (Appellant, Shareholder of Corporate Debtor), Sarbat Cotfab Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), Manoj Sehgal (RP), Tejinder Singh Kocher (Resolution Applicant), Bhupinder Singh Mann (Suspended Director). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution plan submitted by Tejinder Singh Kocher. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan submitted on 06.06.2018, approved by CoC on 14.08.2018, approved by Adjudicating Authority on 08.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant produced public GST and Income Tax returns showing the Resolution Applicant and the Suspended Director were active partners in two firms (Prabh Films and Prabh International) well after the alleged retirement date of 31.10.2017, proving them to be related parties. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority originally approved the plan on 08.06.2020 relying on private retirement deeds, ignoring the public tax documents.
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Applicant was a related party to the suspended director under Section 29A of the IBC, thereby rendering him ineligible to submit a Resolution Plan?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan submitted by an ineligible related party under Section 29A is void and must be rejected. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A strictly prohibits related parties of the corporate debtor's management from acting as resolution applicants. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Public documents such as GST and Income Tax returns carry higher evidentiary value and render private, unregistered retirement deeds suspect, especially when discrepancies like age differences appear on the deeds. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded the resolution applicant was a related party at the time of submission, contravening Section 30(2) of the IBC, and set aside the approval.
operative_order: The impugned order approving the Resolution Plan is set aside. The Resolution Plan is rejected. Actions taken under it are declared null and void. The matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to pass liquidation orders under Section 33. The RP is to be replaced and a new Liquidator appointed. Costs of Rs. 4 lakhs imposed on Respondents 2 and 3.
summary: A shareholder challenged the approval of a resolution plan, alleging the successful resolution applicant was a related party to the suspended director. Despite private retirement deeds claiming otherwise, public tax returns proved ongoing partnership. The NCLAT held the applicant was ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC, set aside the plan's approval, ordered liquidation, and directed the replacement of the Resolution Professional.

case_title: Dr. A.G. Jayakrishnan vs. M/S. Omega Hospitals Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 395 of 2021 in COMPANY APPEAL (AT) No. 77 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dr. A.G. Jayakrishnan (Applicant/Respondent No. 5), M/S. Omega Hospitals Pvt. Ltd. (Company), and two factions of Directors (Dr. Joe Verghese group vs. Dr. K. Mukund group). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management of a hospital providing critical care. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Application filed seeking appointment of an Interim Board/Chairperson during pendency of appeals. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resignation of Dr. Errol Pinto on 02.11.2020 resulted in a 4-4 split in the 8-member Board. Disputed board meeting on 27.02.2021 where the Applicant was denied virtual participation until the end, and the Chairman could not be elected. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appeals were pending against NCLT order dated 24.01.2019 regarding oppression and mismanagement. IA filed to resolve the current board deadlock.
legal_issues: Whether a deadlock in the Board of Directors of a hospital company warrants the appointment of an independent Chairperson to manage day-to-day affairs pending final disposal of oppression and mismanagement appeals?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In cases of severe board deadlock affecting public interest and critical operations, the tribunal may appoint an independent administrator/chairperson to manage the company's affairs pendente lite. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The tribunal utilized its inherent powers to ensure smooth functioning of a critical care hospital undergoing management disputes. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The 4-4 split in the board and the failure to elect a chairman or conduct proper meetings provided sufficient evidence of a deadlock detrimental to public interest. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the deadlock was unhealthy for the company, shareholders, and public, justifying the interim appointment of an independent Chairperson.
operative_order: The application is allowed. Parties are directed to file a panel of three names within 10 days, consenting to act as an Independent Chairperson with full administrative powers, along with a declaration of non-relationship. The Tribunal will appoint a suitable person from the panel or independently if parties fail to do so.
summary: Amidst an ongoing oppression and mismanagement dispute, the resignation of a director caused a 4-4 deadlock in the Board of Omega Hospitals. Citing the hospital's critical care functions and the inability of the factions to conduct board meetings, an applicant sought interim management. The NCLAT allowed the application, directing the appointment of an independent Chairperson with full administrative powers to manage the hospital pending the final disposal of the appeals.

case_title: Punjab National Bank vs. Mr. Subrata M Maity
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Punjab National Bank (Financial Creditor/Appellant), Subrata M Maity (Replacement RP/Respondent), Bhatia Coke and Energy Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank guarantee/Letter of Credit (LC) facilities extended to the Corporate Debtor pre-CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Rs. 17,95,04,271.79 appropriated by PNB during the CIRP period to settle devolved LCs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 22.05.2019. LCs debited during the moratorium. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: PNB claimed the erstwhile IRP approved the debiting of the cash credit account to keep the entity as a going concern. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: New RP demanded a refund of the appropriated amount. The Adjudicating Authority allowed the RP's application on 29.05.2020, directing PNB to refund the amount to the Corporate Debtor's account.
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor can appropriate funds from the Corporate Debtor's account during the moratorium period to settle pre-CIRP Letters of Credit, even if allegedly permitted by the erstwhile IRP?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a moratorium is declared, no creditor can recover or appropriate any amount from the corporate debtor's account towards its own dues. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 strictly prohibits the recovery of any pre-CIRP debt during the moratorium, and an IRP has no authority to bypass this statutory bar. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The fact that the amount was appropriated post-CIRP admission to settle pre-CIRP LCs is a direct violation of the moratorium, regardless of the former IRP's alleged consent. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench affirmed that the bank illegally appropriated the funds during the moratorium and upheld the NCLT's direction to refund the amount.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The NCLT order directing the Appellant bank to deposit the amount of Rs. 17,95,04,271.79 back into the Corporate Debtor's account is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Punjab National Bank debited the Corporate Debtor's account during the CIRP moratorium to settle pre-CIRP Letters of Credit, claiming the erstwhile IRP had consented to keep the company a going concern. The new RP demanded a refund, which the NCLT granted. The NCLAT upheld the decision, ruling that Section 14 of the IBC strictly prohibits creditors from appropriating the corporate debtor's funds during a moratorium, and an IRP's unauthorized consent cannot override the statute.

case_title: Mr. Dhan Prakash Gupta vs. M/S Daehsan Trading India Pvt Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Dhan Prakash Gupta (Successful Auction Purchaser/Appellant), S. Rajendran (Liquidator of M/S Daehsan Trading India Pvt Ltd./Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: E-auction sale of the Corporate Debtor's commercial office space. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute over payment of an additional Rs. 6 Lakhs for Maintenance Security Deposit (MSD) to DLF. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: E-auction completed on 17.04.2020. Letter of Intent issued on 21.04.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Process Memorandum and the LoI clearly stated that the successful bidder must pay Rs. 6 Lakhs towards MSD over and above the bid price. The Liquidator also informed the Appellant via email on 10.04.2020 that this amount was non-negotiable. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an IA claiming the Rs. 130 Lakhs bid was inclusive of MSD. NCLT dismissed it on 08.09.2020, ordering the Appellant to pay the separate MSD.
legal_issues: Whether an auction purchaser is bound to pay statutory maintenance deposits separately when the Process Memorandum and Letter of Intent explicitly mandate it over and above the final bid price?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A successful bidder in a liquidation auction is strictly bound by the terms of the Process Memorandum and Letter of Intent they accepted. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Auction sales under liquidation are governed by the explicitly published terms; buyers cannot retroactively alter conditions they knowingly bid under. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documentary evidence (Process Memorandum, LoI, and pre-auction emails) conclusively proved the Appellant was informed of the separate MSD charge before bidding. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the Appellant had full knowledge of the separate MSD requirement and could not claim the bid amount was inclusive of it.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. However, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Liquidator is directed to accept the balance sale consideration of Rs. 120 Lakhs plus Rs. 6 Lakhs (MSD) without charging interest, provided it is deposited within 10 days. No order as to costs.
summary: The successful bidder in a liquidation e-auction challenged the Liquidator's demand for a separate Rs. 6 Lakhs Maintenance Security Deposit (MSD), claiming his Rs. 130 Lakhs bid was inclusive of it. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that the Process Memorandum, pre-auction emails, and the Letter of Intent explicitly stated the MSD was to be paid over and above the bid amount. The purchaser was directed to pay the full amount, though interest was waived due to the pandemic.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Subodh Kumar Agrawal & Ors.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 1110 of 2021 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1377 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: ICICI Bank Ltd. (Applicant), State Bank of India (Appellant in main appeal), Taguda Pte Ltd. (Resolution Applicant/Respondent No. 2), Subodh Kumar Agrawal (RP/Respondent No. 1). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Clarification sought on the enforceability of corporate guarantees under a revised resolution plan. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Main appeals were disposed of on 08.04.2021, remanding the revised plan to the CoC. Voting scheduled for 22.06.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: ICICI Bank sought a legal clarification on whether their corporate guarantee would subsist if their debt was converted into preference shares or assigned to a third party under the proposed plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The IA was filed in an already disposed-of appeal, seeking a preemptive ruling before the CoC voted on the plan.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal can issue legal clarifications on the terms of a proposed Resolution Plan while it is still pending consideration and voting by the Committee of Creditors?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal cannot pre-judge or issue clarifications on hypothetical questions regarding a Resolution Plan that has not yet been voted on by the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The commercial wisdom of the CoC must operate first; the Adjudicating Authority only evaluates the legality of a plan after it has been approved by the CoC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Asking for preemptive judicial clarification sets a wrong precedent and interferes with the CoC's exclusive domain to accept or reject plans. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench refused to entertain the application, stating that the applicant must make its own commercial decision to consent or dissent, and legality will be tested subsequently.
operative_order: The application for clarification is rejected. No orders as to costs.
summary: ICICI Bank filed an interlocutory application seeking clarification on whether its corporate guarantees would survive if debt was converted into preference shares under a pending Resolution Plan. The NCLAT rejected the application, ruling that it cannot pre-judge hypothetical issues or interfere with the commercial wisdom of the CoC before voting occurs. The legality of the plan is only to be tested by the Adjudicating Authority after the CoC makes its final decision.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Limtex Tea & Industries Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 966 of 2021 IN Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1496 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Applicant), Legal heirs of Late Durga Prasad Agarwal (Appellants/Promoters), Limtex Tea & Industries Ltd (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Land leased to the Corporate Debtor, over which SBI claimed symbolic possession under SARFAESI Act. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim of Rs. 96,67,40,673.31 by SBI. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Main appeal was allowed on 03.03.2021 setting aside CIRP. IA filed on 27.05.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SBI, a non-party to the original NCLT and NCLAT proceedings, sought a modification/clarification of the 03.03.2021 judgment, requesting the RP to hand over specific mortgaged land to the Bank instead of the Corporate Debtor's directors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed the IA under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules after the final judgment had been pronounced.
legal_issues: Whether a non-party to an appeal can introduce new facts and seek modification of a final judgment via an Interlocutory Application under Rule 11 after the appeal has been fully disposed of?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interlocutory application introducing fresh facts by a non-party is not maintainable in an appeal that has already been finally decided. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules cannot be invoked to reopen or substantively modify a final judgment based on new claims by third parties. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since SBI was never a party to the proceedings and never filed an intervention application during the pendency of the appeal, bringing new facts post-judgment is impermissible. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench dismissed the application as not maintainable.
operative_order: I.A. No. 966 of 2021 is dismissed as not maintainable.
summary: After the NCLAT set aside the CIRP of a Corporate Debtor, State Bank of India (SBI) filed an application seeking to modify the order. SBI claimed it held symbolic possession of certain leased lands and asked that the property be handed over to the Bank rather than the Corporate Debtor's directors. The NCLAT dismissed the application as not maintainable, noting that SBI was never a party to the original proceedings and could not introduce new facts after the appeal had been finally decided.

case_title: Rupa Rajesh Sony vs. Anil Kumar
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rupa Rajesh Sony (Appellant/Partner), Anil Kumar (Liquidator of Pearl Vision Pvt. Ltd./Respondent 1). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged unregistered partnership deed for running 'Color Cafe Wellness Solutions' from the Corporate Debtor's residential premises. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Partnership allegedly entered on 17.07.2017. CIRP started in 2018. RP terminated partnership on 26.03.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The property belonged to the Corporate Debtor. The Appellant failed to produce any document proving the Director who signed the unregistered partnership had the authority to do so. Non-cooperation by directors persisted throughout CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT passed orders directing the Commissioner of Police to assist the Liquidator in taking possession of the property, which the Appellant challenged.
legal_issues: Whether a party claiming rights under an unregistered and unauthorized partnership deed can resist the Liquidator's statutory duty to take control of the Corporate Debtor's assets?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Liquidator is statutorily mandated to take control of assets owned by the Corporate Debtor, and unauthorized third-party occupants cannot thwart this process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 18, 25, and 35 of the IBC cast a strict duty on the IRP/RP/Liquidator to take custody of assets, backed by police assistance if necessary under Section 429 of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An unregistered partnership deed executed by a Director without proven authority cannot grant a valid right of possession against the Corporate Debtor's estate in liquidation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench found no merit in the appeal, upholding the NCLT's order for police assistance to evict the Appellant.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed without admitting the same as there is no substance.
summary: The Appellant claimed the right to occupy the Corporate Debtor's premises based on an unregistered partnership deed to run a business. Despite repeated requests and earlier tribunal orders, she refused to vacate during the CIRP and liquidation. The NCLT ordered police assistance to help the Liquidator take possession. The NCLAT dismissed her appeal, holding that the Liquidator has a statutory duty to take custody of the debtor's assets, and the unauthorized partnership deed provided no valid defense.

case_title: Naresh Kumar vs. Durgesh Kumar Sharma & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Naresh Kumar (Appellant/Third Party), Durgesh Kumar Sharma (Operational Creditor/Respondent No. 1), M/s North Rajasthan Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim of property ownership by the Appellant versus a registered sale deed held by the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt of Rs. 1,81,021/- for which CIRP was initiated. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 application admitted on 18.12.2020. Appellant executed power of attorney and filed a civil suit in April 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant produced an old allotment letter from 1995. The RP produced a chain of title ending in a Registered Sale Deed dated 29.06.2009 in favor of the Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant challenged the Section 9 admission order, alleging collusion between the Operational Creditor and the defunct Corporate Debtor to usurp his property.
legal_issues: Whether a third party can challenge the initiation of CIRP by claiming title over the Corporate Debtor's property based on an unregistered historical allotment letter against a registered sale deed?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Appellate Tribunal under the IBC will not conduct a mini-trial to adjudicate complex disputes of property title at the instance of a third party holding mere historical allotment papers. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 moratorium bars the institution of new civil suits regarding the Corporate Debtor's property; the Appellant's post-admission civil suit was invalid. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A registered sale deed in the name of the Corporate Debtor carries strong evidentiary weight over a 25-year-old unregistered society allotment letter and receipt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench declined to entertain the allegations of collusion or decide the title dispute, dismissing the appeal.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed. The Appellant may pursue appropriate remedy in the appropriate forum.
summary: A third party appealed the admission of a Section 9 CIRP petition, alleging it was a collusive attempt to usurp land he claimed to own based on a 1995 society allotment letter. The Resolution Professional countered with a 2009 registered sale deed in the Corporate Debtor's name. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, refusing to adjudicate property title disputes or entertain allegations of collusion based on weak historical documents, advising the appellant to seek remedy in an appropriate civil forum.

case_title: Jasjit Singh Sawhney vs. Net 4 India Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jasjit Singh Sawhney (Suspended Director/Appellant), Net 4 India Limited (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 1), Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. (Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: N/A (Focus on limitation). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned NCLT order passed on 08.03.2019. Appeal filed on 21.12.2020, with a delay of 624 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant argued the Adjudicating Authority wrongly relied on Article 62 of the Limitation Act, citing a Supreme Court precedent. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IA filed seeking condonation of a 624-day delay in filing the appeal against the CIRP admission order.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal has the statutory jurisdiction to condone a delay of 624 days in filing an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Appellate Tribunal has no power or jurisdiction to condone a delay beyond the strict statutory limit prescribed under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) strictly mandates that an appeal must be filed within 30 days, and the Tribunal's power to condone delay is capped at a maximum of 15 additional days. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The numerical delay of 624 days factually exceeds the absolute 45-day outer limit, depriving the Tribunal of any discretion regardless of the underlying legal merits. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded it had no power to entertain the time-barred appeal and dismissed it.
operative_order: The Appeal being time-barred, the Appeal is dismissed.
summary: The suspended director of the Corporate Debtor filed an appeal against the CIRP admission order with a massive delay of 624 days, arguing the lower tribunal applied the wrong limitation article for the debt. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal outright, reiterating that Section 61(2) of the IBC strictly limits its power to condone delay to a maximum of 15 days beyond the initial 30-day filing period, rendering the appeal statutorily time-barred.

case_title: S. Ramuthai vs. M/s. P dot G Constructions Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: S. Ramuthai (Appellant/Homebuyer), M/s. P dot G Constructions Private Limited (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 1), Sundaresan Nagarajan (Resolution Professional/Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purchase of a flat by the Appellant from the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim of Rs. 28,67,560/-, out of which the RP admitted only Rs. 11,15,520/- due to lack of reflection of the remaining cash payment in the corporate books. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved on 13.12.2019. Application filed by Appellant on 18.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant claimed full payment via cash and RTGS, supported by an executed Sale Deed and Construction Agreement. The RP rejected the cash portion. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority dismissed the Appellant's application because it was filed after the approval of the Resolution Plan.
legal_issues: Whether a creditor's application to admit a partial claim can be entertained after the Resolution Plan has already been approved by the Adjudicating Authority?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a Resolution Plan is approved, no new claims or disputes regarding rejected claims can be entertained against the Corporate Debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Relying on the Supreme Court's decision in Essar Steel, the tribunal held that a Successful Resolution Applicant cannot be faced with 'hydra heads' popping up after the plan's approval. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The strict timeline of the IBC process supersedes the evidentiary merits of a late claim. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the Adjudicating Authority's decision to dismiss the application as it was filed post-approval of the Resolution Plan.
operative_order: The Company Appeal is dismissed without costs.
summary: A homebuyer appealed against the Resolution Professional's rejection of a portion of her claim paid in cash. However, she filed her application before the NCLT months after the Resolution Plan had already been approved. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that per the Supreme Court's precedent in Essar Steel, claims cannot be resurrected after the Resolution Plan is approved, to ensure a clean slate for the resolution applicant.

case_title: Resolution Professional of Venta Realtech Pvt. Ltd. vs. Present
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Resolution Professional of Venta Realtech Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: N/A (Focus on CIRP timeline exclusion). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Initial 270 days of CIRP expired on 14.02.2020. NCLAT had earlier stayed CoC final decisions from 06.08.2020 to 04.09.2020 (39 days). Resolution plan submitted on 22.10.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Adjudicating Authority excluded 68 days (lockdown) but failed to exclude the 39-day period where the NCLAT had stayed the CoC from approving any plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The RP appealed the NCLT's refusal to grant the full exclusion of time required to bring the submitted resolution plan within the 270-day CIRP limit.
legal_issues: Whether the period during which an Appellate Tribunal stays the Committee of Creditors from taking a final decision on a Resolution Plan should be excluded from the computation of the CIRP timeline?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The period during which a judicial stay prevents the CoC from finalizing a resolution plan must be excluded from the statutory CIRP timeline. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Judicial stay periods are an exception to the strict timeline computation to prevent prejudice to the resolution process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The existence of the NCLAT's own prior order explicitly staying CoC action for 39 days justified the exclusion. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held the NCLT erred in not excluding the 39-day judicial stay period alongside the 68-day lockdown period.
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed. The period of 107 days (68 days lockdown + 39 days judicial stay) is excluded from the CIRP timeline. The NCLT is requested to dispose of the pending Resolution Plan hearing expeditiously. No order as to costs.
summary: The Resolution Professional appealed the NCLT's refusal to exclude a 39-day judicial stay period from the CIRP timeline. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, ruling that the 39 days during which the Appellate Tribunal itself had restrained the CoC from approving a resolution plan, along with the 68-day COVID lockdown, must be excluded from the 270-day CIRP period computation.

case_title: Binay Kumar Singhania vs. Genegrow Commercial Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Binay Kumar Singhania (Resolution Professional/Appellant), Genegrow Commercial Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: N/A. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 02.08.2019. NCLAT set aside CIRP admission; NCLT formally closed proceedings on 27.01.2020. Supreme Court stayed the NCLAT order on 03.11.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP convened a CoC meeting and sought to exclude 363 days from the CIRP period, interpreting the Supreme Court's stay as a revival of the CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority dismissed the RP's exclusion application as premature, holding that a Supreme Court 'stay' of the NCLAT order did not automatically revive the closed Company Petition.
legal_issues: Whether a Supreme Court interim order staying an NCLAT judgment automatically revives a Company Petition that was subsequently and formally closed by the Adjudicating Authority?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interim stay of an appellate order does not automatically revive or quash a subsequent closure order passed by the lower tribunal; the original proceedings remain closed until expressly restored. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Supreme Court precedent (Shree Chamundi Mopeds), a 'stay' only suspends operation from the date of the order and does not wipe the challenged order out of existence like a 'quashing' does. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the NCLT had issued a distinct order closing the petition, CIRP could not resume without a specific restoration order. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench agreed with the NCLT that the RP's application to exclude time and resume CIRP was premature because the underlying company petition had not been restored.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's decision that the application was premature. The Appellant may take steps to move the Supreme Court for appropriate directions.
summary: After the NCLAT set aside a CIRP admission, the NCLT formally closed the company petition. Later, the Supreme Court stayed the NCLAT's order. The Resolution Professional then applied to the NCLT to exclude time and resume CIRP. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's dismissal of this application as premature, clarifying that a Supreme Court 'stay' does not automatically quash the NCLT's closure order or restore the petition.

case_title: C. Somaiah Nadar vs. M/s. P dot G Constructions Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: C. Somaiah Nadar (Appellant/Homebuyer), M/s. P dot G Constructions Private Limited (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 1), Sundaresan Nagarajan (Resolution Professional/Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purchase of real estate by a homebuyer. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim provisionally admitted by RP to the extent of Rs. 10,56,820/-, rejecting the rest due to lack of a 'no due certificate'. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved on 13.12.2019. Application filed by Appellant on 18.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant claimed full payment was made to the erstwhile management, including cash payments, but the RP rejected the unverified portion. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority dismissed the application as it was filed after the Resolution Plan's approval.
legal_issues: Whether a creditor's application challenging the partial rejection of a claim can be entertained after the approval of the Resolution Plan?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Post-approval of a resolution plan, no past claims can be entertained or litigated against the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel, the corporate debtor must be handed over on a 'clean slate', and a resolution applicant cannot face unexpected 'hydra head' claims. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The timing of the legal challenge—filed after the plan's approval—rendered the merits of the cash payment dispute irrelevant. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the Adjudicating Authority correctly dismissed the application as legally non-maintainable post-approval.
operative_order: The Company Appeal is dismissed. No costs.
summary: A homebuyer challenged the Resolution Professional's partial rejection of his claim, asserting that the unrecorded cash portion was paid to the former management. He filed his application two months after the Resolution Plan was approved. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, relying on the Essar Steel doctrine that claims cannot be raised after the resolution plan's approval to prevent 'hydra head' liabilities for the successful resolution applicant.

case_title: Daimler Financial Services India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mr. Ankit Kumar Aggarwal & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Daimler Financial Services India Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor/Appellant), Ankit Kumar Aggarwal (Resolution Professional/Respondent No. 1), Consortium of Rajesh Grover & Vishnu Gopal Gupta (Resolution Applicant/Respondent No. 2), M/s Mass Metals Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial debt owed by the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC approved the plan with 79.48% voting share. NCLT reserved orders on the plan on 12.01.2021. Appellant filed claim form (Form-C) belatedly on 25.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant promised to file a claim in August 2020 but failed to do so until after the CoC approved the plan and the NCLT had concluded its hearings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority rejected the Appellant's application to admit the claim and reject the CoC-approved plan, citing the Essar Steel 'hydra head' doctrine.
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor can mandate the admission of its claim and rejection of a CoC-approved Resolution Plan after the Adjudicating Authority has reserved its final orders on the plan?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Claims submitted by a creditor after the Committee of Creditors has approved a Resolution Plan and the Adjudicating Authority has reserved its order cannot be entertained. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Permitting claims at such a belated stage violates the core objective of time-bound resolution and triggers the 'hydra head' claims prohibition laid down by the Supreme Court in Essar Steel. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The documented timeline showed the Appellant slept on its rights from August 2020 until February 2021, rendering the application fatally belated. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench found no illegality in the NCLT's refusal to admit the late claim and disrupt the approved resolution process.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: A Financial Creditor sought to file its claim and halt the approval of a Resolution Plan long after the CoC had approved it and the NCLT had reserved its final order. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT's decision that allowing a claim at such a belated stage would amount to the prohibited 'hydra head' scenario condemned by the Supreme Court in the Essar Steel judgment.

case_title: Kanwar Raj Bhagat vs Gujarat Hydrocarbons And Power Sez Ltd & SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd, Corporate Debtor is Gujarat Hydrocarbons and Power SEZ Ltd., Corporate Guarantor is Assam Company India Ltd. (ACIL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan of Rs. 100 Crores granted to Corporate Debtor by Financial Creditor, guaranteed by ACIL. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on 15.04.2014. Financial Creditor claimed Rs. 648.81 Crores in ACIL's CIRP, later filed against Corporate Debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Debt Repayment and Settlement Agreement (DRSA) signed on 24.03.2015, cancelled on 29.05.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DRSA dated 24.03.2015 and Cancellation Agreement dated 29.05.2017 served as acknowledgment of debt. Resolution plan for ACIL was approved, wherein Financial Creditor accepted Rs. 38.87 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed against Corporate Debtor on 10.02.2020, admitted by Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, New Delhi, Bench-III) on 18.11.2020. Ex-Director appealed.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Application under Section 7 of IBC is barred by limitation? 2. Whether the second Application under Section 7 of IBC is maintainable against the Corporate Debtor given CIRP has already taken place against the Corporate Guarantor?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to IBC; a creditor can simultaneously or sequentially initiate CIRP against both the Principal Borrower and Corporate Guarantor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 extends limitation via written acknowledgment. Section 60(2) and (3) of IBC envisage concurrent proceedings against corporate debtor and guarantor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Cancellation Agreement explicitly acknowledged the debt, extending limitation. The resolution plan of the guarantor did not release the principal borrower from the balance. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held the application was within limitation and legally maintainable, dismissing the appeals.
operative_order: The Appeals are dismissed, however, no order as to costs.
summary: In a challenge against the admission of a Section 7 application, the NCLAT held that the application by SREI Infrastructure Finance against Gujarat Hydrocarbons was within limitation due to acknowledgment of debt in a settlement agreement. It further ruled that a creditor can initiate CIRP against a Corporate Debtor even if CIRP has concluded against its Corporate Guarantor for the same debt, as liability is co-extensive. The appeals by the Ex-Director and Resolution Applicant were dismissed on merits[cite: 10].

case_title: V.G. Selvaraj & Ors vs VGP Housing Pvt Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are minority shareholders/petitioners, Respondents are VGP Housing Pvt Ltd and its majority directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management of a family-owned real estate company and the sale of its land parcels. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original CP 393/2019 filed on 14.03.2019. NCLT passed interim consent order on 16.04.2019 appointing an Observer. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants alleged Respondents were selling land at undervalued rates using brute majority, and the Observer was passive. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CA No. 6/2021 for urgent hearing/interim stay. NCLT Chennai vide order dated 22.01.2021 merely directed expedited mediation. Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in passing the impugned order leaving the valuable properties of the Company unprotected pending adjudication of oppression and mismanagement claims.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Allegations of oppression and mismanagement involving mixed questions of law and fact cannot be conclusively decided at the interim stage, but the Tribunal must act fairly to protect the company's paramount interests. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241 and 242 grant unfettered powers to the Tribunal to bring an end to matters complained of. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Consent orders appointing the Observer cannot be annulled simplistically without adjudication on merits. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench directed NCLT to hear the main petition expeditiously and mandated that if the Observer fails to resolve disputes over property sale rates, the NCLT itself must fix the ERP rates.
operative_order: The NCLAT directed NCLT Chennai to take up the main CP No. 393 of 2019 for hearing and dispose of it on merits. It further directed that if the Observer fails to resolve pricing disputes amicably, the NCLT shall fix the ERP rates to protect the company's interests. Appeal disposed of.
summary: In an appeal concerning alleged oppression and mismanagement in VGP Housing Pvt Ltd, the appellants challenged the NCLT's refusal to grant interim protection against the sale of company properties. The NCLAT held that while mixed questions of fact and law cannot be decided at the interim stage, the paramount interest of the company must be protected. The NCLAT directed the NCLT to hear the main petition expeditiously and mandated the NCLT to fix property sale rates if the court-appointed Observer failed to resolve disputes amicably[cite: 11].

case_title: Directorate Of Economic Offences vs Binay Kumar Singhania & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Directorate of Economic Offences, Govt. of West Bengal (DEO). Respondent 1 is Binay Kumar Singhania (Liquidator). Respondent 3 is Pincon Spirits Ltd (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor allegedly accepted fraudulent deposits from the public, leading to FIR and attachment by DEO. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Fraudulent deposits, leading to DEO sealing registered office on 16.04.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: FIR registered on 19.02.2017. Properties attached in Nov 2017 and Apr 2018. CIRP initiated on 19.07.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Designated Court order dated 03.10.2020 convicted directors under WBPIDFE Act and confiscated properties. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed IA No. 1741 of 2019 under Sec 33(5) & 14 IBC seeking de-attachment of properties. NCLT Kolkata allowed it on 19.02.2020, holding IBC overrides WBPIDFE Act. DEO appealed.
legal_issues: Whether Section 14 and 33(5) of the IBC have an overriding effect on Section 3 of the WBPIDFE Act for properties attached prior to CIRP initiation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 14 (Moratorium) and Section 32A of the IBC do not override prior attachments made under specialized state depositor protection laws if no resolution plan is approved changing the management. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of IBC does not apply to criminal proceedings or penal actions. Section 32A grants immunity only if a Resolution Plan is approved leading to a change in control. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since CIRP yielded no resolution plan and liquidation was recommended, the preconditions of Section 32A were not met. The properties were attached before the CIRP commenced. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the attached properties were legally confiscated by the Designated Court under the WBPIDFE Act, and NCLT erred in directing their de-attachment.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 19.02.2020 was set aside. The Appeal was allowed with no order as to costs, leaving the liquidator at liberty to take available legal action.
summary: The Directorate of Economic Offences, West Bengal appealed an NCLT order directing the de-attachment of properties of Pincon Spirits Ltd. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, ruling that Section 14 of the IBC does not override criminal attachments under the WBPIDFE Act made prior to CIRP initiation. Furthermore, Section 32A immunity does not apply since no resolution plan was approved causing a change in management. The NCLT's order was set aside[cite: 12].

case_title: Bank Of India & Ors vs Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd Through Mr Bhuban Madan
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Financial Creditors (Bank of India, Central Bank of India, SBI, Syndicate Bank). Respondent is Bhuban Madan, Resolution Professional for Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium of banks provided fund-based and non-fund-based limits. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim admitted as on insolvency commencement date (06.07.2017) was over Rs. 41.73 Crores across these banks. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 06.07.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: During the moratorium, the erstwhile RP deposited funds generated by the Corporate Debtor into the Cash Credit accounts, which the banks appropriated to square off their liabilities, recovering Rs. 41.73 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed CA 92/CTB/2019 seeking reversal of these amounts as violating Section 14. NCLT Cuttack allowed it on 02.03.2020. Banks appealed.
legal_issues: Whether banks can appropriate funds deposited into the Corporate Debtor's cash credit account during the CIRP moratorium period towards their pre-CIRP dues.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a moratorium is declared under Section 14 of the IBC, financial creditors cannot unilaterally appropriate amounts deposited in the Corporate Debtor's accounts towards their own outstanding pre-CIRP dues. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 14 and 17(1)(d), banks must act on the RP's instructions and cannot debit amounts for recovery. Such unilateral appropriation grants preferential treatment over other creditors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the claims were already filed and crystallized. The banks' recovery of Rs. 41.73 Crores out of the company's running cash flows resulted in unjust enrichment violating the Code. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's direction ordering the banks to reverse the appropriated amounts.
operative_order: The Appeal was dismissed. I.A. No. 156 of 2020 was allowed, directing the Appellant Banks to release the title deeds for the effective implementation of the approved Resolution Plan.
summary: In a dispute over the appropriation of funds during the CIRP moratorium, the NCLAT ruled against a consortium of banks led by Bank of India. The banks had adjusted Rs. 41.73 Crores from the Corporate Debtor's cash flows against their outstanding dues. The NCLAT held this violated Section 14 of the IBC, emphasizing that banks cannot unilaterally recover pre-CIRP dues during the moratorium, as it grants preferential treatment. The appeal was dismissed, and banks were ordered to reverse the amounts and release title deeds[cite: 13].

case_title: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner vs Vandana Garg & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Regional Provident Fund Commissioner (EPFO). Respondent 1 is Vandana Garg, Resolution Professional of GVR Infra Projects Ltd (Corporate Debtor). Respondent 2 is UV Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd (Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory provident fund dues deducted from employees' wages but not remitted. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: EPFO claimed Rs. 1,95,01,301 in Form B during CIRP, which was admitted. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 15.10.2018. Resolution plan approved by NCLT on 20.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Despite filing a claim for Rs. 1.95 Crores (which was subsumed in the approved plan), the Appellant later raised a claim of Rs. 2,84,69,797 on appeal. The Corporate Debtor had not maintained a separate PF corpus. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai approved the Resolution Plan. EPFO appealed, arguing PF dues cannot be waived and must be excluded from the liquidation estate under Section 36(4).
legal_issues: 1. Whether Provident Fund dues can be partially waived or settled under a Resolution Plan. 2. Whether Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC, which excludes PF from the liquidation estate, applies during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a Resolution Plan is approved under Section 31 of the IBC, it binds all stakeholders including statutory authorities, and any claims outside the plan stand extinguished. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36(4)(a)(iii) excluding PF dues from the liquidation estate applies only during liquidation, not when the corporate debtor undergoes resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the corporate debtor had not created a separate PF fund and was being resolved (not liquidated), the RP could not exclude non-existent funds. The Appellant's original claim was fully admitted and dealt with per the plan; raising a subsequent enhanced claim is impermissible. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded the approved Resolution Plan was legally compliant and extinguished any enhanced PF claims not part of the plan.
operative_order: The Appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: The Regional Provident Fund Commissioner appealed an NCLT order approving a Resolution Plan for GVR Infra Projects Ltd, arguing PF dues cannot be waived and are excluded from the liquidation estate under Section 36 of the IBC. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 36 applies only during liquidation, not resolution. Furthermore, once a Resolution Plan is approved under Section 31, it binds all statutory authorities, and the creditor cannot subsequently raise enhanced claims outside the approved plan[cite: 14].

case_title: Antanium Holdings Pte. Ltd. vs M/s. Sujana Universal Industries Limited & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Antanium Holdings Pte. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant). Respondent is Sujana Universal Industries Limited (Corporate Debtor) through RP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution of the corporate debtor involving total debt of Rs. 1956.75 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved by CoC on 15.09.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Resolution Plan contained conditions seeking waivers of statutory tax liabilities and CBDT approvals. NCLT approved the plan but noted that the approval does not construe a waiver of statutory obligations, which must be dealt with by appropriate authorities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad approved the plan on 24.12.2020 with the caveat in Para 22. The Resolution Applicant appealed against Para 22.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction by adding an observation that the approval of the Resolution Plan does not automatically grant statutory waivers and that specific waivers must be approved by the relevant authorities.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority can express its views on the limitations of a Resolution Plan regarding statutory waivers without it constituting an unauthorized modification of the plan's commercial terms. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 requires subjective satisfaction. Directing the applicant to seek statutory waivers from relevant authorities does not violate the binding nature of the plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the NCLT merely observed that statutory waivers sought in the plan are subject to approval by the concerned authorities. This was an expression of legal reality, not an imposition of a new commercial condition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the NCLT's observations in Para 22 were within its limits to express its opinion and did not illegally modify the Resolution Plan.
operative_order: The Appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: The Successful Resolution Applicant (Antanium Holdings) appealed an NCLT order approving its Resolution Plan for Sujana Universal Industries Ltd, challenging a paragraph stating that statutory waivers sought in the plan require approval from relevant authorities. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that the Adjudicating Authority did not exceed its jurisdiction or alter the commercial wisdom of the CoC. The NCLT's observation was merely an expression of the legal reality that statutory waivers must be processed by the appropriate authorities[cite: 15].

case_title: Rajratan Babulal Agarwal vs Solartex India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Rajratan Babulal Agarwal, Ex-Director of Honest Derivatives Pvt Ltd (Corporate Debtor). Respondent 1 is Solartex India Pvt Ltd (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purchase order dated 27.10.2016 for supply of 500 MT Indonesian Coal. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: 20 invoices issued between 28.10.2016 and 02.11.2016 amounting to Rs. 15,73,279 plus interest. Default date 10.11.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued on 05.02.2018, delivered 08.02.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate debtor sent an email on 03.11.2016 complaining about coal quality. Creditor replied on 04.11.2016 explaining the moisture and stopped delivery. Corporate debtor consumed the coal, never issued a debit note, and only filed a civil suit for damages on 26.03.2018, after receiving the statutory notice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application filed on 30.07.2018. NCLT Ahmedabad admitted it on 28.05.2020. Ex-Director appealed.
legal_issues: 1. Whether there was a pre-existing dispute regarding the quality of goods under Section 8(2) of the IBC. 2. Whether the impugned order was passed in contravention of NCLT Rules by delayed pronouncement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A spurious or hypothetical defense raised to avoid liability does not constitute a 'pre-existing dispute' under the IBC. A civil suit filed after the receipt of a statutory demand notice cannot establish a pre-existing dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2)(a) requires the dispute or suit to be pending *before* the receipt of the demand notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The corporate debtor's failure to return the goods or issue a debit note after the creditor's clarification, combined with filing a civil suit only post-demand notice, proved the dispute was an afterthought. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the admission of the Section 9 application, finding no genuine pre-existing dispute and dismissing procedural objections about delayed judgment.
operative_order: The Appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: The Ex-Director of Honest Derivatives Pvt Ltd appealed the admission of a Section 9 application filed by Solartex India Pvt Ltd (Operational Creditor). The appellant claimed a pre-existing dispute over coal quality. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the corporate debtor consumed the coal, never issued a debit note, and only filed a civil suit for damages after receiving the statutory demand notice. Thus, the defense was an afterthought, and no genuine pre-existing dispute existed under Section 8(2) of the IBC[cite: 16].

case_title: Mrs. Manasi Indrajit Wadkar vs Union Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Manasi Indrajit Wadkar, Ex-Director of Krishna Knitwear Technology Ltd (Corporate Debtor). Respondent 1 is Union Bank of India (formerly Andhra Bank, Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Working capital and term loans provided by a consortium of banks led by Andhra Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount was Rs. 245,31,64,521. Account declared NPA on 29.06.2012. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NPA on 29.06.2012. SARFAESI notice issued on 31.01.2015. Section 7 application filed on 21.05.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor sent letters on 23.03.2015 and 05.04.2016 requesting restructuring and offering OTS. Balance sheets of 2015-16 and 2017-18 acknowledged the debt. Part payments were made in July and Sept 2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the Section 7 application on 13.01.2020. Ex-director appealed on the ground of limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application was barred by limitation given the NPA date of 29.06.2012 and the filing date of 21.05.2018.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Acknowledgments of debt in letters, balance sheets, and part-payments extend the limitation period under Section 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act for filing a Section 7 application under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies mutatis mutandis to IBC proceedings. Balance sheets and OTS proposals qualify as valid acknowledgments. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the Corporate Debtor's letters in 2015 and 2016, balance sheets up to 2017-18, and part payments in 2017 to conclude that a fresh period of limitation was triggered repeatedly. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the debt was not time-barred and upheld the NCLT's admission order.
operative_order: The Appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: The Ex-Director of Krishna Knitwear Technology Ltd challenged the admission of a Section 7 application by Union Bank of India, arguing the debt was time-barred since the account was declared NPA in 2012. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the corporate debtor's letters proposing settlement, balance sheets for 2015-16 and 2017-18, and part payments in 2017 constituted valid acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, thereby extending the limitation period[cite: 17].

case_title: Ronak Kundanlal Bhagat & Ors. vs Parthiv Parikh & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are shareholders/promoters of Sanghvi Forging and Engineering Ltd (Corporate Debtor). Respondent 1 is Parthiv Parikh, Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of the corporate debtor culminating in an approved resolution plan. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Suspended management failed to act on their OTS proposal by 31.12.2019. Resolution plan approved by CoC. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC approved the Resolution Plan with 100% voting share. The promoters failed to comply with their one-time settlement proposal within the given timeframe. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT approved the Resolution Plan. The promoters appealed to NCLAT seeking a stay on CIRP to pay the amount.
legal_issues: Whether shareholders/promoters can challenge an approved Resolution Plan without demonstrating material irregularity by the Resolution Professional under Section 61(3)(ii) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal against an order approving a Resolution Plan is only maintainable on the specific grounds enumerated in Section 61(3) of the IBC, such as material irregularity. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(3)(ii) restricts appeals against approved plans to cases of material irregularity in the exercise of powers by the RP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The appellants merely offered to pay the amount accepted from the successful applicant but failed to allege or prove any material irregularity by the RP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT summarily dismissed the appeal for failing to meet the statutory threshold for challenging an approved Resolution Plan.
operative_order: The Appeal was dismissed summarily with no costs.
summary: Shareholders and promoters of Sanghvi Forging and Engineering Ltd appealed an NCLT order approving a Resolution Plan, offering to match the successful applicant's payment. The NCLAT summarily dismissed the appeal, ruling that under Section 61(3)(ii) of the IBC, an approved plan can only be challenged on grounds such as material irregularity by the Resolution Professional. Since the appellants failed to demonstrate any such irregularity and had previously failed to honor their settlement proposal, the appeal was not maintainable[cite: 18].

case_title: Ramasamy Palaniappan vs Radhakrishnan Dharmarajan & Others
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ramasamy Palaniappan, Shareholder of Corporate Debtor. Respondent 1 is Radhakrishnan Dharmarajan, Resolution Professional of Appu Hotels Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Appu Hotels Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 05.05.2020. 180-day timeline ending on 04.11.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, CIRP activities were delayed. The Committee of Creditors (CoC) passed a resolution with 100% voting share to seek an exclusion of 179 days from the CIRP timeline. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Chennai) allowed the RP's application under Regulation 40C, excluding the period from 05.05.2020 to 31.10.2020. The Appellant challenged this, arguing the entire CIRP process should have been restarted.
legal_issues: Whether the commercial decision of the Committee of Creditors to seek exclusion of time under Regulation 40C of the IBBI Regulations instead of re-issuing Form G is subject to judicial review.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors is paramount and non-justiciable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 40C allows the exclusion of the COVID-19 lockdown period from the CIRP timeline for activities that could not be completed. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The CoC unanimously voted to seek a time exclusion rather than issuing a fresh Form G; this commercial decision cannot be interfered with by the Adjudicating or Appellate Authority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the NCLT was justified in granting the exclusion of time based on the CoC's resolution and dismissed the appeals.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) Nos. 19 and 20 of 2021 are dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: A shareholder of the Corporate Debtor appealed the NCLT's order excluding 179 days from the CIRP timeline under Regulation 40C due to the COVID-19 lockdown[cite: 19]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that the Committee of Creditors' decision to seek an extension rather than restarting the process by re-issuing Form G was a protected exercise of its commercial wisdom, which is non-justiciable[cite: 19].

case_title: Lakshmi Narayan Sharma vs Punjab National Bank & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Lakshmi Narayan Sharma, Promoter/Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor (Saptarishi Hotels Pvt Ltd). Respondent 1 is Punjab National Bank (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium loan aggregating Rs. 170 Crores sanctioned on 11.08.2011 to develop a hotel on BOT basis. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount of Rs. 78.74 Crores against Term Loan 1 and Rs. 4.15 Crores against Term Loan 2 as on 31.03.2016. Total dues as of 30.06.2019 were Rs. 144.02 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account became NPA on 30.06.2013/30.06.2016. Section 7 application filed on 18.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Guarantors executed Balance and Security Confirmation Letters on 20.02.2018 acknowledging the debt. The Corporate Debtor made a part-payment of Rs. 15,262.75 to the loan account on 15.10.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad admitted the Section 7 application on 18.01.2021. The Promoter appealed, arguing the application was barred by limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the application filed by the Financial Creditor under Section 7 of the IBC was barred by limitation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Balance and Security Confirmation Letters and part-payments constitute valid written acknowledgments of debt under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963, thereby initiating a fresh period of limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act is fully applicable to IBC Section 7 applications, extending the 3-year limit from the date of the acknowledgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The execution of Balance Confirmation Letters on 20.02.2018 and the part-payment on 15.10.2018 extended the limitation period, bringing the application filed in July 2019 well within the permissible 3-year window. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the debt was validly acknowledged, effectively renewing the limitation period, and thus upheld the NCLT's admission order.
operative_order: The Instant Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 01 of 2021 is dismissed, but without costs.
summary: A suspended director appealed against the admission of a Section 7 IBC application by Punjab National Bank, arguing the debt was time-barred[cite: 20]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that the Corporate Debtor's execution of Balance and Security Confirmation Letters and a part-payment made to the loan account constituted valid acknowledgments of debt under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, effectively renewing the limitation period[cite: 20].

case_title: Vijaya Sai Poultries Pvt. Ltd vs Vemulapalli Sai Prameela & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Vijaya Sai Poultries Pvt. Ltd. Respondents are Vemulapalli Sai Prameela and others (Petitioners before NCLT). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged illegal transfer of shares, siphoning of company funds, and unauthorized purchase of immovable properties by Managing Director Naveen Kishore. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Respondents made vague allegations of forgery and fund diversion spanning 15 years, unsupported by documentary evidence. A criminal FIR on the same facts resulted in a closure report. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents filed a petition under Sections 241/242 of the Companies Act. The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Amaravati) passed an interim order allowing a forensic audit covering 15 years through a one-line order lacking any reasoning. The Company appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can pass an order directing a forensic audit of a company without recording reasons or making prima facie findings of fact.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A quasi-judicial authority must record cogent and clear reasons in support of its conclusions; cryptic and non-speaking orders violate the principles of natural justice and fairness. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(4) of the Companies Act requires a prima facie finding of oppression or mismanagement before passing interim orders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the allegations were vague and lacked documentary support, concluding that the NCLT's one-line order providing no reasoning for ordering a 15-year forensic audit was arbitrary and legally unsustainable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT set aside the impugned order for being unreasoned and arbitrary.
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed, however, no order as to costs. The Impugned Order is set aside.
summary: In an oppression and mismanagement petition, the NCLT directed a 15-year forensic audit of the appellant company via a one-line, unreasoned interim order[cite: 21]. The NCLAT set aside the order, emphasizing that quasi-judicial bodies must provide cogent reasons for their decisions to prevent arbitrariness and ensure fairness, thereby holding the cryptic order legally unsustainable[cite: 21].

case_title: R V Tyagarajan vs R. Raghavendran
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is R. V. Tyagarajan, Chairman and MD of Corporate Debtor (Thiru Arooran Sugars Ltd) prior to CIRP. Respondent is R. Raghavendran, Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of the Corporate Debtor, primarily involving sugar production and large dues owed to sugarcane farmers (Operational Creditors). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted claims included Rs. 65.90 Crores owed to farmers. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Final Resolution Plan rejected by CoC on 07.12.2020. Promoters submitted a revised Compromise Settlement offer on 23.11.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Sole Resolution Applicant's plan was rejected by 76.02% of the CoC voting share. The Promoters' OTS offer (Rs. 243 Crores) lacked additional upfront payment and was not considered for approval by the CoC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following the CoC's rejection of the plan, the RP filed an application for liquidation under Sec 33. NCLT Chennai ordered liquidation on 08.04.2021. Appellant challenged the liquidation.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in ordering liquidation when the CoC rejected the resolution plan but did not consider the Promoters' One Time Settlement offer.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The decision to liquidate a corporate debtor upon the rejection of a resolution plan by the requisite majority of the Committee of Creditors is a non-justiciable exercise of commercial wisdom. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(2) of the IBC mandates liquidation if the CoC rejects the resolution plans and decides to liquidate. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The CoC, with a 76.02% voting share, rejected the sole resolution plan after assessing its feasibility and viability. The Tribunal cannot interfere with this commercial decision. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority correctly ordered liquidation based on the CoC's commercial wisdom, dismissing the appeal.
operative_order: The Instant Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 59 of 2021 is dismissed. No costs.
summary: The former Chairman of Thiru Arooran Sugars Ltd appealed an NCLT liquidation order, arguing the CoC wrongly ignored the promoters' settlement offer which would fully pay sugarcane farmers[cite: 22]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, reinforcing that the CoC's rejection of a resolution plan by a 76.02% majority is a binding commercial decision. Under Section 33(2) of the IBC, the NCLT rightly ordered liquidation[cite: 22].

case_title: Vivek Raheja Resolution Professional vs Na
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Vivek Raheja, Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 26.02.2020. The 330-day limit ended on 21.01.2021. IA 4208 of 2020 (to replace RP) was pending for 123 days (from 27.09.2020 to 27.01.2021). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT excluded 97 days for the COVID-19 lockdown but refused to exclude the time lost to judicial intervention. This left the RP with an insufficient 43 days to conclude the nascent CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected the exclusion of judicial delay on 17.03.2021. RP appealed to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the time consumed by judicial intervention and pandemic lockdowns should be excluded from the mandatory 330-day limit for completing CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Time lost due to judicial intervention and pandemic lockdowns qualifies as exceptional circumstances, warranting exclusion from the 330-day CIRP limit to prevent the corporate debtor from being effortlessly pushed into liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Section 12(3) mandates completion within 330 days, the Supreme Court has clarified this can be extended in exceptional cases where delay is attributable to the adjudicatory process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that CIRP was at a nascent stage due to COVID-19 and the 123-day pendency of an application to replace the RP. Denying exclusion would unfairly force liquidation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT modified the NCLT's order, excluding 92 days for judicial delay and 160 days for lockdown, emphasizing resolution over liquidation.
operative_order: A total period of 92 days (judicial intervention) and 160 days (lockdown) are excluded. The appeal is disposed of. No order as to costs.
summary: A Resolution Professional appealed the NCLT's refusal to exclude time lost to judicial delays from the 330-day CIRP limit[cite: 23]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, excluding 92 days for judicial intervention and 160 days for the COVID-19 lockdown. The Tribunal emphasized that liquidation should be the last resort, and delays attributable to the pandemic and the Adjudicating Authority constitute exceptional circumstances warranting an extension under Section 12(3) of the IBC[cite: 23].

case_title: Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. vs. Nagaur Water Supply Company Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor (Assignee) is Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor is Nagaur Water Supply Company Pvt. Ltd., Assignor is L&T Infrastructure Finance Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed Rs. 40 Crores from L&T Infrastructure Finance on 14 June 2011 to be repaid in 120 monthly installments at 13% interest. Debt was assigned to Appellant on 30 December 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account became NPA on 30 November 2013, outstanding amount claimed Rs. 40,42,00,020 as of January 2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding up notice issued on 9 January 2015; winding up petition filed 7 April 2015; section 7 application filed on 15 September 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Winding up petition was pending in Gujarat High Court; Balance sheets for 2014-15 to 2016-17 acknowledged the debt; cheque of Rs. 25 lakhs was issued on 16 April 2015. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed Section 7 petition on 27 May 2020 on the ground of limitation as NPA date was 2013.
legal_issues: Whether the application under Section 7 of IBC was barred by limitation considering the pendency of a winding-up petition and entries in balance sheets acknowledging the debt?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Entries in balance sheets and partial payments by cheque can constitute acknowledgment of debt extending the period of limitation under sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 applies to applications under IBC, meaning acknowledgments in Annual Returns extend limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the balance sheets of 2014-15 to 2016-17 without any reservations by directors, finding them valid acknowledgments. 4.
