DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held the application under Section 7 was not barred by limitation, setting aside the NCLT order.
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed. The Impugned Order is quashed and set aside. The Section 7 application is restored to the file of the Adjudicating Authority to be admitted unless parties settle.
summary: The case involves Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd., assignee of L&T Infrastructure, appealing the NCLT's dismissal of a Section 7 application against Nagaur Water Supply Company for being time-barred. The NCLAT analyzed the effect of pending winding-up petitions, part payments, and balance sheet entries acknowledging the debt. Finding that the balance sheets from 2014-15 to 2016-17 contained clear acknowledgments and that a partial payment was made in 2015, the NCLAT held that the limitation period was extended under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act. The appeal was allowed, and the NCLT order was set aside.

case_title: Sandeep Jindal vs. State Bank of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is State Bank of India. Corporate Debtor is represented by Sandeep Jindal (Suspended Director). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor took loans from SBI in tranches totaling Rs. 69.67 Crores between 2008-2012. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account declared NPA on 30 September 2012. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application was filed on 3 October 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: State Bank of India relied on balance sheets for the years ending 31 March 2015 and 31 March 2016, and an OTS letter dated 20 January 2017, demonstrating acknowledgment of debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh admitted the Section 7 petition on 3 March 2020, rejecting the defense that it was time-barred. The suspended director appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the entries in the balance sheets of the corporate debtor constitute an acknowledgment of debt extending the period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgment of debt in the balance sheets or through a One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal extends the period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act for IBC proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act is applicable to proceedings under the IBC, meaning the three-year limitation period from the date of default can be reset. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the auditor's notes and found that even if balances were 'subject to confirmation', it did not negate the acknowledgment of liability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the limitation period was validly extended by balance sheet entries and the OTS proposal, affirming the NCLT's admission of the CIRP.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: Sandeep Jindal, suspended director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed against the NCLT's admission of a Section 7 application filed by State Bank of India. The appellant argued the application was time-barred as the default (NPA date) was in 2012, while the application was filed in 2018. The NCLAT held that the balance sheets for 2015 and 2016, along with a 2017 OTS proposal, validly constituted an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, resetting the limitation period. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the initiation of CIRP.

case_title: Next Orbit Ventures Fund vs. Print House India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Next Orbit Ventures Fund (Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant). Corporate Debtor is Print House India Pvt. Ltd. Respondent 3 is Sify Technologies Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was in printing and leasing, which became non-viable. Sify proposed to transform the infrastructure into Data Centers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly quantified in this appeal as it pertains to the resolution plan approval stage. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT initiated CIRP on 9 October 2018. CoC approved Sify's plan on 26 August 2019. NCLT approved the plan on 23 June 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sify's plan secured 70.05% voting share from the CoC, proposing to pay Rs. 56.91 Cr compared to Appellant's plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved Sify's resolution plan despite objections that it changed the nature of the business. Next Orbit appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Plan can be approved under the IBC if it alters the core business of the Corporate Debtor, and whether the Adjudicating Authority can interfere with the commercial wisdom of the CoC in approving such a plan?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The IBC does not inhibit a Resolution Applicant from changing the Corporate Debtor's line of business to maintain it as a going concern, especially if the original business is obsolete. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2) and Section 31 leave the feasibility and viability assessment exclusively to the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal analyzed the CoC's evaluation matrix, where Sify's plan scored higher and won the requisite majority vote. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the NCLT's decision, reiterating that courts cannot trespass into the commercial wisdom of the CoC as long as statutory compliance is met.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 417 of 2020 is rendered infructuous and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 744 of 2020 is dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: Next Orbit Ventures Fund challenged the NCLT's approval of a resolution plan submitted by Sify Technologies for Print House India. The appellant argued that Sify's plan would change the corporate debtor's business from printing to data centers, allegedly violating the IBC's intent. The NCLAT affirmed that the IBC permits a change in the line of business to ensure the entity's survival and maximization of value. The Tribunal emphasized the supremacy of the CoC's commercial wisdom in evaluating plan feasibility and viability, ultimately dismissing the appeal and upholding Sify's resolution plan.

case_title: Sree Bhadra Parks And Resorts Ltd vs. Sri Ramani Resorts And Hotels Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sree Bhadra Parks And Resorts Ltd (Corporate Debtor). Respondent is Sri Ramani Resorts And Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent paid Rs. 1 Crore advance under a Share Purchase Agreement dated 21.11.2012 for buying 100% shares for Rs. 33.08 Crores. The transaction did not fructify. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 4,25,32,016.405 with 24% interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed on 21.01.2020. Settled initially on 26.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor acknowledged debt on 28.11.2018. A settlement agreement was reached to pay Rs. 2.25 Crores, with Rs. 1 Lakh paid upfront, Rs. 10 Lakhs later, and a post-dated cheque for Rs. 2.14 Crores which eventually bounced in December 2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT initially disposed of the petition on 24.09.2020 based on the settlement, granting liberty to file fresh. Upon default, Respondent filed a restoration application under Rule 11, which NCLT allowed on 28.01.2021.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the inherent power under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to restore a Section 7 application disposed of on the basis of a settlement agreement when the corporate debtor subsequently defaults on the settlement terms?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to restore a withdrawn or disposed of insolvency petition if the settlement terms leading to the withdrawal are breached. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 11 allows NCLT to pass orders necessary for meeting the ends of justice, independent of the right to file a fresh application. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the admitted default on the post-dated cheque and the corporate debtor's failure to honor the settlement. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the NCLT's restoration of the CIRP, ruling that the corporate debtor cannot avoid obligations on technicalities after breaching a settlement.
operative_order: The instant Company Appeal is dismissed. No costs. IA No.17 of 2021(Stay Application) is closed.
summary: Sree Bhadra Parks appealed an NCLT order restoring a Section 7 application filed by Sri Ramani Resorts. The original application had been disposed of after a settlement was reached between the parties. However, the appellant defaulted on the final settlement payment, prompting the respondent to seek restoration of the insolvency petition under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules. The NCLAT rejected the appellant's argument that the NCLT lacked power to review its order, affirming that the NCLT has inherent jurisdiction to restore proceedings when a settlement is breached to prevent injustice. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Victory Iron Works Limited vs. Jitendra Lohia Resolution Professional of Avani Towers Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant 1 is Victory Iron Works Ltd (Licensee). Appellant 2 is Energy Properties Pvt Ltd (Landowner). Respondent is Jitendra Lohia (RP of Avani Towers Pvt Ltd - Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Landowner entered a Development Agreement on 16.06.2008 with Corporate Debtor for developing 10.19 acres of land. Licensee was granted leave and license for 10,000 sq ft on 11.08.2011. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly defined for the core debt, relates to asset possession during CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP of Corporate Debtor commenced on 15.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Development Agreement was never terminated before CIRP. A Memorandum of Recording Possession dated 24.06.2010 confirmed Corporate Debtor's exclusive development rights. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT directed local police assistance to the RP to protect the Corporate Debtor's development rights but clarified Victory Iron could continue business on its 10,000 sq ft. Victory and Energy Properties appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the intangible development rights of a Corporate Debtor over a property not owned by it can be protected under the moratorium provisions of Section 14 of the IBC during the CIRP?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Intangible assets, such as possessory and development rights arising from a subsisting Development Agreement, fall within the purview of the Corporate Debtor's assets protected by the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(d) prohibits the recovery of property occupied by or in possession of the Corporate Debtor, thereby freezing the landowner's ability to evict the developer or terminate the agreement during CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found that the 2008 Development Agreement was active at the onset of CIRP, preserving the Corporate Debtor's developmental rights. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the NCLT's decision protecting the RP's possession and development rights over the property, while allowing the licensee to continue using its specific portion.
operative_order: The appeals are dismissed with observations. Pending Interlocutory Application(s), if any, stands disposed of. No order as to costs.
summary: Victory Iron Works and Energy Properties appealed against the NCLT's order protecting the Resolution Professional's possession of a 10.19-acre property. Energy Properties owned the land, but the Corporate Debtor (Avani Towers) held subsisting developmental rights under a 2008 agreement. The NCLAT held that these intangible development rights constitute an asset of the Corporate Debtor, which is protected by the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC. The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's order preserving the RP's rights to the property while permitting Victory Iron to retain its licensed 10,000 sq. ft. area. Both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Ashish Mohan Gupta vs. The Liquidator Of M/S Hind Motors India Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ashish Mohan Gupta (Promoter/Director). Respondent is the Liquidator of M/s. Hind Motors India Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was engaged in sale and service of cars. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly specified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation ordered on 12 September 2017. E-auction of spare parts proposed for 16 August 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The promoter submitted a scheme for amalgamation/compromise under Sec 230-232 of the Companies Act, but it lacked economic rationale and proposed discharging liabilities without infusing additional funds. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh rejected the application to stay the e-auction of spare parts and later rejected the proposed amalgamation scheme holding the promoter ineligible under Sec 29A. Promoter appealed both orders.
legal_issues: Whether a promoter, ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC, can propose a scheme of compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act during the liquidation phase of the Corporate Debtor?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The disqualifications stipulated under Section 29A of the IBC apply to schemes of compromise or arrangement proposed under Section 230 of the Companies Act when a company is undergoing liquidation under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 230 of the Companies Act cannot be used as a backdoor by ineligible promoters to regain control of the corporate debtor during IBC liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the scheme proposed by the appellant lacked fresh fund infusion and was merely an attempt to delay liquidation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench dismissed the appeals, relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Arun Kumar Jagatramka, confirming the promoter's ineligibility and rejecting the scheme.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 875 of 2019 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 07 of 2020 are dismissed. Interim Orders dated 29th August 2019 are withdrawn. No order as to costs.
summary: Ashish Mohan Gupta, promoter of Hind Motors India Ltd, appealed against NCLT orders refusing to halt the e-auction of the company's spare parts and rejecting his proposed scheme of compromise/amalgamation under Section 230 of the Companies Act. The NCLAT referenced the Supreme Court's precedent in Arun Kumar Jagatramka, holding that promoters ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC cannot propose a Section 230 scheme to regain control of a corporate debtor in liquidation. The Tribunal found the scheme lacked economic rationale and was a delaying tactic, subsequently dismissing both appeals.

case_title: Technology Development Board vs. Anil Goel Liquidator Of Gujarat Oleo Chem Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Technology Development Board (Secured Creditor). Respondent 1 is Anil Goel (Liquidator of Gujarat Oleo Chem Ltd). Respondent 2 and 3 are Stressed Asset Stabilisation Fund and Gujarat State Finance Corporation (First Charge Holders). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial loans provided to the Corporate Debtor by multiple creditors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant submitted a claim of Rs. 24,78,68,595 during liquidation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation initiated on 17 January 2018. Stakeholder meeting held on 9 May 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator distributed entire sale proceeds to first charge holders (Respondents 2 and 3), giving nothing to the Appellant (second charge holder) despite holding a 14.54% voting share. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed Appellant's application, ruling inter-se priorities of secured creditors remain valid in liquidation. Appellant challenged this.
legal_issues: Whether inter-se priorities among secured creditors (such as first and second charge) subsist when they relinquish their security interest to the liquidation estate under Section 52, for the purpose of distribution under Section 53 of the IBC?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When secured creditors relinquish their security interest to the liquidation estate, all such secured creditors rank equally for the distribution of assets under Section 53(1)(b)(ii), rendering their prior inter-se priorities irrelevant. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 53 of the IBC overrides conflicting provisions like Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act. Relinquishment of security under Section 52 places all secured creditors in the same equitable class. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated that since the first charge holders relinquished their interest instead of enforcing it, they forfeited their hierarchical priority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT set aside the NCLT order, directing the liquidator to distribute the proceeds equally among all secured creditors who relinquished their interest.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed and the impugned order is set aside. I.A. 514 of 2019 is allowed with direction to the Liquidator to treat all Secured Creditors relinquishing the security interest as one class ranking equally under Section 53(1)(b)(ii) and distribute proceeds accordingly.
summary: The Technology Development Board appealed against the NCLT's refusal to grant it a share of the liquidation proceeds of Gujarat Oleo Chem Ltd. The liquidator had paid the entire proceeds to the first charge holders, ignoring the Appellant, a second charge holder. The NCLAT held that under Section 53 of the IBC, if secured creditors relinquish their security interest to the liquidation estate, inter-se priorities (like first or second charge) are dissolved. Consequently, all relinquishing secured creditors rank equally. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and directed equitable distribution among all such secured creditors.

case_title: Mr. K.N. Rajakumar vs. Mr. V. Nagarajan & 2 Others
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is K.N. Rajakumar (Suspended Director of Aruna Hotels Ltd). Respondent 1 is V. Nagarajan (Resolution Professional). Respondent 3 is HDFC Bank. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Relates to the constitution of the Committee of Creditors for the Corporate Debtor, Aruna Hotels Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details not fully listed, but HDFC Bank claims funding balance of Rs. 36 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP originally admitted in 2017. Restored by Supreme Court on 3 March 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Following SC's restoration, the RP allegedly reconstituted the CoC with current creditors, which was challenged as some original 2017 creditors had withdrawn claims. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT directed the RP to convene a meeting of the original 2017 CoC members to consider a withdrawal application under Section 12A and suspended the newly constituted CoC. Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Professional has the adjudicatory power to alter or reconstitute the Committee of Creditors after its original formation under the IBC?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional has no adjudicatory power to alter the composition or status of the Committee of Creditors once it has been validly constituted. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While an RP can update the list of claims, they cannot review or change the fundamental status of a creditor or unilaterally reconstitute the CoC in derogation of the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found the NCLT's direction to restore the original 2017 CoC members for considering the 12A withdrawal to be free from legal infirmities. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the NCLT order suspending the RP's newly constituted CoC and directing the convening of the originally constituted CoC.
operative_order: The present Company Appeal AT INS 48 of 2021 is dismissed. No Costs. I.A.106/2021 (Stay Application) is dismissed.
summary: K.N. Rajakumar, suspended director of Aruna Hotels, challenged an NCLT order that directed the Resolution Professional (RP) to convene the originally constituted 2017 Committee of Creditors (CoC) to consider a Section 12A withdrawal application. The NCLT had suspended a newly constituted CoC formed by the RP. The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's decision, emphasizing that an RP acts in an administrative capacity and lacks the adjudicatory power to unilaterally alter or reconstitute the CoC once formed. Finding no legal infirmity in the NCLT's directions, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: M/s Renganayaki Agencies vs. Sreenivasa Rao Ravinuthala
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Renganayaki Agencies (Successful Resolution Applicant, KALS Group). Respondent is Sreenivasa Rao Ravinuthala (RP for Samyu Glass Pvt Ltd). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution of the Corporate Debtor (Samyu Glass Pvt Ltd). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not detailed in the judgment as it focuses on plan approval. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT ordered rebidding on 24 February 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC approved the Appellant's Resolution Plan with a 100% voting share. Another applicant secured only 55.58%. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Despite the 100% CoC approval, NCLT Hyderabad directed the CoC to invite fresh bids to maximize value because the difference between the two plans was deemed meager. The Appellant challenged this.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to direct a fresh bidding process for value maximization after a Resolution Plan has been approved by the CoC with a 100% majority?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority cannot direct a fresh bidding process or interfere with the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a Resolution Plan, provided the plan complies with statutory requirements. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30 and 31 limit the Adjudicating Authority's review to statutory compliance. Value maximization is a commercial decision falling exclusively within the CoC's domain. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the Supreme Court's ruling in Kalpraj Dharamshi, confirming the supremacy of the CoC's commercial wisdom. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench struck down the NCLT's rebidding order, ruling it acted in excess of jurisdiction by interfering with the CoC's conscious commercial decision.
operative_order: The instant Comp App (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 23/2021 is allowed. No costs. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to approve the Resolution Plan approved by the Committee of Creditors with 100% voting in favour of KALS Group. I.A. applications are closed.
summary: Renganayaki Agencies (KALS Group) appealed an NCLT order that directed the CoC to invite fresh bids for Samyu Glass Pvt Ltd to maximize value, despite the CoC having already approved the Appellant's resolution plan with a 100% voting majority. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, relying on Supreme Court precedents which establish that the commercial wisdom of the CoC is paramount and non-justiciable. The NCLAT held that the NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction by demanding a rebid solely for value maximization, and directed the NCLT to approve the CoC-endorsed resolution plan.

case_title: Centrum Financial Services Ltd. vs. CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Centrum Financial Services Ltd. (Financial Creditor). Corporate Debtor is Sri Aranath Logistics Limited. Respondent 1 is CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim by a financial creditor against the corporate debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified debt amount. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 8 November 2019. 90-day claim deadline was 6 February 2020. Claim was filed 37 days late on 7 April 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant's claim was delayed beyond the 90-day statutory limit. The new RP rejected the claim on 9 October 2020 due to delay. A resolution plan was already formulated and pending before the CoC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an application before NCLT Kolkata to condone the delay, which was scheduled for hearing on 28 April 2021 (after the CIRP expiry date of 16 April 2021). Appellant appealed to NCLAT for urgent intervention.
legal_issues: Whether a delay in filing a claim by a financial creditor beyond the stipulated 90-day period should be condoned by the Appellate Tribunal to prevent the exclusion of the creditor from the CoC?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The IBC is a time-bound process, and strict adherence to statutory timelines for filing claims is essential to prevent destructive delays in the resolution process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 12(2) specifically restricts the submission of claims beyond 90 days from the insolvency commencement date, overriding previous flexible provisions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed the appellant had knowledge of the CIRP from the beginning and failed to file the claim before the pre-Covid deadline of February 2020. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT declined to intervene, noting that entertaining the late claim would further delay an already prolonged CIRP, though it left the NCLT free to decide the pending application independently.
operative_order: In the facts and circumstances of the present matter, we decline to entertain the Appeal. The Appeal is dismissed.
summary: Centrum Financial Services appealed to the NCLAT over the Resolution Professional's rejection of its delayed financial claim against Sri Aranath Logistics. The appellant had submitted its claim 37 days after the 90-day statutory deadline had passed. The NCLAT emphasized the time-bound nature of the IBC and noted that the appellant was aware of the CIRP but failed to act before the deadline, which preceded the Covid-19 lockdowns. Refusing to cause further delays to the resolution process, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal but left the NCLT free to rule on the pending condonation application.

case_title: The Directorate of Enforcement vs. Manoj Kumar Agarwal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Directorate of Enforcement (ED). Respondents are Resolution Professionals for Corporate Debtors Sterling SEZ & Infrastructure Ltd and Sterling International Enterprises Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CBI registered FIR against Sterling Biotech Ltd and promoters for bank fraud. ED provisionally attached properties of the Corporate Debtors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged fraud turning loan into NPA. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Provisional attachment order issued 29.05.2018. CIRP admitted 16.07.2018. PMLA attachment confirmed 20.11.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Attached assets were purchased prior to the alleged offenses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai directed the release of attached properties, holding the attachment a nullity under IBC Sec 14 and 238. ED appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority under IBC has jurisdiction to quash provisional attachment orders passed under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), and whether IBC overrides PMLA attachments during CIRP?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Properties of a Corporate Debtor attached under PMLA prior to or during CIRP must become available to the Resolution Professional to fulfill the objects of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 (moratorium) applies to PMLA adjudication proceedings because they are civil in nature. Section 238 overrides conflicting provisions in PMLA. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that PMLA attachments would hinder the CIRP's time-bound value maximization process. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the NCLT's order releasing the attachments, dismissing ED's appeals.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 575 of 2019 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 576 of 2019 are dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: The Directorate of Enforcement appealed NCLT orders that released the Corporate Debtors' properties from PMLA attachments. The NCLAT held that PMLA adjudication proceedings are civil and hit by the IBC Section 14 moratorium. Furthermore, Section 238 of IBC overrides PMLA, ensuring that attached properties are available for the CIRP to achieve value maximization. The appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Brillio Technologies Pvt. Ltd. vs. Registrar Of Companies & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Brillio Technologies Pvt. Ltd. Respondents are Registrar of Companies, Karnataka and Regional Director, South Eastern Region. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Reduction of equity share capital by paying off non-promoter shareholders from the Securities Premium Account. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board resolved to reduce capital on 24.01.2019. EGM passed special resolution on 04.02.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: 100% members voted for reduction. Notices served to 186 unsecured creditors with no objections received within 3 months. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the Section 66 petition, holding selective reduction using Securities Premium Account must fall under Sec 230-232, not Sec 66. Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a company can selectively reduce its share capital using its Securities Premium Account under Section 66 of the Companies Act without resorting to a scheme of compromise/arrangement under Sections 230-232?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A company can selectively reduce its share capital and utilize its Securities Premium Account for paying off non-promoter shareholders under Section 66 of the Companies Act, provided fair value is paid and creditors are not prejudiced. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66 permits reduction 'in any manner', encompassing selective reduction. Securities Premium Account is treated as paid-up capital under Section 52 and can be reduced following Section 66 procedures. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tribunal noted notices were served to creditors without objection, and non-promoter shareholders were being paid a premium. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench set aside the NCLT order, confirming the reduction of share capital under Section 66.
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed. The impugned order passed by the Tribunal is set aside. The reduction of equity share capital resolved on 04.02.2019 is confirmed.
summary: Brillio Technologies appealed against the NCLT's dismissal of its petition to selectively reduce its share capital by paying off non-promoter shareholders using its Securities Premium Account. The NCLAT held that Section 66 of the Companies Act permits selective reduction 'in any manner'. It further clarified that the Securities Premium Account can be utilized for this purpose under Section 52. Since no creditors objected and fair value was being paid, the NCLAT allowed the appeal and confirmed the capital reduction.

case_title: Pradeep Kumar Sekar vs. Solar Semiconductor Energy Systems (India) Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Pradeep Kumar Sekar (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor). First Respondent is Solar Semiconductor Energy Systems (Corporate Debtor). Second Respondent is Orix Leasing and Financial Services India Limited (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial Creditor entered into a Lease Agreement dated 03.04.2017 to provide lease finance assistance for furniture and fixtures. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default sum claimed was Rs. 1,16,98,242.60. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Disbursals made in April and November 2017. Section 7 application admitted by NCLT on 19.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease agreement required 36 monthly rentals, after which the asset would be purchased by the Corporate Debtor. Demand notice was issued. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad admitted the Section 7 petition. Suspended director appealed arguing the lease was not a financial lease.
legal_issues: Whether the lease agreement for furniture and fixtures constituted a 'financial lease' under Section 5(8)(d) of the IBC, qualifying the lessor as a Financial Creditor?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A lease agreement structured as lease finance assistance with a predefined repayment schedule and an option for the lessee to purchase the asset at the end of the term qualifies as a 'financial lease' imparting the time value of money. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Such a transaction falls within the ambit of 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, distinguishing it from an operational debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tribunal analyzed the lease terms, noting the capital disbursal to the manufacturer and the residual value purchase option, indicating a financial lease. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the NCLT's admission of the Section 7 application, confirming the debt was financial in nature.
operative_order: The instant Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 2/2021 is dismissed, but without costs.
summary: The suspended director of Solar Semiconductor appealed the NCLT's admission of a Section 7 application filed by Orix Leasing. The appellant contended the lease for furniture and fixtures was an operational lease, not a financial debt. The NCLAT examined the lease terms, noting it involved lease finance assistance with a 36-month repayment schedule and a residual purchase option, which satisfied the 'time value of money' requirement. Concluding it was a financial lease under Section 5(8) of the IBC, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal and upheld the CIRP initiation.

case_title: Neeta Shrinivas Zanvar & Anr. vs. Nagarjuna Agro Chemicals Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Neeta Shrinivas Zanvar & Anr. Respondents are Nagarjuna Agro Chemicals Pvt Ltd and its directors (Respondent No. 2 to 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Disputes between two family groups jointly managing a quasi-partnership company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Allegations of siphoning off funds amounting to Rs. 55,99,68,131 by Respondent No. 2. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board resolution passed on 19.11.2019 to change bank operation mandate. NCLT passed interim order on 05.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Both factions alleged mismanagement and siphoning of funds against each other. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad passed an interim order directing joint operation of bank accounts and directed the Registrar of Companies to investigate the company's affairs. Appellants challenged this order.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has the statutory power to direct the Registrar of Companies to conduct an investigation into the affairs of a company under Sections 210 and 213 of the Companies Act, 2013?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The NCLT can direct an investigation into a company's affairs only by ordering the Central Government to appoint inspectors under Sections 210 and 213, not by directly assigning the investigation to the Registrar of Companies. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 206 and 207 vest inspection and inquiry powers with the ROC, whereas the power of investigation strictly lies with the Central Government under Sections 210-213. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tribunal noted NCLT failed to record sufficient 'satisfaction' or 'good reasons' required under Section 213. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's direction to the ROC for investigation, while modifying the bank operation directive to include a weekly transaction report.
operative_order: The Appeal is partly allowed. The directions of the NCLT regarding investigation by the ROC are set aside. A weekly report of all transactions over Rs. 1000 from all bank accounts must be circulated to all directors.
summary: In a dispute between two promoter groups of Nagarjuna Agro Chemicals, the NCLT directed the Registrar of Companies to investigate the company's affairs and ordered joint operation of bank accounts. The NCLAT partially allowed the appeal, holding that under Sections 210 and 213 of the Companies Act, 2013, the NCLT can only direct the Central Government to conduct an investigation, not the ROC directly. The NCLAT set aside the investigation directive but maintained interim measures to prevent siphoning of funds by ordering weekly transaction reporting to all directors.

case_title: Amit Suresh Bhatnagar vs. Bhuvan Madan
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Amit Suresh Bhatnagar (Suspended Director of Diamond Power Infrastructure Ltd). Respondent is Bhuvan Madan (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of Diamond Power Infrastructure Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (Procedural irregularity in CIRP). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced 24.08.2018. CoC meetings held in October/November 2019 resulting in liquidation resolution. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP failed to provide notice to one suspended director and gave less than 24 hours' notice to the Appellant. RP refused to provide video conferencing links and copies of resolution plans to the Appellant. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the Appellant's application challenging the RP's actions, citing bail conditions that were actually modified earlier. Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the failure of the Resolution Professional to provide adequate notice, video conferencing options, and copies of resolution plans to suspended directors invalidates the CoC meetings and subsequent resolutions?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Suspended directors have a statutory right to receive at least five days' notice, video conferencing links, and copies of resolution plans for CoC meetings; failure to provide these constitutes material irregularity invalidating the proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 24(3)(b) of IBC and CIRP Regulations 19, 21, and 23 strictly mandate the RP to facilitate the participation of suspended management. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tribunal observed the RP acted arbitrarily by citing lack of legal clarity to deny video conferencing despite having a favorable legal opinion on record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT set aside the NCLT order and the resolutions passed in the 9th, 10th, and 11th CoC meetings due to procedural violations.
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed. The Impugned order as well as the Resolutions passed in 9th, 10th, and 11th CoC meetings are set aside. The RP is directed to provide all relevant documents to the suspended directors and call fresh meetings with proper notice and video conferencing options.
summary: The suspended director appealed against the NCLT's dismissal of his application challenging the Resolution Professional's conduct during the CIRP. The NCLAT found that the RP committed material irregularities by failing to serve proper notice of CoC meetings to the suspended directors, refusing video conferencing access, and denying them copies of resolution plans, violating Section 24 of the IBC and CIRP Regulations. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT order and nullified the CoC resolutions (including the liquidation resolution) passed in the flawed meetings, directing the RP to conduct fresh proceedings compliantly.

case_title: Sanjay Lamba vs. Union Bank Of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sanjay Lamba (Ex-Managing Director of Sainov Spirits Pvt Ltd). Respondent 1 is Union Bank of India (Financial Creditor). Respondent 2 is Pawan Trivedi (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Cash credit, term loan, and working capital limits taken from the bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount is Rs. 70,34,19,678.23. Account declared NPA on 30.09.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition filed on 22.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor acknowledged debt via revival letters on 21.06.2017, proposed OTS in 2019, and made part payments of Rs. 8.28 Crores between May and July 2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 7 petition. Appellant appealed, arguing the petition was time-barred since it was filed more than 3 years after the NPA date.
legal_issues: Whether written acknowledgments of debt and part payments extend the three-year limitation period for filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgment of liability in writing or a part payment made before the expiration of the limitation period initiates a fresh period of limitation under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: By virtue of Section 238A of the IBC, Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act apply to IBC proceedings, thereby allowing the extension of the limitation period beyond three years from the original date of default (NPA date). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tribunal noted the 2017 revival letter and 2019 part payments constituted valid acknowledgments resetting the limitation clock. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the NCLT's admission, concluding the Section 7 application filed in November 2019 was well within the extended limitation period.
operative_order: The appeal deserves to be dismissed and is dismissed. Pending application, if any, stands disposed of. No order as to costs.
summary: Sanjay Lamba, ex-managing director of Sainov Spirits, appealed the NCLT's admission of a Section 7 application by Union Bank of India, claiming it was barred by limitation since the NPA date was September 2016 and the petition was filed in November 2019. The NCLAT applied the Supreme Court's rulings confirming that Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act apply to the IBC. Noting that the corporate debtor had acknowledged the debt in 2017 and made part payments in 2019, the NCLAT ruled that a fresh period of limitation had commenced. The appeal was dismissed, upholding the CIRP.

case_title: Sunil Parmanand Kewalramani vs. Kestrel Import & Export Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Sunil Parmanand Kewalramani and family members. Respondents are Kestrel Import & Export Pvt Ltd, Modlite Holdings Pvt Ltd, and Urban Sanctuaries Developers Pvt Ltd (Family-owned companies). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants allegedly advanced loans/quasi-capital to the respondent family companies. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Demanded repayment in 2017; respondents lacked funds. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petitions dismissed by NCLT on 30.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT dismissed the petitions holding the funds were quasi-capital, not financial debt. NCLT also remarked that the appellants colluded with family members to issue and reply to demand notices. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed appeals to expunge the NCLT's remarks of 'unlawful collusion'. Respondents filed cross-appeals seeking penal action under Sections 65, 72, and 75 against the appellants.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in making observations of 'unlawful collusion' and 'malicious intent' against the Petitioners without sufficient evidence, and whether penalties under Sections 65, 72, and 75 of IBC were warranted?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Adverse remarks of collusion or malicious intent cannot be recorded by a tribunal based solely on unsubstantiated suspicion or familial relationships without affording the parties an opportunity to be heard. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Dismissal of a Section 7 petition because the debt is deemed quasi-capital rather than 'financial debt' does not automatically imply the petition was filed with malicious intent under Section 65. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that issuing a demand notice under Section 7 is not even a legal requirement, thus doing so within a family context does not prove sinister collusion. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT expunged the adverse remarks against the appellants and dismissed the cross-appeals seeking penal action.
operative_order: The Appeal Nos. 847, 848 and 853 of 2020 are allowed. We expunge the remarks/observations in para 18 and 19 of the impugned judgements. Cross Appeal Nos 1016, 1018 and 1019 of 2020 sans merit hence dismissed.
summary: The appellants challenged NCLT orders dismissing their Section 7 petitions against family-owned companies, specifically seeking to expunge adverse remarks of 'unlawful collusion' and 'malicious intent'. The respondents filed cross-appeals demanding penal action against the appellants under IBC Sections 65, 72, and 75. The NCLAT held that the NCLT's remarks were based on mere suspicion and misunderstanding of family dynamics rather than evidence. Finding that dismissing a petition because the debt was quasi-capital does not equate to malicious intent, the NCLAT allowed the appeals to expunge the remarks and dismissed the cross-appeals.

case_title: AKJ Fincap Limited vs. Bank of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is AKJ Fincap Limited (Corporate Debtor). Respondent is Bank of India (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial debt owed to the bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Ex-parte order passed against Corporate Debtor on 18.03.2020. Application to set aside ex-parte order dismissed on 09.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: First notice returned due to 'insufficient address'. Fresh notice served via email. NCLT had issued a general notice suspending hearings from 16.03.2020 to 27.03.2020 due to COVID-19, except for urgent matters. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati proceeded ex-parte on 18.03.2020 and later dismissed the Corporate Debtor's application to set it aside, stating it had no power to review an admission order. Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the power under Rule 49(2) of the NCLT Rules to set aside an ex-parte order, and whether proceeding ex-parte during a declared COVID-19 suspension period violated principles of natural justice?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses the power under Rule 49(2) of the NCLT Rules to set aside an ex-parte order if satisfied that there was sufficient cause preventing the party's appearance. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An order setting a party ex-parte is an interim procedural order, not a final admission order under Section 7, and is thus subject to recall under Rule 49(2). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tribunal noted the ex-parte order coincided with the NCLT's own notification suspending regular hearings due to the pandemic, justifying the appellant's non-appearance. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT set aside the ex-parte order and remanded the matter, allowing the appellant to participate upon payment of costs.
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed and the Order of the Adjudicating Authority is set aside. Both parties are directed to appear before the Adjudicating Authority on 26th April 2021, subject to payment of Rs. 25,000 costs by the Appellant.
summary: AKJ Fincap appealed an NCLT order that refused to set aside an ex-parte proceeding against it in a Section 7 application filed by Bank of India. The NCLT had incorrectly reasoned it lacked the power to review an 'admission' order. The NCLAT clarified that the order was merely setting the party ex-parte, which can be recalled under Rule 49(2) of the NCLT Rules. Given that the ex-parte order was passed on 18.03.2020, during a period when the NCLT had suspended regular hearings due to COVID-19, the NCLAT set aside the ex-parte order to uphold natural justice, subject to costs, and remanded the matter.

case_title: SRLK Enterprises LLP vs. JALAN Transolutions (India) Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is SRLK Enterprises LLP (Financial Creditor). Respondent is JALAN Transolutions (India) Ltd (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debt settlement resulting in withdrawal of Section 7 petition. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor issued 27 post-dated cheques in settlement, but only 4 were honored. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP originally terminated on 09.05.2019 upon withdrawal. Application to recall withdrawal filed later and dismissed on 26.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The settlement deed was executed outside the Tribunal. The withdrawal order did not grant the creditor liberty to revive the petition in case of default on the settlement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi rejected the application to recall the withdrawal order, stating no liberty to revive was granted. Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 insolvency petition can be revived upon the breach of a settlement agreement if the withdrawal order was a simpliciter withdrawal without granting liberty to revive the proceedings?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency petition cannot be revived upon a breach of settlement if the prior withdrawal order was a simpliciter withdrawal without the Tribunal explicitly granting liberty to restore the proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The IBC is not a debt recovery mechanism. Parties cannot repeatedly approach the Adjudicating Authority to enforce private settlement defaults unless specifically permitted by the withdrawal order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tribunal examined the order dated 09.05.2019 and confirmed no liberty was reserved by the creditor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the NCLT's refusal to recall the withdrawal order, directing the appellant to pursue other legal remedies.
operative_order: We do not find any substance in the Appeal to entertain the Appeal. The Appeal is dismissed.
summary: SRLK Enterprises appealed the NCLT's refusal to recall an order that terminated a CIRP against JALAN Transolutions. The CIRP had been previously withdrawn based on a private settlement involving post-dated cheques, most of which subsequently bounced. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision, emphasizing that the withdrawal was a 'simpliciter' withdrawal without any recorded liberty to revive the petition in case of default. Noting that the IBC is not a recovery forum, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal, leaving the creditor to seek alternative legal remedies.

case_title: Mr. Ambika Prasad Sharma vs Horizon Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Financial Creditor is Mr. R. Tarkeshwar Narayanan, a home buyer, and the Corporate Debtor is Horizon Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. (HBPL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An Apartment Buyer Agreement was executed on 14.02.2014 for a flat in the IRIDIA project, where Horizon Concept Private Limited (HCPL) acted as the marketing arm of HBPL. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The home buyer paid Rs. 32,34,108 out of a total consideration of Rs. 49,76,500, but possession was not delivered within the stipulated 36 months by 14.02.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against HCPL was initiated previously and withdrawn; no Section 8 notices were applicable as this was a Section 7 petition. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Core evidence included the Collaboration Agreement dated 28.08.2012, Marketing Agreement dated 06.07.2013, and the Apartment Buyer Agreement establishing HBPL as the developer and HCPL as its agent. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The original Section 7 petition (IB) No. 266/ND/2019 was admitted by the NCLT New Delhi Bench on 08.11.2019.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Flat Buyer is a Financial Creditor vis-a-vis HBPL. 2. Whether HBPL falls within the ambit of the definition of Corporate Debtor, as defined under Section 3(8) of the Code.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity acting as a principal is liable as a Corporate Debtor for funds collected by its marketing agent on its behalf. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Amounts paid by home buyers to a developer's agent fall within the definition of Financial Debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC, as it carries the essential elements of disbursal and consideration for time value of money. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court evaluated the agency relationship under Section 182 of the Indian Contract Act and the covenants of the real estate agreements, concluding the marketing arm had express consent to act on the developer's behalf. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: HBPL is the Corporate Debtor and the home buyer is a Financial Creditor because the amounts were collected by HCPL for and on behalf of HBPL.
operative_order: The NCLAT concurred with the finding of the NCLT admitting the Section 7 application against HBPL and dismissed the appeal. However, the bench directed that the CIRP should be Project-based and confined strictly to the subject Project (IRIDIA). No order as to costs was passed.
summary: The home buyer (Financial Creditor) filed a Section 7 application against the developer, Horizon Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. (HBPL), which was admitted by the NCLT. The appellant argued that the buyer paid money directly to HCPL, a marketing arm, thus there was no privity of contract or financial debt with HBPL. The NCLAT held that HCPL acted merely as an agent for HBPL, the principal developer, meaning the financial debt was indeed owed by HBPL. The tribunal upheld the NCLT's admission of CIRP but directed that the resolution process be confined only to the specific IRIDIA real estate project.

case_title: New Okhla Industrial Development Authority vs Mr. Anand Sonbhadra
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA). Respondent is Anand Sonbhadra, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Shubhkamna Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: NOIDA leased a plot of land to the Corporate Debtor for 90 years via a lease deed dated 30.07.2010 for developing a residential complex. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding dues claimed against the lease of the plot amounted to Rs. 99,32,55,183. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor was required to pay the upfront premium in 16 half-yearly instalments from 11.09.2010 till 11.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NOIDA initially submitted Form B as an Operational Creditor and later filed Form C seeking Financial Creditor status based on the lease deed and Indian Accounting Standards. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NOIDA filed CA 257/ND/2019 seeking Financial Creditor status, which was rejected by NCLT New Delhi on 30.09.2019.
legal_issues: Whether the lease of land granted by NOIDA to the Corporate Debtor qualifies as a 'financial lease' under Indian Accounting Standards and constitutes a 'Financial Debt' under Section 5(8)(d) or 5(8)(f) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A lease of land by a development authority cannot be treated as a financial lease if it does not transfer substantially all risks and rewards incidental to ownership. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(d) requires the lease to be deemed a finance or capital lease under Indian Accounting Standards. Since NOIDA retained significant control and ownership rights over the land, it did not meet the criteria. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluated the lease deed clauses against paragraphs 61-67 of the Indian Accounting Standards, finding no bargain purchase option or transfer of ownership. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The lease deed does not fit the requirements of a financial lease or have the commercial effect of a borrowing; thus, NOIDA is not a Financial Creditor.
operative_order: The NCLAT found no substance in the appeal and dismissed it without costs, upholding the NCLT's decision.
summary: NOIDA appealed the NCLT's refusal to classify it as a Financial Creditor for a 90-year land lease granted to the Corporate Debtor. The NCLAT analyzed the lease deed against Indian Accounting Standards and held that it did not transfer substantially all risks and rewards of ownership to the lessee. Consequently, the transaction was not a financial lease under Section 5(8)(d) of the IBC, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Mr Joseph Jayananda vs Navalmar (UK) Ltd & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Navalmar (UK) Ltd; Corporate Debtor is Navalmar Shipping (India) Pvt Ltd. Appellant is Joseph Jayananda, a suspended director of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under a General Agency Agreement dated 31.08.2003, the Corporate Debtor was appointed as an agent for booking cargo and collecting freight in India for the Operational Creditor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The claimed debt included USD 1,766.09 (freight collections), USD 61,119.45 (yacht payment), and other advances totalling USD 2,53,591.50 and USD 13,38,807.80. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Operational Creditor terminated the agreement on 05.09.2018 and issued a Section 8 demand notice on 12.06.2019. Corporate Debtor replied on 01.07.2019 admitting parts of the debt. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: General Agency Agreement, email acknowledgment dated 23.10.2018, and audited balance sheets for FY ending 31.03.2018 showing trade payables. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru admitted the Section 9 petition on 29.05.2020.
legal_issues: 1. Whether advance payments made by the Operational Creditor for future services constituted an Operational Debt. 2. Whether the debt was barred by limitation. 3. Whether there was a pre-existing dispute.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Advance payments made for the provision of future services under an agency agreement constitute Operational Debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpreted Section 5(21) to include advances for services, distinguishing it from Financial Debt per the Supreme Court's Pioneer Urban Land judgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applied to audited balance sheets and email communications, constituting valid acknowledgments extending limitation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was an Operational Debt, within limitation due to continuous acknowledgment, and there was no pre-existing dispute.
operative_order: The NCLAT found no reason to interfere with the NCLT's admission order and dismissed the appeal with no order as to costs.
summary: A suspended director of the Corporate Debtor appealed the admission of a Section 9 CIRP petition, arguing the debt was not an operational debt and was time-barred. The NCLAT held that advance payments for future services under an agency agreement qualify as operational debt. Furthermore, the debt was not time-barred due to continuous acknowledgments in the Corporate Debtor's balance sheets and emails, leading to the dismissal of the appeal.

case_title: Ambuja Cements Limited vs NA
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ambuja Cements Limited (Amalgamated/Transferee Company), holding 100% shares of DIRK India Pvt. Ltd. (Amalgamating/Transferor Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Scheme of Merger was approved by the Board of Directors on 11.10.2019 to amalgamate the wholly-owned subsidiary into the parent company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There was no default; Appellant's net worth post-merger is Rs. 22,714.77 crores, with zero secured creditors and unsecured trade creditors worth Rs. 1,108 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Transferor Company obtained an order dispensing with its meetings from NCLT Mumbai on 12.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Scheme showed no issuance of new shares, no dilution of shareholding, and all liabilities of the subsidiary assumed by the parent company. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CA (CAA) 50 of 2020 before NCLT Ahmedabad for dispensing with shareholder and creditor meetings, rejected on 10.12.2020 due to lack of written consent affidavits.
legal_issues: Whether a Transferee Company that is a 100% holding company of the Transferor Company is required to hold meetings of its equity shareholders and creditors for a merger, when there is no reorganization of share capital or compromise with creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a merger between a wholly-owned subsidiary and its holding company where no new shares are issued and the net worth remains highly positive, meetings of shareholders and creditors of the transferee company can be dispensed with. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 230-232, if an arrangement does not affect the rights of members or creditors, a rigid requirement for consent affidavits can be relaxed. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tribunal noted the highly positive net worth and absence of any compromise affecting creditors' rights, following the Bombay High Court in Mahaamba Investments Ltd. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in ignoring judicial precedents by insisting on written affidavits when the scheme clearly did not prejudice stakeholders.
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the NCLT Ahmedabad's order dated 10.12.2020, dispensed with the meetings of the equity shareholders, secured, and unsecured creditors of the Appellant Company, and remanded the matter to the NCLT for further consideration.
summary: Ambuja Cements appealed an NCLT order that refused to dispense with meetings of its shareholders and creditors regarding the merger of its 100% subsidiary, DIRK India Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT held that since no new shares were being issued, no creditor rights were compromised, and the parent company had a highly positive net worth, the meetings were unnecessary. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's order, emphasizing adherence to judicial precedents.

case_title: Mr. Sumat Gupta (Resolution Professional) vs Sh. RD Sharma & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sumat Gupta, Resolution Professional for Corporate Debtor Agro Dutch Industries Limited. Respondents are RD Sharma and Mars Envirotech Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Mars Envirotech Limited purchased a plot of land adjacent to the Corporate Debtor's plant on 09.10.2015 from the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor was in CIRP, and the RP claimed the Respondents broke a wall to use the Corporate Debtor's premises for access. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 27.11.2019; RP appointed on 25.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The registered sale deed dated 09.10.2015 explicitly mentioned a common road having a width of 26 ft. 10 inches on the south side of the plot. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 234/2020 before NCLT Chandigarh to prevent trespass, but NCLT on 22.09.2020 directed that the Respondents' use of the common road could not be objected to unless the sale deed was invalidated.
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional could restrict the Respondents from using a common passage during the moratorium period under Section 14 of the IBC, despite the registered sale deed indicating its existence.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional cannot unilaterally restrict access rights granted via a registered sale deed without having the deed legally invalidated. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 moratorium protects the Corporate Debtor's assets but does not automatically extinguish third-party easement or access rights explicitly documented in pre-CIRP registered instruments. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Adjudicating Authority correctly relied on the registered sale deed and Schedule-1 which clearly showed the existence of the common road. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT's finding that the usage of the common road by the Respondent cannot be objected to (provided they do not cause disturbance) was affirmed as legally sound.
operative_order: The NCLAT affirmed the findings of the NCLT and dismissed the appeal as devoid of merit, with no order as to costs.
summary: The Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor appealed an NCLT order that allowed a neighboring entity (Respondent) to use a common road traversing the Corporate Debtor's property. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that since the Respondent's registered sale deed from 2015 explicitly included the right to the common road, the RP could not unilaterally block access under the guise of IBC moratorium provisions without having the deed legally invalidated.

case_title: Tek Travels Private Limited vs Altius Travels Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Tek Travels Private Limited (Operational Creditor); Respondent is Altius Travels Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational Creditor sought to initiate CIRP for recovery of an operational debt based on business transactions. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt recovery dispute, specific default amount not central to the procedural rejection. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Application was filed in 2019 relying on a Board Resolution passed in 2013. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The application included a Board Resolution/Authorization from 2013, predating the IBC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: On 13.12.2019, NCLT Ahmedabad rejected the Section 9 application on maintainability grounds because the authorization was from 2013, without giving time to rectify the defect.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an authorization letter issued prior to the enactment of the IBC can be treated as a valid authorization for filing a Section 9 petition. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority must grant 7 days to rectify the defect under the proviso to Section 9(5)(ii)(a) instead of outright dismissal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for CIRP cannot be dismissed outright for a curable defect, such as an older authorization, without first granting the applicant the statutory 7-day period to rectify it. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Proviso to Section 9(5)(ii)(a) mandates that before rejecting an incomplete application, the Adjudicating Authority must give notice to rectify the defect within seven days. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on precedents (Surendra Trading, Palogics Infrastructure), a general power of attorney or authorization from before 2016 remains valid for IBC proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in dismissing the petition on maintainability for a 2013 authorization without providing an opportunity to cure the defect.
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's dismissal order and allowed the appeal, directing the Adjudicating Authority to decide the application afresh at the earliest.
summary: The Operational Creditor's Section 9 petition was dismissed by the NCLT solely because the board resolution authorizing the filing was from 2013, before the IBC existed. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, ruling that pre-IBC general authorizations are valid and that, statutorily, the NCLT must grant a 7-day notice period to rectify such defects rather than outright dismissing the petition.

case_title: Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner vs Laxman Digambar Pawar
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner (EPFO). Respondent is Laxman Digambar Pawar, Liquidator of Infinity Fab Engineering Co. Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: EPFO claimed statutory PF dues from the Corporate Debtor, undergoing liquidation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default centered on the timeline of appealing the NCLT order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned NCLT order was passed on 22.11.2019. Appellant filed appeal with a 15-day delay beyond the 30-day period from the date of claimed knowledge. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant admitted via their 'List of Dates and Events' that they had knowledge of the CIRP admission as early as 07.09.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IA No. 72 of 2021 was filed to condone a 15-day delay in filing the appeal against the NCLT Bengaluru's order dated 22.11.2019.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal has the jurisdiction to condone a delay beyond the statutory maximum of 45 days (30 days + 15 days extension) under Section 61 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Appellate Tribunal under the IBC has no power to condone any delay in filing an appeal beyond the strict statutory limit of 45 days. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC is a special law and strictly limits condonation of delay to 15 days beyond the 30-day appeal period. Supreme Court's Suo Motu Covid-19 extension did not apply as the order was from November 2019. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on Mobilox Innovations and Glaxo Smith Kline cases, the limitation is mandatory and uncondonable beyond the absolute ceiling. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The delay application was not maintainable because it fell outside the maximum permissible 45-day window from the date of the order/knowledge.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed IA No. 72 of 2021 (Application for Condonation of Delay) without costs, and consequently rejected the main appeal Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 31 of 2021.
summary: The Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner appealed an NCLT order passed in November 2019, seeking condonation of delay by citing the COVID-19 lockdown and claiming late knowledge. The NCLAT rejected the application and the appeal, enforcing the strict interpretation of Section 61 of the IBC that bars any condonation of delay beyond the absolute maximum period of 45 days.

case_title: Ministry of Corporate Affairs vs Amit Chandrakant Shah & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. Respondent 1 is Amit Chandrakant Shah (RP of BCIL Red Earth Developers India Pvt Ltd). Respondents 2-6 are related parties/directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor allegedly wrote off receivables amounting to Rs. 1,25,45,046 from Respondent 4. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Fraudulent/wrongful trading alleged to the tune of Rs. 1.25 crores written off. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RP filed an application under Section 66 of IBC. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP presented a Review Report by a Chartered Accountant indicating potential fraudulent write-offs. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru on 09.08.2019 directed the Central Government to refer the matter directly to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) for investigation.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority under the IBC has the jurisdiction to directly order the Central Government to refer a matter to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) without following the procedure under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority cannot bypass statutory procedures and directly order an SFIO investigation; it must refer the matter to the Central Government to initiate the process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 213(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires the Central Government to form an opinion and follow natural justice before directing an investigation by its Inspectors or the SFIO. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following the precedent in Mr. Lagadapati Ramesh vs Mrs. Ramanathan Bhuvaneshwari, NCLT must give notice to parties and refer it to the Central Government, who then decides the appropriate investigative body. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in directly mandating an SFIO probe instead of directing the Central Government to adopt the procedure under Section 213(b).
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal and modified the NCLT's order, directing the Central Government to adopt the procedure under Section 213(b) of the Companies Act, 2013, and directed the RP to recall the matter sent directly to the SFIO.
summary: The Ministry of Corporate Affairs appealed an NCLT order that directly mandated the Central Government to refer the Corporate Debtor's fraudulent activities to the SFIO. The NCLAT modified the order, holding that under Section 213 of the Companies Act, the NCLT can only refer the matter to the Central Government, which must then follow due procedure to decide whether an SFIO investigation is warranted.

case_title: Mr. Thomas George vs Union Bank of India & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Thomas George, suspended director of Mathstraman Manufacturers and Traders Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondent is Union Bank of India (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facilities granted to the Corporate Debtor by the erstwhile Corporation Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The account was declared a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 31.12.2010. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application was filed on 06.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Financial Creditor produced OTS proposals dated 05.01.2012, 10.07.2014, and 09.08.2014, plus a balance sheet approved on 18.01.2017 acknowledging the debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi admitted the Section 7 application on 20.11.2020, relying on SARFAESI/DRT proceedings to hold it within limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the application under Section 7 filed in 2020 for a debt declared NPA in 2010 was barred by the 3-year limitation period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Continuous acknowledgments of debt in writing before the expiration of the limitation period provide a fresh period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to IBC proceedings. Balance sheets and OTS proposals constitute valid acknowledgments of a subsisting liability. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on Sesh Nath Singh, the court held that the series of OTS proposals and the 2014-15 balance sheet approved in 2017 effectively extended the limitation period. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was not barred by limitation because the Corporate Debtor continuously acknowledged the debt.
operative_order: The NCLAT found no substance in the appeal and dismissed it with no order as to costs, upholding the admission of the Corporate Debtor into CIRP.
summary: The suspended director of the Corporate Debtor appealed the admission of a Section 7 CIRP petition, arguing the debt (NPA since 2010) was time-barred. The NCLAT upheld the admission, citing recent Supreme Court jurisprudence that One Time Settlement (OTS) proposals and audited balance sheets act as valid acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, thereby extending the limitation period.

case_title: SMS Integrated Facility Services Private Limited vs Expat Educational Institute
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is SMS Integrated Facility Services Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor). Respondent is Expat Educational Institute (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational Creditor provided housekeeping services to the Corporate Debtor's institute under various work orders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid invoices from March to December 2017; total debt claimed is Rs. 22,69,778. Date of last invoice was 01.12.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice in Form 3 issued on 12.06.2019. Section 9 application filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence included emails dated 15.11.2017 and 15.07.2020 where the Corporate Debtor admitted the financial crisis and acknowledged the debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru on 23.02.2021 held the petition barred by laches and limitation, noted the Corporate Debtor's non-appearance, and directed the ROC to take action for non-compliance, rather than admitting the petition.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Section 9 application was barred by limitation and laches. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority could decline to admit a valid Section 9 application and instead direct the ROC to strike off the company.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When debt and default are established within the period of limitation, and the Corporate Debtor fails to appear despite valid service of notice, the Adjudicating Authority must admit the insolvency application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The petition filed in 2019 for defaults occurring in 2017 was well within the 3-year limitation period. NCLT has no jurisdiction under Section 9 to arbitrarily refer the matter to the ROC for strike-off instead of adjudicating the insolvency. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on NCLT Rule 49 (Ex parte hearing), since notice was served and the debt acknowledged via email, the NCLT should have proceeded ex parte and admitted the petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT's findings of delay and laches were legally unsustainable, and its directions to the ROC were improper.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the NCLT's order dated 23.02.2021, and directed the Adjudicating Authority to restore the petition and pass an 'order of admission' under Section 9 of the IBC.
summary: The Operational Creditor appealed after the NCLT refused to admit its Section 9 petition for unpaid housekeeping services. Instead of deciding the case, the NCLT claimed it was barred by laches and directed the ROC to investigate the Corporate Debtor. The NCLAT set aside the order, noting the petition was filed well within the 3-year limitation period and the debt was acknowledged. It directed the NCLT to admit the Corporate Debtor into CIRP.

case_title: Decan Value Investors L.P vs Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian & Ors[cite: 11]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Deccan Value Investors L.P., the Successful Resolution Applicant. Respondent No.1 is Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian, RP for Corporate Debtor Amtek Auto Ltd. Respondent No.2 is State Bank of India, Lead Lender for CoC[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Amtek Auto Ltd., wherein the Appellant submitted a Resolution Plan[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant sought to avoid implementing the plan citing non-fulfillment of conditions related to Ace Complex Land[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Resolution Plan was approved by CoC on 07.02.2020, and the NCLT approved it on 09.07.2020[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant claimed that executing a 20-year lease for the Ace Complex Land with prior written consent of the mortgagee (Vistra) was a condition precedent that was ignored[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh approved the plan in IA 225/2020; the Appellant challenged this approval arguing the NCLT went beyond its jurisdiction by waiving the prior consent requirement[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction in approving the Resolution Plan by concluding that the requirement for prior written consent from the mortgagee of the Ace Complex Land was rendered infructuous[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Execution of commercial terms such as a long-term lease stipulated in a Resolution Plan acts as a condition precedent for the effective date/implementation of the plan, not for its approval by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 of the IBC focuses on overall compliance; securing post-approval consents for property leases does not prevent the Adjudicating Authority from approving the plan[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed the RP had already executed the 20-year lease and deemed the Appellant's challenge a frivolous attempt to renege on solemn commitments, noting the Supreme Court's prior warnings against withdrawal[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The execution of the lease was an effective date condition precedent, not an approval condition precedent, and the Adjudicating Authority did not exceed its jurisdiction[cite: 11].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal for lacking merit and being frivolous, imposing costs of Rs. 1 Lakh on the Appellant to be deposited within 15 days[cite: 11].
summary: The successful Resolution Applicant appealed the NCLT's approval of its own Resolution Plan for Amtek Auto Ltd., arguing that a condition requiring prior consent from a mortgagee for a land lease was bypassed[cite: 11]. The NCLAT held that this condition was for the effective implementation of the plan, not a prerequisite for the Adjudicating Authority's approval, and dismissed the appeal with costs as a contumacious attempt to wriggle out of the resolution process[cite: 11].
