case_title: Simran Kaur vs M/s. Haiko Logistics India Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 12]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Simran Kaur, claiming to be a shareholder of the Corporate Debtor, Datawind Innovations Pvt. Ltd. Respondent No.1 is Haiko Logistics India Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational Creditor provided freight forwarding and import services to the Corporate Debtor between August and December 2016[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Pending dues demanded by the Operational Creditor amounted to Rs. 86,07,122[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 sent on 09.05.2018[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor alleged a pre-existing dispute regarding delayed shipments and lost goods, presenting emails and a complaint to the Metropolitan Police in the UK[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh admitted the Section 9 petition on 13.11.2019, initiating CIRP. The Appellant filed this appeal claiming pre-existing disputes were ignored[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether the Appellant, claiming to be a shareholder but failing to provide evidence of her shareholding or authorization to represent the Corporate Debtor, has locus standi to prefer an appeal under Section 61(1) of the IBC[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A person preferring an appeal under Section 61(1) of the IBC must establish their locus standi by proving they are an aggrieved party[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(1) requires the appellant to be a 'person aggrieved' by the order of the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the Appellant failed to provide any documentary proof (like a share certificate) of being a shareholder, and the authorized representative of the Corporate Debtor had chosen not to appeal[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is not maintainable at the threshold due to the Appellant's failure to establish locus standi as an aggrieved party[cite: 12].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal on the grounds of maintainability with no order as to costs, leaving the NCLT's admission order undisturbed[cite: 12].
summary: An individual claiming to be a shareholder of the Corporate Debtor challenged the admission of a Section 9 CIRP petition, alleging that pre-existing disputes regarding delayed and lost freight were ignored[cite: 12]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal at the threshold, holding that the Appellant failed to provide any evidence of her shareholding to establish locus standi under Section 61(1) of the IBC[cite: 12].

case_title: EVO Green Trading Pvt. Ltd. vs Volkswagen Finance Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 13]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is EVO Green Trading Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondent is Volkswagen Finance Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial Creditor filed a Section 7 application for recovery of debts[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed overdue amount was Rs. 74,97,822[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed on 09.01.2020. Notice issued on 11.02.2020[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's counsel repeatedly failed to file a reply and pay costs of Rs. 15,000 imposed on 16.12.2020[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: On 16.02.2021, NCLT New Delhi closed the Corporate Debtor's right to file a reply due to non-compliance. The Corporate Debtor appealed, blaming the previous counsel's professional negligence[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in closing the Corporate Debtor's right to file a reply due to repeated failures and non-compliance with cost orders[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority may close a party's right to file a reply if they persistently fail to adhere to timelines and disregard orders imposing costs[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Timely disposal of IBC applications is paramount; delays attributed to counsel negligence without formal complaints do not mandate leniency[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the Appellant failed to show proof of any formal complaint against the previous counsel to the Bar Council, and also filed the present appeal after the next NCLT hearing date had expired, showing a lack of seriousness[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly exercised its discretion to close the right to reply after multiple unutilized opportunities[cite: 13].
operative_order: The NCLAT affirmed the Impugned Order and dismissed the appeal[cite: 13].
summary: The Corporate Debtor appealed an NCLT order that closed its right to file a reply in a Section 7 proceeding due to repeated delays and failure to pay costs[cite: 13]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting the Appellant's lack of seriousness in pursuing the matter and the absence of any formal complaint against the allegedly negligent former counsel[cite: 13].

case_title: M/s. Micra Systems Pvt. Ltd. vs M/s. Masters India Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 14]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s. Micra Systems Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor). Respondent is M/s. Masters India Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational Creditor was hired in October 2016 to design and develop a GST Portal software solution at Rs. 1 Lakh per person per month[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Pending bills amounted to Rs. 88,37,700[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice sent on 22.05.2019[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor had sent an email on 09.11.2017 alleging incomplete product and service disruption, and legal notices in March/April 2018 raising issues of delay and defective work[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi (Bench-V) rejected the Section 9 application on 29.05.2020 due to the existence of a pre-existing dispute[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether the allegations of defective services and delays raised by the Corporate Debtor in emails and legal notices prior to the Section 8 demand notice constitute a genuine pre-existing dispute under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 9 application must be rejected if there is evidence of a pre-existing dispute regarding the quality of goods or services communicated prior to the demand notice[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Relying on the Mobilox Innovations judgment, the Adjudicating Authority must only ensure that a dispute truly exists in fact and is not a spurious defense; it does not need to examine the merits of the dispute[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Emails from November 2017 and legal notices from early 2018 clearly established that the Corporate Debtor had raised grievances regarding service disruption, delays, and incomplete software long before the Section 8 notice[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The existence of a genuine pre-existing dispute bars the initiation of CIRP under Section 9[cite: 14].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, finding no reason to interfere with the NCLT's rejection order, with no order as to costs[cite: 14].
summary: The Operational Creditor appealed the rejection of its Section 9 application for unpaid software development invoices. The NCLAT upheld the rejection, confirming that emails and legal notices sent by the Corporate Debtor months before the statutory demand notice—complaining of incomplete products and service disruptions—constituted a valid pre-existing dispute[cite: 14].

case_title: K G Somani & Co vs Arvind Garg[cite: 15]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is K G Somani & Co (Forensic Auditor). Respondent is Arvind Garg, Liquidator of Carnation Auto India Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 15] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant was initially appointed by Punjab National Bank to conduct a forensic audit of the Corporate Debtor prior to CIRP[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed Rs. 5,31,000 in fees for forensic audit services allegedly continued during the CIRP[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 25.09.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant produced emails showing PNB negotiated fees and marked copies to the IRP, but produced no formal engagement letter or CoC resolution confirming their appointment by the IRP[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi rejected the IA on 09.02.2021, refusing to direct the Liquidator to admit the fees as CIRP costs[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether a forensic auditor originally appointed by a single Financial Creditor prior to CIRP is entitled to claim fees as CIRP costs in the absence of a formal appointment or CoC resolution during the CIRP period[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Professional fees for a forensic auditor cannot be classified as CIRP costs if the auditor was acting at the behest of an individual financial creditor without formal engagement by the Resolution Professional or approval by the CoC[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: IBBI Circulars dictate what constitutes CIRP costs; continuing an auditor unilaterally appointed by one stakeholder does not automatically convert their fees into CIRP costs[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Emails from a bank copying the IRP do not constitute a formal engagement by the IRP. Disciplinary proceedings noted that it is improper for an RP to use a forensic auditor engaged by a single stakeholder[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant failed to produce any valid document of engagement or continuation by the IRP/RP, justifying the rejection of the fee claim[cite: 15].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, agreeing with the Adjudicating Authority that the claim was not payable as CIRP costs[cite: 15].
summary: A forensic auditor appealed to have its fees (Rs. 5,31,000) recognized as CIRP costs, arguing it was continued by the IRP after the CIRP began[cite: 15]. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's rejection, noting that the auditor was originally hired by a single financial creditor (PNB) and there was no formal engagement or CoC resolution approving their appointment by the Resolution Professional[cite: 15].

case_title: Rakesh Kapoor vs Mr. Ashok Kumar Juneja & Anr[cite: 16]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Rakesh Kapoor (Operational Creditor and CoC member). Respondent No.1 is Ashok Kumar Juneja (Liquidator). Respondent No.2 is Andhra Bank[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor Mas Project Engineers Pvt. Ltd. was undergoing liquidation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant held post-dated cheques worth Rs. 20 Lakhs issued by suspended directors, which were presented and mistakenly cleared by the bank during liquidation[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation ordered on 30.10.2019; cheques presented on 19.11.2019[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The bank mistakenly honored the cheques despite a change in official signatories. The Appellant claimed he presented them to trigger a Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act case[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT directed the Appellant to refund the Rs. 20 Lakhs with 8% interest to the liquidation estate[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether a creditor holding post-dated cheques can lawfully present and encash them during the liquidation phase, and retain the proceeds resulting from a bank's error[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Encashment of post-dated cheques during the liquidation process to recover pre-existing claims constitutes unjust enrichment and violates the statutory distribution waterfall under Section 53 of the IBC[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A CoC member or creditor who has already filed claims in liquidation cannot bypass Section 53 to extract preferential payments from the liquidation estate assets[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal rejected the Appellant's defense that he intended the cheques to bounce, finding that retaining the mistakenly cleared funds amounted to mala fide action taking advantage of the bank's negligence[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's order directing the refund of the Rs. 20 Lakhs to the liquidation estate was fully justified and legally sound[cite: 16].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal and upheld the NCLT's order directing the refund, with no orders as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: An Operational Creditor presented post-dated cheques worth Rs. 20 Lakhs during the Corporate Debtor's liquidation, which the bank mistakenly cleared[cite: 16]. The NCLT ordered the creditor to refund the money to the liquidation estate. The NCLAT dismissed the creditor's appeal, holding that taking advantage of a banking error to extract preferential payment violates the Section 53 waterfall mechanism under the IBC[cite: 16].

case_title: Sanjay Kumar Dewani Interim Resolution Professional of ADI Automotives Pvt. Ltd. vs NA[cite: 17]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sanjay Kumar Dewani, Interim Resolution Professional of ADI Automotives Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 17] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Extension of the statutory timelines for the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP)[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: 180-day CIRP period expired; IRP filed multiple applications for exclusion of time lost due to lockdowns and judicial delays[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced 08.01.2020. IRP originally granted exclusion for 25.03.2020 to 31.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: IRP filed an application seeking further exclusion for time utilized in litigating previous extension applications, including bar association strikes[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh on 15.03.2021 granted exclusion only for the period from 03.09.2020 to 14.12.2020. IRP appealed for further exclusion of periods consumed in adjudicating the new application[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether the time taken by the Adjudicating Authority to decide an application for exclusion of time, and the time spent pursuing an appeal, should be excluded from the statutory 180-day CIRP period[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Time consumed by the Adjudicating Authority and Appellate Tribunal in adjudicating applications for the extension or exclusion of CIRP timelines can be validly excluded from the strict statutory CIRP period[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: To prevent the CIRP from becoming frustrated through no fault of the IRP or CoC, judicial delays should not eat into the 180-day limit mandated by Section 12 of the IBC[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal accepted the detailed chronological affidavit demonstrating that the delay from 07.01.2021 to 15.03.2021 (NCLT delay) and up to 12.04.2021 (NCLAT delay) was purely judicial/administrative in nature[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Impugned Order required modification to add a further 73 days to the excluded CIRP period[cite: 17].
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal to a limited extent, modifying the Impugned Order to exclude a further 73 days (from 07.01.2021 to 15.03.2021, and from the appeal filing to disposal) from the CIRP period[cite: 17].
summary: The IRP of a Corporate Debtor appealed to exclude additional days from the statutory CIRP period, specifically the time the NCLT took to hear his extension application and the time spent in the current appeal[cite: 17]. The NCLAT modified the NCLT's order, granting an additional 73-day exclusion to ensure the CIRP was not penalized for delays in the judicial process[cite: 17].

case_title: Sintex Industries Ltd. vs Punjab National Bank[cite: 19]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sintex Industries Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondent is Punjab National Bank (Financial Creditor)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Section 7 application for initiating CIRP was pending against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly discussed in the order; the issue was purely procedural regarding mediation[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLAT had previously ordered the Adjudicating Authority on 15.03.2021 to pass an order on the Section 7 application within one week[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Adjudicating Authority had already reserved its order on the Section 7 application on 25.03.2021[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed the current appeal asking NCLAT to direct the Adjudicating Authority to first consider its application for mediation under Section 442 of the Companies Act before deciding on the Section 7 admission[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority should be directed to consider an application for mediation under Section 442 of the Companies Act before pronouncing its reserved order on the admission or rejection of a Section 7 IBC application[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a tribunal has reserved its order on the merits of an insolvency admission application following strict appellate directives, it cannot be compelled to halt the pronouncement to consider a collateral mediation application[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The strict timelines of the IBC and previous binding directives of the Appellate Tribunal (upheld by the Supreme Court) take precedence over a request for mediation under the Companies Act[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Permitting a mediation detour after the order on the main Section 7 application was already reserved would wrongly dilute the NCLAT's earlier order mandating swift disposal[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal has no merit as the Adjudicating Authority must proceed with pronouncing the reserved order[cite: 19].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal finding no merit, allowing the Adjudicating Authority to deliver its reserved order on the Section 7 application[cite: 19].
summary: The Corporate Debtor appealed to halt the NCLT from pronouncing a reserved order on a Section 7 CIRP application, arguing that the NCLT should first consider a mediation application under the Companies Act[cite: 19]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that since a prior appellate directive (upheld by the Supreme Court) mandated the immediate disposal of the Section 7 application, introducing mediation at the reserved-order stage would improperly dilute the mandate[cite: 19].

case_title: Shailja Nagar vs. Canara Bank & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Canara Bank is the Financial Creditor, and the Corporate Debtor is a real estate entity managing a home-buyers project. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial debt extending from Canara Bank to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Specific underlying default amounts are not detailed, but the OTS settlement amount negotiated was Rs. 37.80 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 11th March 2021, the creditor rejected the initial OTS proposal. The NCLT admitted the petition on 22nd March 2021. On 30th March 2021, the creditor formulated terms for an improved OTS. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The evidence relied upon during the appeal were the letters dated 11th March 2021 and 30th March 2021 from the Financial Creditor regarding the OTS conditions (requiring Rs. 3.78 Crores upfront deposit). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The original application was filed under Section 7 of the IBC by Canara Bank and was admitted by the NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court-II) on 22nd March 2021 on the grounds of debt and default.
legal_issues: Whether the pendency or subsequent formulation of terms for an One-Time Settlement (OTS) proposal by a Financial Creditor constitutes a valid legal ground to set aside an otherwise legally sound order of admission under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The mere pendency or post-admission negotiation of a settlement proposal does not invalidate an insolvency admission order that was properly passed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 admission is contingent solely on the existence of debt and default; parties intending to settle post-admission must utilize the statutory exit routes available within the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) framework. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal reviewed the post-admission OTS correspondence and determined it did not highlight any legal infirmity in the original NCLT admission order. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since the impugned admission order suffered from no legal infirmity, the pending OTS could not justify setting it aside.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. However, the bench clarified that this dismissal shall not act as a bar for the Appellant to seek an appropriate remedy (such as withdrawal or settlement) before the Adjudicating Authority.
summary: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's admission of a Section 7 insolvency petition filed by Canara Bank against the Corporate Debtor. The appellant challenged the admission order solely on the ground that an One-Time Settlement (OTS) proposal was pending consideration at the time. The tribunal ruled that ongoing settlement negotiations do not render an otherwise valid admission order legally infirm, and directed the parties to utilize standard CIRP exit mechanisms if they wish to resolve the matter amicably.

case_title: India Resurgence ARC Private Limited vs Amit Metaliks Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: India Resurgence ARC Pvt Ltd (Dissenting Secured Financial Creditor), Amit Metaliks Ltd (Successful Resolution Applicant), VAP Udyog Pvt Ltd (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed, but ARC was an assignee of a secured financial debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: ARC's admitted claim exceeded Rs. 13 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan was approved by CoC with 95.35% voting share and NCLT order passed on October 20, 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Resolution Plan offered ARC slightly over Rs. 2 Crores despite its security interest being valued at approximately Rs. 12 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata admitted the CP(IB) 1221/KB/2018 and subsequently approved the Resolution Plan via order dated 20 October 2020; the ARC appealed the approval.
legal_issues: Whether a dissenting secured financial creditor is entitled to a higher payout in a Resolution Plan strictly based on the value of its underlying security interest.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in deciding the manner of distribution in a Resolution Plan is paramount and not subject to judicial review unless similarly situated creditors are treated inequitably. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpreted amended Section 30(4) of the IBC to hold that considering the value of security interest is merely a guideline for the CoC to arrive at a business decision, not a mandatory entitlement for a dissenting secured creditor to receive payout equivalent to its security value. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court evaluated whether the CoC exercised its commercial wisdom equitably among the same class of creditors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the Resolution Plan, concluding that the CoC acted within its discretion and the dissenting creditor was not entitled to preferential treatment solely based on the valuation of its security interest.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: India Resurgence ARC Pvt. Ltd., a dissenting secured financial creditor, appealed against the NCLT's approval of Amit Metaliks Ltd.'s Resolution Plan for VAP Udyog Pvt. Ltd. The appellant argued that the payout of slightly over Rs. 2 Crores was disproportionate to its admitted claim of Rs. 13 Crores and security value of Rs. 12 Crores. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the distribution mechanism is a commercial decision of the CoC under Section 30(4) of the IBC and cannot be judicially reviewed merely because a dissenting creditor holds a higher security interest.

case_title: Office of the Asst. State Tax Commissioner vs Parthiv Parikh & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Tax Department, Govt of Maharashtra (Operational Creditor), Jaihind Projects Ltd (Corporate Debtor), Parthiv Parikh (Resolution Professional), Parixit Irrigation Ltd (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor defaulted on statutory tax dues to the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Department. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid statutory dues amounting to Rs. 5,62,29,528. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated and public notice issued on 02-11-2018; 90-day extended claim period expired 31-01-2019; Tax Department filed its claim on 20-12-2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The claim was filed more than a year after the public announcement and after the Resolution Plan was submitted to the Adjudicating Authority for approval. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad initiated CIRP in CP(IB) 172/AHM/2018. The RP rejected the delayed claim on 31-12-2019, which was upheld by the NCLT on 17-03-2020, followed by plan approval on 19-03-2020.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory operational creditor's claim can be admitted by the Resolution Professional if filed well beyond the 90-day extended timeline and after the CoC-approved Resolution Plan has been submitted to the Adjudicating Authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Claims filed after the expiration of the statutorily mandated period and after the Resolution Plan is pending approval cannot be entertained, as it would derail the time-bound CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Emphasized that Regulation 12(2) strictly curtails the period for submission of claims to 90 days from the insolvency commencement date to allow prospective resolution applicants to prepare viable plans. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the factual delay of over a year in filing the claim and the critical stage of the CIRP (plan pending NCLT approval). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that allowing the delayed claim would reset the CIRP clock, defeating the IBC's objective of timely resolution, thereby justifying the rejection.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: The Assistant State Tax Commissioner of Maharashtra appealed the rejection of its claim of Rs. 5.62 Crores against Jaihind Projects Ltd. The Resolution Professional rejected the claim because it was filed in December 2019, over a year after the public announcement and after the CoC-approved Resolution Plan was submitted to the NCLT. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that accepting belated claims at the final stage of CIRP would disrupt the time-bound resolution process mandated by the IBC.

case_title: Abhishek Jain vs Puerto Life Science Pvt Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Abhishek Jain (Appellant/Minority Shareholder & Director), Puerto Life Sciences Pvt Ltd (Respondent No.1/Company), Pramod Kumar Sharma and other Directors (Respondents 2-6). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant acquired 30% equity (12 lakh shares) via MoU and provided short-term unsecured loans of Rs. 6.90 Crores through his parents to fund a pharmaceutical manufacturing unit. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Company defaulted on repaying the Rs. 6.90 Crores unsecured loan; cheques issued were dishonoured. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Board resolved to increase authorized share capital from Rs. 4 Crores to Rs. 16 Crores on 09-05-2020 and issued a rights issue offer letter on 27-06-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The bank stopped term loan disbursal due to the Appellant's refusal to provide a personal guarantee, prompting the majority to initiate a rights issue which the Appellant claimed was a scheme to dilute his shareholding. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi vacated an interim stay on the rights issue on 06-11-2020, prompting the Appellant to appeal under oppression and mismanagement grounds.
legal_issues: Whether the majority shareholders' decision to issue rights shares to raise capital was a bona fide corporate action or an oppressive tactic to dilute the minority shareholder's stake.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In allegations of oppression and mismanagement involving rights issues, appellate courts may preserve the status quo regarding the contested shares while remanding factual disputes requiring evidentiary review to the lower tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241 and 242 of the Companies Act 2013 require a comprehensive review of complex factual allegations, such as fund rotation and bad faith, which should be assessed by the NCLT first. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT declined to rule on the merits of newly submitted bank statements showing alleged fund rotation, determining they must be evaluated by the NCLT. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench remanded the petition to the NCLT for full adjudication on merits while granting interim protection to the Appellant by restraining the allotment/renunciation of his proportionate rights shares.
operative_order: The matter was remanded back to the NCLT for a decision on merits. The Respondents were directed not to allot or renounce the shares offered to the Appellant until the disposal of the Company Petition. The earlier order deferring the AGM was vacated, allowing the company to hold its AGM.
summary: Abhishek Jain, a 30% shareholder in Puerto Life Sciences Pvt. Ltd., challenged a rights issue initiated by the majority directors, alleging it was a coercive tactic to dilute his shareholding after disputes arose over unpaid unsecured loans and personal bank guarantees. The NCLT vacated an interim stay on the rights issue. The NCLAT remanded the case to the NCLT to assess new evidence regarding alleged fund rotation, but directed that the rights shares offered to Jain must not be allotted to others pending final disposal.

case_title: Rajendrakumar Kundanmal Jain vs Vijal A. Jain & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vijal A. Jain / EPPAJ India (Operational Creditor), Rajendrakumar Kundanmal Jain / Bothra Metals and Alloys Ltd (Corporate Debtor/Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale, supply, and delivery of plastic sheets and box goods across twelve invoices between 18-10-2014 and 14-02-2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid principal operational debt of Rs. 6,75,940 along with 12% interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor made a part payment of Rs. 40,000 on 16-02-2016 and issued a cheque for Rs. 44,298 on 12-01-2016 which was dishonoured. Section 8 Demand Notice was issued on 16-10-2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A cheque dated 12-01-2016 was dishonoured with the remark 'Payment stopped by drawer', acting as an acknowledgment of debt extending limitation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 9 petition via order dated 13-02-2020; the Corporate Debtor appealed arguing the claim was time-barred.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 9 petition was barred by limitation when the underlying invoices dated back to 2014-2015, given the issuance of a subsequently dishonoured cheque in 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The issuance of a cheque towards the payment of dues constitutes an acknowledgment of debt, which provides a fresh period of limitation under Section 20 of the Limitation Act, even if the cheque is subsequently dishonoured. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The court interpreted Section 20 of the Limitation Act, confirming that the date of the cheque (12-01-2016) falls within the original limitation period and successfully extends it. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluated the dishonoured cheque and the unreplied Section 8 demand notice as concrete evidence of an extended limitation period and undisputed debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The petition filed on 03-06-2019 was within the extended three-year limitation period starting from the date of the dishonoured cheque (12-01-2016).
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the NCLT's admission of the CIRP.
summary: The Corporate Debtor appealed the NCLT's admission of a Section 9 petition, arguing that the operational debt arising from 2014-2015 invoices was time-barred. The NCLAT upheld the CIRP initiation, holding that a cheque issued by the Corporate Debtor on January 12, 2016—even though later dishonoured—acted as a valid acknowledgment of debt under the Limitation Act. Consequently, the petition filed in June 2019 was well within the extended limitation period.

case_title: Palm Products Pvt Ltd vs Tvl Narsimha Rao & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Palm Products Pvt Ltd (Appellant/Assignee), Tvl Narsimha Rao (Resolution Professional), SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd (Respondent No.2/Assignor), Amrit Jal Ventures Pvt Ltd (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SREI, a related party, assigned its debt of Rs. 60.48 Crores due from the Corporate Debtor to Palm Products for a consideration of Rs. 10 Lakhs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total admitted claim of SREI was Rs. 43,24,16,087, with an unreconciled portion of Rs. 17.76 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Assignment Deed was executed on 18-05-2020 but was not registered when the claim was filed; it was later registered on 15-07-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP rejected the assignee's claim because the deed was initially unregistered, there was no credible bank statement proving the Rs. 10 Lakhs consideration changed hands, and SREI retained the shares while only assigning the debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad dismissed the Appellant's IA No. 486 of 2020 on 12-08-2020, affirming the RP's refusal to induct the assignee into the CoC as a non-related Financial Creditor.
legal_issues: Whether an assignee stepping into the shoes of a related party Financial Creditor via an initially unregistered and allegedly undervalued assignment deed is entitled to join the CoC as a non-related Financial Creditor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An assignee of a debt steps into the shoes of the assignor; if the assignor is classified as a related party to the Corporate Debtor, the assignee inherits that disability regarding CoC participation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 17 of the Registration Act necessitates the registration of the assignment deed. Since it was unregistered at the time of claim submission, the RP legally disregarded it. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the lack of concrete financial evidence (no bank statements) proving the payment of the Rs. 10 Lakh consideration, affirming suspicions of a surrogate transaction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the RP's decision to treat the Appellant as having stepped into the shoes of a related party, thereby barring it from entering the CoC.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. The RP was permitted to treat the Appellant as having stepped into the shoes of the related party if valid evidence of consideration is eventually produced.
summary: Palm Products Pvt. Ltd. sought entry into the CoC of Amrit Jal Ventures after acquiring a Rs. 60.48 Crore debt from SREI Infrastructure for a mere Rs. 10 Lakhs. SREI was previously barred from the CoC for being a related party. The Resolution Professional rejected Palm's claim due to the assignment deed being unregistered at the time and lacking proof of consideration. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that the assignee steps into the shoes of the assignor and inherits the related-party disqualification, preventing surrogate entry into the CoC.

case_title: Radico Khaitan Ltd vs BT & FC Pvt Ltd And Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Radico Khaitan Ltd (Appellant/Operational Creditor), BT & FC Pvt Ltd (Corporate Debtor 1), Bangalore Dehydration and Drying Equipment Co Pvt Ltd (Corporate Debtor 2), SBI & Ugro Capital (Financial Creditors). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: BT & FC operated a bottling unit on land and warehouse owned by Bangalore Dehydration. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: BT & FC defaulted on an operational debt of Rs. 5,72,49,000 to the Appellant; Bangalore Dehydration stood as guarantor for BT & FC's financial debts to SBI and Ugro exceeding Rs. 25 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT admitted CIRP for BT & FC on 27-09-2019 and for Bangalore Dehydration on 27-01-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Both companies shared common promoters (Murlidher family), common directors, interdependent assets, and cross-guaranteed liabilities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru rejected the Operational Creditor's application to consolidate the two CIRPs on 02-09-2020, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an Operational Creditor has the locus standi to seek consolidation of CIRPs of two interdependent associate companies, and whether the group companies meet the parameters for consolidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: CIRPs of distinct but deeply intertwined corporate entities can be consolidated if there is common control, common directors, intermingled assets and liabilities, and business interdependence, to maximize asset value and achieve resolution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While the IBC does not explicitly provide for consolidation, the Tribunal exercised its inherent powers, noting that the associate company relationship satisfies common control criteria analogous to Companies Act definitions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal applied an 8-parameter test (common control, directors, assets, liabilities, interdependence, pooling of resources, intricate links, common creditors) and found all were satisfied. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that consolidation would prevent imminent liquidation and maximize value, and that the Operational Creditor had sufficient locus to file the application.
operative_order: The NCLT's impugned order was set aside, and the appeal was allowed without costs. The NCLT was directed to appoint a single common Resolution Professional/Liquidator for the consolidated CIRP of both Corporate Debtors.
summary: Radico Khaitan Ltd., an operational creditor, applied to consolidate the CIRPs of BT & FC Pvt. Ltd. and its associate company, Bangalore Dehydration, arguing they were inextricably linked. The NCLT rejected the plea, citing lack of locus standi and CoC's preference for liquidation. The NCLAT reversed the decision, applying an 8-parameter test to find that the companies shared promoters, assets, and liabilities. The NCLAT ordered the consolidation of the two CIRPs under a single Resolution Professional to facilitate a comprehensive resolution and prevent piecemeal liquidation.

case_title: State Bank of India vs Animesh Mukhopadhyay
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Appellant/Financial Creditor), Zenith Finesee India Pvt Ltd (Corporate Guarantor), Purple Advertising Services Pvt Ltd (Principal Borrower), Animesh Mukhopadhyay (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SBI granted a term loan to the Principal Borrower, which was secured by the Corporate Guarantor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total outstanding debt of approximately Rs. 29 Crores as of 20-11-2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against Principal Borrower on 29-10-2019 and against Corporate Guarantor on 20-11-2019; SBI filed claim on 11-02-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP rejected SBI's claim against the Guarantor solely because SBI had already filed a claim in the CIRP of the Principal Borrower. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata dismissed SBI's IA on 02-02-2021, affirming the RP's refusal to admit simultaneous claims.
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor can simultaneously file and maintain claims for the same debt in the separate CIRPs of both the Principal Borrower and the Corporate Guarantor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A creditor's right to pursue remedies against the principal borrower and surety is co-extensive, allowing simultaneous claims in their respective CIRPs subject to proportional adjustments upon actual recovery. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(2) and 60(3) of the IBC contemplate parallel insolvency proceedings against a borrower and its guarantor, necessitating that claims be admissible in both. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal held that until the creditor actually receives payment in one CIRP, the debt remains legally 'due' in the other. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that barring a claim against a guarantor merely because a parallel claim exists against the borrower is legally flawed; both claims are fully maintainable.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed, and the NCLT's impugned order was set aside. The Resolution Professional was directed to consider the Appellant's claim and appropriately include SBI in the Committee of Creditors.
summary: State Bank of India appealed the rejection of its Rs. 29 Crore claim against a Corporate Guarantor (Zenith Finesee) by the Resolution Professional. The RP and NCLT held that SBI could not claim the same debt simultaneously in the CIRPs of both the Principal Borrower and the Guarantor. The NCLAT reversed this, ruling that under the IBC, a creditor's rights against a borrower and guarantor are co-extensive. SBI is legally entitled to maintain claims in both CIRPs concurrently, subject to final adjustments upon actual recovery.

case_title: State Bank Of India vs Vibha Agro Tech Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Appellant/Financial Creditor), Vibha Agro Tech Ltd (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Various credit facilities granted by a consortium of lenders since March 2011, later restructured under a Master Restructuring Agreement (MRA) on 26-09-2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The account was declared a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 30-04-2013 due to failed restructuring. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor exited the CDR package on 31-01-2015. SBI filed the Section 7 application on 12-09-2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SBI relied on an OTS proposal dated 19-06-2015 as an acknowledgment of debt to extend limitation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad dismissed the Section 7 petition as time-barred on 27-02-2020, prompting the Bank to appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application was barred by limitation, and whether the Master Restructuring Agreement or an OTS proposal extended the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation period for filing an insolvency application runs from the date of default (NPA date); documents produced as acknowledgments must fall within the unexpired three-year period to validly extend limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applied Article 137 of the Limitation Act to determine that the three-year period expired on 30-04-2016. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the MRA (dated 2013) and the OTS proposal (dated June 2015) and found that even if the OTS was considered, the application filed in September 2018 remained beyond the three-year extension. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since no valid written acknowledgment was proven to extend the limitation up to September 2018, the petition was hopelessly time-barred.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed as devoid of merits with no order as to costs.
summary: State Bank of India appealed the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 7 petition against Vibha Agro Tech Ltd. The account was classified as an NPA in April 2013, but SBI filed for insolvency in September 2018. SBI argued that a 2013 Master Restructuring Agreement and a 2015 One Time Settlement proposal constituted acknowledgments of debt extending the limitation period. The NCLAT rejected this, ruling that even if the 2015 OTS was considered, the three-year limitation period expired before the 2018 filing. (Note: This decision was later overruled by the Supreme Court on grounds of balance sheet acknowledgments).

case_title: Kishanlal Likhmichand Bothra vs Canara Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Canara Bank (Financial Creditor/Assignee of Syndicate Bank), Kishanlal Likhmichand Bothra (Appellant/Erstwhile Director of Bothra Metal and Alloys Ltd). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Syndicate Bank provided financial assistance via Cash Credit, Letter of Credit, Term Loan, and Forward Cover. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total outstanding debt of Rs. 61,47,52,521; account declared NPA on 03-12-2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application was filed on 04-07-2019, beyond three years from the NPA date. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor recorded the debt in its balance sheets and submitted multiple One Time Settlement (OTS) plans between July 2018 and August 2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the CIRP on 06-07-2020, rejecting the defense that the debt was time-barred.
legal_issues: Whether an insolvency application filed more than three years after the NPA date is saved from limitation by acknowledgments of debt in the Corporate Debtor's balance sheets and OTS proposals.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Entries in balance sheets and formal settlement proposals (OTS) constitute valid written acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, effectively resetting the three-year limitation clock. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to IBC proceedings, meaning any acknowledgment made before the expiration of the original limitation period grants a fresh period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the Corporate Debtor's own reply affidavit which admitted the principal debt of Rs. 41.67 Crores and confirmed the submission of OTS plans. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the CIRP admission, concluding that the continuous acknowledgments in financial records kept the debt legally alive and within limitation.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed, confirming the initiation of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against the Corporate Debtor.
summary: The erstwhile director of Bothra Metals appealed the initiation of CIRP by Canara Bank, arguing the Section 7 petition filed in July 2019 was time-barred as the account became an NPA in December 2015. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the Corporate Debtor's continuous recording of the debt in its balance sheets and its submission of multiple One Time Settlement proposals constituted valid acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, thereby extending the limitation period.

case_title: Aashish Jhunjhunwala & Ors vs Kshitiz Chhawhharia, RP of Ramsarup Industries Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: SS Natural Resources Pvt Ltd (Successful Resolution Applicant/Appellant), Ramsarup Industries Ltd (Corporate Debtor), Kshitiz Chhawchharia (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution of the Corporate Debtor involving multiple manufacturing units and extensive land lease. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted claims ran into hundreds of crores, with Financial Creditors owed approximately Rs. 5853 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan was approved by CoC on 28-06-2019 and by NCLT on 04-09-2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The SRA sought waivers of lease transfer fees and penalties from WBIDC, which the NCLT left for the relevant authorities to decide rather than granting outright. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata approved the Resolution Plan but did not grant the specific waivers requested; SRA and other stakeholders appealed challenging various aspects including the viability of the plan, differential treatment of creditors, and Section 29A eligibility.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can unilaterally modify a CoC-approved Resolution Plan by refusing to grant requested waivers, and whether the plan violated Section 30(2) by differentiating between classes of creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors is paramount; an Adjudicating Authority directing a Resolution Applicant to seek statutory waivers from respective authorities rather than granting them outright does not amount to a unilateral modification of the plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2) and Section 30(4) of the IBC permit differential treatment/payments to different classes of creditors as long as the minimum statutory requirements are met. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluated whether the SRA's plan explicitly stated that non-grant of waivers would not jeopardize implementation, concluding the SRA was bound to implement it. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the approval of the Resolution Plan, dismissing all appeals, and directed the Monitoring Agency to commence immediate implementation.
operative_order: All appeals were dismissed. The Monitoring Agency was directed to take immediate steps for implementation, failing which an application for liquidation should be moved.
summary: Multiple appeals were filed against the NCLT's approval of SS Natural Resources Pvt Ltd's Resolution Plan for Ramsarup Industries. The SRA argued the plan was unviable because NCLT didn't grant waivers on lease transfer fees. Promoters argued the plan was discriminatory and the SRA was ineligible under Section 29A. The NCLAT dismissed all appeals, ruling that the NCLT merely directed the SRA to approach relevant authorities for waivers (which was in line with the plan's own provisions) and reaffirmed that the CoC's commercial wisdom regarding distribution and viability is non-justiciable.

case_title: Tarun International Ltd vs Vikram Bajaj
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Tarun International Ltd (Appellant/Auction Purchaser), Vikram Bajaj (Resolution Professional), Anil Special Steel Industries Ltd (Corporate Debtor), Allahabad Bank (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: E-auction sale of Unit No. 1 (land, plant, machinery) of the Corporate Debtor by Allahabad Bank under the SARFAESI Act. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on loans, prompting Allahabad Bank to invoke SARFAESI. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Auction held on 20-12-2017; Sale Certificate registered on 09-02-2018; CIRP commenced against Corporate Debtor on 05-03-2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The auction notice and subsequent communications explicitly stated the sale was on an 'as is where is' basis and that statutory dues (including EPF and workers' dues) would be borne by the purchaser. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Jaipur held the Appellant liable to pay the workers' and statutory dues related to the unit. The Appellant challenged the NCLT's jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Whether a bona fide auction purchaser who bought an asset under the SARFAESI Act prior to the commencement of CIRP can be held liable for the Corporate Debtor's statutory and workers' dues pertaining to that asset under Section 60(5) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An auction purchaser acquiring property on an 'as is where is' basis with explicit notice of pending statutory and workers' encumbrances inherits the liability to clear those dues. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: EPF dues constitute a first charge on the establishment under Section 11(2) of the EPF Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the auction notice and pre-sale correspondence proving the purchaser was fully aware of the EPF and workers' claims before completing the purchase. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: By a 2:1 majority, the NCLAT concluded that the Appellant consciously accepted the encumbrances, and thus the Adjudicating Authority correctly fastened the liability on the auction purchaser, not the Corporate Debtor.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. The Appellant/auction purchaser remains liable for the workers' and EPF dues pertaining to the purchased unit.
summary: Tarun International purchased a unit of the Corporate Debtor via a SARFAESI auction conducted by Allahabad Bank just before CIRP commenced. The RP approached the NCLT, which ruled that the auction purchaser must bear the unit's pending workers' and EPF dues. The NCLAT (by majority) upheld this decision, stating that since the auction was 'as is where is' and the purchaser was explicitly informed of the statutory liabilities before the sale certificate was issued, it could not evade paying those dues.

case_title: Next Education India Pvt Ltd vs K12 Techno Services Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Next Education India Pvt Ltd (Appellant/Operational Creditor), K12 Techno Services Pvt Ltd (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Master License Agreement dated 03.01.2011 for providing digital classroom solutions. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid invoices totaling Rs. 2,39,85,521.35. The first date of default was 12.03.2011. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: 187 invoices were raised between March 2011 and June 2017. Section 8 demand notice was issued on 08.08.2017. Section 9 petition was filed on 26.10.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Demand Notice cumulatively claimed the entire amount from 2011. Emails from 2015/2016 were produced as acknowledgments. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru rejected the Section 9 application on grounds of pre-existing dispute and limitation. NCLAT initially allowed the appeal, but the Supreme Court set it aside and remanded it for fresh consideration.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 9 application was barred by limitation when the earliest invoice dated back to 2011, and whether a pre-existing dispute existed prior to the demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation period for Section 9 under Article 137 begins from the first date of default. A creditor cannot arbitrarily shift the date of default to a later period by relying on subsequent invoices when the demand notice claims the cumulative amount. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act requires acknowledgment of debt within the three-year limitation period; acknowledgments made in 2015 for a 2011 default are invalid to extend limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that routine service complaints from 2012-2015 did not constitute a 'pre-existing dispute' under the IBC as no serious dispute was raised prior to the Section 8 notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While finding no pre-existing dispute, the bench definitively concluded the application was barred by limitation because the three-year period from the 2011 default expired in 2014, and subsequent acknowledgments were too late.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the NCLT's rejection of the application on the ground of limitation.
summary: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application claiming Rs. 2.39 Crores for digital services provided between 2011 and 2017. The NCLT rejected it for limitation and pre-existing disputes. On remand from the Supreme Court, the NCLAT analyzed the facts afresh. While it found that no valid pre-existing dispute existed prior to the demand notice, it upheld the dismissal on limitation grounds. The NCLAT ruled that the default occurred in 2011, and emails from 2015/2016 could not legally extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.

case_title: Devinder Parkash Kalra & Ors vs Syngenta India Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Devinder Parkash Kalra & Ors (Appellants/Minority Public Shareholders), Syngenta India Ltd (Respondent/Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Selective capital reduction under Section 66 of the Companies Act to extinguish 3.59% public shareholding. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: EGM held on 08.12.2017; NCLT order passed on 27.10.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Independent valuers in Oct 2017 valued shares at Rs. 2445/share. In the 3-year interim before NCLT approval, the company's net worth and PAT substantially increased, and a 2020 tax amendment shifted the Dividend Distribution Tax (DDT) burden to shareholders. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the capital reduction in 2020 based on the 2017 valuation. Minority shareholders appealed to secure current fair value.
legal_issues: Whether a selective capital reduction can be approved based on a three-year-old valuation when the company's financial health has substantially improved and tax liabilities have fundamentally shifted to the detriment of minority shareholders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a capital reduction scheme, extinguishing minority shares based on a stale valuation violates equity and fair play if the company has experienced substantial financial growth during a prolonged judicial process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Section 66 permits selective capital reduction in any manner, the payout to exiting minority shareholders must reflect the true and fair current value of their shares. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal contrasted the 2016-17 financials with the 2018-19 financials, noting a near doubling of PAT and substantial net worth increase. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that while the reduction process was lawful, compensating the shareholders based on 2017 figures in 2020 unjustly deprived them of the company's interim profits.
operative_order: The NCLT order was modified. The Company was directed to appoint an independent valuer to revalue the shares based on the latest audited accounts and pay the higher fair value to the extinguishing shareholders.
summary: Minority shareholders of Syngenta India appealed the NCLT's approval of a selective capital reduction scheme. They argued that the payout price of Rs. 2445 per share was based on a 2017 valuation, which was obsolete by the time the NCLT passed its order in October 2020, especially given the company's substantial profit growth and a 2020 tax law change shifting DDT to shareholders. The NCLAT agreed, modifying the NCLT's order to direct the company to conduct a fresh valuation based on current financials to ensure the minority shareholders are fairly compensated.

case_title: Piyush Dilipbhai Shah & Ors vs Syngenta India Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Piyush Dilipbhai Shah & Ors (Appellants/Minority Public Shareholders), Syngenta India Ltd (Respondent/Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Selective capital reduction under Section 66 to extinguish 3.59% public shareholding. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: EGM held on 08.12.2017; NCLT order passed on 27.10.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuers in Oct 2017 priced shares at Rs. 2445. Between 2017 and 2020, the company's PAT increased from Rs. 288.33 lakhs (2016-17) to Rs. 503.52 lakhs (2018-19). Tax amendments in 2020 shifted DDT burden to the shareholders. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the capital reduction in 2020 based on the 2017 valuation. Shareholders appealed.
legal_issues: Whether compensating minority shareholders in 2020 based on a 2017 share valuation is just and equitable in a selective capital reduction scheme when the company's profits have significantly increased.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Extinguishing minority shares based on a stale valuation is contrary to the principles of equity; exiting shareholders are entitled to a fair value that incorporates the company's financial growth up to the date of execution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66 of the Companies Act allows selective reduction, but courts must ensure the compensation to exiting shareholders is fair and reflects current value. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the 2018-19 Annual Report demonstrating massive profit growth compared to 2016-17 to rule that the 2017 valuation was obsolete. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the capital reduction itself but mandated a fresh valuation to ensure minority shareholders receive a fair, updated price.
operative_order: The NCLT order was modified. The Company was directed to appoint an independent valuer to revalue the shares based on the latest audited accounts and pay the higher fair value to the extinguishing shareholders.
summary: In a companion appeal to CA No. 220 of 2020, minority shareholders of Syngenta India challenged the NCLT's approval of a capital reduction scheme using a 3-year-old share valuation. The NCLAT modified the NCLT order, ruling that while the selective capital reduction was legally permissible, relying on a 2017 valuation in 2020 unjustly deprived the minority shareholders of the company's interim financial growth. The company was directed to conduct a fresh valuation.

case_title: Indian Overseas Bank vs Rcm Infrastructure Ltd & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Indian Overseas Bank (Appellant/Financial Creditor), Rcm Infrastructure Ltd (Respondent 1/Corporate Debtor), Koneru Subbiah Chowdry (Respondent 2/Erstwhile MD). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank initiated SARFAESI proceedings against the Corporate Debtor and successfully auctioned its property. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: NPA declared on 13.06.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Auction held on 12.12.2018; 25% bid amount received on 13.12.2018; CIRP commenced on 03.01.2019; remaining 75% received on 08.03.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The sale was not fully paid for, nor was the Sale Certificate issued, before the NCLT declared the moratorium under Section 14. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor's ex-MD applied to NCLT under Section 60(5) to set aside the sale. NCLT set aside the sale as it violated the moratorium. The Bank appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an auction sale under the SARFAESI Act, where only 25% of the bid amount was paid prior to CIRP commencement, can be completed by receiving the balance payment after the imposition of a moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An auction sale is not complete until full payment is received and the sale certificate is issued; any completion steps taken after the imposition of an IBC moratorium are illegal and void. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the IBC explicitly prohibits transferring, encumbering, alienating, or disposing of any of the Corporate Debtor's assets, overriding SARFAESI proceedings via Section 238. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the factual chronology that 75% of the payment was received two months after CIRP began, confirming the asset legally belonged to the Corporate Debtor on the insolvency commencement date. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that receiving the balance consideration post-moratorium violated Section 14, justifying the NCLT's cancellation of the sale.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed with no orders as to cost, upholding the NCLT's decision to set aside the auction sale.
summary: Indian Overseas Bank auctioned the Corporate Debtor's property under SARFAESI, receiving 25% of the payment just before CIRP was initiated. The bank accepted the remaining 75% two months into the CIRP moratorium. The NCLT set aside the sale. The NCLAT upheld the decision, ruling that the sale was incomplete on the insolvency commencement date and completing it thereafter directly violated the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, which has overriding effect over the SARFAESI Act.

case_title: Kolla Koteswara Rao vs Dr Sk Srihari Raju & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kolla Koteswara Rao (Appellant/Suspended Director), Dr. Sk Srihari Raju (Respondent 1/Financial Creditor), Anjaneyulu Sadhu (Respondent 2/IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent 1 paid Rs. 2.34 Crores directly to SBI to fulfill the Corporate Debtor's OTS. In exchange, the CD executed an Agreement to Sell its property to Respondent 1. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The CD failed to secure the necessary NOC from TSIIC, nullifying the sale, triggering a refund obligation under the Agreement with 24% interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreement executed on 10.12.2017; TSIIC cancelled allotment in Feb 2018; Demand Notice issued Oct 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clause 12 of the Agreement clearly stipulated a refund with 24% interest if the sale failed. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad admitted the Section 7 petition. The suspended director appealed, arguing the transaction was not a 'financial debt'.
legal_issues: Whether amounts paid by a purchaser directly to a lender on behalf of a Corporate Debtor under an Agreement to Sell, which contains a refund-with-interest clause upon failure, qualifies as a 'Financial Debt' under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any amount raised under an agreement (including an Agreement to Sell) that involves an obligation to refund with interest upon failure of the core transaction has the 'commercial effect of a borrowing' and constitutes a Financial Debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpreted the residuary clause Section 5(8)(f) as a 'catch-all' provision, relying on the Supreme Court's Pioneer Urban Land ruling that money advanced for temporary use with profit as a main aim satisfies the criteria of financial debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified the tripartite-like nature of the payment (to the Bank on behalf of the CD) and the explicit indemnity clause requiring a 24% interest refund. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench definitively concluded that the transaction met the criteria of 'disbursal', 'time value of money', and 'commercial effect of borrowing', classifying the purchaser as a Financial Creditor.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs, confirming the admission of the Corporate Debtor into CIRP.
summary: The suspended director of the Corporate Debtor appealed the admission of a Section 7 petition. The creditor had paid Rs. 2.34 Crores directly to SBI on the Corporate Debtor's behalf under an Agreement to Sell land. When the land transfer failed, the creditor invoked the agreement's clause demanding a refund with 24% interest. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's ruling, classifying the transaction as a 'Financial Debt' under the residuary clause of Section 5(8)(f) because it had the commercial effect of a borrowing.

case_title: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd vs Gwalior Bypass Projects Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd (Appellant/Financial Creditor), Gwalior Bypass Projects Ltd (Respondent/Corporate Guarantor), Adel Landmarks Ltd (Principal Borrower). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Adel Landmarks took a Rs. 170 Crore loan from ECL Finance, later assigned to EARCL. Gwalior Bypass executed a Corporate Guarantee. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account declared NPA on 31.12.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against Principal Borrower admitted on 05.12.2018; CIRP against Guarantor admitted on 29.05.2019. EARCL filed claim against Guarantor on 11.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP rejected EARCL's claim against the Guarantor solely because EARCL had already filed a claim in the CIRP of the Principal Borrower. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed EARCL's application to admit the claim, relying on the NCLAT's earlier 'Piramal' judgment. EARCL appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor can simultaneously file and maintain claims for the same debt in the separate CIRPs of both the Principal Borrower and the Corporate Guarantor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A creditor's remedies against the principal borrower and surety are co-extensive under the contract of guarantee; thus, the creditor can file claims in the respective CIRPs of both entities simultaneously. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(2) and (3) of the IBC contemplate parallel insolvency proceedings against a corporate debtor and its corporate guarantor before the same Adjudicating Authority, explicitly validating simultaneous claims. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal explicitly disagreed with and overruled its previous interpretation in the 'Piramal' case, noting that adjustments can be made at the distribution stage. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that barring a claim against a guarantor merely because a parallel claim exists against the borrower is legally incorrect and violates the fundamental tenets of guarantee contracts.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed. The NCLT's impugned order was quashed. The matter was remitted to the NCLT to direct the RP to consider EARCL's claim, and any pending Resolution Plan was to be sent back to the CoC for reconsideration.
summary: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company's claim of Rs. 458 Crores against Corporate Guarantor Gwalior Bypass was rejected by the RP and NCLT because EARCL had already claimed the same debt in the CIRP of the Principal Borrower, relying on the 'Piramal' judgment. The NCLAT reversed this decision, explicitly rejecting its own reasoning in 'Piramal'. It ruled that under Section 60 of the IBC and general guarantee laws, simultaneous claims against both the borrower and the guarantor are completely valid, subject to final adjustments upon recovery.

case_title: Interups Inc vs Kuldeep Kumar Bassi & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Interups Inc (Appellant/Unsuccessful Bidder), Kuldeep Kumar Bassi (RP of Asian Colour Coated Ispat Ltd), Committee of Creditors (Respondent 2), JSW Steel Coated Products Ltd (Respondent 3/Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Asian Colour Coated Ispat Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC approved JSW's plan on 28.06.2019; RP filed for NCLT approval on 10.07.2019. Appellant submitted an Expression of Interest much later on 12.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant did not participate in the CIRP timelines, submitted no formal resolution plan, and only sought to intervene a year after the CoC had already approved JSW's plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT approved JSW's Resolution Plan on 19.10.2020. The Appellant challenged this approval, seeking to submit a higher bid.
legal_issues: Whether a third party who failed to participate in the CIRP within stipulated timelines qualifies as an 'aggrieved person' under Section 61(1) of the IBC with the locus standi to challenge a CoC-approved resolution plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity that fails to submit an Expression of Interest within the prescribed timelines and does not participate in the CIRP is a mere outsider and lacks the locus standi to challenge a legally approved resolution plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpreted 'any person aggrieved' under Section 61(1) to include only legitimate stakeholders in the CIRP, explicitly excluding busybodies attempting belated interventions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the Appellant submitted an EOI a full year after the CoC had approved the SRA's plan, rendering the intervention highly disruptive to the time-bound IBC process. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded the Appellant was neither a Resolution Applicant nor an aggrieved party, and entertaining such belated bids would make a mockery of the time-bound CIRP mechanism.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed as not maintainable for lack of locus standi, with no order as to costs.
summary: Interups Inc appealed the NCLT's approval of JSW Steel's Resolution Plan for Asian Colour Coated Ispat Ltd. Interups claimed it could offer a significantly higher amount but had only submitted its Expression of Interest in June 2020, a year after the CoC approved JSW's plan. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal at the threshold, ruling that an entity that completely ignores CIRP timelines and attempts to intervene at the final approval stage is an outsider lacking locus standi under Section 61 of the IBC.

case_title: Mr Kuldeep Verma (RP) vs State Bank Of India And Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kuldeep Verma (Appellant/Resolution Professional), K.S Oils Ltd (Corporate Debtor), State Bank of India & Ors (Respondents/CoC). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of K.S. Oils Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: 270-day CIRP limit expired on 16.04.2018. Liquidation application filed in April 2018. NCLT heard the matter 31 times over 981 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC repeatedly rejected 5 addendums to SREI's resolution plan with over 66% voting share. Despite this, the NCLT continuously adjourned the liquidation application and eventually dismissed it as infructuous on 01.01.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA 165/2018 for liquidation. NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the IA as not maintainable and infructuous, prompting the RP to appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the discretion to continuously adjourn and subsequently dismiss a liquidation application despite the expiry of the maximum statutory CIRP period and repeated rejections of resolution plans by the CoC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 33(1) of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority is statutorily mandated to pass a liquidation order if the maximum CIRP period expires without the receipt of a CoC-approved resolution plan; it has no discretion to delay this indefinitely. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 mandates time-bound resolution. The AA's repeated demands for the CoC to reconsider rejected addendums directly violated the CoC's commercial wisdom and the strict timelines of the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the egregious delay of 981 days and 31 hearings without passing a liquidation order, viewing it as a defeat of the Code's very purpose. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded the Adjudicating Authority acted erroneously by dismissing the liquidation application and bypassing the statutory mandate of Section 33(1).
operative_order: The appeal was allowed. The NCLT's impugned order was set aside. Liquidation of the Corporate Debtor was ordered under Section 33(1), and the Appellant was appointed as the Liquidator.
summary: The Resolution Professional of K.S. Oils Ltd. appealed against the NCLT's refusal to order liquidation. The 270-day CIRP period expired in 2018, and the CoC repeatedly rejected all resolution plans. Nevertheless, the NCLT dragged the liquidation application through 31 hearings over 981 days before dismissing it. The NCLAT strongly reprimanded this delay, emphasizing that time is of the essence under the IBC. It set aside the NCLT's order and mandated the immediate liquidation of the Corporate Debtor under Section 33(1).

case_title: Pawan Kumar Agarwal vs Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited (Assignee of Union Bank of India). Corporate Debtor is M/s Mohan Jute Mills Limited, represented by Appellant Pawan Kumar Agarwal (Suspended Director). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed a loan from Union Bank of India in 2010. The loan was assigned to the Financial Creditor on 31 December 2012 and restructured via a term sheet dated 21 March 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The claimed default amount is Rs. 42,33,36,044/- as of February 2019, with the original NPA declaration date being 31 December 2009. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Financial Creditor sent a notice for revocation of the settlement package on 3 February 2015. A recall notice was issued on 20 May 2016. The Section 7 application was filed on 15 March 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence included letters from the Corporate Debtor dated 23 July 2015, 14 August 2015, 1 September 2015, and 31 March 2016, acknowledging outstanding principal and interest dues and seeking rescheduling. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata admitted the Section 7 application on 21 October 2019, rejecting the defense of limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application was barred by limitation given that the original NPA date was 31 December 2009, and whether the letters of acknowledgment extended the limitation period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgment of debt in writing signed by the party against whom the right is claimed before the expiration of the limitation period creates a fresh period of limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to applications under Section 7 of the IBC. Successive written acknowledgments of liability continuously extend the limitation period, starting a fresh period of three years from each acknowledgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated multiple letters sent by the Corporate Debtor seeking rescheduling of payments and found they explicitly confirmed outstanding balances, satisfying the requirement of a valid acknowledgment under Section 18. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the date of default was extended by valid written acknowledgments, the last being in March 2016, making the Section 7 application filed in March 2019 well within the extended limitation period.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority admitting the Section 7 application was affirmed. The CoC was directed to send the decision taken to the Adjudicating Authority. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged the initiation of CIRP arguing the debt was time-barred as it was declared NPA in 2009. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the Corporate Debtor had repeatedly acknowledged the debt in writing up until March 2016 to seek restructuring. Applying Section 18 of the Limitation Act, these acknowledgments extended the limitation period, validating the Section 7 petition filed in 2019.

case_title: Abhinandan Jain vs Tanaya Enterprises Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Tanaya Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. Corporate Debtor is Risa International Ltd., represented by Appellant Abhinandan Jain (Suspended Director). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods for which six invoices dating from 27 October 2014 to 31 October 2014 were raised, payable within 90 days. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default amount was Rs. 90,49,843/- plus interest. The date of default was identified as 22 September 2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A demand notice under Section 8 IBC was sent on 10 September 2018. The Section 9 application was filed on 19 October 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Operational Creditor provided a running ledger account and invoices duly stamped by the Corporate Debtor. The Corporate Debtor made a part payment of Rs. 30,30,000/- on 22 September 2016. A postal department report confirmed delivery of the Section 8 notice to the registered address on 21 September 2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 9 application on 31 August 2020.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 8 demand notice was properly served, whether the operational debt was barred by limitation, and whether a pre-existing dispute existed prior to the filing of the application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Service of a statutory demand notice sent to the registered address of the corporate debtor via registered post constitutes valid service, regardless of whether a third party at that address signs the acknowledgment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Default under Section 3(12) occurs when a part or installment of a debt becomes due and payable and is not paid; part payments on a running account refresh the limitation period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To establish a pre-existing dispute, a corporate debtor must present substantive evidence showing a plausible contention requiring further investigation, not merely a patently feeble legal argument or bald denial. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held the part payment in September 2016 extended the limitation period, rendering the October 2018 petition timely.
