It also found the service of the Section 8 notice valid and concluded no pre-existing dispute was proven.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority admitting the Section 9 application was upheld. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged the initiation of CIRP, arguing improper service of the Section 8 notice, a time-barred debt, and a pre-existing dispute. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's admission order, ruling that notice sent to the registered address constitutes valid service. It further held the application was within the limitation period due to a part payment made in September 2016, and found no substantive evidence to establish any pre-existing dispute.

case_title: Vijay Sitaram Dandnaik vs Punjab National Bank & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is Punjab National Bank. Corporate Debtor is Jailaxmi Sugar Products (Nitali) Private Limited, represented by Appellant Vijay Sitaram Dandnaik. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank sanctioned term loan facilities to the Corporate Debtor via agreements in 2010 and 2011. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The account was classified as Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 31 March 2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application was filed by the bank on 10 October 2019. The bank relied on restructuring letters dated 11 June 2017 and a balance confirmation dated 17 June 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A winding-up order had already been passed against the Corporate Debtor by the Bombay High Court on 4 January 2018, and an Official Liquidator was appointed. The bank's Section 7 application relied on acknowledgment letters issued in 2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 7 application on 6 November 2019, holding the debt was acknowledged and the application was within time.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application was barred by limitation when filed more than six years after the date of NPA, and whether acknowledgment letters issued beyond the initial three-year period could extend limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act must be made before the expiration of the prescribed period of limitation to validly extend the limitation period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Article 137 of the Limitation Act applies to Section 7 applications, providing a three-year limitation period starting from the date of default (NPA date). Acknowledgment letters issued after the expiry of this three-year period cannot revive a time-barred debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the dates of the balance confirmation letters (June 2017) against the NPA date (March 2013) and found that no acknowledgment was made within the three-year window from the date of default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since the acknowledgment letters were issued beyond three years from the date of NPA, the debt was time-barred, and the Section 7 application was not maintainable.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed. The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority admitting the Section 7 application was set aside. The matter was remitted to the NCLT for quantifying the fees of the RP to be borne by the Financial Creditor.
summary: The Appellant challenged the NCLT's admission of a Section 7 application filed by Punjab National Bank, arguing the debt was time-barred since the account became an NPA in 2013 and the application was filed in 2019. The NCLAT agreed, noting that the acknowledgment letters relied upon by the bank were issued in 2017, after the initial three-year limitation period had expired. The appeal was allowed, and the CIRP admission was set aside.

case_title: Ram Ratan Kanoongo vs Veda Kumar Nimbagal & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ram Ratan Kanoongo (former Resolution Professional of Sirpur Paper Mills Ltd). Respondent No. 1 is Veda Kumar Nimbagal (Ex-Director/Employee of the Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 2 is J K Paper Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent No. 1 claimed unpaid salary dues for his services as an employee/Ex-Director. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 1 originally submitted a claim for Rs. 13,50,000/- which the RP partially admitted to the tune of Rs. 5,40,000/- up to the CIRP commencement date (18 September 2017). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT approved the Resolution Plan on 19 July 2018 and dismissed the Ex-Director's application for the rejected salary claim of Rs. 8,10,000/-. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Post-approval of the plan, the Ex-Director filed fresh applications in January 2019 seeking Rs. 20,38,300/- as salary and conditioning his cooperation in signing old financial statements on the payment of these dues. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Despite the finality of the July 2018 order, NCLT Hyderabad passed a new order on 4 August 2020 directing the erstwhile RP to pay the salary dues.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to issue directions to an erstwhile Resolution Professional to pay past salary claims after the Resolution Plan has been approved under Section 31 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An approved Resolution Plan is binding on all stakeholders, and a successful resolution applicant acquires the corporate debtor on a clean slate; undecided or belated claims cannot be imposed post-approval. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) strictly binds the Corporate Debtor, its employees, and creditors to the terms of the approved Resolution Plan, extinguishing any past claims not expressly provided for in the plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the claimant's right to salary had already been adjudicated and settled by the NCLT's earlier order rejecting the excess claim, which had attained finality as it was never appealed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that entertaining fresh applications for past claims after the approval and implementation of the Resolution Plan defeats the purpose of the Code, and no directions could be issued to the discharged RP for such settled claims.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed. The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority directing the RP to make payment of the salary was quashed and set aside. No costs.
summary: The erstwhile RP appealed an NCLT order directing him to pay salary dues to an Ex-Director long after the approval of the Corporate Debtor's Resolution Plan. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT order, emphasizing that under Section 31 of the IBC, an approved Resolution Plan is binding and extinguishes all past claims. Since the Ex-Director's claim was already adjudicated during the CIRP, raising it anew post-approval violated the 'clean slate' principle.

case_title: MBev Spirits Pvt. Ltd. vs Mam Chand Goyal & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is MBev Spirits Pvt. Ltd. (Lessee). Respondents 1 and 2 (Mam Chand Goyal and Windsor Buildwell Pvt. Ltd.) are petitioning shareholders of Respondent No. 3 (Uttar Development Pvt. Ltd., the Lessor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent No. 3 purportedly executed an unregistered lease deed on 3 December 2019 to lease 26.76 hectares of land to the Appellant for 5 years, which was later replaced by a registered lease deed on 25 June 2020 for 29 years over 5.659 hectares. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The dispute centers on oppression and mismanagement under the Companies Act, alleging fraudulent transfer of the company's sole asset (land) to a related party. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The initial lease was executed on 3 December 2019. The oppression and mismanagement petition was filed on 23 June 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence showed common directorships (related party transaction), lack of notice to Respondent 1 for the 3 December 2019 board meeting, execution of the initial lease on under-stamped paper, and deposit of the Rs. 3 Crore security into an unauthorized bank account. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Delhi Bench-V passed an interim order on 31 July 2020 restraining the Appellant from construction on the land and directing that possession remain with Respondent No. 3.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in passing an interim restraining order protecting the company's sole property when a prima facie case of fraudulent related-party leasing and oppression/mismanagement was alleged.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal has broad equitable powers under Section 242 of the Companies Act to pass interim orders to protect the substratum of a company from being alienated through suspect related-party transactions pending final adjudication. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Non-compliance with Section 188 (related party transactions), Section 180 (leasing whole undertaking), and Section 17 of the Registration Act (mandatory registration of leases) establishes a strong prima facie case of oppressive conduct prejudicial to shareholders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the unseemly haste of the transaction, the lack of notice to directors, the discrepancies between the unregistered and registered lease deeds, and the unauthorized banking channels to conclude that the transaction lacked bona fides. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the interim order preserving the property and preventing construction was necessary to protect the interest of the company and its shareholders from potential fraud by internal forces.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. The interim order passed by the NCLT restraining construction and preserving possession with Respondent No. 3 was upheld. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged an interim NCLT order restraining it from constructing on land leased from Respondent No. 3. The petitioning shareholders of Respondent No. 3 alleged the lease was a fraudulent related-party transaction executed without proper board approval or compliance with the Companies Act. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the suspicious circumstances, unseemly haste, and statutory violations justified the NCLT's interim intervention to protect the company's sole asset.

case_title: Maldar Barrels Pvt. Ltd. vs Pearson Drums & Barrels Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Maldar Barrels Pvt. Ltd. Corporate Debtor is Pearson Drums & Barrels Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An original operational debt of Rs. 8,82,11,723/- which resulted in an initial Section 9 CIRP that was later settled via a Settlement Agreement dated 11 January 2018 for a reduced sum of Rs. 3.70 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The settlement required payment in 37 monthly installments of Rs. 10 Lakhs each by the 21st of every month. The Operational Creditor alleged default due to minor delays in installment payments ranging from 0 to 22 days between January 2018 and July 2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Operational Creditor issued a demand notice under Section 8 IBC on 27 June 2019, claiming the full original debt of Rs. 9,41,85,391/- had revived due to the delayed payments. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements confirmed that the entire Rs. 3.70 Crore settlement amount was eventually paid in full. The Operational Creditor had accepted the delayed payments without immediate protest and deposited some post-dated cheques late. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata dismissed the second Section 9 application on 13 February 2020, holding it was an attempt to enforce a settlement agreement and would lead to unlawful enrichment.
legal_issues: Whether minor delays in paying installments under a settlement agreement constitute a default reviving the original debt under Section 9 IBC, and whether 'time was of the essence' in the contract.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: If a promisee accepts delayed performance without demur or retaining rights, time ceases to be of the essence in the contract, and such delay cannot be grounds for invoking penal default clauses. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 55 of the Contract Act, 1872, the conduct of accepting late payments implies that strict adherence to timelines is not essential, precluding the creditor from treating the contract as voidable or triggering severe default consequences. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the Operational Creditor accepted delayed payments for months without objection and was itself responsible for late deposit of cheques. Crucially, the entire settlement sum of Rs. 3.70 Crores was fully paid. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since time was not of the essence and the settlement amount was fully paid, there was no actionable default under the IBC to justify initiating a fresh CIRP.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority rejecting the Section 9 application was affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: The Operational Creditor filed a second Section 9 application claiming that minor delays in installment payments breached a Settlement Agreement, thereby reviving the original larger debt. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that by accepting the delayed payments without objection, time was no longer of the essence under Section 55 of the Contract Act. Since the Corporate Debtor had fully paid the agreed settlement amount, no actionable default existed to trigger CIRP.

case_title: Accelyst Solutions Pvt Ltd vs Freecharge Payment Technologies Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Transferor Company is Accelyst Solutions Pvt Ltd. Non-Petitioner/Transferee Company is Freecharge Payment Technologies Pvt Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A scheme of amalgamation was proposed between the Transferor and Transferee companies. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (Merger/Amalgamation, not an insolvency default). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The scheme specified the Appointed Date as 7 October 2017. The Board Resolution approving the scheme was dated 27 March 2018, and the Valuation Report was dated 22 March 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT Delhi had already approved the scheme for the Transferee Company with the Appointed Date of 7 October 2017. The Regional Director's report was erroneously quoted by the NCLT Mumbai as objecting to the date. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai, via order dated 28 February 2020, approved the scheme but unilaterally modified the Appointed Date from 7 October 2017 to 1 April 2018 due to the lapse of time before the valuation report.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has the jurisdiction to unilaterally modify the 'Appointed Date' in a Scheme of Amalgamation agreed upon by the shareholders when all statutory requirements are met.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The jurisdiction of the Company Court/Tribunal in sanctioning a scheme of amalgamation is supervisory; it cannot sit in appeal over the commercial wisdom of the shareholders who approved the scheme. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013, if the statutory procedures are complied with and the scheme is not violative of law or public policy, the Tribunal must respect the Appointed Date mutually agreed upon by the companies. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that altering the Appointed Date would disrupt financial calculations and that the NCLT Delhi had already approved the original date for the corresponding Transferee Company. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that NCLT Mumbai acted beyond its supervisory jurisdiction by modifying the Appointed Date without cogent legal justification, rendering the modification unwarranted.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed. The NCLT Mumbai's modification of the Appointed Date was set aside, and the Appointed Date was fixed as 7 October 2017. Time limits for compliance and filing with the ROC were extended.
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT Mumbai order that approved a scheme of amalgamation but unilaterally changed the 'Appointed Date' from 7 October 2017 to 1 April 2018. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, emphasizing that the NCLT's jurisdiction is supervisory and it cannot alter the commercial wisdom of the shareholders regarding the Appointed Date, especially when NCLT Delhi had already approved the 2017 date for the Transferee Company.

case_title: Mazda Agencies vs Hemant Plastics & Chemicals Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Mazda Agencies (Partnership Firm). Corporate Debtor is Hemant Plastics & Chemicals Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of printing and packaging material by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total outstanding debt acknowledged was Rs. 1,48,11,572/- as of 31 December 2004, with the last payment made on 22 November 2004. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The debt was acknowledged on 11 January 2005. BIFR rehabilitation proceedings under SICA began in 2005. The Operational Creditor filed a civil suit in 2009 after obtaining BIFR consent. SICA was repealed on 1 December 2016. The Section 9 IBC application was filed on 24 November 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Operational Creditor had explicitly rejected the BIFR settlement proposal of 20% and had successfully obtained permission under Section 22(1) of SICA in 2012 to pursue independent civil remedies. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad rejected the Section 9 application on 7 July 2020, holding it was barred by limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the Operational Creditor was entitled to exclude the period during which the Corporate Debtor's rehabilitation proceedings were pending before BIFR under Section 22(5) of SICA for the purpose of computing limitation for a Section 9 IBC application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A creditor cannot claim the benefit of exclusion of time under Section 22(5) of SICA if they were not part of the sanctioned rehabilitation scheme and had actively obtained consent to pursue independent legal remedies. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 22(1) of SICA suspends legal proceedings unless consent is obtained. If a creditor obtains consent and initiates independent civil action, their remedy is not suspended, and they cannot subsequently claim tolling of limitation under Section 22(5). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed that the Operational Creditor rejected the 20% settlement under the BIFR scheme and filed a civil suit in 2009, proving their legal rights were not suspended. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since the Operational Creditor's right to sue was not suspended during the BIFR proceedings, the limitation period was not tolled, rendering the Section 9 application filed in 2017 hopelessly time-barred from the 2004 default.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed ex-parte. The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority rejecting the Section 9 application as time-barred was upheld. No order as to costs.
summary: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application in 2017 for a default dating back to 2004, claiming the limitation period was suspended while the Corporate Debtor was in BIFR proceedings under SICA. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that the creditor had opted out of the BIFR scheme and obtained consent to file a civil suit in 2009. Because their legal remedies were never suspended, they could not claim exclusion of time under SICA, making the IBC petition time-barred.

case_title: B.S. Krishnan vs Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund (Assignee of IDBI). Corporate Debtor is L.S.P. Agro Ltd., represented by Appellant B.S. Krishnan (Ex-Director). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan facilities aggregating Rs. 10.50 Crores were granted by IDBI in 1998 and 2000. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The account was declared Non-Performing Asset (NPA) before 2001. A recall notice was issued on 15 January 2002 for Rs. 11,05,92,701/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IDBI filed an OA before DRT on 6 February 2002. A DRT decree was passed on 29 April 2019, and a Recovery Certificate was issued on 16 January 2020. The Section 7 IBC application was filed on 23 January 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: There was no acknowledgment of debt within three years of the initial NPA date. The Financial Creditor relied solely on the subsequent DRT decree to claim the debt was not time-barred. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai admitted the Section 7 application on 25 January 2020, inferring the debt was not time-barred based on the DRT order.
legal_issues: Whether a judgment or decree passed by the Debt Recovery Tribunal shifts the date of default forward for the purpose of computing the three-year limitation period under Article 137 for filing a Section 7 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A judgment, decree, or recovery certificate passed by a Civil Court or DRT for recovery of money does not shift forward the original date of default for the purposes of limitation under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: For applications under Section 7, the limitation period governed by Article 137 begins from the date the original default occurred (the NPA date). Independent recovery proceedings do not impact this timeline unless there is a valid acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act within the initial three years. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on the prior NCLAT majority decision in 'V. Padmakumar vs SASF', the bench held that since the NPA date was before 2001 and no acknowledgment occurred within three years, the DRT decree of 2019 could not revive the time-barred IBC remedy. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded the Section 7 application filed in 2019 was barred by limitation. (Note: This legal reasoning was subsequently overruled by the Supreme Court in Dena Bank vs C. Shivakumar Reddy, which held that a DRT Recovery Certificate creates a fresh cause of action).
operative_order: The appeal was allowed. The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority was set aside, and the Section 7 application was dismissed. The Corporate Debtor was released from the CIRP and moratorium. The matter was remitted to the NCLT to decide CIRP costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged the initiation of CIRP, arguing the debt was time-barred since the account became an NPA before 2001. The Financial Creditor argued a 2019 DRT decree extended limitation. Relying on its own precedent, the NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that a DRT decree does not shift forward the original date of default for IBC purposes, rendering the Section 7 application time-barred. This specific legal position was later overturned by the Supreme Court.

case_title: Rajesh Goyal vs. Babita Gupta & Ors.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 2166 of 2020 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1056 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Applicant: Rajesh Goyal (Promoter of Corporate Debtor M/s Rajesh Projects (India) Pvt. Ltd. acting as outsider Financial Creditor/Lender); Respondents No. 1-3: Babita Gupta, Manoj Kumar Gupta, Sweta Gupta (Allottees/Original Section 7 Applicants); Other Parties: Indiabulls Commercial Credit Pvt. Ltd., IIFL Home Finance Ltd. (Financial Creditors), Interim Resolution Professional Gaurav Katiyar, and RG Luxury Home Buyers Association / Jan Kalyan Samiti. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development project ('RG Luxury Homes') involving allottees/homebuyers and lenders, subject to a 'Reverse Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process' framed under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules, 2016 via order dated 05.02.2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by promoter in timely infusing agreed amounts (infusion of Rs. 13.88 crores within 30 days was delayed; promoter infused Rs. 5.24 crores and undertook the rest) and missing construction milestone dates. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Timelines fixed in 05.02.2020 order expired between March and August 2020; I.A. No. 2166 of 2020 filed seeking extension of 11 months citing nationwide COVID-19 lockdown from 25.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Nationwide COVID-19 disruption, government recognition of real estate hardship, sanction letter dated 04.08.2020/21.08.2020 from IIFL Home Finance Ltd. extending financial assistance of Rs. 15 crores, and revised construction schedules submitted on 12.01.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application initially filed by homebuyers; on appeal, NCLAT formulated Reverse CIRP on 05.02.2020 allowing promoter to infuse external funds and finish flats; promoter filed interlocutory application seeking enlargement of timelines due to pandemic.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal can extend the timelines prescribed for completion of a real estate project and payment to creditors under the Reverse Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process on account of force majeure circumstances and disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an ongoing Reverse Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process for real estate projects, the Appellate Tribunal has inherent jurisdiction to grant extension of project completion and payment timelines to mitigate genuine hardship arising from unprecedented force majeure disruptions such as a pandemic, provided the foundational structure of the resolution is preserved. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Exercise of inherent powers under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules, 2016 in Reverse CIRP allows flexibility in timeline adjustments to promote the economic welfare and maximization of assets for all stakeholders over mechanical procedural dismissal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where non-adherence to infusion milestones is attributable directly to nationwide lockdown and credit bottlenecks rather than willful disobedience, a single pre-lockdown delay may be treated as an aberration to advance substantial justice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Granting reasonable extension of project timelines serves the larger interests of allottees awaiting homes and secured lenders, with a strict forfeiture condition if the promoter fails to adhere to the revised schedule.
operative_order: Application I.A. No. 2166 of 2020 allowed; project completion, refund, and payment timelines extended as per revised schedule (flats to 15.09.2021, internal fit-outs to 15.10.2021, common areas and refunds to 15.11.2021); allottees balance payment date extended to 15.06.2021; failure by promoter will forfeit invested sums and revert CIRP to NCLT; RP to report compliance monthly.
summary: Rajesh Goyal, promoter of a distressed real estate project undergoing a court-monitored Reverse CIRP under NCLAT's earlier order dated 05.02.2020, sought an extension of project completion and creditor settlement timelines due to the COVID-19 pandemic and resultant lockdowns[cite: 10]. Financial creditors including IIFL Home Finance and various homebuyer associations supported the extension to avoid project collapse[cite: 10]. The NCLAT held that the extraordinary economic disruption caused by the nationwide lockdown justified a magnanimous approach to keep the experiment of Reverse CIRP alive[cite: 10]. Extending the milestones up to September/November 2021 without altering substantive terms, the Tribunal warned that any future non-compliance by the promoter would result in forfeiture of invested funds and resumption of ordinary CIRP before NCLT[cite: 10].

case_title: Gyanchand Mutha vs. Aditya Birla Money Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor/Respondent No. 1: M/s Aditya Birla Money Ltd. (stockbroker); Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 2: M/s Arkay International Finsec Ltd. (registered NBFC); Appellant: Gyanchand Mutha (Shareholder of Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor opened trading account No. 1070913 with Operational Creditor at Jaipur in September 2017 to trade in shares and securities, purchasing 1,00,000 shares of Steel Exchange of India Ltd. for Rs. 1,30,38,956.27. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Debit balance of Rs. 90,24,817.40 arose on 30.11.2017; after selling shares held in margin, unpaid operational debt stood at Rs. 28,83,058.80 with interest totaling Rs. 28,90,835.10. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice sent on 21.12.2017; Section 8 statutory demand notice issued on 15.03.2018; Section 9 application filed in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Reserve Bank of India Certificate of Registration No. 10.00021 dated 03.03.1998 recognizing Corporate Debtor as Non-Banking Financial Institution; RBI letter dated 06.11.2019 confirming corporate debtor holds valid NBFC certificate and filed all returns up to date; KYC Form where Corporate Debtor ticked 'Public Limited Company' instead of 'Financial Institution'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Jaipur Bench admitted Section 9 application via order dated 14.02.2020 on the ground that the Corporate Debtor deceived the creditor by not declaring itself as an NBFC in the KYC form; Shareholder appealed.
legal_issues: Whether Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 9 of the IBC can be initiated against an entity holding a valid Certificate of Registration as an NBFC from the Reserve Bank of India, in view of the statutory exclusion under Section 3(7) of the Code.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A company registered with and regulated by the Reserve Bank of India as a Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) is a 'financial service provider' and is expressly excluded from the definition of 'corporate person' under Section 3(7) of the IBC; consequently, CIRP cannot be initiated against it under Section 9 of the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(7) explicitly carves out any 'financial service provider' from the ambit of corporate persons; under Section 3(8), an entity cannot be treated as a 'corporate debtor' under the Code if it does not qualify as a corporate person. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once the entity produces a subsisting Certificate of Registration issued by the RBI and demonstrates up-to-date filing of regulatory returns, the adjudicating authority must hold its hands; errors, omissions, or misstatements in private commercial KYC forms cannot estop statutory immunity under the Code. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor being a validly registered NBFC, NCLT had no jurisdiction to initiate CIRP against it as punishment for omissions in a KYC form.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 14.02.2020 passed by NCLT Jaipur Bench quashed and set aside; Section 9 application dismissed; all actions taken by IRP/RP quashed; Corporate Debtor restored to its Board; IRP costs/fees to be determined by NCLT; no costs.
summary: Gyanchand Mutha, shareholder of Arkay International Finsec Ltd., challenged an NCLT Jaipur order admitting Aditya Birla Money Ltd.'s Section 9 IBC application for trading account dues[cite: 11]. NCLT had admitted the petition on the premise that the Corporate Debtor failed to disclose its NBFC status in the broker's KYC form[cite: 11]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, ruling that Section 3(7) of the IBC explicitly excludes financial service providers from the definition of a corporate person[cite: 11]. Since the Corporate Debtor held a valid NBFC registration certificate from the RBI and had regularly filed its regulatory returns, the provisions of the IBC could not be invoked against it, irrespective of any private KYC omissions[cite: 11].

case_title: Durga Prasad Agarwal & Anr. vs. Limtex Tea & Industries Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor: Limtex Tea & Industries Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); Corporate Debtor/Appellants: Durga Prasad Agarwal (later represented by legal heirs Smt. Sangita Agarwal, Ankur Agarwal, Harsh Agarwal) and Biswanath Mondal; Interim Resolution Professional: Manish Jain (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Short-term loan of Rs. 25,00,000 disbursed via bank on 06.06.2011 with interest, acknowledged by letter dated 06.06.2011. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed default in Part-IV was Rs. 40,10,274 (principal Rs. 25,00,000 + interest @ 15% from 01.04.2014 to 10.04.2018 of Rs. 15,10,274); date of default recorded as 01.04.2014. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Dishonor of repayment cheque on 22.06.2015; Demand Notice under NI Act issued on 29.06.2015 (received 30.06.2015); follow-up letter dated 23.02.2018; Section 7 application filed on 17.04.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Cheque No. 930562 dated 27.04.2015 for Rs. 25,00,000 drawn on SBI, dishonored for 'Fund Insufficient'; Corporate Debtor disputed cheque signature as a forgery and filed application before NCLT to send it to Questioned Document Investigation Department, CID West Bengal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted Section 7 application CP (IB) No. 535/KB/2018 on 21.11.2019 without adjudicating limitation or deciding the forensic verification plea; Corporate Debtor appealed.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a Section 7 IBC application filed on 17.04.2018 is barred by limitation when the date of default pleaded in Part-IV of Form-1 is 01.04.2014. 2. Whether a disputed and unverified dishonored cheque can be relied upon to establish acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act without examining allegations of forgery.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The period of limitation for filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC is three years from the date of default under Article 137 of the Limitation Act; in the absence of properly pleaded and proved acknowledgments under Section 18, an application filed beyond three years from the default date stated in Part-IV cannot be maintained. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Supreme Court ruling in Babulal Vardharji Gurjar, limitation is a mixed question of fact and law; where the creditor specifically pleads a default date in Form-1 and fails to lay a proper evidentiary foundation for extension in its pleadings, it cannot alter the default date at a later stage. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A cheque whose authenticity and signature are actively disputed as forged cannot serve as valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 when the court fails to determine its genuineness or address forensic verification pleas. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The default having occurred on 01.04.2014 and the Section 7 petition being filed on 17.04.2018 without an established acknowledgment, the application was barred by limitation.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 21.11.2019 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench set aside; Section 7 application dismissed; Corporate Debtor released from CIRP; IRP/RP to hand back assets and records; matter remitted to NCLT to decide IRP fees/costs payable by Financial Creditor; no costs.
summary: The legal heirs of Durga Prasad Agarwal and Biswanath Mondal appealed an NCLT Kolkata order admitting Limtex Tea & Industries Ltd.'s Section 7 IBC application for a loan disbursed in 2011[cite: 12]. In Form-1, the Financial Creditor stated the date of default as 01.04.2014, but filed the Section 7 petition on 17.04.2018, arguing that a subsequent cheque dishonor in June 2015 reset limitation[cite: 12]. The Corporate Debtor vehemently disputed the cheque as a forgery and sought forensic examination[cite: 12]. The NCLAT set aside the admission order, holding that under Babulal Vardharji Gurjar, limitation runs from the pleaded default date (01.04.2014), rendering the 2018 application time-barred under Article 137[cite: 12]. Furthermore, an unverified, disputed cheque could not be relied upon to extend limitation under Section 18[cite: 12].

case_title: M/s Orator Marketing Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s Samtex Desinz Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor/Appellant: M/s Orator Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (assignee); Original Lender: M/s Sameer Sales Pvt. Ltd.; Corporate Debtor/Respondent: M/s Samtex Desinz Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan agreement dated 20.01.2019 under which sister concern Sameer Sales advanced Rs. 1.60 crores as an interest-free, unsecured loan to Corporate Debtor to meet business working capital needs, repayable on or after 01.02.2020 upon demand; loan subsequently assigned to Appellant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed of Rs. 1,56,89,740 (principal debt; zero interest). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan repayable on or after 01.02.2020; demand notices issued on 03.02.2020 and 14.02.2020; Corporate Debtor replied on 18.02.2020 requesting installments; Section 7 petition filed in 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreement dated 20.01.2019 expressly stipulating an interest-free advance; balance sheets showing unsecured loan entry; correspondence acknowledging debt and seeking time. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-VI dismissed Company Petition (IB)-908(ND)/2020 on 23.10.2020 holding that an interest-free loan lacking time value of money does not constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8); Assignee appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an interest-free, unsecured loan advanced by a sister concern to assist a company's business development constitutes a 'financial debt' disbursed against 'consideration for the time value of money' under Section 5(8) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interest-free loan that does not stipulate payment of interest or provide any commercial consideration for the time value of money to the lender does not qualify as a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and non-payment cannot trigger Section 7 insolvency. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(8), the core requirement is that money must be disbursed against consideration for the time value of money; the mere fact that the borrower utilized the money to develop its business does not constitute time value of money from the perspective of the lender. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the underlying loan contract; if the contract reveals a simple, interest-free loan devoid of return, consideration, or commercial borrowing effect, the debt remains a simple debt rather than a financial debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Neither default nor assignment of an interest-free loan to a third party changes the intrinsic character of the debt; hence Section 7 was rightly rejected.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; impugned order dated 23.10.2020 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-VI affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Orator Marketing Pvt. Ltd., as assignee of Sameer Sales Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its Section 7 IBC application against Samtex Desinz Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 13]. The debt arose from an interest-free loan of Rs. 1.60 crores advanced by a sister concern to assist the Corporate Debtor with business operations[cite: 13]. The appellant argued that business development constituted sufficient consideration for the time value of money[cite: 13]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 5(8) of the IBC, the 'time value of money' must represent a commercial consideration accruing to the lender[cite: 13]. An interest-free advance lacking such consideration remains a simple debt and cannot qualify as a financial debt to maintain a Section 7 petition[cite: 13].

case_title: Reserve Bank of India vs. SREI Equipment Finance Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Reserve Bank of India (statutory banking and financial regulator); Respondent: SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. (SEFL, Non-Banking Financial Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Proposed Scheme of Arrangement between SEFL and certain classes of its creditors (debenture holders, ECB lenders) under Section 230 of Companies Act, 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Regulatory moratorium/classification issue; no specific monetary debt default adjudicated in this appeal. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Kolkata order passed on 30.12.2020; RBI served with Section 230(5) notice on 01.01.2021; intervention applications listed in February/March 2021 without effective orders; appeal filed on 19.03.2021 (77 days from service). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RBI Master Circular dated 01.07.2015 on prudential norms on income recognition, asset classification (IRAC), and provisioning; NCLT direction in Para 34 estopping all regulatory authorities from reporting or changing account status. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In SEFL's application C.P. No. 1492/KB/2020 under Section 230, NCLT Kolkata on 30.12.2020 granted directions restraining regulatory authorities from taking coercive actions or altering account classifications; RBI appealed via I.A. No. 596/2021 (condonation of delay) and I.A. No. 595/2021 (ad-interim stay).
legal_issues: 1. Whether the appeal filed by RBI within 77 days of service of notice is within limitation in view of the Supreme Court's Suo Motu limitation extension orders and Section 421(3) proviso. 2. Whether the NCLT exercising jurisdiction under Section 230 of the Companies Act has authority to issue an ex-parte injunction restraining the Reserve Bank of India from enforcing statutory prudential norms and regulating asset classifications.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory limitation extensions granted by the Supreme Court in Suo Motu Writ Petition (Civil) No. 3 of 2020 enlarge the period for filing appeals where limitation expired during the pandemic, and the Appellate Tribunal retains discretion under Section 421(3) proviso of the Companies Act, 2013 to condone delay up to 45 days upon sufficient cause. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 230 read with inherent powers cannot be utilized by an Adjudicating Authority to usurp the statutory powers of the Reserve Bank of India under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 or interfere with regulatory asset classification norms. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Directions curtailing the statutory functions of a sectoral regulator without providing a hearing or examining regulatory circulars warrant immediate ad-interim stay to prevent prejudice to the financial system. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Delay was condoned under Supreme Court extension orders, and NCLT's direction estopping regulatory authorities from reporting or altering account status was stayed pendente lite.
operative_order: I.A. No. 596 of 2021 allowed and delay condoned; I.A. No. 595 of 2021 allowed granting ad-interim stay of the direction in Para 34 of NCLT Kolkata's order dated 30.12.2020 estopping governmental/regulatory authorities from coercive steps or changing SEFL's account status.
summary: The Reserve Bank of India appealed against an order of NCLT Kolkata Bench passed in a Section 230 Companies Act scheme proceeding initiated by SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. (SEFL)[cite: 14]. In the impugned order, NCLT had directed that all governmental and regulatory authorities be estopped from taking coercive steps, reporting, or altering the account status of SEFL[cite: 14]. RBI filed applications for condonation of delay and ad-interim stay[cite: 14]. The NCLAT condoned the delay under the Supreme Court's COVID-19 suo motu limitation extension order and the proviso to Section 421(3)[cite: 14]. Holding that staying the restraint against RBI would not prejudice the company petition, the Tribunal stayed the NCLT's direction restraining regulators pendente lite[cite: 14].

case_title: Rajalakshmi Vardarajan, RP of Arudaavis Labs Pvt. Ltd. vs. G. Dhananjaya Naidu
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Ms. Rajalakshmi Vardarajan, Resolution Professional of Arudaavis Labs Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent: G. Dhananjaya Naidu (Landowner/Lessor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lease of land and godown-cum-shed building measuring 95 Cents and 10,504 sq. ft. situated in Chennivakkam Village, Tiruvallur District, initially executed in 2011 and renewed on 23.11.2013 for 11 months, expired without further extension. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Rental arrears totaling Rs. 66,79,260 with interest for the period from 01.04.2014 to 01.08.2019, fully admitted by the RP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 9 on 30.07.2019; initial 180-day period expired on 26.01.2020 with no extension sought; CoC resolved to liquidate on 20.01.2020; liquidation application filed on 14.02.2020; Lessor filed IA No. 626/2020 on 05.08.2020; liquidation approved on 12.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease agreement; admitted claim statement of Rs. 66,79,260; landlord requiring premises to prevent financial loss in storing agricultural produce; lack of any CIRP extension application on record. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Special Bench Chennai allowed IA/626/2020 on 04.11.2020 directing RP to vacate and handover premises within 30 days and permitting Lessor to file CIRP rental claims; RP appealed alleging violation of Section 14(1)(d).
legal_issues: Whether a lessor can recover possession of leased premises occupied by the Corporate Debtor after the statutory 180-day CIRP period has expired without any order of extension, resolution plan approval, or liquidation order being in place.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC endures only until the completion of the CIRP period; upon the expiry of the statutory CIRP period (180 days or extended duration) without an extension order, resolution plan approval, or liquidation order, the moratorium automatically ceases to operate under Section 14(4). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 14(1)(d) read with Section 14(4), the prohibition against recovery of occupied properties applies strictly during the operative subsistence of the moratorium; it does not protect the Corporate Debtor once the CIRP timeline has lapsed by efflux of time. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proof that 180 days elapsed without the RP applying for extension under Section 12 establishes as a matter of law that the moratorium came to an end. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The moratorium having expired on 26.01.2020, the RP had no legal right to retain possession of the premises or resist handing over vacant possession to the rightful lessor.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; impugned order dated 04.11.2020 passed by NCLT Special Bench Chennai directing the RP to vacate and handover possession within 30 days affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: The Resolution Professional of Arudaavis Labs Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT Chennai order directing her to handover vacant possession of leased factory premises and pay rental arrears to the landlord, G. Dhananjaya Naidu[cite: 15]. The RP argued that recovering possession violated the statutory moratorium under Section 14(1)(d) of the IBC[cite: 15]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that the mandatory 180-day CIRP period expired on 26.01.2020 and the RP had not applied for any extension under Section 12[cite: 15]. Under Section 14(4), the moratorium automatically terminated upon the expiration of the CIRP period[cite: 15]. Consequently, the RP had no legal authority to retain possession of the landlord's property after January 2020[cite: 15].

case_title: Subhash Agrawal vs. AU Small Finance Bank Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor: AU Small Finance Bank Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); Corporate Debtor: M/s SRK Devbuild Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 2); Appellant: Subhash Agrawal (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sanction and release of a Term Loan facility of Rs. 4.00 Crores secured by a registered charge with ROC Gwalior created on 09.02.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default date established as 31.05.2016; last repayment made on 31.05.2017; failed OTS proposal executed on 26.05.2017; claimed default amount was Rs. 3,34,96,299 as on 25.07.2018 (Corporate Debtor acknowledged at least Rs. 1.23 Crores in balance sheets). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 31.05.2016; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 370/7/NCLT/AHM/2018 filed on 02.08.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certificate under Section 2A of Bankers Book Evidence Act, 1891; charge creation certificate from ROC; balance sheet notes as on 31.03.2018 admitting unsecured debt of Rs. 1.23 crores owed to the bank. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Indore Bench at Ahmedabad admitted the Section 7 petition on 03.01.2020; Appellant appealed on grounds that the application was defective, calculations included recovery from mortgaged assets, and interest was disputed.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 IBC application is liable to be rejected as incomplete or defective when the exact quantum of default is disputed, provided that the financial debt due and in default exceeds the statutory threshold of Rupees One Lakh.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: At the stage of admission under Section 7(5) of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority is required only to satisfy itself that a financial debt is due, that default has occurred, and that the default exceeds the statutory threshold; disputes regarding exact calculations, interest rates, or adjustments of mortgaged recoveries do not bar admission and are to be resolved by the Resolution Professional during CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(6) defines 'claim' to include a right to payment even if disputed; reading Section 3(11), 3(12), and Section 7 together under the Innoventive Industries doctrine, default means non-payment of whole or any part of an admitted debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of loan sanction letters, ROC charge documents, and statement of accounts certified under the Bankers Books Evidence Act, supported by admissions of liability in balance sheets exceeding the threshold, satisfies the requirement of Section 7(5). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The existence of debt and default exceeding Rs. 1 Lakh being established, the application was complete and rightly admitted.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; impugned order dated 03.01.2020 passed by NCLT Indore Bench at Ahmedabad admitting Section 7 application affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Subhash Agrawal, Suspended Director of SRK Devbuild Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order admitting AU Small Finance Bank's Section 7 IBC application[cite: 16]. The appellant contended that the bank's application failed to properly account for proceeds realized from selling mortgaged properties, charged disputed interest, and was defective under Section 7(5)(b)[cite: 16]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding under the Innoventive Industries doctrine that the Adjudicating Authority only needs to ascertain whether a financial debt exists and whether an unrectified default exceeding the threshold (Rs. 1 Lakh at the time) occurred[cite: 16]. Since the Corporate Debtor's own balance sheets admitted over Rs. 1.23 Crores as due, minor accounting disputes must be addressed before the Resolution Professional during CIRP rather than stalling admission[cite: 16].

case_title: Vidharbha Industries Power Ltd. vs. Axis Bank Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor: Axis Bank Limited (Respondent); Corporate Debtor: Vidharbha Industries Power Limited (Appellant, 600 MW thermal power producer). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with Reliance Infrastructure Limited approved by MERC; credit facilities extended by consortium of banks led by Axis Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of approximately Rs. 553 crores claimed by Axis Bank; Corporate Debtor had an APTEL tariff award of Rs. 2,100 crores pending in appeal before Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 372 of 2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed on 15.01.2020; Corporate Debtor filed stay application IA No. 570/2020 in January 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor did not dispute the financial debt or default; instead, it relied on pending tariff appeals before the Supreme Court against MERC orders and a fuel supply writ petition in Delhi High Court as grounds of liquidity distress. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court No. II rejected IA No. 570/2020 on 29.01.2021 holding regulatory disputes extraneous to Section 7; Corporate Debtor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the discretion to stay the consideration of an application filed under Section 7 of the IBC on grounds that the Corporate Debtor faces liquidity distress due to pending appeals before the Supreme Court and regulatory authorities that could potentially realize sufficient funds to settle the debt.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once the existence of a financial debt and an event of default are established and the application is complete, the Adjudicating Authority has a mandatory obligation under Section 7(5)(a) of the IBC to admit the application; external litigation, regulatory disputes, or liquidity woes are extraneous and cannot justify staying insolvency proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(4) and Section 7(5) require time-bound adjudication of default within 14 days; the word 'may' in Section 7(5) cannot be interpreted to allow indefinite postponement of CIRP to await external litigation recoveries. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Innoventive Industries doctrine, all that must be proved is the occurrence of default on a legally enforceable financial debt; solvency or prospective realization of receivables is irrelevant. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and default being admitted, the Adjudicating Authority rightly refused to stay its hands; external tariff litigations cannot be permitted to impede the time-bound CIRP.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; order dated 29.01.2021 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in I.A. No. 570/2020 affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Vidharbha Industries Power Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order refusing to stay Section 7 CIRP proceedings initiated by Axis Bank for a default of Rs. 553 crores[cite: 17]. The power generating company argued that its financial distress arose from regulatory delays and that an APTEL tariff award of Rs. 2,100 crores pending before the Supreme Court would wipe out the debt if upheld[cite: 17]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under the binding Supreme Court mandate in Innoventive Industries, the Adjudicating Authority is bound to admit a complete Section 7 application once debt and default are established[cite: 17]. External regulatory disputes and pending recovery proceedings are extraneous considerations that cannot stall time-bound insolvency proceedings[cite: 17].

case_title: Gursharan Singh vs. The State Trading Corporation of India Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 2596 of 2019 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 853 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor: The State Trading Corporation of India Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); Corporate Debtor: Spacevision Impex Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 2); Appellant: Gursharan Singh (Director and Shareholder of Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial trading transactions forming the subject matter of an operational debt petition under Section 9 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics and operational debt adjudicated in original ex-parte Section 9 admission order dated 08.05.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT admission order passed on 08.05.2019; IRP served order on Appellant's residence on 07.06.2019; inspection applied on 28.06.2019; certified copy applied on 08.07.2019 and received on 15.07.2019; appeal filed on 13.08.2019 (total 58 days from knowledge/service). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: IRP proved service via registered post letter dated 30.05.2019 received by appellant's wife in first week of June 2019; emails sent to MCA registered email address; WhatsApp message sent to caretaker; physical delivery receipt signed by co-director Ravi Gupta on 13.06.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court No. 4 admitted Section 9 application CP No. IB-697/ND/2018 on 08.05.2019; Appellant filed appeal on 13.08.2019 with IA No. 2596/2019 for condonation of delay.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal has the statutory jurisdiction under Section 61(2) of the IBC to condone a delay exceeding 15 days beyond the initial 30-day appeal period, where notice and a copy of the impugned order were served on an adult family member at the appellant's registered address.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 61(2) of the IBC, the statutory period for filing an appeal is 30 days, extendable by a maximum of 15 days upon sufficient cause; the Appellate Tribunal has no statutory authority or jurisdiction to condone any delay beyond the aggregate period of 45 days. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) strictly confines appellate limitation; delivery of an order or communication to an adult family member at the party's residence constitutes valid service of notice in law. The absence of a statutory requirement to serve free copies under the IBC precludes relying on Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 to indefinitely defer limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Official postal delivery and contemporaneous records produced by an IRP acting in official capacity rebut self-serving pleas of lack of personal knowledge. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Even computing limitation from service on 07.06.2019, the appeal filed on 13.08.2019 after 58 days was hopelessly barred beyond the maximum condonable window of 45 days.
operative_order: Application for condonation of delay (I.A. No. 2596 of 2019) rejected; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 853 of 2019 dismissed as barred by limitation.
summary: Gursharan Singh, Director of Spacevision Impex Pvt. Ltd., appealed an ex-parte NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 9 IBC application by The State Trading Corporation of India Ltd.[cite: 18]. The appellant sought condonation of delay via I.A. No. 2596 of 2019, contending he learned of the order belatedly because his wife received the postal delivery in his absence[cite: 18]. The NCLAT rejected the explanation, finding that the IRP had served the order at his residence on 07.06.2019 and via email[cite: 18]. Under Section 61(2) of the IBC, the maximum delay the Tribunal can condone is 15 days beyond the 30-day appeal period[cite: 18]. Because 58 days had elapsed since service, the appeal exceeded the statutory 45-day ceiling and was dismissed as time-barred[cite: 18].

case_title: K.C. Industries vs. Prasol Chemicals Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor/Appellant: K.C. Industries; Corporate Debtor/Respondent: Prasol Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and supply of industrial chemicals; last commercial invoice raised on 13.08.2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed of slightly in excess of Rs. 31 Lakhs; Sales Tax Authorities claimed Rs. 70.42 Crores due from Operational Creditor, giving rise to an offsetting liability. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Last invoice raised 13.08.2013; Section 9 application filed on 16.04.2019 (nearly six years later); NCLT dismissal order dated 20.12.2019; appeal filed with IA No. 489/2021 seeking condonation of 411 days delay. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor demonstrated pre-existing sales tax liability of Rs. 70.42 Crores attributable to Appellant which, when set off against the Rs. 31 Lakh claim, completely extinguished liability; no certified copy applied for by Appellant. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed the Section 9 petition on 20.12.2019 on limitation and existence of a genuine dispute regarding sales tax set-off; Appellant appealed with a 411-day delay application.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an appeal filed after 93 days from the date of the impugned order prior to the COVID-19 lockdown can be condoned under Section 61(2) of the IBC. 2. Whether an application under Section 9 filed six years after the last invoice is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC must be filed within 30 days, extendable by no more than 15 days; where the period consumed prior to the commencement of the Supreme Court's COVID-19 lockdown exclusion exceeds the maximum allowable period of 45 days, the appeal is non-est and cannot be entertained. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) prescribes an inflexible limitation scheme; failure of an applicant to apply for a certified copy despite having knowledge of the adverse dismissal order precludes establishing sufficient cause. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Invoices dated beyond three years without written acknowledgment are time-barred under Article 137; claims exceeding the debt payable to statutory authorities establish a plausible, non-illusory pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was hopelessly time-barred both at the appellate stage and on original filing before NCLT, and was devoid of merit due to valid pre-existing set-off claims.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; I.A. No. 489 of 2021 seeking condonation of delay dismissed; impugned order dated 20.12.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench affirmed; no costs.
summary: K.C. Industries appealed an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing its Section 9 IBC application against Prasol Chemicals Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 19]. The Section 9 application was based on an invoice from August 2013 and filed in April 2019, nearly six years later, and the Corporate Debtor established an offsetting sales tax claim of Rs. 70.42 Crores[cite: 19]. The appeal itself was filed with a delay of 411 days[cite: 19]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal as time-barred, noting that 93 days had elapsed between the impugned order and the onset of the COVID-19 lockdown, far exceeding the maximum 45-day condonable period under Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 19]. The Tribunal also upheld the dismissal on the merits due to limitation and a genuine pre-existing dispute[cite: 19].

case_title: Rajratan Babulal Agarwal vs. Agarwal Coal Corporation India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Agarwal Coal Corporation India Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); Corporate Debtor is Shri Tradco Deesan Private Limited represented by its Director/Appellant Rajratan Babulal Agarwal; Fanendra Harakchand Munot was the appointed Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of high-grade imported boiler coal by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default amount was Rs. 21,82,821/-, scaled down by NCLT to Rs. 9,50,005/- by excluding an unrelated debit entry of Rs. 12,32,816/-; default arose after invoices dated 22nd January, 2018 and 31st January, 2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 8 of the IBC was issued on 09.04.2019; Reply to Demand Notice raising disputes and denying receipt of invoices was issued on 18.04.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor relied on consolidated tax invoices STC-01-18/4042 and STC/01-18/4135; Corporate Debtor proved via GSTIN portal data that no such invoices existed or were supplied, and showed the creditor ledger improperly debited Rs. 12,32,816/- pertaining to a sister concern (Agarwal Transport Corporation Pvt. Ltd.), alongside earlier correspondence alleging short supplies causing losses of Rs. 95,70,000/-. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 petition C.P. (IB) No. 2361/NCLT/MB/2019; NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the application on 16.07.2020 holding that short supply is not a dispute and scaling down the claim to Rs. 9,50,005/-.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority in a summary Section 9 IBC proceeding can adjudicate and scale down disputed ledger accounts like a Civil Court when the underlying invoices are suspect and disputed prior to the demand notice; and whether an application under Section 9 should be admitted where the operational debt claimed is based on unreliable records and includes third-party dues.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority exercising summary insolvency jurisdiction under Section 9 cannot sit to reconcile, adjust, or scale down disputed and inaccurate running accounts in the manner of a plenary Civil Court; an application grounded on unreliable, suspect, or inflated invoices reflecting third-party claims must be rejected where a pre-existing dispute is demonstrated. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 and Section 9 demand notices require an undisputed and crystal-clear operational debt; inclusion of dues of sister concerns and invoices not reflected on statutory tax platforms (GSTIN) constitutes a bonafide pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6), negating CIRP initiation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court applied the test of plausibility and reliability of the foundational accounts, holding that where the ledger contains obvious disparities, fabricated split invoices, and foreign debts, the defense raised in reply to Section 8 notice cannot be brushed aside as spurious. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed a fatal error by scaling down the claim from Rs. 21.82 Lakhs to Rs. 9.5 Lakhs instead of dismissing the Section 9 petition for genuine pre-existing disputes and unreliability of claimed debt.
operative_order: Appeal is allowed; the Impugned Order dated 16.07.2020 admitting the Section 9 petition is quashed and set aside; the Section 9 petition is dismissed; all actions taken by the IRP/RP including the hastily formed COC are quashed; Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP to function under its Board of Directors; RP directed to hand back records; CIRP expenses and fees directed to be examined by NCLT for directions on payment; liberty granted to report IRP's conduct to IBBI; no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, Director of Corporate Debtor Shri Tradco Deesan Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Mumbai order admitting an operational insolvency petition filed by Agarwal Coal Corporation India Pvt. Ltd. The Operational Creditor issued a Section 8 notice for Rs. 21,82,821/- based on invoices not verifiable on the GSTIN portal and including debts of an unrelated sister entity. NCLT scaled down the claim to Rs. 9,50,005/- and admitted the petition. NCLAT set aside the admission, ruling that the Adjudicating Authority cannot sit as a civil court to settle disputed accounts in summary proceedings. Since a genuine pre-existing dispute existed regarding unsupplied goods and inflated accounts, the Section 9 application was dismissed.

case_title: Solenis Chemicals India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Arjun Pulp and Paper (India) Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor/Appellant is Solenis Chemicals India Pvt. Ltd.; Corporate Debtor/Respondent is Arjun Pulp and Paper (India) Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and supply of industrial chemicals and allied materials on a day-to-day basis under eleven distinct invoices raised between 12.05.2015 and 23.11.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed a total default of Rs. 63,54,412/- along with interest at 24% per annum from the alleged date of acknowledgment on 07.11.2017 until realization. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor issued a Legal Notice (Notice of Dispute) on 01.08.2018; Operational Creditor issued a Section 8 Demand Notice on 05.09.2018 (delivered 15.09.2018); Corporate Debtor submitted a formal statutory reply on 17.09.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor proved pre-existing disputes through Tax Invoice No. RM-RTN-001 dated 06.02.2017 for goods valued at Rs. 17,12,649/- returned due to quality defects and acknowledged by the Creditor, a joint debit note dated 17.07.2017 for Rs. 8,20,833/- prepared during site inspection, an independent Chartered Accountant reconciliation report submitted by the Official Liquidator indicating advance payments of Rs. 17,30,000/-, and unauthorized belated alteration of claim via affidavit dated 16.05.2019 to include debts belonging to Connel Bros. Company (India) Pvt. Ltd. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application CP/1456/IB/2018 was filed before NCLT Chennai Division Bench, which dismissed it on 05.05.2020 finding genuine pre-existing disputes requiring deeper investigation.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in dismissing the Section 9 application on the ground of a pre-existing dispute where the Corporate Debtor raised contemporaneous quality issues, returned defective goods, executed joint debit notes, and where the Operational Creditor impermissibly modified its claim by incorporating third-party debts.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 9 IBC petition is not maintainable where the record reveals a plausible, non-illusory pre-existing dispute regarding quality of goods, debit adjustments, and return of consignments existing prior to the Section 8 demand notice, which requires comprehensive investigation outside the summary purview of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The mandate of Section 8 and Section 9 under the doctrine of Mobilox Innovations requires that any dispute regarding supply or quality raised prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice completely divests the NCLT of jurisdiction to trigger CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mobilox test; the Corporate Debtor need not prove its defense to the final standard of a civil trial but only show a plausible contentious dispute that is not spurious, hypothetical, or illusory. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Evidenced returns of defective chemicals, joint inspection debit notes, reconciliation gaps, and unilateral introduction of claims of a third-party entity establish genuine pre-existing disputes, affirming the rejection of the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 707 of 2020 is dismissed; the impugned order dated 05.05.2020 passed by NCLT Division Bench Chennai in CP/1456/IB/2018 is confirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Solenis Chemicals India Pvt. Ltd. challenged the NCLT Chennai order dismissing its Section 9 IBC petition against Arjun Pulp and Paper (India) Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 63,54,412/-. Corporate Debtor showed that materials worth Rs. 17,12,649/- had been returned due to quality issues under acknowledged invoices, a debit note was jointly formulated on site, and the creditor attempted to belatedly add claims of another entity without notice. NCLAT held that these facts demonstrated genuine, plausible pre-existing disputes prior to the Section 8 notice, affirming the dismissal of the Section 9 petition.

case_title: M/s Albanna Engineering LLC vs. M/s Sanghvi Movers Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Albanna Engineering LLC (foreign parent company incorporated in UAE); Corporate Debtor is M/s Albanna Engineering (India) Private Limited (wholly-owned Indian subsidiary, Respondent No. 5); Respondent Nos. 1 to 4 are Operational Creditors led by Sanghvi Movers Limited; Respondent No. 8 is Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL); Respondent No. 7 is the Committee of Creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: BPCL invited global tenders for execution of Mechanical Works for VGO HDT and DHDT Units at Kochi Refinery in 2014; BPCL awarded the contracts worth Rs. 205,59,20,098/- to the Appellant, which appointed its subsidiary (Corporate Debtor) as a sub-contractor; Appellant provided two performance bank guarantees to BPCL. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in payments by the Corporate Debtor to sub-vendors/operational creditors who supplied crane hiring and civil services for the refinery contract. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP of Corporate Debtor was admitted on 25.10.2019 under Section 9; Operational Creditors filed M.A./25/KOB/2020 on 09.03.2020 under Section 60(5); impugned order was passed on 20.04.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditors alleged Corporate Debtor had no independent assets and sought invocation of performance bank guarantees issued by parent Albanna Engineering LLC; parent company was never arrayed as a party respondent in the cause title of M.A. 25/KOB/2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench admitted Section 9 CIRP on 25.10.2019; on 20.04.2020, NCLT allowed M.A. 25/KOB/2020, directing BPCL to invoke the two bank guarantees given by the parent entity and place proceeds in a fixed deposit under RP control.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can direct the invocation of performance bank guarantees issued by a third-party foreign parent company and appropriate its proceeds towards CIRP liabilities of its subsidiary without impleading the parent company or giving it an opportunity to be heard; and whether such directions violate the principles of natural justice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any judicial or quasi-judicial order passed in insolvency proceedings that adversely impacts or appropriates the assets, guarantees, or property rights of a separate legal entity without impleading it as a party and without serving notice violates fundamental principles of natural justice and is void ab initio. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) of the IBC does not confer jurisdiction upon the Adjudicating Authority to bypass constitutional and natural justice protections to pierce the corporate veil or issue adverse coercive orders against a non-party foreign entity. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the application record and cause title establishing that the affected guarantor/parent entity was omitted from the array of parties, thereby rendering the order passed strictly ex-parte and behind its back. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because M/s Albanna Engineering LLC was never made a party to M.A./25/KOB/2020, the NCLT's direction to encash its performance guarantees is legally unsustainable and must be set aside on grounds of natural justice breach.
operative_order: Impugned order dated 20.04.2020 passed by NCLT Kochi Bench is set aside; matter is remitted back to NCLT Kochi Bench for fresh adjudication after hearing all parties; parties directed to appear on 15.04.2021 with matter to be disposed of within six weeks; time spent in M.A. 25/KOB/2020 excluded from CIRP period; Respondents 9 and 10 directed to renew the Performance Bank Guarantees for six months from the date of the order; appeal disposed of without costs.
summary: Sanghvi Movers Ltd. and other operational creditors obtained an order from NCLT Kochi Bench under Section 60(5) directing BPCL to encash two bank guarantees furnished by UAE-based parent company Albanna Engineering LLC to secure debts of the Corporate Debtor Albanna Engineering (India) Pvt. Ltd. The foreign parent company appealed, arguing it was never made a party to the application. The NCLAT held that directing encashment of bank guarantees belonging to a distinct entity behind its back without impleadment was a flagrant violation of natural justice. The Appellate Tribunal quashed the NCLT order and remitted the matter for fresh hearing, ordering the bank guarantees to be renewed.

case_title: Sunil Kumar Agrawal, Resolution Professional, GSS Procon Pvt. Ltd. vs. Committee of Creditors, GSS Procon Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sunil Kumar Agrawal, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s GSS Procon Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Committee of Creditors (represented by Homebuyers' Authorized Representative Ajay Kumar Siwach); Respondent No. 2 is Crossroad Welfare Society (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of a real estate corporate debtor involving construction projects and homebuyer allottees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Insolvency was initiated under IBC with CIRP commencement dated 10.10.2019; statutory 180 days expired on 07.04.2020; extension of 90 days ended on 07.07.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Nationwide COVID-19 lockdown imposed on 25.03.2020; resolution plan received on 30.10.2020 and approved by CoC with 93.43% majority voting share on 04.12.2020; plan approval application I.A. No. 5670/2020 filed before NCLT; exclusion application I.A. 411/ND/2021 filed seeking exclusion of 221 days from 25.03.2020 to 31.10.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC voting sheet confirming 93.43% approval of the Resolution Plan and documented disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic during CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi on 09.02.2021 in I.A. 411/ND/2021 restricted the exclusion to 68 days (25.03.2020 to 31.05.2020) merely following a previous routine order, thereby causing CIRP to theoretically expire on 14.09.2020 prior to plan approval.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing to grant full exclusion of 221 days spent during nationwide COVID-19 disruptions when a viable resolution plan had already been received, approved by the Committee of Creditors with a 93.43% majority, and was pending final sanction under Section 31.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a resolution plan has received overwhelming approval by the Committee of Creditors and is pending formal sanction, the outer statutory time limits under Section 12 must yield to allow exclusion of lockdown disruption periods, avoiding liquidation in keeping with the primary objective of corporate resolution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 proviso, as interpreted in Essar Steel, permits the exercise of judicial discretion beyond 330 days in exceptional cases where delays are attributable to extraordinary external factors and a short extension saves the corporate debtor from liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Application of the Essar Steel proportionality test: weighing the prejudice of liquidation against the advanced progress of CIRP where a compliant resolution plan already carries 93.43% voting support. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Mechanically limiting lockdown exclusion to 68 days was improper; full exclusion of 221 days is granted to extend the CIRP deadline up to 29.01.2021, regularizing the approval of the resolution plan.
operative_order: Impugned order dated 09.02.2021 modified; exclusion of 221 days from 25.03.2020 to 31.10.2020 on account of COVID-19 disruptions is granted; CIRP period is extended up to 29.01.2021 including the prior 90-day extension granted on 11.02.2020; appeal disposed of without costs.
summary: The Resolution Professional of GSS Procon Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT New Delhi order which granted only 68 days of COVID-19 lockdown exclusion instead of the 221 days prayed for. The CoC had approved a resolution plan on 04.12.2020 with 93.43% voting share, but the restricted extension would have caused CIRP to expire before plan approval. Relying on the Supreme Court ruling in Essar Steel, NCLAT held that where a viable plan has already been approved and awaits formal sanction, procedural timelines must be flexibly extended to prevent corporate death. NCLAT modified the order and granted the full 221-day exclusion up to 29.01.2021.

case_title: Ajit Kumar, Resolution Professional of K-Lifestyle & Industries Limited vs. Manasi Wadekar & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ajit Kumar, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor K-Lifestyle & Industries Ltd.; Respondents include suspended management personnel and Brijendra Mishra, Resolution Professional of sister concern Krishna Knitwear Technology Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Competing asset possession claims in parallel Corporate Insolvency Resolution Processes of two sister companies. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in credit facilities extended by UCO Bank leading to CIRP of K-Lifestyle on 05.02.2020; CIRP had earlier commenced against Krishna Knitwear on 04.10.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated in Krishna Knitwear on 04.10.2019; CIRP initiated in K-Lifestyle on 05.02.2020; NCLT order in I.A. 864/2020 passed on 05.01.2021; impugned order in I.A. 53/2021 passed on 02.02.2021. 5.
