FACTUAL EVIDENCE: K-Lifestyle asserted title over immovable property at Survey No. 65/2 and 65/4, Krishna Nagar, Samarvani, Silvassa, which was physically possessed and held by sister concern Krishna Knitwear Technology Ltd. under its own CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed I.A. 864 of 2020 seeking directions against the suspended management to hand over property, disposed of on 05.01.2021; Appellant then filed rectification application I.A. No. 53 of 2021 seeking directions compelling the RP of Krishna Knitwear to deliver possession; NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed it on 02.02.2021 for want of material and jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Professional administering CIRP of one company can summarily seize and take over possession of properties held by another corporate debtor undergoing an independent CIRP without seeking consolidation of CIRPs or initiating group insolvency proceedings under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of an order of consolidation of CIRP or statutory group insolvency proceedings, a Resolution Professional appointed in one corporate debtor has no unilateral authority to seize or command takeover of properties in the possession and control of another corporate debtor undergoing independent CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Duties of RP under Section 18 and Section 25 to take custody and control of assets do not empower summary dispossession of assets held under the statutory moratorium and administration of another ongoing CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Requirement of substantive evidentiary record establishing undisputed right to immediate physical possession and recourse to statutory mechanisms or IBBI dispute resolution rather than summary rectification petitions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: RPs of group companies are required to coordinate and resolve jurisdictional custody issues through formal consolidation or regulatory channels; the appeal against the rejection of the rectification application lacks legal merit.
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal declines to entertain the Appeal; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 185 of 2021 is dismissed; both RPs are instructed to cooperate and coordinate within the provisions of the IBC to preserve corporate assets.
summary: The RP of K-Lifestyle & Industries Ltd. appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order rejecting an application to direct the RP of sister company Krishna Knitwear Technology Ltd. to hand over physical possession of industrial land at Silvassa. Both companies were under independent CIRP proceedings. NCLAT held that without obtaining an order for Group Insolvency or consolidation of CIRPs, the RP of one corporate debtor cannot summarily wrest possession of assets held by another corporate debtor in a parallel insolvency process. Emphasizing professional coordination under IBC and recourse to IBBI, NCLAT refused to entertain the appeal and dismissed it.

case_title: Vipra Containers Pvt. Ltd. vs. Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi & Haryana
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Vipra Containers Pvt. Ltd. (represented by its Authorized Representative); Respondent is the Registrar of Companies (ROC), NCT of Delhi & Haryana. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Incorporation of private company for intended container manufacturing and acquisition of industrial plot. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Complete continuous failure to file statutory annual returns and financial statements from inception in 2010 until striking off in 2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company incorporated on 12.03.2010; ROC struck off the company's name via notice ROC-DEL/248(5)/STK-7/2879 dated 30.06.2017; Appeal No. 386/252/ND/2019 dismissed by NCLT New Delhi Court IV on 31.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant produced an Agreement to Sell dated 08.10.2010 for Rs. 34,15,000/- executed with Director Sajjan Kumar for an HSIIDC-allotted plot; allotment letter dated 31.07.2007 stood solely in Sajjan Kumar's individual name; no title transfer was ever executed, no business operations occurred, and no financial statements were placed on public record since 2010. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi dismissed the Section 252 appeal for company revival on 31.10.2019 finding no proof that the company was carrying on business or had assets.
legal_issues: Whether a company struck off by the ROC under Section 248 can be revived under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 when it has failed to file financial statements since its incorporation and fails to demonstrate that it was in bona fide operation or holding title to commercial assets.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A struck-off company cannot seek restoration under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 on grounds of equity or justness where it has remained completely dormant since inception, filed zero statutory returns, and failed to establish active commercial operations or ownership of corporate assets. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The 'otherwise just' requirement under Section 252 requires tangible, contemporaneous documentary proof of active operations, statutory compliance attempts, or legitimate asset holdings belonging directly to the corporate entity. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict evidentiary assessment of actual business activities; private unperfected agreements to purchase land from a promoter without conveyance or statutory filings fail to satisfy the threshold of an active enterprise. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The company was never operational and owned no property in its own name since 2010; the ROC acted well within statutory authority in striking it off.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 38 of 2020 is dismissed; the impugned order of NCLT Court IV New Delhi dated 31.10.2019 upholding the strike-off is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Vipra Containers Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi decision refusing to restore its name to the Register of Companies under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013. The company was incorporated in 2010 and struck off in 2017 after failing to file any statutory financial returns since incorporation. It claimed it had purchased land via an unexecuted agreement with its director. NCLAT held that the allotment was solely in the director's individual name, the company never engaged in any business operations, and no grounds of equity existed to warrant revival. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Board Ltd. & Ors. vs. C.A. Jalesh Kumar Grover, Resolution Professional
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Board Ltd. & Ors. (statutory electricity distribution licensee); Respondent is C.A. Jalesh Kumar Grover, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor GPI Textiles Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Continuous supply of essential high-tension industrial electricity energy to the manufacturing facility of the Corporate Debtor during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding operational electricity dues accumulated during the CIRP period comprising unpaid current energy consumption tariffs alongside statutory electricity duties and late payment surcharges. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP pending; interim application I.A. No. 335 of 2020 filed by the Resolution Professional before NCLT; impugned order passed on 15.12.2020; appeal preferred with a 14-day delay which was condoned under suo motu limitation extension powers. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants produced statutory tariff orders mandating late payment surcharges and accumulated electricity duties showing that the CIRP arrears far exceeded the nominal clearing rate, while the RP demonstrated that a Resolution Plan for GPI Textiles Ltd. was already pending consideration before the Adjudicating Authority which would address statutory CIRP dues on priority. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT disposed of I.A. No. 335 of 2020 on 15.12.2020 directing Appellants not to disconnect electricity supply so long as the Corporate Debtor pays current monthly consumption charges plus Rs. 10 Lakhs per month towards CIRP period arrears.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can restrain an electricity distribution licensee from disconnecting power supply to a Corporate Debtor undergoing CIRP under Section 14 while fixing an installment schedule for CIRP-period power dues that overlooks statutory surcharges and tariff orders; and how the balance between preserving the going-concern status of the Corporate Debtor and the statutory rights of the utility provider must be struck.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While essential utility supplies to a corporate debtor must be protected under Section 14 to preserve its going-concern status and avoid industrial closure, the repayment installment schedule for admitted CIRP consumption dues must remain balanced, reasonable, and proportionate without unjustly impairing the utility provider's statutory tariff recoveries. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(2) and Section 14(2A) require current consumption dues during CIRP to be cleared to avoid disconnection, and any arrangement for past CIRP liabilities must balance the corporate debtor's liquidity constraints with the utility provider's statutory rights, subject to priority payment under the ultimate resolution plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Commercial viability and going-concern balancing test: weighing the risk of shutting down plant operations against the sufficiency of cash flows to liquidate utility debts incurred by the insolvency administration. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: To prevent the debtor from grinding to a halt while more appropriately addressing the utility board's accumulated charges, the monthly installment directed towards CIRP arrears is enhanced from Rs. 10 Lakhs to Rs. 12 Lakhs per month, preserving the licensee's statutory right to disconnect if current monthly consumption charges are not paid.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 15.12.2020 is modified in paragraph 8 by enhancing the monthly installment payable towards CIRP period electricity dues from Rs. 10 Lakhs to Rs. 12 Lakhs per month alongside timely clearance of current monthly consumption bills; in the event of default in clearing current monthly energy consumption bills, the Appellant board is granted liberty to discontinue electricity supply in accordance with law; appeal disposed of with directions communicated forthwith.
summary: Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Board appealed an NCLT order restraining it from disconnecting power supply to GPI Textiles Ltd. provided the company paid current monthly bills plus Rs. 10 Lakhs towards CIRP period arrears. The utility argued that the installment amount overlooked statutory late surcharges and duty. NCLAT held that maintaining the corporate debtor as a going concern is paramount, but the recovery schedule for CIRP utility dues must be equitable. The Appellate Tribunal modified the order by enhancing the monthly installment to Rs. 12 Lakhs, affirming that failure to pay current monthly consumption bills permits disconnection under law.

case_title: M/s. Marinaindia Traexim Pvt. Ltd. vs. Union Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s. Marinaindia Traexim Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 1 is Union Bank of India (Lead Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Approved resolution plan submitted by Appellant for the resolution of the Corporate Debtor in CP IB-343(PB)/2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on total banking credit facilities amounting to approximately Rs. 550 Crores advanced by a consortium of financial creditors; Appellant's resolution plan offered a settlement value of merely Rs. 24 Crores (less than 5% of the total admitted claim). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved by Committee of Creditors with a 72.30% majority voting share; Adjudicating Authority approved the Resolution Plan under Section 31 via impugned order dated 04.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Serious discrepancy revealed between total loans advanced (Rs. 550 Crores) and collateral security held by the financial institutions, with bank officials failing to explain the massive security deficit during NCLT proceedings, prompting NCLT to record adverse remarks in paragraphs 14, 15, and 16 directing RBI and bank CMDs to investigate internal banking malfeasance. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi approved the resolution plan on 04.01.2021 while issuing investigative directions against lending officials; Successful Resolution Applicant appealed challenging solely those adverse observations.
legal_issues: Whether a Successful Resolution Applicant whose resolution plan has been formally sanctioned and approved under Section 31 of the IBC has standing as an 'aggrieved person' under Section 61(1) to challenge internal regulatory and administrative inquiry directions issued by the Adjudicating Authority to the Reserve Bank of India and heads of lending banks regarding collateral deficiencies.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity whose resolution plan has been fully approved without any adverse findings or sanctions directed against it lacks locus standi to appeal under Section 61 of the IBC, as an appeal does not lie against internal administrative inquiry directions issued to banking regulators and lenders. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'person aggrieved' under Section 61(1) of the IBC requires an actual, direct legal injury or deprivation of rights under the code, which does not encompass speculative operational apprehensions regarding future credit facilities from investigated lenders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of direct legal injury; absent an adverse finding or encumbrance on the approved plan itself, speculative assertions that investigated banks might hesitate to extend financing cannot sustain appellate maintainability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is fundamentally frivolous and maintained at the behest of undisclosed parties seeking to insulate bank officials from administrative scrutiny; since the resolution plan stands fully approved, no appeal lies.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 141 of 2021 is dismissed as frivolous; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Marinaindia Traexim Pvt. Ltd., the successful resolution applicant whose resolution plan of Rs. 24 Crores against total bank debts of Rs. 550 Crores was approved by NCLT Principal Bench, appealed against paragraphs 14-16 of the approval order. Those paragraphs directed RBI and CMDs of creditor banks to investigate officials responsible for gross under-collateralization. The Appellant argued that the directions created apprehension that banks would deny future credit. NCLAT dismissed the appeal as frivolous, holding that an applicant whose plan was approved suffered no legal grievance, had no standing to protect bank officials from inquiry, and could not be considered an 'aggrieved person'.

case_title: BRS Ventures Investment Ltd. vs. GIR Logistics Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is BRS Ventures Investment Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is GIR Logistics Pvt. Ltd. (custodian/warehouse bailee); Respondent No. 2 is the Corporate Debtor/Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Custody, storage, and release of commercial goods lying in the warehouse of Respondent No. 1 during corporate insolvency proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Procedural failure by the Appellant to lift and recover admitted goods lying with the logistics provider within the consented 7-day timeline. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned consent order passed by NCLT Guwahati Bench on 23.02.2021 providing a 7-day period to retrieve goods; extension application filed by Appellant before NCLT; simultaneous appeal filed before NCLAT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT record demonstrating that order dated 23.02.2021 was entered into by consensus between both sides, and that an application for enlargement of time to lift the cargo was actively sub judice before the NCLT when the appeal was instituted. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati Bench directed Respondent on 23.02.2021 to release goods within seven days on agreed terms or Appellant's entitlement would stand extinguished; Appellant approached NCLT for time extension while simultaneously preferring this appeal to vacate the forfeiture clause.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC is maintainable against a consent order passed by the Adjudicating Authority based on mutual agreement; and whether a party can simultaneously prosecute an application for extension of time before the NCLT while challenging the underlying conditional forfeiture in the appellate forum.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order passed by the Adjudicating Authority based on consensus and mutual agreement of the parties operates as a consent order and is not subject to appellate review under Section 61; simultaneously pursuing identical extension reliefs before the original forum while filing an appeal constitutes impermissible forum hunting. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61 appellate jurisdiction does not encompass consensual or agreed directions where no contentious legal or factual determination has been adjudicated adversarially by the Adjudicating Authority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Doctrine of consent estoppel and election of remedies; admissions on record showing the underlying order was based on consensus and that identical extension applications were actively pending before the primary bench. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant cannot invoke appellate jurisdiction against its own consented timelines while its extension application remains pending before the lower bench; the appeal is an abuse of process and legally defective.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 232 of 2021 is dismissed without costs; the practice of simultaneous forum hunting is deprecated.
summary: Appellant BRS Ventures Investment Ltd. challenged an order of NCLT Guwahati Bench which directed GIR Logistics Pvt. Ltd. to release goods to the Appellant within seven days pursuant to mutual consensus, failing which rights in the goods would stand extinguished. The Appellant approached NCLT for an extension of time while simultaneously filing an appeal before NCLAT to set aside the forfeiture condition. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that an order founded upon consensus cannot be appealed under Section 61 and that pursuing identical relief across both forums concurrently amounts to impermissible forum hunting.

case_title: Manoharlal Mehta & Ors. vs. Anil Vrijdas Rajkotia, Resolution Professional of K K Welding Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Mr. Manoharlal Mehta & Ors. (shareholders/promoters of the Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Anil Vrijdas Rajkotia, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor K K Welding Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of K K Welding Ltd. wherein statutory invitation for expressions of interest yielded zero viable bids. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt obligations leading to admission of CIRP; complete insolvency failure during resolution period with no Resolution Applicants submitting proposals. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Committee of Creditors (CoC) convened meeting on 03.09.2020 resolving to liquidate Corporate Debtor; Section 33 liquidation application allowed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-1 on 07.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CIRP records confirming that no Expression of Interest (EoI) was received during the CIRP period and the CoC resolved with requisite voting majority to liquidate the Corporate Debtor, with Corporate Debtor participating in and being duly represented during liquidation hearings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed liquidation application under Section 33 following CoC approval; NCLT Mumbai Bench allowed the application on 07.01.2021; Appellants appealed alleging denial of personal hearing and violation of natural justice.
legal_issues: Whether an order of liquidation passed under Section 33(2) of the IBC based on the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in the total absence of any Expression of Interest is subject to judicial review; and whether suspended promoters/shareholders are entitled to challenge liquidation on grounds of natural justice when the Corporate Debtor was duly represented.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution passed by the Committee of Creditors to liquidate a Corporate Debtor in exercise of its commercial wisdom—especially where no Expression of Interest has been received—is non-justiciable and not amenable to judicial review by the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under the Explanation to Section 33(2) inserted by Act No. 26 of 2019, the CoC is vested with paramount statutory authority to liquidate the Corporate Debtor at any stage after constitution and before plan approval, affirming that commercial decisions on liquidation remain beyond the purview of judicial intervention. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective verification of statutory compliance: proof of issuance of Form G, absence of any compliant Expression of Interest, and due passage of the CoC liquidation resolution with the requisite statutory majority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The lack of any prospective resolution applicant left no statutory option but liquidation; because the Corporate Debtor was fully represented before the NCLT, allegations of breach of natural justice are groundless.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 135 of 2021 is dismissed for lack of merit; order of liquidation dated 07.01.2021 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-1 is upheld.
summary: Appellants, shareholders of K K Welding Ltd., challenged an NCLT Mumbai order ordering liquidation under Section 33 of the IBC on grounds of lack of hearing and breach of natural justice. During the CIRP, no Expression of Interest was received, leading the Committee of Creditors to resolve on 03.09.2020 to liquidate the Corporate Debtor. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that under the Explanation to Section 33(2), the CoC possesses absolute pre-eminent commercial authority to resolve upon liquidation, which is not amenable to judicial review, and that natural justice was satisfied since the Corporate Debtor was duly represented.

case_title: Nilesh Sharma (Resolution Professional of Today Homes and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.) vs. Suspended Board of Directors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Nilesh Sharma, Resolution Professional of Today Homes and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is the Suspended Board of Directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ongoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Today Homes and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory CIRP timeline computation; dispute concerned exclusion of 29 days from the 180/270-day CIRP period. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Period of 29 days from 25.12.2019 to 23.01.2020 spent in handing over charge from the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) to the Resolution Professional (RP). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record showing delay during transition between IRP and RP rendering RP unable to take over charge, alongside suo motu nationwide lockdown orders under Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 01 of 2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 3930 of 2020 in (IB)-2130(ND) 2019 seeking exclusion of 131 days (23.03.2020 to 31.07.2020); NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court-II) on 05.02.2021 excluded 97 days but rejected the prayer to exclude 29 days (25.12.2019 to 23.01.2020), prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the period consumed in handing over charge and statutory records from the Interim Resolution Professional to the newly appointed Resolution Professional can be excluded from the computation of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process timeline under Section 12 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Time lost due to administrative deadlock or delays during the formal handover of charge from an Interim Resolution Professional to a Resolution Professional, which renders the resolution professional unable to function, must be excluded from the CIRP timeline. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 CIRP duration is intended to encompass active resolution, justifying exclusion of periods where the resolution process is unavoidably stalled through no fault of the applicant. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Establishing actual inability of the Resolution Professional to take over functional charge and manage debtor operations during the transition window. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in refusing exclusion for the handover window; 29 days from 25.12.2019 to 23.01.2020 plus time spent pursuing IA 3930 of 2020 must be excluded.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order rejecting exclusion of 29 days (25.12.2019 to 23.01.2020) is set aside; time spent pursuing IA No. 3930 of 2020 is also excluded from the CIRP process; no order as to costs.
summary: Nilesh Sharma, Resolution Professional of Today Homes and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT New Delhi order that granted partial lockdown exclusion but refused to exclude a 29-day period (25.12.2019 to 23.01.2020) consumed in handing over charge from the IRP to the RP under Section 12. Relying on established precedent regarding unavoidable administrative transition delays, the NCLAT set aside the rejection, allowing the exclusion of the 29 days as well as the period spent pursuing the interlocutory application.

case_title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. vs. A.P. Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. Through Rajiv Khurana Resolution Professional & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. (major secured financial creditor with 84.35% voting share in the CoC); Respondent No. 1 is Corporate Debtor A.P. Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. through RP Rajiv Khurana; Respondent No. 2 is the Successful Resolution Applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution Plan approved by CoC on 19.07.2019 and confirmed by NCLT on 18.03.2020 in CA No. 610/2019 under CP (IB) No. 119/Chd/CHD/2018 with a 48-month payment timeline. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Out of total upfront payment of Rs. 5,00,17,650, the Resolution Applicant paid Rs. 3,00,17,650 (approx. 60%), leaving Rs. 2,00,00,000 unpaid due to pandemic disruption. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The national lockdown occurred between 25.03.2020 and 31.07.2020; impugned NCLT exclusion order passed on 12.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Applicant took over the Corporate Debtor in May 2020 and remitted 60% of upfront funds despite severe disruption during the COVID-19 pandemic. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Applications IA No. 287/2020 and 483/2020 were filed seeking extension; NCLT Chandigarh Bench on 12.01.2021 excluded the lockdown period (25.03.2020 to 31.07.2020) from the plan payment schedule, which Kotak Mahindra Bank challenged.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the power to exclude the COVID-19 lockdown period from the schedule of payments in an approved Resolution Plan without requiring prior approval or consent from the Committee of Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a Resolution Plan is approved under Section 31(1), the Committee of Creditors becomes functus officio/irrelevant, governance shifts to the Monitoring Committee, and the Adjudicating Authority holds jurisdiction to extend payment timelines by excluding COVID-19 lockdown disruptions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) transfers debtor supervision away from the CoC; Regulation 40C of the IBBI CIRP Regulations along with suo motu judicial orders empowers exclusion of lockdown periods from IBC activity timelines. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Substantial bona fide compliance during severe disruption, evidenced by the Resolution Applicant paying 60% of the upfront amount during a global pandemic. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority acted within jurisdiction and sound discretion in excluding the lockdown period from the payment schedule; CoC consent was unnecessary.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT Chandigarh Bench order dated 12.01.2021 excluding the lockdown period from 25.03.2020 to 31.07.2020 from the approved Resolution Plan payment timeline.
summary: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Chandigarh Bench which excluded the lockdown period (25.03.2020 to 31.07.2020) from the payment schedule of an approved Resolution Plan for A.P. Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. The bank argued that as the majority financial creditor, its CoC consent was mandatory for any schedule extension. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that upon plan approval under Section 31(1), the CoC becomes functus officio and the Monitoring Committee assumes control. Considering Regulation 40C, Supreme Court suo motu directives, and the applicant's 60% upfront payment, the exclusion was valid.

case_title: Chandra Shekhar Ramrakhiya vs. M/s Radhakrishna Acua Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Respondent No. 1 (M/s Radhakrishna Acua Pvt. Ltd.) is the Operational Creditor; Respondent No. 2 (Digital Micron Roto Print Private Limited) is the Corporate Debtor; Appellant (Chandra Shekhar Ramrakhiya) is an erstwhile member of the Suspended Board of Directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational debt arising from the supply of goods under commercial invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default evidenced by the dishonour of 14 post-dated cheques issued by the Corporate Debtor toward discharging its operational liability. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8(1) demand notice was served on the Corporate Debtor on 11th September 2019, which received no response or reply. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational debt and default proved by 14 dishonoured cheques; no documentary evidence or communications demonstrating any pre-existing dispute regarding the quality of goods. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application admitted ex parte by NCLT Indore Bench at Ahmedabad on 11th January 2021 after limited court notices were ignored; appealed by the suspended director alleging lack of notice.
legal_issues: Whether an ex parte Section 9 admission order breaches natural justice when statutory and judicial notices were ignored, and whether debt default is established where 14 post-dated cheques were dishonoured without any pre-existing dispute.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Admission of a Section 9 application ex parte does not violate principles of natural justice where statutory demand and tribunal notices were served and unheeded, and default is established by dishonoured cheques without pre-existing dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Failure to respond to a Section 8(1) demand notice coupled with dishonour of cheques constitutes an unrefuted admission of default under Section 9. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In absence of pre-existing dispute regarding quality of goods or invoice discharge, dishonoured negotiable instruments sufficiently satisfy the threshold of debt and default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor committed default on operational debt, justifying CIRP admission; an MSME debtor seeking settlement must proceed via Section 12A through the CoC.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, sustaining the admission order dated 11th January 2021; liberty is granted to approach the CoC through the IRP for settlement under Section 12A of the Code.
summary: Chandra Shekhar Ramrakhiya, suspended director of Digital Micron Roto Print Pvt. Ltd., appealed an ex parte NCLT order admitting an operational creditor's Section 9 petition. The appellant alleged lack of intimation and denial of natural justice. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that the demand notice served on 11.09.2019 was ignored, 14 post-dated cheques had dishonoured, and no pre-existing dispute regarding goods existed, affirming that settlement attempts must proceed via Section 12A.

case_title: Dr. Krishan Mohan Mendiratta vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Dr. Krishan Mohan Mendiratta, suspended director of the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (financial creditor); Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional; Dr. Rajendar Singh is an unsuccessful resolution applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bidding and evaluation of Resolution Plans during CIRP of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Competing resolution plan figures: Successful Resolution Applicant plan valued at Rs. 30.10 Crores; Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant plan valued at Rs. 32 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC approved the Rs. 30.10 Crore plan, which was pending approval before the Adjudicating Authority. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC evaluated the Rs. 32 Crore bid and determined it was neither viable nor feasible; no procedural illegality in the bidding process was alleged. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an application before NCLT New Delhi (Principal Bench) seeking consideration of the higher Rs. 32 Crore offer; NCLT dismissed it on 13.01.2021 for lack of locus standi, which was appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a member of the suspended Board of Directors, who is statutorily disqualified from submitting a resolution plan, has locus standi to maintain an appeal espousing the cause of an unsuccessful third-party resolution applicant against the commercial wisdom of the CoC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An ineligible, suspended director is a stranger/alien to the resolution bidding arena and has no legal locus standi to champion the cause of an unsuccessful resolution applicant or challenge the commercial decision of the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: IBC policy bars ineligible insiders from entering the CIRP bidding process directly or indirectly; they cannot meddle in resolution evaluation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Absence of any legal authorization to represent the unsuccessful applicant and absence of procedural illegality in the CoC's feasibility assessment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Commercial wisdom of the CoC approving a Rs. 30.10 Crore plan as feasible over an unviable Rs. 32 Crore plan cannot be assailed by an ineligible insider without locus standi.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as not maintainable.
summary: Dr. Krishan Mohan Mendiratta, a suspended director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed an NCLT order dismissing his application to compel the CoC to consider an unsuccessful resolution applicant's higher offer of Rs. 32 Crores over the approved Rs. 30.10 Crore plan. The NCLAT held that because the appellant was disqualified from submitting a plan and did not participate in the bidding process, he had no locus standi to espouse the cause of an unsuccessful bidder or meddle in CIRP proceedings, dismissing the appeal as non-maintainable.

case_title: Pandurang Ramchandra Shinde & Ors. vs. Vijendra Kumar Jain
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Pandurang Ramchandra Shinde & Ors., members of the Suspended Board of Directors; Respondent is Vijendra Kumar Jain, Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP initiated under Section 7 by IDBI Bank against the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure and refusal by suspended directors to hand over possession of corporate debtor assets, specifically a residential bungalow in District Satara, Maharashtra. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Moratorium declared upon Section 7 admission; CoC subsequently approved a resolution plan which was submitted to NCLT for approval. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Undisputed proof that the residential bungalow is an asset belonging to the Corporate Debtor, occupied by the suspended director. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 1390 of 2020 under Sections 19(2), 25(2)(a), and 70 seeking recovery of documents and residential bungalow; NCLT Mumbai Bench on 07.01.2021 directed directors to hand over the property, which was appealed on hardship grounds due to senior citizen status.
legal_issues: Whether personal hardship and senior citizen status of a suspended director can override the statutory duty under Section 19 and Section 25(2)(a) to hand over possession of Corporate Debtor assets covered by a Section 14 moratorium during CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Personal hardship, age, or accommodation difficulties do not create a legal right for suspended directors to retain possession of Corporate Debtor assets, which must be surrendered to the Resolution Professional to ensure resolution completion. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 19(2) and 25(2)(a) mandate the Resolution Professional to take custody and control of all assets belonging to the Corporate Debtor; continued unauthorized occupation obstructs resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Ownership of the asset vesting in the Corporate Debtor and operation of the statutory moratorium under Section 14. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Continued occupation by the suspended director is legally unsustainable and impedes conclusion of the CIRP; dismissal is mandated while allowing reasonable administrative grace to find accommodation.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as legally unsustainable; liberty is granted to the Appellants to approach the Adjudicating Authority for extension of time to find alternative accommodation; copy of order directed to NCLT.
summary: Pandurang Ramchandra Shinde, a suspended director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed an NCLT Mumbai order directing him under Sections 19(2) and 25(2)(a) to vacate and surrender possession of a corporate-owned residential bungalow to the RP. The appellant sought to retain possession citing senior citizen status and difficulty in finding alternative housing. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that personal hardship cannot override the statutory mandate requiring delivery of corporate debtor assets to the RP, but granted liberty to seek time extension before the NCLT.

case_title: Commercial Tax Department Government of Rajasthan vs. Mr. Kalpraj Dharamshi & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Commercial Tax Department, Government of Rajasthan (Government Authority/Creditor); Respondents are Mr. Kalpraj Dharamshi & Ors. (Successful Resolution Applicants/Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory tax dues/operational debts payable to the Commercial Tax Department arising during resolution proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Condonation of delay of 341 days sought in filing appeal against NCLT order dated 28th November 2019; free certified copy received on 23rd January 2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 28-11-2019; certified copy made available on 23-01-2020; prescribed 30-day period and 15-day extendable period expired on 08-03-2020; suo moto limitation extension by Supreme Court/NCLAT commenced w.e.f. 25-03-2020; appeal filed on 29-01-2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Free-of-cost certified copy dated 23-01-2020 showing that the ordinary and condonable limitation period had already lapsed prior to the COVID-19 lockdown. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appeal was filed challenging the order of NCLT Mumbai Bench dated 28th November 2019 along with I.A. No. 338 of 2021 for condonation of 341 days delay, which was rejected by NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal has jurisdiction to condone a delay in filing an appeal beyond the maximum 45-day statutory limit (30 days plus 15-day discretionary extension) prescribed under Section 61(2) of the IBC, where the limitation period expired before the COVID-19 pandemic suo moto extension commenced on 25th March 2020.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate authority created under a special statute does not possess jurisdiction to condone delay beyond the outer statutory limit prescribed within the statute, and general suo moto extensions of limitation do not revive claims whose statutory condonable window already lapsed prior to the effective date of the extension. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC mandates a 30-day period extendable by a maximum of 15 days upon sufficient cause; the tribunal is not conferred with jurisdiction to condone any period beyond the total 45-day limit. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Calculation of the calendar limitation from the date of supply of the certified copy to determine if the outer boundary of 45 days expired prior to 25th March 2020. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The extended 45-day period expired on 8th March 2020, leaving a 16-day unexplainable gap before the 25th March 2020 suo moto relief, rendering the appeal hopelessly time-barred without jurisdiction to condone.
operative_order: I.A No. 338 of 2021 seeking condonation of delay is dismissed; consequently, Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 148 of 2021 is dismissed.
summary: The Appellant, Commercial Tax Department, Government of Rajasthan, preferred an appeal along with an application seeking condonation of 341 days delay against an order of the NCLT Mumbai Bench dated 28th November 2019. The certified copy was received on 23rd January 2020, meaning the 30-day statutory limitation under Section 61(2) of the IBC, along with the permissible 15-day extended period, expired on 8th March 2020. As the COVID-19 lockdown suo moto extension only operated from 25th March 2020, the NCLAT held that the 16-day delay beyond the outer limit could not be condoned due to lack of jurisdiction, dismissing both the application and the appeal.

case_title: Chandralekha Constructions Pvt. Ltd. vs. Khandelwal Group Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Chandralekha Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Khandelwal Group Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational transactions between the parties forming the subject matter of an insolvency application filed under Section 9 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and specific date arising out of operational debt subject to adjudication under the pending Section 9 application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Application under Section 9 pending at pre-admission stage; impugned rectification order passed on 4th March 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Interchanged application records and inadvertently swapped documents between two separate applications seeking initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Respondent/Operational Creditor applied before NCLT New Delhi (Court-IV) to rectify exchanged documents; the Adjudicating Authority permitted the curing of defects on 04-03-2021; Appellant challenged this interlocutory permission before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the legal duty and jurisdiction under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code to permit an applicant to rectify formal defects and swap back interchanged documents in a Section 9 application prior to the stage of admission or rejection.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses an affirmative statutory duty to permit an applicant to cure procedural defects and place complete, correct documents on record before proceeding to evaluate the admission or rejection of an insolvency petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5) of the IBC mandates that before deciding whether to admit or reject an application, opportunity must be provided to rectify any defect, making the pre-admission curing of formal errors mandatory and standard procedural law. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of whether the proposed rectification alters the substantive cause of action or merely rectifies a bona fide clerical and administrative error (exchanged documents). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Permitting substitution of misplaced records does not cause prejudice or amount to legal infirmity, but rather satisfies the statutory scheme of Section 9.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as devoid of merit. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to adhere to the mandate of Section 9(5) of the IBC and pass an order of admission or rejection within one week and report compliance to the Appellate Tribunal.
summary: Chandralekha Constructions Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an interlocutory order dated 4th March 2021 passed by NCLT New Delhi, which allowed the Operational Creditor, Khandelwal Group Pvt. Ltd., to rectify a clerical defect where documents between two Section 9 applications had been interchanged. The NCLAT held that it is the bounden statutory duty of the Adjudicating Authority to allow an applicant to cure defects before deciding on admission. Finding no infirmity in the order, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal and directed the NCLT to decide the Section 9 petition within one week pursuant to Section 9(5) of the IBC.

case_title: Delhi Gymkhana Club Ltd. vs. Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 94 of 2020 & Company Appeal (AT) No. 95 of 2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs (Petitioner/Appellant in CA 94/2020) and Delhi Gymkhana Club Ltd. along with its General Committee members (Respondents/Appellants in CA 95/2020). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operation and management of Delhi Gymkhana Club Ltd., incorporated in 1913 as a non-profit company limited by guarantee under Section 26 of the Companies Act, 1913 (now Section 8, Companies Act, 2013), occupying 27.03 acres of prime State perpetual leasehold land. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Waitlisted applicants deposited Rs. 44.79 Crores up to FY 2017-18 as application/registration fees; average vacancy was 120-135 per annum against a 37-year non-government waitlist; Club incurred over 60% expenditure on recreational pastimes and food/beverages (30.34% on catering, wine, and cigarettes) while expending less than 3% on its core objective of sports. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Inspection ordered under Section 206(5) on 16-03-2016; report submitted on 31-07-2019; MCA directed further probe on 13-09-2019; supplementary inspection report issued on 03-03-2020; Central Government sanction to file petition granted on 18-03-2020; interim NCLT order passed on 26-06-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Inspection reports revealing gross diversion of funds, unauthorized increase and retrospective revision of applicant fees, creation of fast-tracked hereditary user categories (dependents, Green Cards, UCPs) conferring benefits exclusively on relatives of permanent members while using applicant funds and accrued interest to subsidize recreational facilities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Union of India petitioned under Section 241(2) alleging prejudice to public interest and sought interim suspension of the GC; NCLT granted limited interim relief on 26-06-2020 (appointing two government observers and a special inquiry committee); Club appealed against the interim order/maintainability and Union of India appealed seeking full management takeover.
legal_issues: Whether subjective formation of opinion by the Central Government under Section 241(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 is justiciable on the ground of sufficiency of reasons; whether exclusionary, nepotistic governance and diversion of State perpetual leasehold resources by a Section 8 company constitute acts prejudicial to public interest; and whether NCLT's interim relief was inadequate warranting total suspension of the General Committee under Section 242(4).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An administrative opinion of the Central Government formed to trigger statutory investigative or remedial jurisdiction under corporate oppression/mismanagement provisions requires only the existence of objective material and not judicial scrutiny into the sufficiency of reasons; furthermore, where an entity operates on State largesse, exclusionary and hereditary monopolization of its facilities at the cost of public applicants violates public interest. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241(2) empowers the Central Government to petition the tribunal based on its subjective opinion supported by factual material; 'public interest' under Section 241(2) is not confined to the entirety of the populace but extends to any identifiable section of society whose rights or economic welfare are prejudiced; Section 242(4) permits broad, effective interlocutory orders regulating corporate affairs to prevent ongoing prejudice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of prima facie case, balance of convenience, and necessity of efficacious prevention where documentary inspection reports disclose structural illegality, financial manipulation, and hereditary monopolization. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Central Government possessed ample factual material to form its opinion, and the limited interim relief granted by NCLT was toothless; effective protection of public interest necessitated complete supersession of the General Committee and appointment of an Administrator.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 95 of 2020 filed by the Club is dismissed; Company Appeal (AT) No. 94 of 2020 filed by Union of India is allowed. The interim order of the NCLT is modified to suspend the General Committee of the Club and appoint an Administrator nominated by the Union of India to manage the Club's affairs, with an embargo on accepting new memberships or fee increases until disposal of waitlisted applications, to be implemented within two weeks.
summary: The Union of India initiated proceedings under Section 241(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 against Delhi Gymkhana Club Ltd., alleging gross mismanagement, diversion of prime leased land away from sports promotion towards elite recreational pastimes, and hereditary conferring of memberships using Rs. 44.79 Crores collected from long-pending waitlisted applicants[cite: 11]. On cross-appeals from an interlocutory order of NCLT New Delhi, the NCLAT affirmed that the Central Government formed a valid opinion based on extensive inspection reports and that public interest was heavily implicated[cite: 11]. Holding NCLT's interim relief inadequate, NCLAT suspended the Club's General Committee and directed the appointment of a Government-nominated Administrator[cite: 11].

case_title: Ashok Agarwal vs. Amitex Polymers Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ashok Agarwal, Sole Proprietor of M/s Shree Marketing (Operational Creditor); Respondent is Amitex Polymers Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply and sale of chemicals and operational materials pursuant to purchase order dated 17.02.2011 with payment agreed within 30 days of invoice. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal debt of Rs. 7,50,000/- based on unpaid invoices from 19.02.2011 to 26.03.2011 plus Rs. 1,35,000/- penalty (Rs. 5,000/- per instalment per month for default) totaling Rs. 8,85,000/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Civil Suit No. 6912/2016 compromised vide Settlement Agreement dated 16.08.2018; Consent Decree passed on 25.10.2018; Section 8 demand notice issued on 11.03.2019 and dispatched on 13.03.2019 and 01.04.2019 via official email. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purchase orders, acknowledged delivery invoices, settlement agreement dated 16.08.2018, written undertaking and consent decree dated 25.10.2018 before Saket Court, dishonored post-dated settlement cheques, and MCA portal master data email records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 9 petition (CP (IB) No. 1895/ND/2019); NCLT New Delhi dismissed it on 08.06.2020 holding that a decree holder is not an operational creditor and that demand notice was not delivered at the physical registered office.
legal_issues: Whether a decree holder holding a consent decree arising out of an underlying operational transaction constitutes an 'Operational Creditor' entitled to trigger CIRP under Section 9 of the IBC, and whether service of a demand notice to the official corporate email ID available on the MCA portal constitutes valid service under Section 8 read with statutory presumptions.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The crystallisation of an underlying operational or commercial debt into a civil court decree or consent decree does not extinguish the intrinsic character of the debt, and a decree holder remains an eligible operational or financial creditor entitled to maintain insolvency proceedings under the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(10) defines 'creditor' inclusively to include decree-holders; reading Section 3(10) with Section 5(20) and Section 5(21), an operational creditor does not lose standing merely because the operational claim has merged into a decree of a competent court; furthermore, delivery of a demand notice to the company's registered official email satisfies Section 8. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification that the claim originates from the supply of goods/services and that subsequent consent decrees and undertakings constitute continuous, valid admissions of operational liability without creating a jurisdictional bar. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A decree-holder founded on an operational transaction is an Operational Creditor under Section 5(20); the NCLT committed reversible error in holding the petition non-maintainable and ignoring valid email service.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated 08.06.2020 passed by NCLT New Delhi in IB No. 1895/ND/2019 is quashed and set aside. Appellant is directed to file the certified copy of the impugned order within two weeks. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant supplied chemicals to the Corporate Debtor in 2011, and following a civil suit, parties executed a Settlement Agreement leading to a Consent Decree dated 25.10.2018 for Rs. 7,50,000/- plus penalty[cite: 12]. When post-dated cheques bounced, Appellant issued a Section 8 notice to the registered email and filed a Section 9 application[cite: 12]. NCLT New Delhi dismissed the petition on the premise that a decree-holder is excluded from the definition of an Operational Creditor and notice service was defective[cite: 12]. The NCLAT reversed the decision, ruling that obtaining a decree does not destroy the operational nature of the debt or creditor status under Section 5(20) and that official portal email dispatch constitutes valid service, setting aside the dismissal[cite: 12].
ALLOW

case_title: Om Prakash Agrawal vs. Chief Commissioner of Income Tax (TDS) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Om Prakash Agrawal, Liquidator of S. Kumars Nationwide Limited (Corporate Debtor in Liquidation); Respondent No. 1 is Chief Commissioner of Income Tax (TDS); Respondent No. 2 is UPL Limited (Successful Auction Purchaser). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale of immovable assets of the Corporate Debtor by the Liquidator in a public auction for a total sale consideration of Rs. 43 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Attempted 1% TDS deduction of Rs. 43,00,000/- under Section 194-IA of the Income Tax Act, 1961 from the total sale consideration. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Assets auctioned in liquidation; Respondent No. 2 sought to deduct TDS; Liquidator filed application before NCLT Principal Bench; application dismissed by NCLT on 11.06.2020; appeal heard and disposed of on 08.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: E-auction documentation, correspondence from auction purchaser seeking to deduct 1% TDS, and proof of deposit of TDS amount with the Income Tax Department. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an application before NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi seeking directions to restrain the bidder from deducting 1% TDS and directing full payment under the waterfall mechanism of Section 53; NCLT dismissed the application holding TDS is not a preferential recovery; Liquidator appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the requirement to deduct 1% Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on the sale of immovable property under Section 194-IA of the Income Tax Act, 1961 is inconsistent with the statutory distribution waterfall under Section 53(1)(e) of the IBC, and whether Section 53 overrides Section 194-IA by operation of Section 238 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory provisions mandating advance deduction/collection of taxes at source from asset sales during corporate liquidation impermissibly siphon estate proceeds outside the statutory priority regime, and must yield to the non-obstante distribution waterfall established under insolvency law. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Deduction of 1% TDS under Section 194-IA of the Income Tax Act constitutes advance capital gains tax recovered directly by the revenue; under Section 53(1)(e) of the IBC, government dues are relegated to fifth priority; because Section 53 contains a non-obstante clause while Section 194-IA does not, Section 53 overrides Section 194-IA by virtue of Section 238 of the IBC; furthermore, liquidators under the Code have no statutory obligation to file income tax returns or pursue administrative refund claims. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Conflict analysis between fiscal withholding mechanisms and the mandatory insolvency distribution framework. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Deduction of TDS under Section 194-IA directly disrupts the Section 53 waterfall; the Income Tax Department cannot recover tax in priority through deduction at source on liquidation sales, and any deposited amount must be refunded to the liquidator.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order of NCLT Principal Bench dated 11.06.2020 is set aside. Respondent No. 1 (Income Tax Department) is directed to refund the TDS amount deposited by Respondent No. 2 to the Appellant-Liquidator. No order as to costs.
summary: During the liquidation of S. Kumars Nationwide Limited, the Liquidator sold immovable property to UPL Limited for Rs. 43 Crores[cite: 13]. UPL Limited deducted 1% TDS (Rs. 43 Lakhs) under Section 194-IA of the Income Tax Act, 1961 and deposited it with the revenue[cite: 13]. The NCLT refused to direct non-deduction, holding TDS is merely collection and not priority recovery[cite: 13]. On appeal, the NCLAT reversed the order, holding that Section 194-IA TDS is advance capital gains tax which conflicts with the statutory waterfall under Section 53(1)(e) of the IBC[cite: 13]. Exercising Section 238 override, the NCLAT directed Respondent No. 1 to refund the deducted TDS amount to the Liquidator[cite: 13].

case_title: Bharat Aluminium Co. Ltd. vs. M/s J.P. Engineers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Bharat Aluminium Company Limited (Beneficiary/Creditor); Respondent No. 1 is M/s J.P. Engineers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is Andhra Bank/Union Bank of India (Guarantor/Surety Bank). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement dated 01.04.2019 for the sale and purchase of aluminium products between Appellant and Corporate Debtor, secured by a financial bank guarantee. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in supply payments; bank guarantee issued on 22.04.2019 for Rs. 1,60,00,000/- with extended validity up to 21.04.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 26.02.2020; Appellant issued bank guarantee invocation letter on 03.03.2020; legal notice issued on 20.03.2020; Bank refused encashment on 27.03.2020 citing moratorium; NCLT order passed on 31.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Irrevocable and unconditional bank guarantee No. 016219/GPR0021 dated 22.04.2019, written bank extension letter dated 21.10.2019, demand letters, and refusal communications from Andhra Bank. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed I.A. No. 2085/ND/2020 to encash guarantee; Bank filed I.A. No. 2572/ND/2020 to restrain invocation; NCLT New Delhi (Bench-II) restrained Appellant on 31.07.2020 holding financial guarantees are security interests hit by Section 14; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an unconditional and irrevocable financial bank guarantee executed by a bank on behalf of a Corporate Debtor can be invoked and encashed by the beneficiary during the moratorium period in light of Section 14(3)(b) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A moratorium operating against a corporate debtor does not interdict the invocation and encashment of an independent, irrevocable, and unconditional financial bank guarantee issued by a third-party lending institution as surety. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(3)(b) of the IBC expressly exempts a surety in a contract of guarantee to a corporate debtor from the scope of Section 14(1) moratorium; the 2018 amendment is clarificatory and retrospective, restricting moratorium protection strictly to the corporate debtor's assets and not extending it to third-party bank sureties. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Autonomous contract principle governing unconditional bank guarantees, where the bank is bound to pay upon demand without demur, independent of disputes or insolvency of the principal debtor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT failed to consider the amended Section 14(3)(b); the bank guarantee does not form part of the corporate debtor's estate, and the beneficiary has an absolute right to encash the guarantee against the surety bank.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 31.07.2020 passed by NCLT New Delhi is set aside. Respondent No. 2's application (I.A. No. 2572/ND/2020) is dismissed, and Appellant's application (I.A. No. 2085/ND/2020) is allowed, declaring that the bank guarantee in question can be invoked and encashed during the moratorium period. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant held an unconditional financial bank guarantee of Rs. 1.60 Crores issued by Andhra Bank to secure payment for aluminium supplies to J.P. Engineers Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 14]. After the Corporate Debtor entered CIRP on 26.02.2020, Appellant sought encashment of the guarantee on 03.03.2020, which the bank refused citing Section 14 moratorium[cite: 14]. The NCLT restrained the Appellant from encashing the guarantee[cite: 14]. On appeal, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT order, ruling that under Section 14(3)(b) of the IBC, moratorium does not protect third-party sureties, allowing the Appellant to encash the guarantee against the bank[cite: 14].

case_title: Narayan Singh Pathania vs. Valuelabs LLP & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Narayan Singh Pathania, Managing Director of Global Energy Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Valuelabs LLP (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Corporate Debtor through IRP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Solar Power Purchase Agreement (SPPA) dated 18.06.2013 and addendums dated 09.10.2014, 10.07.2015, and 13.12.2016 for supply of solar electricity generated by Respondent No. 1 into the grid for consumption by consumers under wheeling/banking arrangements. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 1,08,77,104/- under initial unpaid invoices and Rs. 2,09,81,027/- under subsequent invoices dated 21.02.2017 to 20.04.2018, totaling an operational debt exceeding Rs. 3.18 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised periodically from 07.01.2016; Section 8 demand notice issued on 08.05.2018; delayed reply issued on 01.06.2018; Section 9 petition filed on 06.06.2018; admission order passed on 02.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SPPA contracts, DISCOM Generation Credit Notes and monthly Energy Settlement Reports, unpaid invoices, and continuous email correspondence from 03.08.2017 to 07.04.2018 showing repeated payment reminders. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application CP (IB) No. 2520/MB/2019 before NCLT Mumbai Bench; NCLT admitted CIRP on 02.12.2019; Managing Director appealed under Section 61 asserting pre-existing dispute over tariff/banked energy.
legal_issues: Whether an unverified, generic plea of 'pending account reconciliation' and data corruption, raised without disputing invoice rates prior to the Section 8 demand notice, satisfies the threshold of a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 8(2) and Section 9 of the IBC pursuant to the Mobilox standard.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A vague plea of pending account reconciliation or data corruption raised in response to repeated commercial demands does not constitute a genuine pre-existing dispute under the IBC, and an after-thought dispute regarding pricing raised post-notice or during litigation is a moonshine defense. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5) of the IBC, the dispute must exist prior to the receipt of the statutory demand notice; where operational debt above the statutory threshold is unpaid and supported by billing records, the adjudicating authority is mandated to admit the application in the absence of a plausible pre-existing controversy. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Mobilox Innovations test—determining whether the debtor raised a plausible, substantiated contention requiring further inquiry or merely put forth a patently feeble and spurious assertion. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor never disputed the applicable tariff or billing mechanism prior to the statutory notice and merely delayed payment under the pretext of reconciliation; the dispute is illusory and CIRP admission was valid.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the impugned order dated 02.12.2019 in CP (IB) No. 2520/MB/2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench is affirmed. Intervenor Application I.A. 46 of 2021 is rejected. No order as to costs.
summary: Valuelabs LLP supplied solar energy to Global Energy Pvt. Ltd. under a Power Purchase Agreement[cite: 15]. When invoices exceeding Rs. 3.18 Crores remained unpaid, Valuelabs issued a Section 8 demand notice on 08.05.2018 and subsequently filed a Section 9 application, which NCLT Mumbai admitted on 02.12.2019[cite: 15]. The Corporate Debtor's Managing Director appealed, claiming a pre-existing dispute regarding tariffs for 'banked energy'[cite: 15]. The NCLAT held that contemporaneous emails revealed only delays citing software corruption and pending reconciliation, with no dispute raised regarding rates prior to the demand notice[cite: 15]. Dismissing the defense as spurious under the Mobilox doctrine, NCLAT upheld the admission of CIRP[cite: 15].

case_title: Jyoti Strips Private Limited vs. JSC Ispat Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Jyoti Strips Private Limited (Operational Creditor); Respondent is JSC Ispat Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and supply of steel strip goods by the Appellant to the Respondent under diverse commercial invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding operational debt claimed under invoices with default occurring upon failure of Respondent to pay balance sums. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Prior legal notice served on registered office on 18.09.2019; Section 8 demand notice dispatched on 23.10.2019; NCLT dismissal order passed on 18.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Postal tracking slips showing return endorsement 'addressee left without instructions' from a New Delhi branch address; company master data showing registered office at Faridabad, Haryana; email dispatch to a general email address without specifying whole-time directors or KMP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 9 application CP (IB) No. 495/ND/2020 before NCLT New Delhi (Bench-V); NCLT dismissed it on 18.06.2020 for non-delivery of Section 8 demand notice under Rule 5; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether sending a Section 8 demand notice to an operational branch address where it is returned as 'addressee left without instructions', coupled with an email sent to a generic company address, constitutes valid delivery under Section 8 of the IBC read with Rule 5 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules, 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory requirement of delivering a demand notice under Section 8 to the corporate debtor's registered office or to specified key managerial personnel via electronic mail is mandatory, and strict compliance is a jurisdictional condition precedent to maintaining a petition under Section 9. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(1) read with Rule 5(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 prescribes delivery either at the registered office by hand/registered post/speed post or via email to a whole-time director, designated partner, or key managerial personnel; failure to serve the registered office cannot be saved by presumptions of service where the postal remark is 'addressee left without instructions'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict proof of actual or legally valid constructive service of the demand notice prior to triggering CIRP; non-service of a bankruptcy demand notice is an incurable jurisdictional defect. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant had actual knowledge of the registered office in Faridabad but sent the notice to a vacated Delhi address, and failed to prove email delivery to designated officers; therefore, the Section 9 petition was legally non-maintainable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The impugned order dated 18.06.2020 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-V is affirmed, granting liberty to the Appellant to issue a fresh notice and file a fresh application under Section 9 in accordance with law. No order as to costs.
summary: Jyoti Strips Pvt. Ltd. dispatched a Section 8 demand notice to a New Delhi address of JSC Ispat Pvt. Ltd., which returned with the endorsement 'addressee left without instructions', and emailed a general address[cite: 16]. The registered office of the Corporate Debtor was in Faridabad, Haryana, which had received earlier legal notices[cite: 16]. NCLT New Delhi dismissed the Section 9 application for failure of statutory service under Rule 5[cite: 16]. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that service of a Section 8 demand notice at the registered office or upon key managerial personnel is mandatory and strictly construed, though granting liberty to issue a fresh notice[cite: 16].

case_title: Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Ltd. vs. Bhuvesh Maheshwari & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Ltd. (IREDA, Secured Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 1 is Bhuvesh Maheshwari (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2 is Committee of Creditors of Shree Kedarnath Sugar and Agro Products Ltd.; Respondent No. 3 is Shri Sai Priya Sugars Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 4 is Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan facility extended by Appellant to the Corporate Debtor secured by an equitable first pari passu charge by way of mortgage. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted financial claim of Rs. 69.48 Crores; Resolution Plan provided total consideration of Rs. 60 Crores, out of which Rs. 54.25 Crores was allocated to Secured Financial Creditors pro rata based on COC voting share; Appellant allocated Rs. 6.61 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 21.08.2019; 9th COC meeting held on 26.02.2020; e-voting concluded on 09.03.2020; NCLT Mumbai approved plan on 21.09.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Information Memorandum showing first charge of Appellant; Minutes of 9th and 10th COC meetings; e-voting records proving Appellant voted affirmatively in favor of the Resolution Plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I approved Respondent No. 3's resolution plan on 21.09.2020; Appellant appealed contending distribution must follow first charge priority under Section 48 Transfer of Property Act rather than voting share.
legal_issues: Whether a secured financial creditor who actively deliberated and voted in favor of a resolution plan in the COC can subsequently challenge the distribution mechanism, and whether Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act overrides the commercial wisdom of the COC under Section 30(4) of the IBC regarding pro-rata distribution amongst secured creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A financial creditor who votes in favor of a resolution plan is legally estopped from challenging the distribution of proceeds approved by the committee of creditors, and the non-obstante provisions of the insolvency regime override general property law concerning priority of charges. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(4) of the IBC confers complete commercial discretion on the COC to determine the manner of distribution; the word 'may' indicates that considering priority under Section 53 or value of security is directory; Section 238 gives IBC overriding effect over Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Estoppel by conduct based on positive e-voting participation in approving the resolution plan, coupled with the judicial restraint doctrine regarding the commercial wisdom of the COC under the Essar Steel precedent. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The COC acted within its lawful discretion in distributing proceeds pro-rata according to voting share rather than charge priority, and the Appellant's consent bars any subsequent collateral challenge.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The impugned order dated 21.09.2020 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I approving the Resolution Plan is upheld. No order as to costs.
summary: IREDA, a secured financial creditor holding a first pari passu charge with an admitted claim of Rs. 69.48 Crores, challenged the approval of a resolution plan by NCLT Mumbai for Shree Kedarnath Sugar and Agro Products Ltd.[cite: 17]. Under the plan, Rs. 54.25 Crores was distributed among secured creditors pro-rata based on voting share, allotting IREDA Rs. 6.61 Crores[cite: 17]. IREDA claimed the distribution violated Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act[cite: 17]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that IREDA had voted in favor of the plan and was estopped from disputing it, and affirmed that the COC's commercial discretion under Section 30(4) overrides Transfer of Property Act provisions via Section 238[cite: 17].

case_title: Pinakin Shah, Liquidator of M/s Brew Berry Hospitalities Pvt. Ltd. vs. The Assistant Commissioner of State Tax & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Pinakin Shah, Liquidator of M/s Brew Berry Hospitalities Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is The Assistant Commissioner of State Tax, Vadodara; Respondent No. 2 is Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debtor maintained Bank Account No. 08432090000149 with Respondent No. 2; Respondent No. 1 sought recovery of sales tax/VAT arrears. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid Value Added Tax dues claimed under the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 29.05.2019; liquidation ordered on 02.07.2020; Respondent No. 1 issued notice under Section 44 of GVAT Act on 01.09.2020 directing bank to freeze account; NCLT dismissal order passed on 04.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 44 GVAT notice dated 01.09.2020 freezing bank account; claim filed by State Tax Department before Liquidator in liquidation proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed I.A. No. 769 of 2020 before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-2 seeking direction to defreeze the bank account; NCLT dismissed it on 04.12.2020 holding liquidator must approach State Tax Authorities; Liquidator appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a State Tax Department, as an operational creditor, can exercise statutory recovery powers to attach and freeze a corporate debtor's bank account during liquidation, or whether such actions are barred by the priority waterfall under Section 53 and overriding provisions of Section 238 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Following the commencement of liquidation proceedings under the IBC, state statutory authorities possessing tax claims cannot utilize pre-existing provincial recovery statutes to freeze corporate debtor accounts or execute independent recoveries outside the collective insolvency process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC confers an overriding effect over inconsistent provisions of state enactments, including Section 44 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003; tax liabilities constitute operational debts governed strictly by the waterfall distribution mechanism in Section 53. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Supremacy of central insolvency law over provincial tax attachment orders where a claim has already been lodged before the liquidator. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT failed to exercise jurisdiction by remitting the liquidator back to tax authorities; tax authorities cannot march over other creditors and must await distribution under Section 53.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated 04.12.2020 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad is quashed and set aside. I.A. No. 769 of 2020 is allowed, and Respondent No. 2 (Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd.) is directed to defreeze Account No. 08432090000149 held in the name of the Corporate Debtor. No order as to costs.
summary: During liquidation of M/s Brew Berry Hospitalities Pvt. Ltd., the Assistant Commissioner of State Tax issued a notice under Section 44 of the Gujarat VAT Act directing Kotak Mahindra Bank to freeze the Corporate Debtor's bank account[cite: 19]. The NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the Liquidator's application to defreeze the account, holding he should approach the tax authorities[cite: 19]. On appeal, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT order, ruling that tax claims are operational debts subject to the waterfall mechanism of Section 53[cite: 19]. Section 238 of the IBC overrides the GVAT Act, and NCLAT directed Kotak Mahindra Bank to immediately defreeze the account[cite: 19].

case_title: Adish Jain vs. Sumit Bansal & Anr.
appeal_number: Review Application No. 13 of 2020 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 379 of 2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Review Applicant is Adish Jain, Shareholder of M/s J.P. Engineers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Sumit Bansal (IRP); Respondent No. 2 is Worldwide Metals Private Limited (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational transactions between Corporate Debtor and Respondent No. 2 leading to admission under Section 9 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in operational dues claimed by Respondent No. 2, disputed on the basis of alleged sister-concern ledger entries of Rs. 1,95,79,294/- and Rs. 1,95,34,823/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original appeal dismissed on 10.08.2020; Supreme Court dismissed Civil Appeal No. 2960/2020 on 04.09.2020; review before Supreme Court rejected on 03.11.2020 with liberty to file review before NCLAT if permissible; review order passed on 03.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Alleged reconciled ledgers, confirmatory letters signed by a resigned employee (Mr. Vikas Gandhi) dated 30.04.2018, and disputed journal entries. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Applicant appealed NCLT admission under Section 9; NCLAT dismissed appeal on 10.08.2020; Supreme Court affirmed; Applicant then filed Review Application No. 13 of 2020 before NCLAT under Rule 11 and Section 22 of RDBA.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT possesses inherent power or statutory jurisdiction under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules or Section 420 of the Companies Act, 2013 to review its own final appellate judgment on merits by re-appreciating evidence.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The power of substantive review is not an inherent judicial power and cannot be exercised by an appellate tribunal unless expressly conferred by statute. 2.
