STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: NCLAT is established under the Companies Act, 2013; Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules provides procedural inherent power to prevent abuse of process but does not confer substantive jurisdiction to revisit findings of fact; Section 420(2) of the Companies Act is confined solely to rectifying errors apparent on the face of the record and cannot be used as an appeal in disguise. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An error apparent must be manifest and self-evident without requiring a long-drawn process of reasoning or reappraisal of documents. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The review applicant merely sought a rehearing on the evaluation of disputed ledgers and signatures; absent any patent ministerial mistake, the review application is legally impermissible.
operative_order: Review Application No. 13 of 2020 is dismissed as impermissible in law with no mistake apparent on the face of the record. No order as to costs.
summary: A suspended director of J.P. Engineers Pvt. Ltd. sought a substantive review of NCLAT's final judgment dated 10.08.2020, which had upheld the admission of CIRP under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 18]. After the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and subsequent review, the Applicant invoked Rule 11 and Section 420 of the Companies Act, arguing that ledger entries and a pre-existing dispute had been erroneously analyzed[cite: 18]. The NCLAT dismissed the application, holding that review is not an inherent power and cannot be used to re-argue matters on merits or re-evaluate evidence under the guise of rectifying mistakes[cite: 18].

case_title: Krishna Garg & Anr. vs. Pioneer Fabricators Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Krishna Garg & Anr. (Financial Creditors); Respondent is Pioneer Fabricators Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial debt that formed the basis of an application under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in financial debt leading to initial CIRP admission on 12.06.2019, followed by private settlement through post-dated cheques. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 12.06.2019; CIRP withdrawn and terminated on 27.06.2019; NCLT rejected revival application on 07.12.2020; NCLAT appeal decided on 12.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement arrived outside tribunal record; post-dated cheques received by Financial Creditors; absence of settlement terms incorporated into the withdrawal order; subsequent dishonor of post-dated cheques. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following post-dated cheque defaults, Appellants applied before NCLT New Delhi (Court-III) to revive CIRP; NCLT rejected revival on 07.12.2020; Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor can seek revival or restoration of a terminated CIRP upon the dishonor of post-dated settlement cheques where the settlement terms were not incorporated into the court order and no explicit liberty to revive was granted.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where insolvency proceedings are terminated and withdrawn unconditionally on the basis of a private settlement without incorporating the settlement terms into the judicial order or reserving express liberty to revive, the insolvency process cannot subsequently be restored upon a breach of the settlement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Termination of CIRP under Section 7 pursuant to Swiss Ribbons doctrine completely discharges the moratorium and the resolution process; an unincorporated private compromise does not acquire the character of an executable court decree under the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the withdrawal order to verify whether specific liberty to restore the petition upon default was explicitly reserved by the adjudicating authority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The withdrawal order contained no incorporation of terms or revival liberty; hence, CIRP cannot be reopened and the creditor must seek alternative recovery remedies.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, clarifying that dismissal does not preclude the Appellants from pursuing alternative legal remedies.
summary: Appellants initiated CIRP under Section 7 against Pioneer Fabricators Pvt. Ltd., admitted on 12.06.2019[cite: 20]. The parties privately settled, leading NCLT to terminate CIRP on 27.06.2019[cite: 20]. However, the settlement terms were not incorporated into the order, nor was liberty reserved to revive CIRP[cite: 20]. When post-dated cheques bounced, Appellants sought to revive CIRP, which NCLT rejected[cite: 20]. The NCLAT affirmed the rejection, ruling that an unincorporated private settlement cannot be treated as a decree of the court to revive a terminated CIRP, leaving the creditors to pursue other legal avenues[cite: 20].

case_title: M/s. M+R Logistics (India) Private Limited vs. M/s AGA Publications Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor/Appellant is M/s. M+R Logistics (India) Private Limited (formerly PL Shipping & Logistics Private Limited) engaged in freight forwarding and customs clearance; Corporate Debtor/Respondent is M/s AGA Publications Limited, a newsprint publisher. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 01.01.2010, the Respondent issued a contractual order engaging the Appellant as a forwarding agent to handle sea import capital consignments; Appellant handled consignments between 01.01.2010 and 29.05.2010 and raised 14 invoices between 12.05.2010 and 29.05.2010. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed operational debt was Rs. 30,62,583 (or gross claim Rs. 30,51,583.28) with interest at 18% per annum from 06.07.2010 (the date Respondent remitted a last payment of Rs. 1,89,000). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellant issued a winding up notice under Section 434 of the Companies Act, 1956 on 09.12.2010; following IBC enactment and transfer from the High Court, Appellant issued a Demand Notice under Section 8 of the IBC dated 21.02.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Counter Affidavit filed on 26.09.2011 in CP No. 34/2011 before the Andhra Pradesh High Court alleging abnormal delays, demurrage charges, and failure to clear consignments; emails dated 08.07.2010 and 16.07.2010 from Appellant agreeing to absorb detention charges/delay costs of Rs. 1,10,799 and Rs. 2,60,000; and Written Statement dated 20.06.2014 in OS No. 778/2013 before the City Civil Court, Hyderabad asserting a counter-claim of Rs. 41 Lakhs for business losses and appointing a substitute agent. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed winding up CP No. 34 of 2011 before the High Court of Andhra Pradesh; subsequently filed IA No. 5/2018 for transfer to NCLT Hyderabad, which was ordered on 18.07.2018 and registered as CP (IB) No. 636/9/HDB/2019 on 05.09.2019; NCLT Hyderabad rejected the application on 26.06.2020 on the ground of a pre-existing real dispute.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 9 Application was maintainable under the IBC when there was record of pre-existing disputes regarding delay, deficiency of service, and mutual counter-claims raised in prior legal proceedings and email correspondence before the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process by an operational creditor cannot be admitted if there is a bona fide, pre-existing dispute between the parties evidenced in records prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice, as summary insolvency jurisdiction cannot displace plenary trial proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Construing Section 8(2)(a), Section 9, and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) read with Section 5(6) of the IBC, the threshold of dispute requires that a controversy regarding the quality of goods/services, breach of contract, or account reconciliation must exist prior to the receipt of the Section 8 demand notice or invoices; once a plausible pre-existing dispute is demonstrated, the rigours of CIRP cannot be invoked. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applied the test laid down in Mobilox Innovations v. Kirusa Software: the Adjudicating Authority must only determine whether there is a plausible contention requiring further investigation that is not a patently feeble legal argument or an assertion unsupported by evidence. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Corporate Debtor raised issues of demurrage, delay, and deficiency in pleadings before the High Court and Civil Court as early as 2011 and 2014, and the creditor explicitly acknowledged delays in emails of July 2010, there existed a genuine pre-existing dispute warranting dismissal of the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 667 of 2020 is devoid of merits and is dismissed without interference to the order of the Adjudicating Authority; no order as to costs.
summary: Operational Creditor M/s M+R Logistics appealed the dismissal of its Section 9 IBC application by NCLT Hyderabad against Corporate Debtor M/s AGA Publications Limited regarding unpaid freight forwarding charges of Rs. 30,62,583. The Corporate Debtor resisted admission on grounds of pre-existing disputes concerning abnormal delays, customs demurrages, and counter-claims of Rs. 41 Lakhs, which had been raised in a prior 2011 company petition before the Andhra Pradesh High Court and a 2013 civil suit. Citing Mobilox Innovations, the NCLAT held that the emails acknowledging delays and the prior litigations clearly established a genuine pre-existing dispute predating the Section 8 demand notice, thereby affirming the rejection of the Section 9 petition and dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Oase Asia Pacific Pte Ltd. vs. Axis Bank Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Oase Asia Pacific Pte Ltd. (Operational Creditor and sole CoC member of DCCL); Respondent No. 1 is Axis Bank Ltd. & Other Financial Creditors (through Union Bank of India); Respondent No. 2 is Lavasa Corporation Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/holding company under CIRP); Respondent No. 3 is Warasgaon Assets Maintenance Ltd. (100% subsidiary under CIRP); Dasve Convention Centre Ltd. (DCCL) is another 100% subsidiary under CIRP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Group township development where LCL as lessee of Maharashtra Krishna Valley Development Corporation sub-leased convention centre property to subsidiary DCCL via an unregistered, unstamped Deed of Sub-Lease dated 30.09.2010 for a 20-year term with a lease premium of Rs. 110 Crores and token Re. 1 annual rent; DCCL's sole business was operating and maintaining the convention centre within the township. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not specified in the judgment; DCCL faced admitted claims of Rs. 21.33 Crores from Operational Creditors, while substantial multi-thousand crore debts were owed across LCL group entities. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against LCL admitted on 30.08.2018; CIRP against DCCL admitted on 05.02.2019; Axis Bank filed consolidation Application M.A. No. 3664 of 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sub-lease was unregistered and unstamped and barred by Clause 18 of the head lease dated 23.09.2002; Resolution Professional of LCL cancelled the sub-lease; Resolution Plans submitted for LCL were conditioned upon extinguishing consolidated group debt; DCCL lacked revenue or standalone resolution viability. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench allowed M.A. No. 3664 of 2019 on 26.02.2020, directing procedural and substantive consolidation of CIRPs of LCL, WAML, and DCCL under LCL's Resolution Professional based on the Videocon doctrine.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in ordering the consolidation of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Processes of holding company Lavasa Corporation Ltd. and its 100% subsidiaries (including DCCL, whose CoC comprised exclusively of Operational Creditors and opposed consolidation) based on group insolvency principles.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where group companies demonstrate extensive inter-dependence, common ownership and control, operational integration, and where standalone resolution is commercially unfeasible and detrimental to value maximization, the Adjudicating Authority possesses the jurisdiction to order substantive consolidation of their insolvency resolution processes. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The overarching objective of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 is value maximization of stressed assets through viable resolution rather than mere individual recovery of debts by single creditors; lack of common financial creditors does not bar consolidation when economic entity unity is established. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluated the consolidation criteria established in State Bank of India v. Videocon Industries Ltd. (including common control, common assets and liabilities, inter-dependence, resource pooling, and inter-lacing of finance). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since DCCL had no independent assets, held an invalid unregistered sub-lease with nominal rent Re. 1, had received zero standalone resolution plans, and was inextricably tied to LCL's township, consolidation was necessary to achieve meaningful resolution and preserve value.
operative_order: The impugned order consolidating the CIRPs of LCL, WAML, and DCCL is upheld; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 783 of 2020 is dismissed; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Oase Asia Pacific Pte Ltd., an operational creditor and CoC member of Dasve Convention Centre Ltd. (DCCL), appealed an NCLT Mumbai order consolidating the CIRP of DCCL with its parent Lavasa Corporation Ltd. (LCL) and sister subsidiary Warasgaon Assets Maintenance Ltd. (WAML). Appellant contended that DCCL had distinct operational creditors and no common financial liabilities. The NCLAT rejected the appeal, holding that DCCL was wholly dependent on LCL, operated on land leased for nominal rent under an invalid sub-lease, and had received no standalone resolution plans. Applying the Videocon criteria for substantive consolidation, the NCLAT affirmed that group consolidation was essential to prevent value destruction and achieve comprehensive insolvency resolution.

case_title: Macquarie SBI Infrastructure Investment Pte Ltd. & Anr. vs. Soham Renewable Energy India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Macquarie SBI Infrastructure Investment Pte Ltd. & Anr. (shareholders/investors); Respondents are Soham Renewable Energy India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (company and individual directors/shareholders K. Sadananda Shetty and others). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate governance dispute regarding the management and affirmative voting rights of the Appellants concerning employment agreements and executive board appointments in Soham Renewable Energy India Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; petition concerns corporate oppression and mismanagement rather than debt/insolvency default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellants filed CP No. 78/BB/2020 under Sections 241 and 242; Respondents filed cross-petition CP No. 77/BB/2020; both matters heard on 16.06.2020 by NCLT Bengaluru. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants challenged illegal circular resolutions extending employment agreements of Respondent Nos. 2 to 4 in alleged violation of Appellants' contractual affirmative voting rights and sought appointment of professional management. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru vide order dated 16.06.2020 admitted Respondent's petition CP No. 77/BB/2020 for final hearing, but summarily disposed of Appellants' seven interim applications (IA Nos. 179-184 & 189 of 2020 in CP No. 78/BB/2020) on the threshold finding that separate interim applications are maintainable only after the question of admission of the main petition is decided.
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal can summarily reject interlocutory applications for interim relief on the procedural ground that separate interim applications cannot be filed or entertained prior to the formal admission of a company petition under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interlocutory application seeking interim relief in an oppression and mismanagement petition is maintainable at the pre-admission stage, and the tribunal cannot adopt an extra-statutory bar deferring or dismissing such applications on the ground that admission of the main company petition must precede interim consideration. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 empowers the Tribunal 'on the application of any party to the proceedings' to make 'any interim order which it thinks fit for regulating the conduct of the company affairs'; this statutory power is plenary and not contingent upon formal admission of the main petition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Procedural legality and fairness; the Tribunal committed jurisdictional error by refusing to consider urgency and merits of interim relief while simultaneously admitting the cross-petition and listing the deferred interim prayers without formal admission. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The summary disposal of Appellants' interlocutory applications was without legal foundation, contrary to the Act and NCLT Rules, and required restoration and reconsideration on merits.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 134 of 2020 is allowed; the impugned order dated 16.06.2020 in CP No. 78/BB/2020 is set aside and IA Nos. 179 to 184 and 189 of 2020 are restored to their original files with directions to NCLT Bengaluru to decide them on merits after giving reasonable opportunity; Company Appeal (AT) No. 135 of 2020 is disposed of without interference to CP No. 77/BB/2020.
summary: Appellants Macquarie SBI Infrastructure Investment Pte Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order summarily disposing of seven interlocutory applications for interim relief in an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241–242 of the Companies Act, 2013. The NCLT had held that separate interim applications are not maintainable prior to the formal admission of the main petition. The NCLAT set aside the order, ruling that Section 242(4) expressly empowers the tribunal to grant interim relief at any stage of the proceedings and contains no statutory requirement of prior petition admission. The appellate tribunal restored all interim applications and remanded them for expedited disposal on merits.

case_title: Sodexo India Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Chemizol Additives Pvt. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sodexo India Services Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent is Chemizol Additives Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of catering and support services pursuant to an Agreement dated 14.12.2015, which contained an arbitration clause. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed under four unpaid invoices detailed in paragraph 5 of the NCLT order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice demanding outstanding payment was served on the Corporate Debtor on 18.12.2018; Corporate Debtor did not issue any reply or notice of dispute. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant produced the service agreement dated 14.12.2015, four unpaid invoices, and proof of service of demand notice dated 18.12.2018; Corporate Debtor offered no evidence of dispute or repayment and chose not to appear before the Appellate Tribunal despite notice delivery. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition filed by Appellant before NCLT Bengaluru Bench; NCLT passed an order on 08.06.2020 refusing to either admit or reject the application, instead observing that the Corporate Debtor appeared solvent and directing it to endeavor resolution, failing which Appellant could invoke arbitration under the agreement.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority under Section 9(5) of the IBC has the statutory jurisdiction to dispose of a Section 9 application without either admitting or rejecting it, by directing the parties to resolve the dispute or invoke an arbitration clause, on the grounds of the corporate debtor's solvency and ease of doing business.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9(5) of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority is strictly confined to a binary choice: it must either admit the application or reject it; it has no jurisdiction to devise an alternative disposal by relegating the operational creditor to arbitration or mediation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5) is mandatory and exhaustive; the existence of an alternate remedy or arbitration clause in a commercial contract does not bar CIRP initiation, especially given Section 238 of the IBC which overrides conflicting laws or contractual terms; further, a roving inquiry into the corporate debtor's general solvency is alien to Section 9 adjudication. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once the operational creditor establishes that an application is complete, demand notice delivered, debt and default proved, and no notice of a pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2) or in information utilities exists, admission is statutorily mandated. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's disposition delegating the claim to arbitration on notions of solvency and ease of doing business was contrary to law, requiring reversal and a direction to admit the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed and the impugned order dated 08.06.2020 is set aside; the Adjudicating Authority is directed to pass an order of admission under Section 9 within two weeks of communication of the order, with liberty to afford the Respondent an opportunity to settle the claim.
summary: Operational Creditor Sodexo India Services appealed an NCLT Bengaluru order disposing of its Section 9 IBC application without admission or rejection. The NCLT had reasoned that Corporate Debtor Chemizol Additives appeared solvent and directed parties to attempt resolution failing which arbitration could be invoked. The NCLAT set aside the decision, holding that Section 9(5) provides a mandatory binary choice to either admit or reject an application. Relegating the creditor to arbitration despite an undisputed default and absence of a pre-existing dispute violates Section 9 and ignores the overriding effect of Section 238. The NCLAT remanded the case with a direction to admit the petition within two weeks.

case_title: Vekas Kumar Garg vs. DMI Finance Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mr. Vekas Kumar Garg (Resolution Professional of M/s. Ninex Developers Ltd. and M/s. Redtopaz Real Estate Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is DMI Finance Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is the Corporate Debtor facing Section 7 proceedings. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial debt facility extended by DMI Finance Pvt. Ltd. to Respondent No. 2; Appellant is the RP of Ninex Developers Ltd. (NDL), which holds 46.59% equity shares in Respondent No. 2. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed by Respondent No. 1 against Respondent No. 2 under Section 7 of IBC (specific quantum not mentioned in the order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition CP IB-2115/ND/2019 was pending adjudication at pre-admission stage before NCLT New Delhi (Court-VI). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant argued that NDL is an undergoing CIRP corporate debtor and holds 46.59% shares in Respondent No. 2, meaning CIRP against Respondent No. 2 would prejudice NDL and homebuyers, citing Piramal Enterprises. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an impleadment application to be joined as a necessary party respondent in CP IB-2115/ND/2019; NCLT New Delhi rejected the impleadment on 10.12.2020 holding Appellant is not a necessary party.
legal_issues: Whether a third party (including a substantial shareholder or a Resolution Professional managing an entity holding 46.59% equity shares in the corporate debtor) has the legal right to intervene or be impleaded as a necessary party at the pre-admission stage of a Section 7 CIRP application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: At the pre-admission stage of an application under Section 7 of the IBC, only the Financial Creditor and the Corporate Debtor are necessary parties, and third-party intervention or impleadment is not permissible. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(4) and Section 7(5) mandate a summary and expedited determination within 14 days solely to ascertain whether a financial debt is due and in default and whether the application is complete; the statutory scheme admits no third-party adjudication, shareholding disputes, or inter-se managerial conflicts at this threshold. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Necessary party test strictly limited to the creditor asserting debt and the debtor facing CIRP; shareholder rights or external impact on other CIRPs cannot expand the locus standi under Section 7. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Professional of a major shareholder entity is not a necessary or proper party in Section 7 proceedings; the appropriate course is only to submit claims before the IRP if and when CIRP is initiated.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without interference to the impugned order; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Vekas Kumar Garg, acting as Resolution Professional of Ninex Developers Ltd. (NDL), appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order rejecting his application to be impleaded as a necessary party in a Section 7 petition filed by DMI Finance against a corporate debtor in which NDL held 46.59% equity. Appellant argued that admission would jeopardize NDL's assets and homebuyers. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that at the pre-admission stage of Section 7 proceedings, only the financial creditor and corporate debtor are necessary parties. The tribunal is solely confined to ascertaining financial debt and default without entertaining third-party interventions or shareholder disputes.

case_title: JJE Adornment Pvt. Ltd. vs. Pingle Builders Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is JJE Adornment Pvt. Ltd. (contractor/claimant); Respondents are Pingle Builders Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in liquidation) and its Liquidator/RP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Execution of four work orders between the Appellant and the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary loss and contractual claims arising from execution and bank accounts under four work orders (exact default amount not quantified in order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP had culminated in an order of liquidation for the Corporate Debtor prior to the disposal of Appellant's miscellaneous application. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Four work orders executed between the parties and operation of a specific current account by the Appellant. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an application before NCLT Mumbai seeking modification of the initial CIRP admission order dated 19.07.2018, directions to the RP to abide by four work orders, and restraints against taking charge of Appellant's current account; NCLT dismissed the application on 11.12.2020 as the company was in liquidation, while preserving Appellant's right to pursue claims before other competent forums.
legal_issues: Whether an application to modify the original admission order and enforce contractual work orders against a Resolution Professional can be entertained by the Adjudicating Authority after the Corporate Debtor has entered liquidation, and what is the appropriate legal recourse for such operational claimants.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a corporate debtor is ordered into liquidation, prior contractual performance applications or modifications of the initial admission order become infructuous, and all monetary and operational claims must be submitted to the liquidator under the statutory claims verification mechanism. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 38 of the IBC, the liquidator is mandated to collect claims within 30 days of liquidation commencement; under Section 40, the liquidator acts as a quasi-judicial authority to admit or reject claims, subject to an appeal before the Adjudicating Authority under Section 42. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Statutory progression test; the culmination of CIRP into liquidation extinguishes interim enforcement reliefs against the RP, channeling all claims into the Section 38/40/42 framework. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rejection of the modification application was legally valid and does not extinguish or curtail the creditor's substantive statutory right to lodge claims before the Liquidator.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of without interfering with the impugned order, granting liberty to the Appellant to approach the Liquidator with its claim within one week from the date of the order.
summary: Appellant JJE Adornment Pvt. Ltd. challenged an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting its application to modify a 2018 CIRP admission order and direct the Resolution Professional to honor four work orders and release a current account. The NCLT declined the relief because the corporate debtor had entered liquidation. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that once liquidation commences, contractual directions against the RP cannot be entertained. Claimants must submit their claims to the Liquidator under Section 38, who adjudicates them quasi-judicially under Section 40, subject to an appeal under Section 42. Appellant was granted one week to file its claim with the Liquidator.

case_title: Anil Tayal, Resolution Professional for M/s. Horizon Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. vs. Committee of Creditors of M/s. Horizon Buildcon Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Anil Tayal, Resolution Professional for M/s. Horizon Buildcon Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent is the Committee of Creditors of M/s. Horizon Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ongoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Corporate Debtor M/s. Horizon Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; appeal arises out of timeline extension/exclusion during CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC resolved to seek a 60-day extension beyond 270 days; extension application was filed on 21.10.2020; NCLT heard and reserved orders between 12.01.2021 and 03.02.2021; NCLT granted a 40-day extension beyond 330 days on 03.02.2021, which expired on 19.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record showed that period from 21.10.2020 to 09.11.2020 was consumed in pursuing the extension application in the first instance, and period from 12.01.2021 to 03.02.2021 was consumed while NCLT reserved orders. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected RP's request to exclude the litigation period from the CIRP calculation while granting a 40-day extension, rendering the extension illusory as the extended timeline lapsed on 19.02.2021 before the order could be effectively implemented.
legal_issues: Whether the time consumed in judicial proceedings before the Adjudicating Authority (including the time spent actively pursuing an extension application and the period during which orders were reserved) must be excluded from the computation of the CIRP statutory timeline under Section 12 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Time spent in judicial intervention before the Adjudicating Authority, particularly when orders are reserved or applications for extension are actively pursued, must be excluded from the computation of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process period to ensure extensions are meaningful and not rendered futile. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Section 12 sets the outer timelines for CIRP, the period of judicial delay cannot penalize the resolution process; courts must exclude periods consumed by judicial intervention to render statutory extensions productive and fulfill the Code's resolution objectives. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Principle of actus curiae neminem gravabit (an act of the court shall prejudice no man) applied to periods of judicial deliberation and reserved orders. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in extending the period by 40 days without excluding the judicial delay periods, and the exclusion of periods from 21.10.2020 to 09.11.2020 and 12.01.2021 to 03.02.2021 was justifiably warranted.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the periods from 21st October, 2020 till 9th November, 2020 and from 12th January, 2021 to 3rd February, 2021 are directed to be excluded from the computation of the CIRP period for M/s Horizon Buildcon Pvt. Ltd.
summary: Resolution Professional Anil Tayal appealed an NCLT order that granted a 40-day extension beyond 330 days for the CIRP of M/s Horizon Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. but refused to exclude the time spent pursuing the application and the time orders were reserved. Because the exclusion was denied, the granted extension lapsed within days, rendering it meaningless. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that the period of judicial intervention—specifically the time spent prosecuting the extension and the period during which orders were reserved—must be excluded when computing the CIRP timeframe under Section 12 of the IBC, thereby restoring productive time for the completion of the resolution process.

case_title: Surender Kumar Singhal vs. Vikram Bajaj, Resolution Professional for AMR Infrastructure Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Surender Kumar Singhal (Successful Resolution Applicant / H1 Bidder); Respondent is Vikram Bajaj, Resolution Professional for Corporate Debtor AMR Infrastructure Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission and approval of a resolution plan in the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of AMR Infrastructure Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; dispute concerns delay in approval of a CoC-approved resolution plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Professional filed an application under Section 31 of the IBC on 27.05.2019 for approval of the CoC-approved resolution plan; application remained unadjudicated until 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution plan submitted by Appellant was approved with requisite majority by the Committee of Creditors and placed before NCLT on 27.05.2019 without any decision rendered for over 20 months. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Aggrieved by the prolonged pendency without adjudication by the Adjudicating Authority, the Successful Resolution Applicant approached NCLAT seeking directions for time-bound disposal of the Section 31 application.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal can issue binding peremptory directions to the Adjudicating Authority to decide a pending Section 31 application for approval of a resolution plan within a defined timeline where inordinate delay has occurred.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Although an appeal by a Successful Resolution Applicant complaining of delay in plan approval is strictly not maintainable since the Resolution Professional is the proper party to seek procedural expedience, the Appellate Tribunal may exercise supervisory jurisdiction to direct time-bound disposal where prolonged statutory delays defeat the essence of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 of the IBC contemplates an expeditious approval process for resolution plans approved by the CoC; inordinate delay running into years undermines the primary objective of time-bound resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Factual concurrence and procedural gridlock; both the Resolution Professional and Resolution Applicant established undisputed pendency since May 2019. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because of excessive delay in adjudicating the Section 31 application, the Adjudicating Authority must be directed to dispose of the CoC-approved plan with top-most priority within two weeks.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with a direction to the Adjudicating Authority to dispose of the Section 31 application for approval of the CoC-approved Resolution Plan within two weeks according top-most priority and report compliance to the NCLAT.
summary: Successful Resolution Applicant Surender Kumar Singhal approached the NCLAT aggrieved by the prolonged delay of over 20 months by the Adjudicating Authority in deciding an application filed on 27.05.2019 under Section 31 of the IBC for approval of a CoC-approved resolution plan for AMR Infrastructure Ltd. The NCLAT observed that while such an appeal is technically not maintainable at the instance of a resolution applicant, the extraordinary delay justified judicial intervention. Acknowledging that the RP was equally aggrieved by the inaction, the NCLAT directed the Adjudicating Authority to dispose of the approval application with top priority within two weeks and report compliance.

case_title: Tuf Metallurgical Private Limited & Anr. vs. Impex Metal & Ferro Alloys Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are purchasers/suppliers Million Link (China) Investment Ltd. and Tuf Metallurgical Pvt. Ltd. (Stakeholders/Claimants); Respondent No. 1 is Impex Metal & Ferro Alloys Ltd. (Corporate Debtor under liquidation); Respondent No. 2 is Samir Kumar Bhattacharyya (Liquidator); Respondent No. 3 is Subodh Kumar Agrawal (Erstwhile Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Advance payments made to the Corporate Debtor during its CIRP to keep it a going concern for purchasing Ferro Silicon Manganese under purchase contracts and addenda executed in September 2018; Corporate Debtor suffered a plant breakdown and delivered only a fraction of the ordered quantities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Undelivered advance balances claimed as CIRP costs were USD 338,834.13 (equivalent to Rs. 2,40,35,301) for Million Link, and Rs. 4,50,54,512 advance refund plus Rs. 43,56,897 raw material damages (totaling Rs. 4,94,11,409) for Tuf Metallurgical. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 09.03.2018; advances paid on 28.09.2018; liquidation ordered on 12.02.2019; claims submitted in Form G on 14.03.2019 and renewed on 03.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purchase contracts dated 24.08.2018, addenda dated 11.09.2018 and 21.09.2018, bank transfer memos, proforma invoices, and commercial invoices bearing the rubber stamp and authorized signature of the Corporate Debtor while managed by the RP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Both appellants filed applications under Section 60(5) before NCLT Kolkata as the Liquidator failed to adjudicate the claims; NCLT Kolkata summarily disposed of CA (IB) Nos. 625/KB/2019 and 615/KB/2019 on 09.12.2019 with a one-line mechanical order: 'Liquidator to consider its claim as per Rules'.
legal_issues: Whether advance payments made to a Corporate Debtor during CIRP for purchase of finished goods to maintain operations as a going concern, which remain unfulfilled due to operational failure/breakdown, constitute CIRP costs under Section 5(13)(c) of the IBC; and whether a Liquidator is statutorily bound to adjudicate such claims under Section 40 instead of indecisively sitting on them.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Advance payments received by a corporate debtor during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process for the supply of goods to keep the debtor running as a going concern constitute Insolvency Resolution Process costs under Section 5(13)(c) if the goods are not delivered, and purchasers cannot be relegated to subordinate waterfall status under Section 53. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 20(1) and Section 20(2)(e) mandate the RP to manage operations as a going concern; receipts of advances during ordinary trading under CIRP do not constitute interim finance requiring CoC approval under Section 28, but are operational transactions whose unfulfilled liabilities qualify as process costs incurred in running the business. Section 40(2) and Liquidation Regulation 30 are mandatory, requiring the liquidator to verify and admit or reject claims within prescribed timelines and record reasons. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Authentic commercial records; invoices, bank remittances, and delivery notes bearing the debtor's stamp during the CIRP period demonstrate going-concern transactions conducted while under the RP's statutory control. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator cannot evade adjudication on the pretext of missing records from the RP; failure of the debtor to supply paid-for goods during CIRP mandates treating the refund of such advances as CIRP costs.
operative_order: The common impugned order dated 09.12.2019 is set aside; Respondent No. 3/RP is directed to provide all transaction details to the Liquidator within 15 days, failing which the Liquidator must report to the NCLT and IBBI; the Liquidator is directed to adjudicate and admit or reject the claims with reasons under Section 40 of the IBC within 30 days of the judgment; in case of rejection, the Liquidator shall not act upon the order for 14 days to enable the Appellants to approach the Adjudicating Authority under Section 42; both appeals are disposed of.
summary: Appellants Million Link and Tuf Metallurgical appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order that mechanically directed the Liquidator to consider their claims 'as per Rules'. The Appellants had paid substantial advance amounts during CIRP to purchase goods from Corporate Debtor Impex Metal to keep it running as a going concern, but the debtor suffered plant breakdowns and defaulted on supply. The Liquidator refused to treat the undelivered balances as CIRP costs, arguing lack of CoC approval. The NCLAT held that advances received during CIRP to maintain operations as a going concern under Section 20 of the IBC constitute CIRP costs under Section 5(13)(c) upon supply failure. The Liquidator was ordered to adjudicate the claims within 30 days.

case_title: Srei Equipment Finance Limited vs. Mr. Prabhakar Nandiraju, Resolution Professional, MIC Electronics Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 552 of 2019 & Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 976 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Srei Equipment Finance Ltd. (Secured/Dissenting Financial Creditor); Respondent is Prabhakar Nandiraju (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor MIC Electronics Ltd.); Co-Respondents are Consortium Cosyn Ltd., RRK Enterprise, and Sri Siva Lakshmanarao Kakarala (Successful Resolution Applicants). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Four loan facilities rescheduled under a Loan-cum-Hypothecation Agreement dated 22.09.2016 restructuring Rs. 35.02 Crores of debt into a settlement of Rs. 23.50 Crores, consisting of Rs. 10 Crores cash repayment and Rs. 13.50 Crores discharged via allotment of 52 Lakh equity shares at Rs. 26 per share subject to a one-year lock-in. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor allotted 52 Lakh shares at Rs. 20 each (credited value Rs. 10.40 Crores) on 12.05.2017 but defaulted on cash installments; Appellant revoked concessions and recalled the debt, claiming Rs. 39,27,81,934, and subsequently filed Form C claiming Rs. 43,68,84,792. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 13.03.2018; in the 7th CoC meeting on 24.10.2018, the RP reduced Appellant's claim by Rs. 10.40 Crores and reduced voting share from 16.09% to 12.25%; 11th CoC meeting approved the Resolution Plan on 06.12.2018; NCLT Hyderabad approved the plan on 31.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Demat statements showing unencumbered transfer of 52 Lakh equity shares into Appellant's account; Loan Agreement lacking express pledge clauses; independent valuation reports assessing Appellant's secured assets at an average liquidation value of Rs. 12.86 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad dismissed Appellant's IA No. 665/2018 and IA No. 52/2019 on 25.04.2019 upholding the claim reduction by Rs. 10.40 Crores; NCLT subsequently approved the resolution plan allocating Rs. 8.64 Crores to Appellant, prompting cross-appeals CA No. 552/2019 and CA No. 976/2019.
legal_issues: Whether equity shares allotted under a loan restructuring agreement can be treated as a pledge to prevent the reduction of admitted financial debt upon debtor default; and whether a dissenting financial creditor is entitled under amended Section 30(2)(b)(ii) of the IBC to receive its liquidation entitlement under Section 53(1) on priority under an approved resolution plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Equity shares issued, allotted, and credited to a creditor's demat account with the right of unrestricted open-market sale after a lock-in period confer absolute ownership and cannot be construed as a pledge under Section 172 of the Contract Act; thus, their value must be deducted from admitted debt. Under amended Section 30(2)(b)(ii) of the IBC, a dissenting financial creditor must be paid an amount not less than its liquidation entitlement under Section 53(1) on priority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Essar Steel, the 2019 Amendment to Section 30(2)(b) applies to pending appeals as an appellate proceeding is a continuation of original proceedings. The commercial wisdom of the CoC is subject to the statutory floor in Section 30(2)(b)(ii), which guarantees dissenting financial creditors their proportionate liquidation value under Section 53(1), payable on priority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contractual construction and demat ownership records to negate pledge; independent valuation reports and liquidation waterfall calculation submitted via RP affidavit to determine statutory minimum payout. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP correctly reduced the admitted claim by Rs. 10.40 Crores for the allotted shares; however, Appellant as a dissenting financial creditor is entitled to Rs. 8.60 Crores as determined under Section 53(1) to be paid on priority under the approved plan.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 552 of 2019 is dismissed; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 976 of 2019 is partly allowed with directions that the Appellant shall be paid Rs. 8.60 Crores on priority under the approved Resolution Plan.
summary: Appellant Srei Equipment Finance challenged an NCLT Hyderabad order upholding the Resolution Professional's reduction of its claim by Rs. 10.40 Crores based on 52 Lakh equity shares allotted to it under a debt restructuring agreement, and appealed the subsequent approval of a resolution plan allocating it Rs. 8.64 Crores. The NCLAT held that because title to the shares had passed without any pledge creation, the RP rightly reduced the claim. However, applying the amended Section 30(2)(b)(ii) of the IBC and the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel, the NCLAT held that the Appellant, as a dissenting financial creditor, is entitled to its liquidation value entitlement of Rs. 8.60 Crores under Section 53(1) to be paid on priority, partly allowing CA No. 976 of 2019.

case_title: Aparna Enterprise Ltd. vs. SJR Prime Corporation Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Aparna Enterprise Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent is SJR Prime Corporation Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), a real estate developer. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of Ready-Mix Concrete (RMC), tiles, UPVC, and blocks by Appellant under five purchase orders dated 01.07.2017 to 01.03.2018 for construction projects developed by Respondent in Bengaluru. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed in Form 5 was Rs. 8,44,49,943 (including principal and interest at 20% p.a. amounting to Rs. 1,49,65,555) arising from defaulted invoices between 16.04.2018 and 23.02.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 8 sent on 18.11.2019 and delivered on 06.12.2019; Corporate Debtor filed an Arbitration Application under Section 9 of the Arbitration Act on 03.12.2019; Corporate Debtor replied to the Demand Notice within 10 days on 09.12.2019; Section 9 IBC application filed on 13.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debit notes and email communications dating from August 2016, February 2018, September 2018, and April/June 2019 documenting structural cracks, concrete defects, short supply, and snags; unilateral addition of 24% interest not agreed in purchase orders; and pending Section 9 arbitration petition AA No. 25025/2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru disposed of CP(IB) No. 34/BB/2020 on 18.06.2020 on grounds of pending arbitration and pre-existing dispute, granting liberty to pursue remedies subject to arbitration outcome.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 9 IBC application was liable to be rejected under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) due to the existence of a bona fide pre-existing dispute regarding defective goods, short supply, and debit notes raised prior to and in response to the Section 8 demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational debt must be both 'due' and legally 'payable'; where the corporate debtor establishes contemporaneous pre-existing disputes regarding quality, defects, and short supply supported by debit notes and correspondence, an application under Section 9 cannot be admitted to coerce debt recovery. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) mandate the rejection of a Section 9 application if notice of a pre-existing dispute or arbitration proceedings exists; the Code cannot be invoked as a substitute for debt collection or to liquidate a solvent entity amidst genuine contractual disputes. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mobilox Innovations standard: the Adjudicating Authority must ascertain whether there exists a plausible, non-spurious dispute requiring trial, evidenced by contemporaneous quality complaints and debit notes. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor successfully proved genuine pre-existing disputes regarding cracks at project sites, substandard materials, and disputed unilateral interest charges, justifying the dismissal of the Section 9 application.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 632 of 2020 is dismissed; the rejection of the Section 9 application by the Adjudicating Authority is upheld; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Aparna Enterprise Ltd. appealed the rejection of its Section 9 IBC petition by NCLT Bengaluru against SJR Prime Corporation Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid construction material invoices of Rs. 8.44 Crores. The Corporate Debtor resisted admission, citing pre-existing quality disputes, structural cracks, debit notes issued from 2016 to 2019, disputed interest claims, and an arbitration application filed under Section 9 of the Arbitration Act. Applying the principles of Mobilox Innovations, the NCLAT affirmed that the debt was subject to genuine, substantiated pre-existing disputes, holding that IBC summary proceedings cannot be utilized as a recovery mechanism against an ongoing enterprise, and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Mr. Mohanlal Dhakad vs. BNG Global India Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mohanlal Dhakad (representing himself and other individual investors as Financial Creditors); Respondent is BNG Global India Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Monies invested by retail investors under 'Recurring Investment Plan' and 'Lumpsum Investment Plan' schemes floated by the Corporate Debtor in 2012–2013 promising time-value returns, multifold profits, or allotment of agricultural plots upon maturity (terms of 3 to 10 years). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed default was Rs. 16,28,300, comprising Rs. 13,70,000 principal/maturity amount plus Rs. 2,58,300 interest at 12% p.a. calculated up to October 2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Investment schemes matured during 2017–2018; default occurred upon failure to repay or deliver land plots on maturity; joint Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 2978(ND)/2019 filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Investment certificates, registration receipts, dishonored promissory notes issued in lieu of assured returns, and financial deposits classified under long-term borrowings under Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-V dismissed the Section 7 application on 12.03.2020 holding that deposits received under collective schemes do not constitute 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC and relegated the investors to remedies under Chapter V of the Companies Act, 2013.
legal_issues: Whether collective deposits and investment sums entrusted under recurring/lumpsum schemes against assured monetary returns or land allotment constitute a 'financial debt' within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the IBC, entitling retail depositors to maintain a Section 7 petition as Financial Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Monies collected from investors under recurring or lumpsum investment schemes that carry an obligation to pay assured returns or return capital with interest upon maturity are disbursements made against the consideration for the time value of money, squarely constituting a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) hinges on the 'time value of money', signifying compensation paid for the period funds are utilized; the nomenclature of 'deposit' does not strip a transaction of its character as a financial debt. The IBC overrides Chapter V of the Companies Act, 2013, and the existence of an alternative recovery route under company law is no impediment to triggering CIRP under Section 7. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Substantive economic reality test: evaluating investment terms to verify whether funds were disbursed against promised interest/assured returns and whether default in payment or property allotment occurred upon maturity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in concluding that the deposits did not constitute debt; the failure to refund matured amounts or allot land constituted default of a financial debt, requiring restoration and admission of the petition.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 12.03.2020 is set aside; NCLT New Delhi Bench-V is directed to restore CP No. (IB) 2978/(ND)/2019 to its file, admit the Section 7 petition, and proceed in accordance with law; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Mohanlal Dhakad and other investors appealed an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing their Section 7 IBC application against BNG Global India Ltd. The NCLT had held that funds collected under recurring and lumpsum schemes were 'deposits' governed by Chapter V of the Companies Act, 2013 rather than 'financial debt' under the IBC. Reversing the order, the NCLAT held that deposits disbursed with promised assured returns or land allotment are transactions backed by the time value of money, falling squarely within the definition of financial debt under Section 5(8). Concluding that the IBC overrides the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, the NCLAT directed the NCLT to restore and admit the Section 7 petition.

case_title: Gangadhar Udayan Dravid vs. Saurav Keshan & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Gangadhar Udayan Dravid (suspended Director of Corporate Debtor Katalist Viewpaper Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is Saurav Keshan (Proprietor of Inspired Traveller, Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Katalist Viewpaper Pvt. Ltd. through its IRP Pankaj Kumar Singhal. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor placed purchase orders (PO/KVPL/0005, PO/18-19/005) with Operational Creditor for designing advertisements, producing video films, and organizing workshops for 'Honor' smartphones (Huawei Technologies) via advertising network Group M. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt in default was Rs. 17,80,524; four invoices were raised totaling Rs. 45,04,296, against which partial payments were made and the last payment of Rs. 7,52,328 was received on 17.06.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice in Form 3 sent on 04.12.2019; reply denying liability issued on 10.12.2019; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 671/ND/2020 filed thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purchase orders issued directly by Corporate Debtor; invoices raised on Corporate Debtor; Form 26AS TDS certificates naming Corporate Debtor as deductor; and Corporate Debtor's audited balance sheet for FY 2018–2019 reflecting Saurav Keshan as a creditor for Rs. 25,32,852. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor argued it was merely a routing/intermediary agent without payment liability under Section 230 of Contract Act; NCLT New Delhi (Bench-VI) rejected the defense and admitted the Section 9 petition on 18.12.2020.
legal_issues: Whether a company that places purchase orders and accepts invoices for services rendered can disclaim liability as an 'operational debtor' by asserting an informal intermediary/agency defense under Section 230 of the Contract Act, and whether inter-party billing reconciliation constitutes a pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of an express tripartite agreement or disclosed principal agreement in writing, the commercial entity that places purchase orders and receives invoices is the debtor legally liable for operational debt; internal arrangements or pass-through payment structures with third parties cannot be used to evade CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 5(6) read with Section 8(2)(a) must relate directly to the existence, amount, or quality of the goods/services provided by the operational creditor; disputes concerning financial reconciliation between the debtor and third-party buyers do not qualify. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective documentary chain: direct purchase orders, invoices, statutory TDS deductions, and balance sheet acknowledgments prevail over speculative email trails attempting to manufacture an agency defense. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Katalist was the true Corporate Debtor and its agency argument was an illusory, spurious afterthought; the debt was due and defaulted, justifying admission under Section 9.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 01 of 2021 is dismissed without costs; the order of admission passed by the Adjudicating Authority is affirmed.
summary: The suspended director of Katalist Viewpaper Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Saurav Keshan (Inspired Traveller) for unpaid advertising and video production services of Rs. 17.80 Lakhs. Katalist contended that it was merely an intermediary/routing agent for Group M and Huawei and bore no payment liability under Section 230 of the Contract Act. The NCLAT rejected the plea, holding that Katalist issued the purchase orders, received invoices, deducted TDS, and acknowledged the debt in its balance sheet without any formal agency agreement. Concluding that internal disputes between the debtor and third parties do not constitute a pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6), the NCLAT affirmed the CIRP admission.

case_title: Srinivasa Reddy Velagala vs. Sravanthi Infratech Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Srinivasa Reddy Velagala (Director of Corporate Debtor K.P.R. Chemicals Ltd.); Respondent is Sravanthi Infratech Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor/EPC Contractor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: EPC Contract dated 09.02.2011 (awarded via Letter of Award dated 24.12.2010) valued at Rs. 827 Crores for constructing a 225 MW gas-based combined cycle power plant at Bikkavolu, Andhra Pradesh. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor paid Rs. 50.15 Crores towards initial mobilization but defaulted on the remaining advance balance of Rs. 32.55 Crores (out of 10% advance of Rs. 82.7 Crores); last payment received via RTGS was on 25.02.2011. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Contractor issued a work suspension notice on 30.07.2011; Demand Notice under Section 8(1) issued on 02.07.2018; Section 9 petition TCP No. 82/9/AMR/2019 [CP No. 123/9/HDB/2018] filed in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: EPC Contract containing explicit termination procedures under Clauses 14.1 and 14.2 which were never invoked by either party; letter dated 05.01.2012 by Corporate Debtor to the Central Electricity Authority affirming project construction was in full swing; and absence of any reply or dispute notice to the Section 8 demand notice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Amaravati admitted the Section 9 petition on 13.12.2019, holding the debt to be an operational debt arising from a continuing contract not barred by limitation under Article 137.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act where work was suspended in 2011 but the underlying EPC contract was never formally terminated, and whether an EPC agreement can be deemed frustrated by efflux of time without contractual termination.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a commercial contract prescribes specific contractual mechanisms for termination and neither party terminates the contract following work suspension, the contract remains legally subsisting as a continuing contract, and an unfulfilled operational debt thereunder is not barred by limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) encompasses unpaid operational claims arising under ongoing EPC contracts; limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act read with Section 238A of the IBC does not run to bar a claim arising under an unterminated, continuing contractual relationship. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contractual clause enforcement: in the absence of an automatic termination or frustration clause by efflux of time, the failure to invoke contractual termination clauses (Clauses 14.1/14.2) leaves the contractual obligations and corresponding default subsisting. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The contract was never terminated, no dispute was raised in response to the Section 8 notice, and the operational default was continuous, rendering the Section 9 petition fully maintainable and timely.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 188 of 2020 is dismissed; the admission of the Section 9 application by the Adjudicating Authority is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Director of K.P.R. Chemicals Ltd. challenged an NCLT Amaravati order admitting a Section 9 application filed by EPC contractor Sravanthi Infratech Pvt. Ltd. regarding a defaulted Rs. 32.55 Crore balance on an Rs. 827 Crore power plant contract. Appellant argued that work had been suspended in July 2011 and the claim was barred by limitation under Article 137, having frustrated by efflux of time. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the contract contained specific termination clauses that were never exercised by either party, making it a subsisting, continuing contract. Furthermore, as the debtor failed to respond to the Section 8 demand notice, the CIRP admission was upheld.

case_title: Elektronik Lab India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Pinnacle (Air) Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Elektronik Lab India Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent is Pinnacle (Air) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Aircraft Operator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of satcom and airtime communication services initiated in May 2010 for a Falcon 2000 LX aircraft leased by the Respondent from M/s Bajaj Hindustan Sugar Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding operational debt claimed was Rs. 37,02,761; last payment received was Rs. 6,89,524 via cheque cleared on 12.07.2012. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Services terminated on 01.06.2012; legal notice sent on 30.09.2014; winding up petition CP No. 06/2015 filed against third-party Bajaj Hindustan on 10.07.2015; Demand Notice under Section 8 issued on 03.12.2019; Section 9 application filed on 06.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Invoices from 2012; email of 29.05.2012 terminating services; Allahabad High Court order dismissing winding up petition on merits due to lack of privity with Bajaj Hindustan; medical certificates asserting bed rest of authorized representative. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi (Bench-VI) dismissed CP No. IB-303/(ND)/2020 on 25.02.2020 as barred by limitation, rejecting the application of Section 14 of the Limitation Act.
legal_issues: Whether the period spent bona fide prosecuting a winding-up petition against a third-party aircraft owner can be excluded under Section 14(2) of the Limitation Act, 1963 to save limitation for a Section 9 IBC application filed against the aircraft operator; and whether unexplained delay exceeding two years can be condoned under Section 5.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 14(2) of the Limitation Act applies only when a prior civil proceeding was prosecuted against the same party for the same relief in a court lacking jurisdiction; dismissal of a petition on merits against an entirely different entity constitutes non-joinder, not misjoinder, and cannot yield Section 14 exclusion. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(2) requires identity of parties and relief, combined with dismissal arising from a jurisdictional defect or cause of a like nature; an adjudication on evidentiary failure/merits does not qualify. Condonation of delay under Section 5 requires sufficient and continuous explanation for each period of default. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict construction of statutory limitation: medical certificates covering temporary illness do not explain long, multi-year intervals of procedural inertia. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application filed nearly eight years after the date of default was hopelessly time-barred, as Section 14 was inapplicable and the delay remained largely unexplained under Section 5.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 510 of 2020 is dismissed; the impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority dismissing the Section 9 application as time-barred is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Operational Creditor Elektronik Lab India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its Section 9 IBC application against Pinnacle (Air) Pvt. Ltd. as time-barred. The operational debt arose from satcom services defaulted on 12.07.2012, whereas the Section 9 petition was filed in January 2020. Appellant sought exclusion of time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act for period spent pursuing a company winding-up petition against aircraft owner Bajaj Hindustan Sugar Ltd. The NCLAT held that Section 14 requires proceedings against the same party dismissed for want of jurisdiction, whereas the earlier petition was dismissed on merits against a different entity. Citing failure to explain long delays under Section 5, the NCLAT affirmed the dismissal.

case_title: Union Bank of India vs. Siripuram Developers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Union Bank of India (erstwhile Andhra Bank, Secured Financial Creditor); Respondents Nos. 1 to 4 are Siripuram Developers Pvt. Ltd., Tirumani Developers Pvt. Ltd., IVR PUDL Resorts & Clubs Pvt. Ltd., and IVR Prime Developers (Tuni) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Guarantors/subsidiaries of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 5 is Sutanu Sinha (Liquidator of IVRCL Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate guarantees and exclusive equitable mortgages of 133 properties (75.94 acres in Tamil Nadu) executed by Respondents 1 to 4 to secure credit facilities availed by parent company IVRCL Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by principal borrower IVRCL Ltd. resulted in admitted liquidation claim of Rs. 660.15 Crores for Appellant; exclusive security charged to Appellant valued at approximately Rs. 75.94 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IVRCL admitted to CIRP on 23.02.2018; liquidation ordered on 26.07.2019; Appellant issued SARFAESI Demand Notice on 18.12.2019 and Possession Notice on 11.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deeds of Guarantee and title deeds showing exclusive mortgage of subsidiary assets in favor of Appellant; CoC minutes dated 22.09.2019 confirming charges on subsidiary assets were excluded from the liquidation estate. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate guarantors filed IA No. 335 of 2020 before NCLT Hyderabad to restrain enforcement during going-concern sale of IVRCL; NCLT injuncted the Bank from taking coercive steps or selling mortgaged properties till liquidation closure, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under the IBC to restrain a secured financial creditor from enforcing SARFAESI remedies against third-party mortgaged properties owned by subsidiary corporate guarantors that are excluded from the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(d).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to interdict or restrain a secured creditor from proceeding under the SARFAESI Act against mortgaged assets owned by corporate guarantors or subsidiaries where such assets do not form part of the corporate debtor's liquidation estate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36(4)(d) of the IBC contains an express statutory bar providing that 'assets of any Indian or foreign subsidiary of the corporate debtor' shall not be included in the liquidation estate; therefore, statutory protections and stays attendant to liquidation cannot be extended to protect subsidiary-owned assets. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Estate asset boundary test: verifying title and records to confirm whether mortgaged assets belong to the corporate debtor or to independent corporate entities/guarantors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The mortgaged properties were exclusive assets of subsidiary guarantors and statutorily excluded from IVRCL's liquidation estate; the NCLT's injunction was impermissible and must be vacated.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 890 of 2020 is allowed; the impugned order dated 20.08.2020 passed in IA No. 335 of 2020 restraining Union Bank of India from enforcing its security is set aside.
summary: Appellant Union Bank of India appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order that restrained it under Section 60(5) from enforcing SARFAESI actions against 75.94 acres of mortgaged land owned by corporate guarantors (subsidiaries of Corporate Debtor IVRCL Ltd.) during IVRCL's liquidation. The NCLT had reasoned that enforcement would jeopardize the sale of IVRCL as a going concern. The NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that under Section 36(4)(d) of the IBC, assets of subsidiaries are expressly excluded from the liquidation estate. Consequently, the Adjudicating Authority lacked jurisdiction to restrain the secured creditor from proceeding against guarantor assets outside the liquidation estate, and the injunction was vacated.

case_title: Surendra Singh Hada & Ors. vs. Arfat Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Surendra Singh Hada & Ors. (Operational Creditors); Respondent is Arfat Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying supply of goods or operational services resulting in unpaid operational debt claims against the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of operational debt asserted under Section 9 of the IBC (specific debt amount not quantified in the order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 application remained pending adjudication at pre-admission stage before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench (Court No. 1) for over 840 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Prolonged court docket entries and records reflecting pendency of the Section 9 petition exceeding statutory time limits without an order of admission or rejection. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Frustrated by the prolonged delay exceeding 840 days, the Operational Creditors approached NCLAT seeking directions for time-bound disposal.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal can issue supervisory directions to the Adjudicating Authority to ensure strict adherence to statutory timelines for adjudicating Section 9 applications when cases remain pending for over 840 days at the pre-admission stage.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Inordinate delays at the pre-admission stage of insolvency applications defeat the fundamental objective of time-bound dispute resolution under the IBC, and the Appellate Tribunal possesses supervisory authority to direct expedited disposal within a fixed schedule. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5) mandates that the Adjudicating Authority decide admission or rejection within fourteen days; prolonged pendency spanning hundreds of days is contrary to statutory intent and must be curbed. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Gross procedural delay demonstrated on the face of the record (840+ days of pendency at pre-admission stage). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority must scrupulously adhere to statutory timelines and dispose of the pending Section 9 application preferably within four weeks.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with directions to NCLT Ahmedabad Court No. 1 to adhere scrupulously to IBC timelines and make all endeavors to dispose of the Section 9 application with utmost expedition, preferably within four weeks, and report compliance to the NCLAT.
summary: Appellants Surendra Singh Hada and other operational creditors appealed to NCLAT against the prolonged pre-admission pendency of their Section 9 IBC application against Arfat Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd., which had been languishing before NCLT Ahmedabad for over 840 days. Noting that such extreme delays violate the core IBC mandate of time-bound resolution, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal by issuing peremptory directions to NCLT Ahmedabad to decide the application expeditiously, preferably within four weeks, and report compliance.

case_title: Devas Employees Mauritius Private Limited vs. Antrix Corporation Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Devas Employees Mauritius Pvt. Ltd. (3.48% shareholder in Devas Multimedia); Respondent No. 1 is Antrix Corporation Ltd. (Government company/commercial arm of ISRO); Respondent No. 2 is Ministry of Corporate Affairs; Respondent No. 3 is Devas Multimedia Pvt. Ltd. (in provisional liquidation). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Devas Agreement dated 28.01.2005 entered into between Antrix and Devas Multimedia for delivering broadband wireless access and audio-visual services via hybrid satellite-terrestrial systems, involving Rs. 58.37 Crore reservation fees and substantial foreign investments. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Antrix terminated the contract on 25.02.2011; international arbitration followed; winding-up petition based on massive allegations of fraud, sham transactions, and money laundering rather than commercial debt default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Antrix filed winding-up petition CP No. 06/BB/2021 on 18.01.2021; served on Devas at 4:30 PM on 18.01.2021; listed and heard on 19.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CBI charge-sheets, MCA investigation reports under Companies Act, foreign Letter Rogatory findings confirming misrepresentation of non-existent IPR, and provisional liquidator's initial report indicating Devas was an empty sham paper company. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru on 19.01.2021 admitted the winding-up petition under Section 271(c) of the Companies Act, 2013 and appointed the Official Liquidator as Provisional Liquidator under Section 273; Appellant shareholder appealed alleging breach of natural justice.
legal_issues: Whether a minority shareholder has standing under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 to challenge an ad-interim order appointing a Provisional Liquidator over a company on grounds of fraud, and whether the NCLT had jurisdiction under Section 273(1)(c) to appoint a Provisional Liquidator upon short notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal possesses inherent statutory powers under Section 273(1)(c) and 273(1)(e) of the Companies Act, 2013 to pass urgent ad-interim orders appointing a Provisional Liquidator at the admission stage to preserve assets and prevent ongoing fraud, even where notice is short; a minority shareholder's remedy is to apply for impleadment before the original bench. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 273(1)(c) and (e) confer broad authority on the Tribunal to issue any interim order necessary for winding up; principles of natural justice are flexible and do not prevent ad-interim protective orders when a prima facie case of fraud is established. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prima facie fraud standard: documented findings from statutory investigative agencies and initial liquidator reports showing an entity operates as a sham justify immediate protective sequestration. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's ad-interim appointment of a provisional liquidator was lawful and within its discretion; the shareholder must seek impleadment before the NCLT rather than attacking the ad-interim order directly in appeal.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 02 of 2021 is disposed of without interfering with the appointment of the Provisional Liquidator; Appellant is granted liberty to file an interlocutory application before NCLT Bengaluru seeking impleadment, which the Tribunal shall decide on merits after hearing both sides.
summary: Appellant Devas Employees Mauritius Pvt. Ltd., a 3.48% shareholder of Devas Multimedia Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Bengaluru order admitting a winding-up petition filed by Antrix Corporation Ltd. under Section 271(c) of the Companies Act, 2013 and appointing a Provisional Liquidator. Appellant contended that the order was passed with undue haste on one day's notice, violating natural justice. The NCLAT dismissed the challenge to the provisional liquidation, ruling that under Section 273(1)(c), the Tribunal has wide discretion to pass urgent ad-interim orders to prevent fraud and preserve corporate assets. The NCLAT relegated the shareholder to filing an impleadment application before the NCLT.

case_title: Surajbari Traders Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Sumit Binani & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Surajbari Traders Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant No. 1, shared premises owner/occupant), Kavita Jagatramka (Appellant No. 2, Director of Appellant No. 1), Sumit Binani (Respondent No. 1, Liquidator of Corporate Debtor), M/s Gujarat NRE Coke Ltd. (Respondent No. 2, Corporate Debtor in liquidation), and Arun Kumar Jagatramka (Respondent No. 3, suspended director). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resumption of operations and access to the shared registered office premises of the Corporate Debtor at 22, Camac Street, Block C, 5th Floor, Kolkata during Covid-19 lockdown relaxations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; matter arises from alleged non-cooperation and refusal to hand over office keys to the Liquidator rather than monetary loan default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respondent No. 1 was appointed Liquidator in January 2018; lockdown enforced w.e.f. 25.03.2020 with relaxations starting 31.05.2020; Liquidator issued emails demanding office reopening; clarification application filed on 28.07.2020; contempt order passed on 14.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 21.07.2020 where Liquidator admitted he never sought exclusive possession of the shared premises; proof that over 20 independent companies maintain registered offices and records at the same premises. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed an application under Section 19(2) r/w Section 34(3) without arraying the Appellants; NCLT Kolkata Bench on 17.07.2020 ordered keys to be handed over; Appellants sought clarification; NCLT on 14.08.2020 issued contempt show-cause and police assistance orders to break locks without hearing the clarification application.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in directing the handing over of keys and authorizing police assistance to break locks of a shared multi-company office premises under Section 19(2) r/w Section 34(3) without hearing affected third parties and without first deciding their clarification application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority cannot pass coercive directions granting exclusive access or ordering locks broken on premises shared with non-debtor third parties without affording them an opportunity of hearing and deciding pending clarification applications. 2.
