STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19(2) read with Section 34(3) of the IBC empowers the Liquidator to obtain cooperation and access to the records/assets of the Corporate Debtor, but does not confer jurisdiction to dispossess third parties or grant exclusive possession over premises jointly utilized by non-corporate debtor entities. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the liquidator explicitly concedes in writing that exclusive possession is not claimed and the premise is proven to house books/records of numerous distinct entities, coercive access mechanisms are unsustainable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The impugned ex parte and contempt directions failed to adhere to natural justice and misapprehended the scope of the Liquidator's right to access.
operative_order: Appeals allowed without costs; the impugned orders dated 17.07.2020 and 14.08.2020 are set aside; the Adjudicating Authority is directed to consider the matter afresh and pass appropriate orders in accordance with law.
summary: Surajbari Traders and its director challenged orders of NCLT Kolkata directing the handover of keys to Gujarat NRE Coke Ltd.'s registered premises and threatening coercive police action to break locks under contempt proceedings. The Appellants contended they were never party to the Liquidator's Section 19(2) application, that over 20 group companies occupied the shared premises, and that their clarification application remained undecided. The NCLAT held that because the Liquidator only had right of access rather than exclusive possession, granting coercive lock-breaking orders without deciding the clarification application violated natural justice. The NCLAT allowed the appeals, set aside the impugned orders, and remitted the matter for fresh consideration.

case_title: Moser Baer Karamchari Union, Gautam Buddh Nagar vs. Mr. Anil Kohli, Liquidator for Moser Baer India Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Moser Baer Karamchari Union (Appellant, registered employees union) and Mr. Anil Kohli (Respondent, Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Moser Baer India Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment relationship and statutory liquidation dues payable to workmen under Section 53 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Disputed calculation of gratuity (inclusion of supplementary allowances under Section 2(s) of Payment of Gratuity Act) and retrenchment compensation under Section 25FFF(1) vs Section 25F(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidator admitted preferential dues via email on 02.04.2019; Appellant filed CA-767(PB)/2019 on 15.04.2019; application withdrawn under mistaken impression on 24.08.2020; NCLT rejected recall on 04.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Calculation sheets and email dated 02.04.2019 demonstrating Liquidator restricted retrenchment compensation to three months' average pay under Section 25FFF proviso, excluding supplementary allowances from gratuity. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench rejected Appellant's recall application holding that the IBC does not provide for review/recall once an application is withdrawn by counsel on instructions.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the inherent power under Rule 11 of NCLT Rules, 2016 and Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 to recall an order dismissing an application as withdrawn due to counsel's bona fide misconception, so as to decide substantial statutory workmen claims on merits.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the interest of justice and guided by principles of natural justice, the Adjudicating Authority may exercise inherent powers under Rule 11 of NCLT Rules to recall an order permitting withdrawal made under a bona fide mistake, ensuring substantive claims are determined on merits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates adherence to natural justice, and Rule 11 preserves inherent powers to make orders necessary to prevent miscarriage of justice, which is not completely eclipsed by the absence of an express review provision under the IBC in exceptional circumstances. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: While voluntary withdrawal upon client instruction ordinarily forecloses reopening, where grave statutory rights of a large labor collective are forfeited by misapprehended procedural moves, the tribunal must lean toward adjudication on merits. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The dismissal of the recall application as completely non-maintainable was overly rigid, justifying restoration of the substantive dispute.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 04.12.2020 quashed and set aside; CA-767(PB)/2019 in CP No. IB-378(PB)/2017 restored to the file of NCLT New Delhi with directions to decide the matter on merits without expressing any opinion on the underlying claim.
summary: The Moser Baer Karamchari Union challenged an order of NCLT New Delhi dismissing their application to recall an earlier order that recorded the withdrawal of CA-767(PB)/2019, which raised disputes on gratuity and retrenchment compensation calculations during liquidation. The Adjudicating Authority had held that IBC contains no provision for review or recall once withdrawn on instructions. The NCLAT held that pursuant to Rule 11 of NCLT Rules and Section 424 of the Companies Act, inherent powers must be exercised ex debito justitiae to prevent substantial injustice to workmen whose counsel withdrew under a misconception of law. The NCLAT set aside the impugned order, restored the union's application, and directed adjudication on merits.

case_title: Victor Vanya Bandlamudi vs. Mercados Energy Markets India Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Victor Vanya Bandlamudi (Appellant, erstwhile Senior Manager/Operational Creditor) and Mercados Energy Markets India Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent, Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment contract dated January 2017 under which the Appellant resigned on 31.10.2018, was relieved on 31.03.2019, and claimed unpaid variable pay (performance bonus). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 10,35,700 towards variable pay/bonus for FY 2018-2019 plus interest, alleged to be defaulted after full and final settlement. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Legal notice sent on 01.08.2019; Respondent replies dated 02.08.2019 and 23.08.2019; Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 09.09.2019; Corporate Debtor's reply sent on 25.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Correspondence including emails dated 02.02.2019, 03.02.2019, 12.03.2019, and 30.03.2019 proving that variable pay was contingent upon signing a 6-month retainership contract, which Appellant refused, and that Appellant formed a competing company (EMA Solutions Pvt. Ltd.) in violation of employment ethics. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 9 application (IB-3006/ND/2019); NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI dismissed it on 28.02.2020 on the threshold ground of pre-existing dispute.
legal_issues: Whether correspondence disputing entitlement to variable pay/bonus due to non-fulfillment of conditions and contractual breach constitutes a genuine pre-existing dispute within the meaning of Section 9(5)(2)(d) of the IBC as expounded in Mobilox Innovations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 must be rejected if the respondent raises a plausible, non-spurious pre-existing dispute supported by prior contemporaneous correspondence, without requiring the court to conduct a trial on the merits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'dispute' under Section 9(5)(2)(d) encompasses bona fide differences over contractual conditions precedent, performance, and counterclaims of breach that pre-date the Section 8 demand notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Mobilox standard: the tribunal must separate grain from chaff to reject spurious defenses; so long as the defense is not a patently feeble legal argument or bluster and truly exists in fact, the petition cannot be admitted. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor's documentation established that bonus payment was inextricably tied to an unexecuted retainership agreement and contested due to competing business activities, proving a genuine pre-existing dispute.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs; the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 28.02.2020 rejecting the Section 9 petition is affirmed, with liberty to the Appellant to pursue ordinary civil remedies if permissible by law.
summary: Victor Vanya Bandlamudi appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dismissing his Section 9 petition against Mercados Energy Markets India Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid performance bonus of Rs. 10,35,700. The Corporate Debtor resisted on grounds that the bonus was conditionally tied to the execution of a subsequent 6-month retainership contract and non-compete clauses, which the Appellant breached by floating a rival entity prior to relieving. Applying the Mobilox Innovations benchmark, the NCLAT affirmed that the dispute raised prior to the Section 8 notice was real, plausible, and not spurious or illusory. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the summary insolvency mechanism cannot resolve contentious employment-linked bonus disputes.

case_title: M/s. Mateshwari Minerals vs. Jet Granito Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Mateshwari Minerals through sole proprietor Piyush Bangar (Appellant/Operational Creditor) and Jet Granito Private Limited (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of minerals/goods by the proprietorship firm to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt including an invoice dated 31.12.2016 for Rs. 5,63,213 plus additional claimed amounts. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Petition filed under Section 9 of IBC in 2019 (C.P. (I.B) No. 518/NCLT/AHM/2019); dismissed on maintainability grounds on 28.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Application in Form 5, Part-1 reflecting the name of the Operational Creditor as 'M/s. Mateshwari Minerals Proprietorship Firm' instead of 'Piyush Bangar, Sole Proprietor of M/s Mateshwari Minerals'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-II dismissed the Section 9 petition holding that a sole proprietorship is not a legal entity or 'person' under Section 3(23) of IBC, rendering the petition a legal nullity without granting opportunity to amend.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC filed strictly in the trade name of a sole proprietorship firm is a non-curable nullity or a curable defect requiring the Adjudicating Authority to allow amendment under the proviso to Section 9(5).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Initiating an insolvency application in the trade name of a sole proprietorship rather than the proprietor's personal name is a curable procedural defect and does not render the petition inherently void. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 2(f) explicitly extends the provisions of the IBC to proprietorship firms, and the proviso to Section 9(5) obligates the tribunal to give notice to rectify defects in the application before rejecting it. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following Supreme Court precedent in Bhagwati Vanaspati Traders, an individual using a fictional trade name does not destroy legal standing; correcting the description by substituting or adding the sole proprietor's individual name cures the technical irregularity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in summarily dismissing the application instead of permitting the applicant to amend Part-1 of Form 5.
operative_order: Appeal allowed without costs; impugned order dated 28.02.2020 quashed and set aside; matter remitted back to NCLT Ahmedabad with directions to allow the Appellant to amend the description of the Operational Creditor and decide admission on merits; parties directed to appear before NCLT on 10.03.2021.
summary: M/s Mateshwari Minerals appealed the dismissal of its Section 9 application by NCLT Ahmedabad, which had held that a sole proprietorship firm is not a distinct legal entity or 'person' under Section 3(23) of the IBC. The NCLAT, relying on Neeta Saha and Supreme Court authority in Bhagwati Vanaspati Traders, held that filing an insolvency petition under a proprietorship trade name is merely a curable technical defect. In light of Section 2(f) and the statutory proviso to Section 9(5), the Adjudicating Authority was obligated to allow the applicant to amend the petition to reflect the proprietor's individual name. The appellate tribunal quashed the dismissal and remitted the petition for substantive adjudication on merits.

case_title: Committee of Creditors of Trading Engineers International Ltd. vs. Trading Engineers International Ltd. Through Resolution Professional
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Committee of Creditors of Trading Engineers International Ltd. (Appellant/CoC) and Trading Engineers International Ltd. through its Resolution Professional (Respondent/RP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ongoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) seeking approval and implementation of a viable resolution plan for the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Expiry of the statutory outer timeline of 330 days under Section 12 on 30.09.2020 while final internal approvals and voting on the resolution plan were underway. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP 330-day limit expired on 30.09.2020; RP moved Section 60(5) application for extension; NCLT rejected extension on 23.12.2020; appeal filed and heard on 02.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Uncontested submissions from the RP and CoC demonstrating that internal approvals for the resolution plan were complete and only a final meeting was required to formally vote and approve the plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Special Bench (Court-II) rejected the application under Section 60(5) r/w 12A on 23.12.2020, declining to extend CIRP beyond the 330-day threshold.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the discretion to extend the CIRP timeline beyond 330 days under exceptional circumstances where the CoC is at the brink of approving a viable resolution plan, in order to prevent mechanical liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The 330-day outer limit for CIRP is not mandatory; adjudicating bodies retain discretion to grant short extensions where delay is attributable to legal proceedings and an extension serves the statutory objective of corporate rescue over liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 must be interpreted in alignment with the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel, where striking down 'mandatorily' permits reasonable extension beyond 330 days under Article 14 and 19(1)(g) if only a short period is required to consummate a resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Exceptional circumstances are established when litigants did not cause the delay, judicial intervention accounted for the lapse of time, and viable plan finalization is imminent. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing extension when the CoC was actively poised to approve a resolution plan, justifying exclusion of litigation time and grant of two additional weeks.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 23.12.2020 set aside; period of judicial intervention from 25.09.2020 to 02.02.2021 excluded from CIRP; extension of time granted by two weeks from the date of order to complete voting on the resolution plan.
summary: The Committee of Creditors appealed against an order of NCLT New Delhi rejecting an application for extension of the CIRP timeline beyond the 330-day outer threshold. The Appellant established that the CIRP was near finalization, all internal approvals were secured, and only a final CoC vote was needed. Grounding its decision on the Supreme Court's precedent in Essar Steel India Ltd. v. Satish Kumar Gupta, the NCLAT held that the statutory deadline is directory in exceptional cases to prevent pushing a viable corporate debtor into liquidation. The appellate bench excluded the period of judicial delay and granted a two-week extension to allow the CoC to approve the resolution plan.

case_title: M/s. Suri Rajendra Rolling Mills vs. M/s. Bengani Udyog Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Suri Rajendra Rolling Mills through Partner Saroj P Jain (Appellant/Operational Creditor) and M/s Bengani Udyog Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial dealings and execution of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) under which operational debt was claimed. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational default amounting to Rs. 5,61,000 based on internal ledger entries. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First Section 8 notice sent on 04.04.2018; reply alleging fraud and pre-existing dispute sent on 21.04.2018; first Section 9 petition (C.P. (IB) 1026/KB/2018) withdrawn without liberty on 04.09.2018; second Section 8 notice sent on 25.01.2019; reply sent on 08.02.2019; second Section 9 petition (C.P. (IB) 605/KB/2019) dismissed on 06.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Existence of prior disputes including Civil Suit No. 1234 of 2016, Criminal Case No. 218 of 2016, SARFAESI proceedings, and allegations of coerced MoU execution raised in contemporaneous reply notices. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the second Section 9 petition on 06.01.2020 because the previous petition on identical cause of action was unconditionally withdrawn without liberty.
legal_issues: Whether a successive Section 9 application under the IBC is maintainable for the identical debt and cause of action after an earlier application was unconditionally withdrawn without obtaining liberty to file afresh, and whether substantial pre-existing disputes barred admission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A litigant who unconditionally withdraws an insolvency petition based on an identical cause of action without securing leave to institute fresh proceedings cannot maintain a successive petition for the same debt by merely serving a subsequent statutory demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 proceedings cannot be abused by issuing repeated demand notices to restart causes of action that were earlier abandoned without court-sanctioned liberty. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pleadings revealing prior civil and criminal litigation and allegations of forced execution of contract constitute undeniable proof of pre-existing disputes, negating any claim that withdrawal was predicated on an unfulfilled settlement. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The second application was both procedurally barred due to unreserved withdrawal and substantively barred by preexisting disputes.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs; liberty granted to the Appellant to pursue ordinary legal remedies in appropriate alternative forums.
summary: M/s Suri Rajendra Rolling Mills appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order dismissing its Section 9 insolvency petition against Bengani Udyog Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 5,61,000. An identical earlier application had been dismissed as withdrawn without liberty to file afresh. The Appellant argued that issuing a fresh Section 8 demand notice gave rise to a new cause of action following a failed settlement. Rejecting this contention, the NCLAT held that repetitive notices cannot cure the unconditional abandonment of an insolvency petition on identical claims. Furthermore, pre-existing civil and criminal litigation between the parties fully barred the Section 9 proceedings on merits. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Union of India vs. K.V. Brahmaji Rao
appeal_number: I.A. No. 3013 of 2020 in Company Appeal (AT) No. 126 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Union of India through Ministry of Corporate Affairs (Applicant/Respondent in main appeal) and K.V. Brahmaji Rao (Respondent/Appellant in main appeal). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Regulatory proceedings arising out of CP No. 277 of 2018 before NCLT Mumbai Bench regarding statutory corporate affairs and investigation orders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Clerical typographical error in a decided appellate tribunal judgment; no monetary loan default involved. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original appeal decided on 17.08.2020; rectification application under Section 420(2) filed in late 2020; decided on 19.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Paragraph 10 of the Reply Affidavit of Regional Director Chiradeep Balooni demonstrating that Central Government Counsel expressly opposed the prayers in the appeal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLAT had decided Company Appeal (AT) No. 126 of 2019 on 17.08.2020, but paragraph 9 inadvertently recorded that Central Government Counsel had 'not opposed' the prayer.
legal_issues: Whether a clear typographical and clerical error in a final judgment regarding the recorded stance of counsel can be rectified under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal possesses the statutory authority to correct inadvertent clerical and typographical mistakes apparent on the face of the record without altering the substantive result or ratio of the decision. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 empowers the tribunal to amend any order passed by it to rectify any mistake apparent from the record when brought to its notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparison between the recorded sentence in the judgment and the explicit averments in the formal counter-affidavit on record showing that an inadvertent negative ('not') was mistakenly inserted. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The mistake was apparent on the record and merited formal correction in the judgment text.
operative_order: Application allowed without costs; Paragraph 9 of the judgment dated 17.08.2020 rectified to read: 'Learned Sr. Panel Central Government Counsel has opposed the prayer'; rectified judgment directed to be retained on record.
summary: The Union of India filed an interlocutory application under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules, 2016 for rectification of a clerical error in paragraph 9 of NCLAT's final judgment dated 17.08.2020 in Company Appeal (AT) No. 126 of 2019. The paragraph had mistakenly recorded that the Senior Central Government Panel Counsel had 'not opposed' the appellant's prayer, contrary to the filed reply affidavit. The NCLAT verified the record, found the error apparent on the face of pleadings, and exercised its rectification jurisdiction to delete the mistaken word 'not' without disturbing the outcome of the appeal.

case_title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. vs. Indian Speciality Fats Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. (Appellant/Assignee Financial Creditor), State Bank of India (Assignor original Financial Creditor), and M/s Indian Speciality Fats Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit/financial debt facility availed from State Bank of India and subsequently assigned to Kotak Mahindra Bank via Assignment Deed dated 16.01.2006. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount decreed by DRT Jabalpur for Rs. 14,20,80,104.61 along with costs and interest; account classified as NPA prior to 16.01.2006. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: DRT recovery proceeding OA No. 196/2000 filed around 2000; DRT final order passed on 23.10.2002 culminating in Recovery Certificate; Section 7 petition filed on 29.10.2018; dismissed by NCLT on 05.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Final decree/recovery certificate issued on 23.10.2002 by DRT Jabalpur, pending execution before Recovery Officer, with no acknowledgment of debt within the preceding three-year period. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack Bench in TP No. 202/CTB/2019 arising out of CP(IB) No. 4202/MB/2018 dismissed the Section 7 petition as barred by limitation under Article 137.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 petition filed more than 16 years after the issuance of a DRT Recovery Certificate and NPA declaration is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and whether ongoing execution before a DRT Recovery Officer keeps the right to trigger CIRP alive.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application to initiate CIRP must be instituted within three years from the date of default or the issuance of a recovery decree under Article 137 of the Limitation Act; ongoing execution proceedings before a recovery forum do not furnish a continuing or fresh cause of action to trigger IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 applications are governed strictly by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, requiring institution within three years from the date the right to apply accrues. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Computing limitation from either the date of NPA classification (prior to 16.01.2006) or the date of issuance of the Recovery Certificate (23.10.2002), the filing of the application on 29.10.2018 is patently beyond three years without any valid statutory acknowledgment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The IBC is not a recovery vehicle to execute decades-old DRT decrees, and the Section 7 petition was rightly rejected as hopelessly time-barred.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs; dismissal clarified not to affect the Appellant's right to pursue pending execution and recovery proceedings before the Debt Recovery Tribunal / Competent Court.
summary: Kotak Mahindra Bank appealed against the Cuttack Bench of NCLT dismissing its Section 7 petition against Indian Speciality Fats Ltd. as barred by limitation. The original debt owed to State Bank of India was declared NPA prior to being assigned in 2006, and DRT Jabalpur had issued a recovery certificate on 23.10.2002 for Rs. 14.20 crores, which was still under execution. The Appellant filed the Section 7 petition on 29.10.2018. The NCLAT affirmed that under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the three-year clock starts from the date of default/decree. Because the petition was filed over a decade after the decree and IBC is not a forum for debt recovery, the dismissal was upheld.

case_title: Aditya Birla Finance Ltd. vs. Sintex Prefab and Infra Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Aditya Birla Finance Ltd. (Appellant/Financial Creditor) and Sintex Prefab and Infra Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan/financial credit facility availed by the Corporate Debtor resulting in default. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount subject to Section 7 application (exact quantum not stated; pending admission adjudication). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed in July 2020; listed repeatedly before NCLT; impugned order listing for 'final hearing' passed on 12.01.2021; decided by NCLAT on 22.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Orders of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-II demonstrating repeated adjournments and fixing the pre-admission application for 'final hearing'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application remained unadmitted since July 2020; NCLT listed the matter for 'final hearing' on 12.01.2021, prompting the Financial Creditor to appeal against procedural procrastination.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the legal competence to treat a Section 7 insolvency application at the pre-admission stage as an ordinary civil suit and list it for 'final hearing' rather than deciding debt, default, and completeness within the statutory 14-day window under Section 7(4).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority cannot list an insolvency petition for 'final hearing' at the pre-admission stage, as the statutory enquiry is strictly confined to verifying debt, default, and application completeness without granting protracted adjournments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(4) of the IBC mandates that the Adjudicating Authority ascertain the existence of default within 14 days and immediately pass an order of admission or rejection; the statute does not contemplate a regular 'final hearing' prior to admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pre-admission hearing requires only limited summary satisfaction regarding the occurrence of default based on creditor records and corporate debtor's limited response. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed a procedural error in treating pre-admission proceedings as a full-scale final hearing and granting repeated adjournments.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of with directions to the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench) to address the issue at the pre-admission stage with utmost expedition, preferably within one week, and pass an order of admission or rejection without granting further adjournments.
summary: Aditya Birla Finance Ltd. approached the NCLAT challenging an order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench which scheduled its pending Section 7 application (pending since July 2020) for 'final hearing'. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority acted contrary to the scheme of the IBC, reaffirming that pre-admission proceedings are solely intended to ascertain debt and default under Section 7(4) within 14 days. Emphasizing that no 'final hearing' is postulated prior to CIRP admission, the NCLAT directed the NCLT to determine admission or rejection within one week without entertaining further adjournments.

case_title: M/s RK Associates & Hoteliers Pvt Ltd vs BW Businessworld Media Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s RK Associates & Hoteliers Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/alleged Operational Creditor) and BW Businessworld Media Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/alleged Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) dated 18.06.2018 and subsequent Shareholders Agreement dated 06.12.2018 entered into to jointly qualify, bid, and execute an IRCTC tender for publishing and distributing the railway magazine 'Rail Bandhu' on a 50:50 profit/equity basis via a Special Purpose Vehicle. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount of Rs. 1,22,09,975 claimed with 18% interest per annum w.e.f. 12.03.2019, comprising Rs. 72,09,975 transferred for the performance guarantee and first-year revenue share, plus Rs. 50,00,000 paid for project execution expenses. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Contract awarded to Respondent on 14/16.08.2018; terminated and performance guarantee encashed by IRCTC on 12.03.2019; Section 8 demand notice sent on 31.05.2019; reply by Corporate Debtor issued on 14.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clauses 5 and 12 of the MOU stipulating equal 50:50 joint venture shareholding, mutual non-liability for project expenses upon failure to reach financial closure, and absence of any invoice, purchase order, or documentation proving supply of goods or services between the parties. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition filed by the Appellant was dismissed by NCLT New Delhi (Court No. II) on 20.02.2020 on the ground that financial contributions towards a joint venture/business proposition do not constitute operational debt.
legal_issues: Whether capital contributions and expense sharing for a performance guarantee in a joint venture/consortium project constitute an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC so as to maintain a CIRP application under Section 9.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Capital contributions, performance guarantee funding, and cost-sharing advances paid by a joint venture partner towards a shared business endeavor do not constitute 'operational debt' under the IBC in the absence of an underlying direct supply of goods or rendering of services to the respondent. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) requires the claim to arise out of the provision of goods or services; joint venturers rendering services jointly to an external principal do not render operational services to each other. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of the contractual framework (MOU and shareholder terms) to establish whether the relationship is a joint venture/partnership rather than a vendor-buyer or service provider-client relationship. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The claimed debt arose out of an aborted joint venture project rather than operational supplies, rendering the Section 9 petition unmaintainable.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs; order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 20.02.2020 rejecting the Section 9 application is affirmed.
summary: RK Associates & Hoteliers appealed against an order of NCLT New Delhi dismissing its Section 9 application against BW Businessworld Media for Rs. 1.22 crores. The funds were advanced to cover the Appellant's 50% share of a performance guarantee and operational expenses for an IRCTC publishing contract awarded under a joint venture MOU. Following contract cancellation by IRCTC, the Appellant sought to recover the amount as operational debt. Reaffirming its earlier ruling in Sree Sankeshwara Foundation, the NCLAT held that financial investments and cost shares in a joint venture do not arise from the supply of goods or provision of services. Consequently, the claim did not constitute an operational debt under Section 5(21), and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: UTI Structured Debt Opportunities Fund-I vs. Ms. Pinkush Jaiswal, IRP of Mercator Petroleum Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: UTI Structured Debt Opportunities Fund-I (Appellant/Financial Creditor/SEBI Category II AIF) and Ms. Pinkush Jaiswal (Respondent/Interim Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Mercator Petroleum Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Subscription of 1,300 Secured Non-Convertible Debentures of face value Rs. 10,00,000 each issued by Mercator Ltd. totaling Rs. 130 Crores, secured by a Deed of Corporate Guarantee dated 26.03.2018 executed by the Corporate Debtor (Mercator Petroleum Ltd.). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Defaulted financial debt claim amounting to Rs. 2,57,84,25,381 lodged with the IRP on 24.09.2020 following CIRP initiation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 31.08.2020; claim lodged on 24.09.2020; rejected by IRP on 02.10.2020; avoidance application IA 1746/2020 served on 03.10.2020; claim challenge IA 1628/2020 filed on 06.10.2020; split decision rendered on 07.01.2021 and referred to a third member. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Non-Convertible Debenture deeds, Corporate Guarantee deed dated 26.03.2018, and contradictory judicial opinions delivered on 07.01.2021 by the two-member NCLT bench on the validity and avoidance of the claim. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP under Section 9; upon split verdict in I.A. 1628/2020 and I.A. 1746/2020, the matter was referred to a third member; NCLT Mumbai Bench (Court-V) on 22.01.2021 declined to stall the CIRP process while awaiting third-member adjudication.
legal_issues: Whether the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process and evaluation of resolution plans can proceed while a split verdict regarding the admission or avoidance of a major financial creditor's claim remains pending for tie-breaking adjudication before a third member.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To prevent irreparable prejudice when a substantial claim determining CoC composition and voting rights is pending resolution before a third member following a split verdict, the CIRP may proceed up to receipt of resolution plans, but final opening and approval must be stayed to preserve status quo. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) and inherent equitable powers permit appellate authorities to harmonize statutory resolution timelines with fair adjudication of creditor rights where divergent judicial opinions have arisen within a two-member bench. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pendency of contradictory opinions on avoidance and claim admissibility that could alter voting share warrants preservation of the res before plans are irreversibly considered. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Professional may collect plans but cannot open or approve them until one week after the third member delivers the decisive opinion.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of with directions: (i) Resolution Professional is permitted to receive Resolution Plans but shall not open them or take any decision; (ii) status quo prevailing shall be maintained until one week after the third Member decides; (iii) third Member of NCLT Mumbai Bench is directed to hear and decide IA 1628/2020 and IA 1746/2020 as expeditiously as possible.
summary: UTI Structured Debt Opportunities Fund-I appealed against an interim order of NCLT Mumbai in the CIRP of Mercator Petroleum Ltd. The IRP had rejected the Appellant's financial claim of Rs. 257.84 crores arising under a corporate guarantee and filed avoidance proceedings. The two-member bench delivered a split verdict, referring the dispute to a third member. The Appellant challenged the continuing CIRP and impending plan submission deadline. Balancing creditor protection and insolvency timelines, the NCLAT permitted the RP to collect resolution plans but strictly injuncted the opening, consideration, or approval of any plan, ordering status quo until one week after the third member decides the claim admissibility.

case_title: Ravinder Kumar Kalra vs. Ricela Health Foods Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ravinder Kumar Kalra (Appellant, Director of Suspended Board of Evershine Solvex Pvt. Ltd.), Ricela Health Foods Ltd. (Respondent No. 1, Operational Creditor), and Evershine Solvex Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial operational transactions regarding supply of goods/services resulting in outstanding operational dues. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount of Rs. 27 Lakhs demanded under Section 8 notice, subsequently reduced to Rs. 19 Lakhs following two part-payments of Rs. 3 Lakhs on 09.04.2019 and Rs. 5 Lakhs on 22.04.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued under Section 8(1) on 08.03.2019 (unreplied); Corporate Debtor set ex-parte on 17.02.2020; Section 9 admission order passed on 27.02.2020; Section 60(5) recall dismissed on 15.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Postal department speed-post tracking report evidencing uncontroverted service of statutory notice; ledger account entries maintained by Operational Creditor documenting unpaid liability and subsequent partial payments. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench set Corporate Debtor ex-parte on 17.02.2020 after finding postal delivery established, admitted the Section 9 petition on 27.02.2020, and subsequently dismissed Corporate Debtor's IA No. 283/2020 filed under Section 60(5) r/w Rules 11, 49, 110 on 15.12.2020.
legal_issues: Whether postal tracking confirmation constitutes valid service to justify proceeding ex-parte under Section 9, and whether an unreplied demand notice coupled with subsequent part-payments deprives the corporate debtor of raising maintainability and pre-existing dispute defenses.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where service via speed post is authenticated by uncontroverted official postal tracking reports free from allegations of fraud or forgery, an Adjudicating Authority is fully justified in proceeding ex-parte and admitting an uncontested Section 9 petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 9(5), the tribunal is mandated to admit the application upon verifying default and completeness; an unreplied Section 8 notice and failure to appear in response to limited pre-admission notice forecloses belated pleas of non-maintainability. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Postal tracking reports serve as unrebutted proof of valid service; partial payments made after the statutory demand notice constitute written acknowledgment of operational liability that negates any pretext of a pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor was served in accordance with law, failed to appear, and acknowledged the operational debt through part-payments, rendering the admission fully valid.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs; the orders of NCLT Chandigarh Bench setting the Corporate Debtor ex-parte and admitting the Section 9 petition are affirmed.
summary: The suspended director of Evershine Solvex Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Ricela Health Foods Ltd. and rejecting its application to set aside the ex-parte proceedings. The Appellant argued that the Corporate Debtor was not served with notice and that operational debt was not established. The NCLAT held that postal department tracking reports constituted conclusive proof of valid service absent allegations of fraud. Furthermore, the Corporate Debtor failed to reply to the Section 8 demand notice and made part-payments reducing the debt from Rs. 27 lakhs to Rs. 19 lakhs, thereby admitting liability. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: IIFL Finance Ltd. vs. AVJ Developers (India) Pvt. Ltd. and Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: IIFL Finance Ltd. (Appellant/Financial Creditor seeking claim adjudication) and AVJ Developers (India) Pvt. Ltd. through its Resolution Professional (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) involving evaluation and approval of a resolution plan alongside pending financial debt claims. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Pending adjudication of financial claim in IA No. 1261(PB)/2020 prior to CoC consideration of the resolution plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLAT directed expedited disposal within two weeks on 10.09.2020 (Company Appeal No. 772 of 2020); Supreme Court ordered disposal within one week on 26.11.2020 (Civil Appeal No. 3512 of 2020); NCLT reserved orders on 12.11.2020, reheard on 09.12.2020, and re-reserved on 14.12.2020; CIRP extended by 60 days on 11.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Successive judicial orders establishing non-compliance by the Adjudicating Authority with binding directions of the Supreme Court and NCLAT to pronounce orders on IA No. 1261(PB)/2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench on 11.01.2021 extended the CIRP period by 60 days w.e.f. 27.12.2020 while keeping IA No. 1261(PB)/2020 unresolved, enabling the CoC to proceed toward approving a resolution plan without resolving Appellant's claim.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors can proceed to consider and approve a Resolution Plan while a financial creditor's claim application remains unadjudicated in violation of peremptory timelines and orders issued by superior appellate courts.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority must decide pending creditor claim applications before permitting the Committee of Creditors to deliberate upon or approve a Resolution Plan, especially where superior courts have issued peremptory disposal directives. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 CIRP timeline extensions granted to consummate a resolution cannot be utilized to frustrate the adjudicatory rights of creditors whose applications challenging claim exclusions are kept pending by the tribunal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted court records showing repeated reservation and reopening of orders in defiance of explicit Supreme Court mandates require appellate interdiction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC must be injuncted from voting on the resolution plan until the Adjudicating Authority delivers its judgment on the pending claim application.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of with directions to the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi) to decide IA No. 1261(PB)/2020 within one week from the date of order and report compliance; Committee of Creditors directed not to consider the Resolution Plan pending before it until such determination.
summary: IIFL Finance Ltd. appealed against an order of NCLT New Delhi extending the CIRP of AVJ Developers (India) Pvt. Ltd. by 60 days, alleging that the CoC was proceeding to approve a resolution plan without determining its financial claim in IA No. 1261(PB)/2020. Despite prior orders from NCLAT and the Supreme Court directing decision within strict timelines, the NCLT had repeatedly reserved and reopened the application without issuing an order. Emphasizing judicial discipline, the NCLAT directed the Adjudicating Authority to decide the application within one week and restrained the CoC from considering the resolution plan until the claim was formally determined.

case_title: Committee of Creditors Through Shri Ashish Kumar Srivastava vs. Sanjay Gupta and Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Committee of Creditors through Ashish Kumar Srivastava (Appellant/CoC), Sanjay Gupta (Respondent No. 1), and Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ongoing corporate insolvency proceedings in CP (IB)-266(ND)2019 regarding claims and resolution process administration. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in procedural timelines; forfeiture of right to file reply to an interlocutory application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Peremptory order barring further adjournments passed on 02.11.2020; matter adjourned to 27.11.2020; right to reply closed on 05.01.2021; review application IA No. 59/2021 rejected on 12.01.2021; appeal decided on 15.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Orders of the Adjudicating Authority granting repeated extensions culminating in a peremptory warning which the Appellant breached by failing to tender its written response. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court II) closed the Appellant's right to file reply on 05.01.2021 due to persistent failure to file despite peremptory directions, and subsequently refused to review the closure order on 12.01.2021.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is justified in forfeiting a party's right to file a reply in CIRP proceedings after non-compliance with peremptory orders, and whether an order refusing review of such closure suffers from legal infirmity.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Insolvency proceedings are time-bound and non-adversarial; procedural accommodations and liberal adjournments customary to regular civil suits cannot be granted, and failure to comply with peremptory filing deadlines justifies forfeiture of the right to file reply. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 and IBC summary mechanisms do not permit review of procedural closure orders absent an error apparent on the face of the record. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Persistent failure to lodge pleadings following an explicit final indulgence constitutes procedural default warranting closure, provided natural justice is mitigated by permitting written submissions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The forfeiture order and subsequent rejection of review were procedurally proper; natural justice is preserved by allowing oral hearing and written submissions.
operative_order: Appeals dismissed without costs; Adjudicating Authority directed to permit the Appellant to place its written submissions on record and afford it an opportunity of being heard prior to final disposal.
summary: The Committee of Creditors appealed against orders of NCLT New Delhi closing its right to file a reply in CP (IB)-266(ND)2019 and dismissing its subsequent review application. The Adjudicating Authority had issued a peremptory order on 02.11.2020 stating no further adjournments would be granted, yet the CoC failed to file its reply by 27.11.2020. The NCLAT held that CIRP is a strictly time-bound process and not ordinary adversarial civil litigation, justifying the strict enforcement of peremptory orders. Upholding the closure, the NCLAT nonetheless directed the Adjudicating Authority to allow the Appellant to place written submissions on record to safeguard the right of hearing.

case_title: Shubh Holdings Pte. Ltd. vs. Anish Niranjan Nanavaty, Resolution Professional of Reliance Infratel Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shubh Holdings Pte. Ltd. (Appellant, erroneously listed in cause list as Doha Bank QPSC) and Anish Niranjan Nanavaty (Respondent No. 1, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Reliance Infratel Ltd.)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Reliance Infratel Ltd. involving pending interlocutory applications directly affecting resolution plan approval and creditor rights[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Pending adjudication of applications challenging CIRP actions and plan considerations[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Delay of 13 days in filing the appeal condoned pursuant to Supreme Court suo moto limitation orders; appeal heard and disposed of on 03.02.2021[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Commonality of issues and reliance on the prior binding judgment of NCLAT dated 19.01.2021 passed in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 19 of 2021[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Interlocutory applications remained undecided before the Adjudicating Authority; identical impugned orders were challenged in connected appeals, with Company Appeal No. 19 of 2021 already disposed of with directions for time-bound disposal[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal involving identical grounds and parties arising from the same CIRP process is entitled to be disposed of in terms of the directions rendered in a previously decided companion appeal[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the subject matter and legal grievances in an insolvency appeal are identical to and covered by a prior coordinate bench ruling in a companion appeal concerning the same corporate debtor, the appeal is to be decided on identical terms to ensure consistency[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) applications affecting resolution plans must be disposed of expeditiously to allow the Adjudicating Authority to reconsider its orders if warranted by subsequent determinations[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Identity of facts and legal questions admitted across companion proceedings in the same CIRP[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is covered in toto by the earlier judgment rendered in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 19 of 2021[cite: 18].
operative_order: Appeal disposed of in terms of the coordinate judgment dated 19.01.2021 in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 19 of 2021, directing the Adjudicating Authority to dispose of the pending applications with utmost expedition, preferably within three weeks, and reconsider the impugned order if the outcome so warrants; registry directed to place a copy of the prior judgment on record[cite: 18].
summary: Shubh Holdings Pte. Ltd. appealed an order of the Adjudicating Authority in the CIRP of Reliance Infratel Ltd., raising issues identical to those adjudicated in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 19 of 2021[cite: 18]. After rectifying a clerical error in the cause list and condoning a 13-day filing delay, the NCLAT held that the dispute was squarely covered by its prior judgment of 19.01.2021[cite: 18]. Disposing of the appeal in identical terms, the appellate tribunal directed the Adjudicating Authority to decide the underlying applications within three weeks and reconsider the impugned order if necessitated by the findings[cite: 18].

case_title: Mani Kumar Singh vs. Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Mani Kumar Singh is a suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 1 Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. is the Financial Creditor; Respondent No. 2 is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial credit facility assigned/extended to the Corporate Debtor for which default occurred. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and specific date of default occurred prior to the cut-off date envisaged under Section 10A of the IBC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application was registered as CP (IB) No. 458/ALD/2019; substitution application was filed and seven opportunities were granted to Corporate Debtor to file response. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor failed to file a reply on judicial record before NCLT; an unfiled response dated 24th August 2020 was produced at Page 166 of Appeal Paper Book Vol. II by a faction of erstwhile Directors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench admitted Section 7 application on 03.09.2020 after finding debt, default, and compliance with Section 10A, appointing an IRP and declaring moratorium; suspended director appealed claiming breach of natural justice.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority breached the principles of natural justice by admitting a Section 7 petition without hearing the Corporate Debtor when the Corporate Debtor failed to file a response despite seven opportunities, and whether individual directors or factions thereof have an independent right of audience distinct from the juristic entity.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party granted ample procedural opportunities who neglects to file its pleadings cannot claim violation of natural justice; at the Section 7 admission stage, proceedings are summary, time-bound, and require only satisfaction of debt and default without protracted pre-admission hearings, and a juristic company is distinct from individual factions of directors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(4) and Section 7(5) mandate prompt disposal within statutory timelines; the Adjudicating Authority requires only limited inquiry into the existence of financial debt and default occurring prior to the Section 10A cut-off date. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Recitals in judicial records that opportunities were provided operate as estoppel by record; unfiled replies submitted by rival director factions do not constitute pleadings of the corporate entity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because seven opportunities were extended and ignored, the Adjudicating Authority rightfully proceeded under Section 7(4) to admit the petition; the appeal was dismissed with liberty to approach the CoC for settlement.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of (dismissed) without disturbing the admission order dated 03.09.2020, granting liberty to the Corporate Debtor to approach the Committee of Creditors with an all-encompassing settlement proposal.
summary: An appeal was preferred by a suspended director of the Corporate Debtor against an NCLT Allahabad Bench order admitting a Section 7 application filed by Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. The Appellant contended that principles of natural justice were violated as the Corporate Debtor was not heard. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority had provided seven opportunities to file a reply, which operated as estoppel by record. The Tribunal ruled that Section 7 proceedings are summary and time-bound, requiring only satisfaction of debt, default, and non-violation of Section 10A, and separate factions of management have no individual right of hearing distinct from the company, thus upholding the admission.

case_title: M/s Dreamz Infra India Ltd. Through Ashok Kriplani (RP) vs. Pratap Chandra Padhy
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s Dreamz Infra India Ltd. represented through Resolution Professional Ashok Kriplani; Respondent is Pratap Chandra Padhy. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate corporate insolvency resolution process initiated under Section 7/9 in C.P. (IB) No. 84/BB/2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in underlying CIRP timeline calculations under Section 12 for completion of CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Statutory CIRP period of 180 days plus 90 days; RP filed I.A. No. 308 of 2020 seeking exclusion of 195 days from 16.05.2020 to 16.09.2020 due to COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Government of India and Government of Karnataka notifications extending lockdown up to 31.08.2020 and 30.09.2020; Bengaluru Urban Covid-19 War Room data dated 30.09.2020 showing escalation of containment zones; evidence that RP resided in New Delhi with New Delhi-Bengaluru flight services suspended. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench vide order dated 16.09.2020 granted only 68 days exclusion (25.03.2020 to 31.05.2020) and rejected the remaining period; RP appealed against said partial exclusion.
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional is entitled to the exclusion of the entire lockdown period (15th May 2020 to 16th September 2020) from the computation of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process timeline when continuous containment restrictions and flight disruptions prevented CIRP activities.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Time periods during which CIRP cannot proceed due to government-imposed lockdowns, containment zone restrictions, and total disruption of interstate transport must be fully excluded from statutory CIRP calculations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 statutory computation of CIRP period excludes extraordinary periods where resolution is rendered impossible due to nationwide/state lockdowns under Rule 11 and Section 60(5). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Official notifications of the Central and State Governments detailing extensions of lockdown, coupled with travel restrictions preventing the RP from discharging duties, constitute conclusive proof justifying exclusion. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in limiting exclusion to 68 days; the entire lockdown period from 15th May 2020 till 16th September 2020 must be excluded in computing the CIRP period.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 16th September 2020 passed by NCLT Bengaluru Bench is set aside; the appeal is allowed, directing that the period from 15th May 2020 till 16th September 2020 be excluded in computing the CIRP period.
summary: The Resolution Professional of Dreamz Infra India Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Bengaluru Bench's order which granted only 68 days of lockdown exclusion instead of the requested 195 days. The RP produced notifications issued by the Government of India and the State of Karnataka showing lockdown extensions up to September 2020, as well as travel restrictions between New Delhi and Bengaluru. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority failed to consider these operational impediments and pandemic restrictions. Setting aside the lower tribunal's order, the Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and directed the exclusion of the period from 15th May 2020 till 16th September 2020 from the statutory CIRP timeline.

case_title: Jalesh Kumar Grover vs. Committee of Creditors of Akme Projects Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Jalesh Kumar Grover is the Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Akme Projects Ltd.; Respondent is the Committee of Creditors of Akme Projects Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development project involving homebuyers and commercial allottees undergoing CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in adhering to the outer statutory CIRP timeline of 330 days under Section 12 of the Code. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Extension sought beyond 330 days; 270 days had previously been excluded; exclusion specifically claimed for litigation from 13.10.2020 to 09.12.2020 and up to 01.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Inclusion of Spade Financial Services Ltd. and AAA Landmark Pvt. Ltd. in CoC was rejected by NCLT, affirmed by NCLAT on 27.01.2020, and carried to the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal Nos. 3063 & 2841 of 2020, which were dismissed on 01.02.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-II rejected the RP's application for extension/exclusion beyond 330 days on 20.01.2021 on the ground that prior exclusions had been granted and CIRP had to conclude; RP appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the period consumed in litigation before the Supreme Court concerning CoC constitution should be excluded from the mandatory 330-day CIRP period in a real estate project involving legitimate interests of homebuyers and stakeholders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Time spent in bona fide judicial intervention determining the constitution of the Committee of Creditors must be excluded from the CIRP timeline using a pragmatic approach to prevent the defeat of justice, especially in real estate insolvencies. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The 330-day outer limit under Section 12 is subject to realistic and pragmatic exclusions where litigation pending before the Apex Court directly impacts CIRP progression. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Sub-judice status of fundamental CoC composition before the highest court warrants equitable judicial exclusion of the exact period of judicial intervention. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority overlooked the pendency of proceedings before the Supreme Court; 112 days spent litigating between 13.10.2020 and 01.02.2021 must be excluded from the 330-day limit.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 20th January 2021 is set aside and the appeal is allowed; a period of 112 days (from 13th October 2020 to 1st February 2021) is excluded from the 330-day CIRP timeline, clarified to not act as a precedent for other cases.
summary: The Resolution Professional of Akme Projects Ltd., a real estate corporate debtor, appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi Bench-II refusing to grant extension/exclusion beyond 330 days. The RP demonstrated that the constitution of the CoC had been sub-judice before the Supreme Court in appeals regarding the inclusion of Spade Financial Services Ltd. and AAA Landmark Pvt. Ltd., which were decided on 01.02.2021. The NCLAT held that real estate insolvencies involving homebuyers require a pragmatic approach and that the period consumed in judicial intervention before the Apex Court must be excluded to prevent CIRP from being defeated. The appeal was allowed, granting an exclusion of 112 days.

case_title: Subrata M. Maity, RP of Eskay K' N' IT (India) Ltd. vs. COC of Eskay K' N' IT (India) Ltd. Through Bank of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Subrata M. Maity is the Resolution Professional of Eskay K' N' IT (India) Ltd.; Respondents are the Committee of Creditors led by Bank of India. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution process of Corporate Debtor Eskay K' N' IT (India) Ltd. following financial default. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in adherence to statutory CIRP duration of 180/270 days due to pandemic lockdown. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: 180 days expired on 17th August 2020; Adjudicating Authority granted a 90-day extension but excluded only 68 days instead of the full lockdown from 25.03.2020 to 25.10.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Government notifications demonstrating continuous lockdown and economic disruption between 25.03.2020 and 25.10.2020 (213 days); impugned order contained adverse remarks attributing 'delaying tactics' to the RP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-2 granted 90 days extension but restricted exclusion to 68 days and passed adverse remarks against the RP; RP appealed seeking full 213-day exclusion and expungement of remarks.
legal_issues: Whether the full COVID-19 lockdown period of 213 days ought to be excluded from the computation of the 270-day CIRP period, and whether adverse remarks alleging 'delaying tactics' by a Resolution Professional can be sustained without demonstrating malafide or a consistent pattern of deliberate default.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The entire duration of lockdown-induced economic disruption must be excluded from CIRP calculations, and judicial remarks imputing dilatory conduct against court officers cannot be sustained absent demonstrated mala fides or a consistent course of deliberate omission. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 computation requires exclusion of nationwide lockdown days from the 180/270-day limit to enable genuine resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Finding an RP guilty of dilatory tactics requires proof of a series of deliberate acts with oblique motives; a solitary act during pandemic disruption is insufficient. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP was entitled to an exclusion of 213 days (25.03.2020 to 25.10.2020), and the adverse remarks against the RP were unwarranted and must be expunged.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed in part; 213 days are directed to be excluded from the CIRP period, and the adverse observations/remarks made by the Adjudicating Authority against the Resolution Professional are expunged from the record.
summary: The Resolution Professional of Eskay K' N' IT (India) Ltd. challenged an order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-2 which limited lockdown exclusion to 68 days and made adverse remarks accusing the RP of delaying tactics. The NCLAT held that the entire lockdown period of 213 days from 25.03.2020 to 25.10.2020 must be excluded in computing the extended 270-day CIRP period. The Appellate Tribunal further held that holding an RP guilty of dilatory tactics requires evidence of mala fide or oblique motives through a series of acts, which was absent in this case during the pandemic. The NCLAT allowed the exclusion and ordered the expungement of the adverse remarks.

case_title: Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi vs. Power Finance Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi is the Liquidator for Ind-Barath Power (Madras) Ltd.; Respondents are Power Finance Corporation Ltd. and other creditors/parties. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation proceedings of Ind-Barath Power (Madras) Ltd. under CP (IB)(150)/9/HDB/2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Repeated delays and non-adjudication of pending interlocutory applications impeding liquidation timelines. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Order dated 07.01.2021 in IA No. 28 of 2021 and IA No. 157 of 2019 adjourned the applications to 29.01.2021; matters were not taken up on 29.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Procedural record demonstrating frequent adjournments of IA No. 28 of 2021 and IA 157 of 2019 without disposal, causing prejudice to liquidation administration. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appeal filed under Section 61 against the adjournment order dated 07.01.2021 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench (Special Bench), seeking expedited hearing.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal should intervene against a routine adjournment order of the Adjudicating Authority to mandate expeditious, time-bound disposal of pending interlocutory applications in liquidation proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Repeated adjournments of interlocutory applications in liquidation proceedings violate the statutory imperative of expedition under the Code, warranting administrative appellate directions to dispose of matters without granting unnecessary adjournments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61 read with the procedural framework of the IBC requires adherence to statutory time limits and elimination of unnecessary delays in hearing interim applications. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Demonstration of persistent adjournments without substantive hearings establishes procedural prejudice warranting supervisory expedition directives. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority must take up and decide the pending interlocutory applications expeditiously, preferably on the next designated date, after providing adequate opportunity of hearing.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with directions to NCLT Hyderabad Bench (Special Bench) to take up IA No. 28 of 2021, IA No. 157 of 2019 and other pending IAs preferably on 25.02.2021 and dispose of them expeditiously without unnecessary adjournments.
summary: The Liquidator of Ind-Barath Power (Madras) Ltd. filed an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC challenging an adjournment order dated 07.01.2021 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench (Special Bench) in IA No. 28 of 2021 and IA No. 157 of 2019. The Appellant contended that continuous adjournments severely prejudiced the liquidation process and delayed the administration of justice. The NCLAT Chennai Bench disposed of the appeal by directing the Adjudicating Authority to take up the applications preferably on 25.02.2021 and dispose of them expeditiously in adherence to the statutory timelines of the Code, ensuring adequate opportunity of hearing to all parties.

case_title: Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. vs. Dilwara Leasing and Investment Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Respondent Dilwara Leasing and Investment Ltd. is the Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial debt advanced by Respondent to Appellant leading to a Section 7 insolvency petition. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid financial debt leading to default, currently at the pre-admission stage. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor was granted time to file reply on 09.11.2020; matter came up on 17.12.2020 (around 40 days later) where right to file reply was forfeited. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor cited internal board conflicts and lack of consensus on appointment of legal counsel as cause of failure to submit reply. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-IV closed the Corporate Debtor's right to file reply on 17.12.2020 due to non-filing over 40 days; Corporate Debtor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in closing the Corporate Debtor's right to file a reply to a Section 7 application after 40 days had elapsed, and whether internal managerial deadlock justifies bypassing statutory timelines under Section 7(5).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Internal directorial disputes within a corporate debtor do not justify protracted delays in filing a defense, and an adjudicating authority acts within its jurisdiction in forfeiting the right to reply when statutory timelines are flouted. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5) mandates that the Adjudicating Authority pass an order of admission or rejection within 14 days; even if directory, it provides mandatory guidelines to ensure summary adjudication and timely CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Availing approximately 40 days without filing a reply constitutes failure of due diligence that forfeits the right of response in summary insolvency proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Granting further adjournments would violate the statutory mandate of Section 7; the Adjudicating Authority's order closing the right to reply is valid.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order closing the Corporate Debtor's right to file its reply.
summary: The Corporate Debtor appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi Court-IV which closed its right to file a reply to a Section 7 application after it failed to do so for over 40 days. The Appellant argued that disputes among its directors prevented timely consensus on appointing counsel. The NCLAT rejected the plea, holding that the mandate under Section 7(5) requires admission or rejection within 14 days and that proceedings are summary in nature, focused only on debt and default. Holding that internal corporate deadlocks cannot defeat the time-bound framework of the IBC, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Manohar Kakumal Keshwani & Ors. vs. Kishore Kakumal Keswani
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Manohar Kakumal Keshwani & Ors.; Respondent is Kishore Kakumal Keswani; dispute involves management and operation of a family/corporate hotel enterprise. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Day-to-day management, control, and commercial operations of a hotel venture disrupted by COVID-19 pandemic. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Intra-company management and control dispute concerning alleged unlawful exclusion/interference in hotel operations. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: An AGM took place on 12.11.2020 prior to the hearing of the company petition; NCLT passed interim injunction on the same day without affording Appellants opportunity to file written reply. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Impugned order ordered hotel operations to continue as run before COVID-19 and barred interference by non-operating parties, without identifying which faction actually held management. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai passed an interim mandatory injunction on 12.11.2020; Appellants appealed claiming denial of natural justice and patent vagueness.
legal_issues: Whether an interim mandatory injunction regarding the management and operation of a company's business can be sustained when it is unreasoned, vague, fails to specify the parties in control, and was issued without granting the opposing party an opportunity to file a written reply.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interim mandatory injunction concerning corporate control must be grounded in precise findings of fact identifying the parties affected and cannot be issued without affording parties an opportunity to file pleadings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241/242 interim powers require specific, reasoned adjudications identifying who was in lawful control prior to the alleged disruption. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An order that is patently vague on its face as to which party was managing the enterprise cannot satisfy judicial scrutiny. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The impugned order was ambiguous, unreasoned, and passed in violation of natural justice, requiring it to be set aside and remanded for a reasoned rehearing.
operative_order: The impugned interim order dated 12.11.2020 is set aside; the appeal is allowed and disposed of with directions to NCLT Mumbai to afford the parties an opportunity to file pleadings, rehear the matter, and pass a reasoned and specific order.
summary: Appellants challenged an interim order passed by NCLT Mumbai in a company petition governing the management of a hotel. The NCLT had directed that operations continue as they were prior to the COVID-19 pandemic and restrained non-involved parties from interfering, without allowing Appellants to file a written reply. The NCLAT held that the order was in the nature of an interim mandatory injunction that was patently vague, as it failed to determine which faction had actually been running the hotel and against whom the restraint operated. Setting aside the order, the Appellate Tribunal remanded the matter to the NCLT for fresh, reasoned adjudication.

case_title: Power Finance Corporation Ltd. vs. Shree Maheshwar Hydel Power Corporation Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Power Finance Corporation Ltd. is the Financial Creditor; Respondent Shree Maheshwar Hydel Power Corporation Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financing of a hydroelectric power project by the Financial Creditor resulting in default. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding financial debt and default leading to filing of Section 7 petition in 2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed in 2018 remained pending at pre-admission stage; impugned order adjourned proceedings to 11.02.2021 for completion of pleadings. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Admitted judicial record that Section 7 petition had been languishing at the pre-admission stage for nearly three years without an admission or rejection order. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application pending before NCLT Indore Bench at Ahmedabad Court No. 1; Financial Creditor appealed against repeated routine adjournments.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can indefinitely keep a Section 7 application at the pre-admission stage through routine adjournments, contrary to the statutory timelines envisaged under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory mandate requiring the Adjudicating Authority to decide Section 7 applications within prescribed timelines must be strictly adhered to, precluding indefinite pre-admission adjournments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(4) and 7(5) require the Adjudicating Authority to ascertain debt and default and pass an order of admission or rejection within statutory limits, subject only to limited hearings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pre-admission pendency of an application filed in 2018 is an inordinate delay requiring appellate supervisory directions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority must conclude the pre-admission stage and decide the application within two weeks after granting a limited hearing.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with directions to the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Indore Bench at Ahmedabad) to decide the Section 7 application in accordance with law within two weeks after providing an opportunity of limited hearing, and report compliance.
summary: Power Finance Corporation Ltd. appealed against an order of NCLT Indore Bench at Ahmedabad adjourning a Section 7 application filed in 2018 for completion of pleadings. The Appellant contended that the application had languished at the pre-admission stage for three years. The NCLAT observed that there was inordinate delay contrary to the mandate and timelines of the IBC. Without delving into past causes of delay, the Appellate Tribunal disposed of the appeal by directing the Adjudicating Authority to strictly adhere to statutory timelines and decide the Section 7 application on admission within two weeks after granting a limited hearing.

case_title: Satish Chand Gupta vs. Servel India Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sh. Satish Chand Gupta is the Financial Creditor/Appellant; Servel India Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Unsecured loans/deposits disbursed by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor over various financial years (Rs. 7,00,000 in FY 2013-14; Rs. 1,00,000 in FY 2014-15; Rs. 2,00,000 in FY 2017-18) carrying an interest rate of 13.5% p.a., credited consistently across five years. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of INR 21,94,771 (principal amount INR 18,63,108 plus unpaid interest of INR 3,31,663) as of 01.07.2019, with failure to credit interest/deposit TDS occurring on 31.03.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued on 21.06.2019 and emailed on 24.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements, ledger accounts of the Corporate Debtor, TDS certificates in Form 16A, and email exchanges between Appellant's son and CEO Rahul Choudhry admitting liability (emails dated 27.12.2018 and 05.03.2019 acknowledging pending repayment). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed on 16.07.2019 ((IB) 1886 (ND)/2019); NCLT New Delhi Bench-V dismissed the petition on 13.02.2020 holding that the amount deposited was a 'deposit' under Chapter V of the Companies Act, 2013, rather than a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of IBC.
legal_issues: Whether money deposited with a corporate debtor bearing interest constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, thereby entitling the depositor to initiate CIRP under Section 7 of the Code.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Money borrowed or deposited against the payment of interest qualifies as consideration for the time value of money, rendering the transaction a financial debt under Section 5(8) regardless of whether it is termed a deposit or unsecured loan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) encompasses money borrowed against payment of interest; the definition of 'deposit' under Section 2(31) of Companies Act and Rule 2(1)(c) of Acceptance of Deposits Rules is inclusive, and invoking Chapter V remedies under the Companies Act does not preclude CIRP remedies under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Ledger entries, consistent credit of interest, deduction of TDS under Form 16A, and unrefuted written email admissions of liability satisfy the test of debt disbursal for time value of money and default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The deposit with an agreed interest component constitutes a financial debt under Section 5(8) and the appellant is a financial creditor under Section 5(7); hence, the Section 7 petition is maintainable.
