operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 13.02.2020 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-V is set aside; application under Section 7 is restored with directions to the Adjudicating Authority to admit the same and proceed in accordance with law.
summary: Financial Creditor Satish Chand Gupta appealed an NCLT order dismissing his Section 7 IBC application against Servel India Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had ruled that the disbursed sums were company deposits governed by Chapter V of the Companies Act, 2013, rather than financial debt under the IBC. The NCLAT held that money disbursed against interest is compensation for the time value of money, squarely falling under Section 5(8) of the IBC. Supported by five years of interest ledger entries and TDS deductions, the debt and default were firmly established. Consequently, NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the dismissal, and directed the Adjudicating Authority to admit the Section 7 application.

case_title: Harkirat Singh Bedi vs. The Oriental Bank of Commerce & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Harkirat Singh Bedi is the Erstwhile Promoter/Resolution Applicant; M/s IDEB Projects Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Oriental Bank of Commerce and State Bank of India are Financial Creditors; Velayudham Jayavel is the RP/Liquidator. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Working capital credit facility availed by the Corporate Debtor from a Consortium of Banks in 2007. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit repayment leading to recovery proceedings in DRT Bangalore (O.A. No. 862 of 2010), failure under a subsequent compromise petition, and issuance of a DRT recovery certificate on 23.03.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7 on 29.03.2019; EOI published on 16.06.2019; Appellant submitted EOI on 28.06.2019; resolution plan submitted on 16.09.2019; CIRP expired on 25.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant classified as a 'wilful defaulter' by SBI, State Bank of Travancore, and OBC (reflected on CIBIL database since 2011/2012); MSME registration procured post-CIRP admission on 05.06.2019; absence of Section 29A affidavit and Regulation 38 undertakings with the submitted plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CoC voted with 92.63% majority to liquidate; NCLT Bengaluru Bench ordered liquidation on 08.11.2019 in C.P. (IB) No. 17/BB/2019 due to Appellant's ineligibility under Section 29A(b).
legal_issues: Whether a promoter declared as a wilful defaulter under RBI guidelines can submit a resolution plan by claiming MSME exemption under Section 240A, and whether the CoC's decision to reject a plan and order liquidation under Section 33(2) is subject to judicial review.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An applicant declared as a wilful defaulter under RBI guidelines is strictly disqualified under Section 29A(b), and the commercial wisdom of the CoC to reject a non-compliant plan or refuse extension of CIRP timelines under Section 33(2) is non-justiciable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 240A exempts MSMEs exclusively from Section 29A(c) and 29A(h), providing no exemption from the disqualification under Section 29A(b); moreover, post-CIRP admission MSME registrations without RP sanction are void. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The subsisting wilful defaulter entry on CIBIL database without any stay from a High Court is conclusive on the RP and CoC as to disqualification. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The promoter was disqualified under Section 29A(b), and the CoC lawfully exercised its commercial wisdom to reject the resolution plan and resolve to liquidate the corporate debtor.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; impugned liquidation order dated 08.11.2019 upheld; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Harkirat Singh Bedi, erstwhile promoter of IDEB Projects Pvt. Ltd., challenged the NCLT Bengaluru order directing liquidation of the Corporate Debtor after the CoC rejected his resolution plan. The CoC and NCLT held the Appellant ineligible under Section 29A(b) of the IBC because he was declared a wilful defaulter by OBC and SBI. The Appellant contended he was entitled to MSME exemptions under Section 240A and was denied adequate CIRP time. The NCLAT held that Section 240A only exempts clauses (c) and (h) of Section 29A, not wilful defaulters under clause (b). Reaffirming the non-justiciability of CoC's commercial wisdom, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Kalinga Allied Industries India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Hindustan Coils Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kalinga Allied Industries India Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant/Appellant; Bindals Sponnge Industries Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Hindustan Coils Ltd. is the Unsuccessful Third-Party Intervenor/Respondent No. 1; Committee of Creditors is Respondent No. 3. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission and approval of a resolution plan in the CIRP of Bindals Sponnge Industries Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was undergoing CIRP; Appellant submitted a final revised resolution plan offering Rs. 45.11 Crore (approx.), which was approved by the CoC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Expression of interest issued by RP on 24.08.2018; revised plan submitted on 19.12.2018 and approved by CoC on 28.12.2018; RP filed Section 30(6) application in January 2019; Respondent No. 1 filed I.A. No. 1513(PB) of 2020 in February 2020 (beyond 330 days of CIRP). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC approved Appellant's plan by requisite majority; Respondent No. 1 did not submit an EOI or plan during CIRP, but intervened before NCLT offering Rs. 50.01 Crore (12% or Rs. 4.9 Crore higher). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Special Bench New Delhi allowed I.A. No. 1513(PB) of 2020 on 27.02.2020, directing CoC to consider Respondent No. 1's late plan for asset value maximization.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under Section 31 of the IBC to direct the CoC to consider a fresh, higher resolution plan submitted by an entity that did not participate in the CIRP, after the CoC had already approved a resolution plan and submitted it for approval.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction under Section 31 of the IBC to direct the CoC to evaluate or consider a late resolution plan from a stranger to the CIRP after a valid plan has already been approved by the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) restricts the Adjudicating Authority's jurisdiction to verifying whether an approved resolution plan complies with Section 30(2); it does not confer authority to reopen bids or override commercial wisdom under the banner of asset maximization. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once the financials and details of an approved resolution plan are publicly disclosed before the Adjudicating Authority, entertaining unsolicited third-party bids frustrates the statutory timeline under Section 12 and compromises CIRP sanctity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Entertaining an uninvited offer beyond statutory CIRP limits is impermissible; the NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction by undertaking a quantitative price analysis.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 27.02.2020 set aside; Adjudicating Authority directed to proceed with the RP's application for approval of the CoC-approved resolution plan in accordance with law; no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, Kalinga Allied Industries, was the successful resolution applicant whose plan for Bindals Sponnge Industries Ltd. was approved by the CoC and submitted to the NCLT under Section 30(6). Over a year later, Respondent No. 1 (Hindustan Coils Ltd.), an outsider who never participated in the CIRP, filed an application offering 12% more. The NCLT directed the CoC to consider Respondent No. 1's plan for value maximization. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's order, holding that under Section 31, the Adjudicating Authority's role is strictly limited to reviewing compliance under Section 30(2). It held that entertaining belated bids from third parties post-CoC approval subverts the statutory CIRP framework and timeline.

case_title: Narendra Kumar Agarwal & Anr. vs. Monotrone Leasing Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Narendra Kumar Agarwal & Suman Agarwal are Appellants/Suspended Directors of Corporate Debtor BD Motors Limited; Monotrone Leasing Private Limited is the Respondent No. 1/Financial Creditor; Bimal Kanti Chowdhry is Respondent No. 2/IRP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Short-term inter-corporate loan of Rs. 25,00,000 extended on 14.06.2017 for 90 days with interest @ 15% per annum. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default date established as 20.01.2018 for an outstanding balance of Rs. 28,03,083 (principal + interest); only Rs. 2,69,075 was repaid between 14.06.2017 and 31.03.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan disbursed 14.06.2017; repayment cheques dishonoured on 11.06.2018; Section 138 NI Act notice replied to on 26.11.2018; Section 7 petition admitted on 12.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Money receipt acknowledging loan of Rs. 25 lacs with 15% interest for 90 days; bank statement showing electronic fund transfer on 14.06.2017 at 19:11:37 hrs; two dishonoured HDFC cheques (Nos. 806211 and 806210); reply to Section 138 NI Act notice admitting receipt of financial assistance and partial repayment of Rs. 2,98,973. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditor filed CP (IB) No. 188/KB/2019 under Section 7; NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted the petition on 12.03.2020.
legal_issues: Whether an inter-corporate loan granted for a fixed period with interest qualifies as a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC in the absence of a formal written loan agreement, and whether non-payment constitutes a default under Section 3(12).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A written contract is not an indispensable prerequisite to prove a financial debt if the core attributes of disbursal against the consideration for the time value of money are conclusively proved by transactional records and party acknowledgments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An inter-corporate loan or deposit carrying interest for a specific duration falls squarely within the definition of 'financial debt' under Section 5(8)(a), as interest represents the time value of money; non-payment of such debt upon maturity constitutes default under Section 3(12). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of money receipts, corroborated by bank transaction logs and written admissions in response to statutory demand notices, fully substantiates the occurrence of default beyond the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 lakh. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was payable and defaulted upon, and the Section 7 petition was complete; therefore, admission of CIRP by the Adjudicating Authority was mandatory under Section 7(5).
operative_order: Appeal dismissed as devoid of merit; NCLT Kolkata Bench's admission order dated 12.03.2020 affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants, directors of BD Motors Ltd., challenged an NCLT Kolkata order admitting an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed by Monotrone Leasing Pvt. Ltd. The Appellants contended there was no formal written financial contract, the transaction was merely an inter-corporate deposit, and no default date was specified in Form-1. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that a written contract is not mandatory when money receipts, bank account statements, and reply letters under Section 138 of the NI Act conclusively establish that Rs. 25 lakhs was disbursed at 15% annual interest for 90 days and defaulted upon. The debt squarely qualifies as a financial debt under Section 5(8).

case_title: Pondicherry Extraction Industries Pvt. Ltd. vs. Bank of Baroda
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pondicherry Extraction Industries Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Applicant/Corporate Guarantor/Appellant; Bank of Baroda is the Financial Creditor/Respondent; JR Foods Ltd. is the Principal Borrower. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate guarantee furnished by the Appellant to Bank of Baroda to secure credit facilities availed by JR Foods Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal borrower defaulted, causing its accounts to be classified as NPA on 30.03.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act issued to borrower and guarantors; Appellant's shareholders approved Section 10 CIRP initiation in an EGM on 12.09.2019; application filed in Form 6 before NCLT Chennai. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited balance sheets as on 31.03.2018, 31.03.2019, and 15.09.2019 showed general reserve depletion which the Adjudicating Authority scrutinized; SARFAESI proceedings initiated by the bank. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Division Bench-I Chennai rejected the Section 10 application on 11.02.2020 under Rule 7, holding the application was filed with ulterior motives to defeat SARFAESI proceedings and contained financial statement discrepancies.
legal_issues: Whether Rule 7 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules empowers the NCLT to conduct an in-depth audit of financial statement discrepancies, and whether the pendency of SARFAESI recovery proceedings justifies rejecting a Corporate Applicant's Section 10 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 10 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority's jurisdiction is strictly confined to verifying the existence of debt, default, and compliance with statutory filing requirements, without authority to evaluate balance sheet movements or motives relating to SARFAESI proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 7 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules is procedural and does not empower roving inquiries into balance sheet reserves; pending proceedings under SARFAESI Act or DRT Act are extraneous to Section 10 admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once debt, default, and shareholder approval are shown, and the applicant is not disqualified under Section 11, the Adjudicating Authority is statutorily bound to admit the Section 10 application. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction by auditing financial statements and rejecting the application on extraneous grounds.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 11.02.2020 set aside; case remitted to NCLT Division Bench-I Chennai to admit the Section 10 application after notice to parties if no defect exists, or allow time to rectify defects; no costs.
summary: Corporate Applicant Pondicherry Extraction Industries Pvt. Ltd., a corporate guarantor to principal borrower JR Foods Ltd., filed an application under Section 10 of the IBC after the borrower's account became NPA and SARFAESI notices were issued. The NCLT Chennai rejected the application, citing discrepancies in general reserves across audited balance sheets and inferring an ulterior motive to stall SARFAESI actions. The NCLAT set aside the rejection, ruling that the NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction. Reaffirming the Unigreen Global precedent, the Appellate Tribunal held that Section 10 mandates admission upon proving debt and default in the absence of Section 11 disqualifications, and parallel SARFAESI proceedings are irrelevant.

case_title: Prakash Shankar Mishra & Ors. vs. Ashok Kriplani & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Prakash Shankar Mishra & Ors. (Homebuyers/CoC members) are Appellants; Ashok Kriplani (IRP) is Respondent No. 1; Viswanathan Sankaran is Respondent No. 2; Dreamz Infra India Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development involving 60+ joint-venture sites; homebuyers are class-of-creditors undergoing CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arising from failed real estate projects leading to admission of CIRP against the Corporate Debtor under Section 7. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: 1st CoC meeting on 01.10.2019; 2nd CoC meeting held approving replacements; I.A. No. 670 of 2019 filed to confirm appointments; impugned replacement orders passed on 17.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: In the 2nd CoC meeting, 90% voting share of CoC approved Mr. Konduru Prasanth Raju as RP and Mr. Hari T. Devadiga as AR; IRP Ashok Kriplani sought a monthly fee of Rs. 6.75-10 Lakhs plus a 10% success fee, which CoC rejected; IRP then unilaterally filed CA No. 669/2019 seeking appointment of an unapproved RP (Mr. Suresh Kannan). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench bypassed the CoC resolutions on 17.12.2019 in IA Nos. 659 & 670 of 2019, directly appointing IRP Ashok Kriplani as RP and Viswanathan Sankaran as AR based on site complexity.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to reject the CoC's majority vote replacing an IRP and appointing an Authorized Representative under Section 22 and Section 21(6-A) of the IBC, and impose an RP/AR of its own choice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority has no statutory power to override the majority commercial wisdom of the CoC to impose an RP or AR of its own choosing, and must strictly abide by statutory forwarding mechanisms. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 22(2)-(4) confers exclusive discretion upon the CoC to replace an IRP by 66% majority vote; upon receipt of such application, Section 22(4) mandates the NCLT to forward the proposed name to IBBI for confirmation rather than appointing an unapproved professional. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification that the CoC passed resolutions with the requisite statutory majority (90% in this case) and adhered to Form CA selection rules under Regulation 16A. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's appointment of Respondents 1 and 2 in defiance of CoC resolutions was ultra vires Section 22 and Section 21(6-A).
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 17.12.2019 set aside to the extent of appointing Respondents 1 and 2; Mr. Hari T. Devadiga declared Authorized Representative; Adjudicating Authority directed to forward the name of Mr. Konduru Prasanth Raju to IBBI under Section 22(4); past actions and fees of Respondents 1 and 2 protected.
summary: The CoC of Dreamz Infra India Ltd. appealed an NCLT Bengaluru order which discarded the CoC's 90% vote selecting Mr. Konduru Prasanth Raju as Resolution Professional and Mr. Hari T. Devadiga as Authorized Representative. The NCLT had instead appointed the existing IRP, Ashok Kriplani, as RP and Viswanathan Sankaran as AR, citing project complexity. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's appointment, ruling that under Section 22 and Section 21(6-A) of the IBC read with Regulation 16A, the NCLT has no power to impose an RP or AR of its choice. The NCLT is bound to forward the CoC's proposed RP name to the IBBI for statutory confirmation.

case_title: Pratap Technocrats (P) Ltd. & Ors. vs. Monitoring Committee of Reliance Infratel Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pratap Technocrats (P) Ltd. and six other entities are Operational Creditors/Appellants; Monitoring Committee of Reliance Infratel Limited and Anish Niranjan Nanavaty (RP) are Respondents; Reliance Projects and Property Management Services Limited is Successful Resolution Applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of infrastructure goods and operational services to Reliance Infratel Limited (Corporate Debtor). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants claimed debt default where Rs. 120 crores of their claims were rejected, and admitted claims were subjected to a 90% haircut under the plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against Reliance Infratel Ltd.; NCLT Court-I Mumbai Bench approved the resolution plan on 03.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved resolution plan allocated Rs. 3,720 crores as upfront payment; Operational Creditors received Rs. 25,36,38,128 against admitted debt of Rs. 1,29,28,99,328 (19.62% recovery), whereas Financial Creditors received Rs. 4,235,77,87,067 against admitted debt of Rs. 41,055,38,58,711 (10.32% recovery). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants challenged the NCLT Mumbai order dated 03.12.2020, asserting breach of equitable treatment and exclusion of fair market/liquidation values (Rs. 800 crores) from their payout corpus.
legal_issues: Whether operational creditors are legally entitled to parity of distribution or identical percentage recovery with financial creditors, and whether allocation of funds under a CoC-approved resolution plan that complies with Section 30(2) and Section 53 can be challenged as inequitable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The principle of equitable treatment applies only to similarly situated creditors within the same class; operational creditors cannot claim parity or equal percentage recovery with financial creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2) read with Section 53 guarantees operational creditors a minimum payment not less than the liquidation value; the commercial wisdom of the CoC governs differential payment distribution across classes of creditors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification from resolution plan financial schedules showing that operational creditors were allocated a higher recovery percentage (19.62%) than financial creditors (10.32%) alongside compliance with Section 53 waterfall priority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Operational creditors who received more than the liquidation value and had priority in upfront payments have no legal basis to allege discrimination or inequity.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed at the threshold stage; NCLT Mumbai Bench approval order dated 03.12.2020 upheld.
summary: Operational Creditors of Reliance Infratel Limited appealed the NCLT Mumbai order approving the resolution plan submitted by Reliance Projects and Property Management Services Ltd., alleging unfair treatment, a 90% haircut, and arbitrary fund distribution. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal at the threshold, observing that the operational creditors received 19.62% of their admitted dues in upfront cash, whereas financial creditors received only 10.32%. Citing the Supreme Court judgments in Swiss Ribbons and Essar Steel, the Appellate Tribunal held that equitable treatment applies only within the same class of creditors, and CoC's commercial wisdom determines inter-class distribution provided the minimum liquidation value threshold is honored.

case_title: Mohit Minerals Ltd. vs. Nidhi Impotrade Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mohit Minerals Ltd. is the Appellant/Operational Creditor; Nidhi Impotrade Pvt. Ltd. is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods/minerals giving rise to unpaid operational debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of outstanding operational dues upon maturity of invoices. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Mandatory statutory demand notice under Section 8(1) in Form 3 delivered by an advocate prior to filing Section 9 petition; Section 9 petition dismissed by NCLT Ahmedabad on 04.09.2020; appeal heard ex-parte on 08.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Demand notice in Form 3 issued by Advocate Mr. Sumit Kumar under express instructions from the Operational Creditor; notice annexed at Page 227, Volume-II of appeal paper book. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench (Court No. II) dismissed the Section 9 petition on 04.09.2020, holding the application non-maintainable because the advocate's demand notice was not accompanied by a specific Board Resolution authorizing the advocate.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory demand notice issued and delivered under Section 8(1) of the IBC by an advocate on behalf of an operational creditor requires an accompanying Board Resolution to be legally valid.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A demand notice issued under Section 8(1) of the IBC by an advocate duly instructed by an operational creditor is legally valid without requiring a specific corporate board resolution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(1) read with Form 3 requires delivery by the operational creditor or an authorized agent; pursuant to Supreme Court precedent, an instructed legal counsel possesses statutory competence to issue the demand notice on behalf of the client. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of whether the notice emanates from a lawyer acting under instructions, without necessity of an antecedent board resolution unless the person issuing notice is an internal representative other than an advocate. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed a legal error by invalidating a demand notice issued by an instructed advocate, departing from binding Supreme Court precedent and its own prior rulings.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 04.09.2020 set aside; matter remitted to NCLT Ahmedabad Bench to assess debt and default and pass an admission order or grant Corporate Debtor an opportunity to settle; Appellant directed to appear on 15.02.2021.
summary: Mohit Minerals Ltd. appealed against an order of NCLT Ahmedabad dismissing its Section 9 IBC application against Nidhi Impotrade Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT held the application non-maintainable because the Section 8 demand notice was issued by an advocate without an supporting Board Resolution. Applying the Supreme Court ruling in Macquaire Bank v. Shilpi Cable Technologies, the NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that an advocate duly instructed by an operational creditor is fully authorized to issue a Section 8 demand notice without any accompanying board resolution. The Appellate Tribunal set aside the dismissal and remitted the matter back to the NCLT for admission.

case_title: Mr. Shailendra Sharma vs. Ercon Composites & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Shailendra Sharma is the Appellant/Director of R&M International Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 2); Ercon Composites is the Respondent No. 1/Operational Creditor; Mr. Nayana Premji Savala is Respondent No. 3/IRP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and supply of Carbon Fibre Reinforced Laminates across 27 consignments pursuant to purchase orders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed for an outstanding principal balance of Rs. 69,76,937 plus 18% interest per annum out of an agreed total of Rs. 79,76,937, after credit of Rs. 10,00,000 paid by the Corporate Debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding-up petition CP/552/2016 filed before Bombay High Court on 03.09.2016 and transferred to NCLT Mumbai on 01.02.2017 as CP (IB) No. 749/2017; Form-3 Demand Notice issued on 25.09.2017; notice to Directors issued on 04.01.2018; Section 9 petition admitted on 01.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor sent demand notice dated 25.09.2017 to 'C-2098, Oberoi Gardens Estate', which returned unserved because Corporate Debtor's registered office had been changed to 'A-3027, Oberoi Garden Estate' as per MCA records (Form INC-22) since January 2016; demand notice was later annexed with the rejoinder filed before NCLT; dishonoured cheque dated 03.03.2015 for Rs. 69,76,937 marked 'exceeds arrangement'; emails exchanged regarding defective goods in January 2014. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV admitted the Section 9 petition on 01.01.2020 holding that default exceeded Rs. 1 lakh and presumption under Section 139 NI Act applied to the dishonoured cheque.
legal_issues: Whether the physical service of a statutory demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC at the correct registered office of the Corporate Debtor is a mandatory prerequisite for maintaining an application under Section 9, and whether service effected via rejoinder pleadings before the Adjudicating Authority cures the defect of non-service.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The effective delivery and service of a statutory demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC at the corporate debtor's actual registered office is an incurable mandatory condition precedent; failure of service renders a Section 9 application non-maintainable and abated. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 read with Rule 5 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules requires delivery directly to the registered address or designated key personnel before petition initiation; appending a demand notice to a rejoinder does not satisfy statutory service under Section 8. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Postal endorsements showing the notice returned unserved due to being addressed to a defunct address when the MCA portal recorded a newly registered address proves absence of service; admissions of debt or negotiable instrument presumptions cannot dispense with mandatory statutory notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 8 demand notice was never served on the Corporate Debtor, invalidating the Section 9 petition and rendering the admission order unsustainable in law.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 01.01.2020 set aside; appointment of IRP, moratorium, and CIRP actions declared illegal and vacated; Section 9 petition dismissed as abated; Corporate Debtor restored to independent operation under its Board; liberty granted to Operational Creditor to issue a fresh Section 8 notice and re-apply under Section 9 if warranted.
summary: Appellant Shailendra Sharma, Director of R&M International Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by Ercon Composites. The Appellant established that the Section 8 demand notice was sent to an incorrect previous address and returned unserved, with the Operational Creditor attempting to effect service by annexing it to a subsequent rejoinder before the Tribunal. The NCLAT held that delivery of a Section 8 demand notice to the Corporate Debtor's correct registered address is mandatory and strict; failure of service is not curable by appending it to pleadings or relying on cheque dishonour admissions. Setting aside the admission order, the NCLAT dismissed the CIRP application as abated.

case_title: Amit Bharana vs. Gian Chand Narang Resolution Professional For Apex Buildsys Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Amit Bharana is the Appellant/Erstwhile Director of Apex Buildsys Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Gian Chand Narang is Respondent No. 1/RP & Liquidator; ICICI Bank is Financial Creditor; employees/workmen are Appellants in connected Appeal No. 291/2020. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities availed by Apex Buildsys Ltd., leading to financial default and initiation of CIRP under Section 7. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Aggregated collated claims against Corporate Debtor amounted to Rs. 444.60 Crores; average liquidation value assessed by valuers stood at Rs. 119.36 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 20.09.2018; 18th CoC meeting held on 22.10.2019 resolving to liquidate; CIRP expiry date was 14.11.2019; NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi ordered liquidation on 09.01.2020 under Section 33(2). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP received 14 EOIs; 2 resolution plans submitted (Alchemist ARC offering Rs. 79.15 cr, and M/s S.C. Agrawal offering Rs. 71.00 cr); both plans were conditional and contingent on selling leased land at Pant Nagar unit, offering values far below assessed liquidation value (Rs. 119.36 cr); long-term leases existed with SIDCUL (90 years from 2006) and MIDC (95 years from 2008); 18th CoC rejected both plans and approved liquidation by 87.30% vote share. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed Section 33(1) liquidation application; NCLT Principal Bench allowed it on 09.01.2020; Appellants appealed challenging the exclusion of plans from formal voting and valuation of government leasehold land.
legal_issues: Whether the CoC has absolute commercial discretion under Section 33(2) to reject conditional, unviable resolution plans and resolve to liquidate the corporate debtor without putting them to formal electronic voting, and whether leasehold industrial land under registered long-term leases can be factored into liquidation valuation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the CoC in assessing the viability and feasibility of resolution plans and deciding to liquidate a corporate debtor under Section 33(2) with the requisite majority is paramount and entirely non-justiciable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(2) and its Explanation empower the CoC to decide to liquidate at any time before confirmation of a plan; conditional plans contingent upon uncertain property sales and below liquidation value do not constitute compliant plans under Section 30 read with CIRP Regulation 37. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Supreme Court ruling in MCGM v. Abhilash Lal applies only where no lease deed exists; where registered long-term leases exist with transferable rights, valuation of leasehold rights is legally sustainable for computing liquidation value. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC lawfully exercised its commercial wisdom with an 87.30% majority to reject non-viable plans and mandate liquidation; the Adjudicating Authority is statutorily bound to order liquidation under Section 33(1).
operative_order: Both appeals dismissed for lack of merit; liquidation order dated 09.01.2020 upheld; interim order restraining disposal of properties vacated; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants Amit Bharana (director) and employees challenged the NCLT Principal Bench order directing liquidation of Apex Buildsys Ltd. under Section 33(2) of the IBC. The Appellants argued that the CoC rejected resolution plans without formal voting, misapplied leasehold land values, and violated MCGM v. Abhilash Lal. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the CoC deliberated and rejected the two submitted plans as conditional, unviable, and below liquidation value. With an 87.30% voting majority, the CoC acted within its commercial wisdom to order liquidation, which is non-justiciable under Section 33(2) and binding precedents such as K. Sashidhar and Essar Steel.

case_title: Arun Gupta & Anr. vs. South Eastern Carriers Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Arun Gupta & Savita Gupta (shareholders/directors holding 33.93% combined) are Appellants; South Eastern Carriers Limited is Respondent No. 1; Yogendra Pal Jain and others are contesting shareholder-directors/Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operation and management of transport business in a closely held family company incorporated in March 1974, with severe intra-family disputes across three branches. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Severe oppression and mismanagement claims alleging turnover plunged from Rs. 222 crores (2015) to Rs. 9 crores (2018) while a competing entity (Care Go Logistics) floated by Appellants grew to Rs. 93.90 crores; siphoning of Rs. 66 lakhs gratuity funds; police FIRs lodged. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP No. 42 of 2016 filed under Section 397/398; various interlocutory applications filed between 2017 and 2019; NCLT Kolkata passed impugned interim order on 01.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Substantial conflicting documentation alleging diversion of customers, parallel business operations, illegal board resolutions, branch divisions under private MOUs, and physical lockouts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP No. 42/KB/2016, NCLT Kolkata appointed Mr. D.C. Agrawal (Retd. CIT) as Special Officer on 01.10.2019 to inspect records, supervise the conduct of business, preside over Board meetings, and submit a fact-finding report within 60 days; Appellants appealed under Section 421 asserting violation of Section 422's 3-month disposal limit.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT possesses the jurisdiction under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 to appoint an independent Special Officer to supervise board meetings and investigate company affairs as an interim measure during the pendency of an oppression and mismanagement petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal has broad discretionary jurisdiction under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 to issue interim orders and appoint an independent supervisory officer to regulate company affairs, preserve assets, and ascertain facts where management is divided. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(4) gives plenary power to pass any interim order deemed just and equitable; the expedition timeline under Section 422 does not divest the Tribunal of its statutory power to conduct necessary factual investigations through an officer of the court. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Appointing an independent investigator/observer is warranted when serious, competing prima facie allegations of business diversion, asset siphoning, and managerial deadlock require ground verification before final adjudication. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The interim appointment of a Special Officer to oversee meetings and report on affairs was well within the NCLT's jurisdiction and does not constitute an impermissible postponement under Section 422.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; interim order of NCLT Kolkata dated 01.10.2019 upheld; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants Arun Gupta and Savita Gupta challenged an interim order of NCLT Kolkata in an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013. The NCLT had appointed a retired Income Tax Commissioner as Special Officer to preside over Board meetings and investigate severe mutual allegations of business diversion and fund siphoning. The Appellants argued that the appointment exceeded jurisdiction and bypassed the three-month disposal mandate in Section 422. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 242(4) grants broad interim powers to regulate company affairs and preserve assets, and that appointing an independent observer to investigate disputed facts prior to final disposal was entirely justified.

case_title: Greenopolis Welfare Association vs. Three C Shelters Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Greenopolis Welfare Association represents 350 homebuyers (Financial Creditors); Straight Edge Contracts Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor; Three C Shelters Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Development and construction of 38 residential towers in the Greenopolis Project launched in 2011. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Defaulted operational debt of Rs. 29,95,91,034/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against the Operational Creditor was set aside by NCLAT on 13.03.2020 pursuant to a settlement, and subsequent Section 9 petition against the Corporate Debtor was admitted prior to restoration of the Operational Creditor's CIRP on 28.09.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor director's admission email dated 27.01.2020 and affidavit dated 05.03.2020 confirming unpaid dues of Rs. 29,95,91,034/-. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP IB-2721/ND/2019 under Section 9; NCLT New Delhi admitted it on 20.07.2020 based on admitted operational debt and dismissed Appellant's intervention IA 3491/2020 on 17.09.2020.
legal_issues: Whether a Corporate Debtor undergoing or recently exited from CIRP is barred under Section 11 of the IBC from filing an operational debt application against another entity, and whether an alleged debt assignment by a Corporate Debtor establishes collusion or a pre-existing dispute.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate entity is entitled to initiate CIRP against another corporate debtor for its independent receivables, and the statutory bar under Section 11 attaches exclusively at the precise time of filing an application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 11(a) and (b) bar the initiation of CIRP, not its continuation; Explanation II clarifies that corporate debtors referred to in clauses (a) to (d) are not prevented from initiating insolvency against another debtor. Furthermore, unlike financial or operational creditors under Sections 5(7) and 5(20), a Corporate Debtor under Section 3(8) cannot legally assign its liabilities to manufacture an operational dispute. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted written acknowledgments and balance confirmations by authorized officers sufficiently prove default, which cannot be dislodged by speculative allegations of fraud or collusion lacking documentary backing. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was valid when filed as CIRP stood quashed on that date, and technical defects in the admission order were cured by subsequent detailed orders.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the admission of CIRP against Respondent No. 1 and disposing of all pending interlocutory applications.
summary: Greenopolis Welfare Association appealed against the NCLT orders admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by Straight Edge Contracts Pvt. Ltd. against Three C Shelters Pvt. Ltd. and dismissing the association's intervention plea. The association alleged collusion, invalid assignment of debt, lack of reason in the initial admission order, and statutory ineligibility of the operational creditor under Section 11. The NCLAT held that Section 11 did not bar the application as the operational creditor's prior CIRP had been vacated at the time of filing, and Explanation II permits corporate debtors to initiate CIRP. The admission order was sustained, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Saboo Tor Private Limited vs. Sanjay Gupta, Liquidator of Case Cold Roll Forming Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Saboo Tor Private Limited is the auction bidder/applicant; Sanjay Gupta is the Liquidator of Case Cold Roll Forming Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in liquidation). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation e-auction for the sale of raw material, scrap, stores, spares, consumables, and finished goods of the Corporate Debtor at a reserve price of Rs. 1.59 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in depositing 25% of the total bid consideration (Rs. 93,75,197/- plus GST out of the bid amount of Rs. 3,75,00,786/-) within the stipulated auction timeline of 25.03.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: E-auction held on 18.03.2020; Letter of Intent issued on 20.03.2020 and unconditionally accepted on 23.03.2020; initial payment deadline was 25.03.2020 (extended to 31.03.2020); EMD forfeited on 23.05.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator's reminder emails dated 01.04.2020, 02.04.2020, 23.04.2020, 15.05.2020, and 18.05.2020 granting final 48 hours before forfeiture; unconditional acceptance of LoI dated 23.03.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 3413 of 2020 before NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi seeking refund of forfeited EMD; NCLT dismissed the application on 05.11.2020 as misconceived due to breach of auction terms.
legal_issues: Whether a liquidator is legally justified under the terms of an e-auction process document in forfeiting the Earnest Money Deposit when the successful bidder fails to deposit the mandatory initial 25% sale consideration citing COVID-19 lockdown disruptions.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A bidder participating in a public auction with full awareness of prevailing circumstances cannot rely on subsequent hardship to breach unconditional auction milestones, and failure to meet threshold deposit covenants triggers absolute forfeiture without requiring proof of actual loss. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Liquidator process documents governed by statutory insolvency liquidation regulations form binding contractual stipulations; clauses permitting interest payment within an extended 90-day window apply strictly to the remaining 75% balance consideration, not the foundational 25% threshold deposit. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unconditional acceptance of the Letter of Intent after the outbreak of known circumstances precludes invocation of force majeure or pre-contractual protections under Section 74 of the Contract Act. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bidder precluded the concluded sale by its own non-compliance despite repeated notices, rendering forfeiture of the Rs. 16,00,000/- EMD valid under Clause J of the process document.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, upholding the NCLT order affirming the liquidator's forfeiture of the Earnest Money Deposit.
summary: Saboo Tor Private Limited emerged as the successful bidder in an e-auction conducted by the liquidator of Case Cold Roll Forming Ltd., offering Rs. 3.75 crores and depositing Rs. 16 lakhs as EMD. After unconditionally accepting the LoI on 23.03.2020, the appellant failed to pay the mandatory 25% consideration by the extended deadline of 31.03.2020, citing pandemic lockdowns. The liquidator forfeited the EMD after multiple reminders. Appellant challenged the forfeiture before NCLT, which dismissed the plea. On appeal, the NCLAT affirmed that the 90-day interest indulgence applied only to the remaining 75% balance, and forfeiture was fully justified under the auction conditions.

case_title: RHI India Private Limited & Ors. vs. Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Transferor Companies are RHI India Pvt. Ltd. and RHI Clasil Pvt. Ltd.; Transferee Company is Orient Refractories Ltd. (listed entity); Respondent is Union of India through Regional Director, MCA Western Region. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate amalgamation and consolidation scheme under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 to simplify group corporate structure of RHI Magnesita. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Scheme envisaged issuance of up to 4,08,57,131 equity shares of the Transferee Company representing 25.38% post-allotment equity to transferor shareholders based on share exchange valuation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respective Board of Directors approved scheme on 31.07.2018; appointed date specified in scheme was 01.01.2019; Regional Director report submitted on 24.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Overwhelming approval by 99.95% of relevant stakeholders including 96.05% of public shareholders; fairness opinion by merchant banker; valuation report dated 31.07.2018; statutory clearances without objection from SEBI, BSE, NSE, CCI, and RBI. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Scheme petition CP No. 2199 of 2019 was rejected by NCLT Mumbai Bench on 02.03.2020 holding that the scheme benefited only promoter-group shareholders, was contrary to public policy, and had a mismatch between valuation date (31.07.2018) and appointed date (01.01.2019).
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can reject a scheme of amalgamation approved by 99.95% of voting stakeholders on subjective notions of public policy and share valuation, and whether the appointed date must strictly correspond with the valuation date.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The company court exercising sanctioning jurisdiction under Sections 230-232 does not sit as an appellate court over the commercial wisdom of shareholders and cannot substitute its own business assessment in the absence of fraud, illegality, or regulatory objection. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 232(6) read with MCA General Circular No. 09/2019 enables companies the commercial freedom to designate a specific calendar appointed date or tie it to events; a discrepancy between the valuation date and appointed date does not invalidate a scheme. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where statutory majorities are established without minority objection or regulatory challenge from SEBI/MCA, courts cannot declare a scheme violative of public policy based on speculative enrichment of certain shareholders. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed judicial overreach by delving into financial valuation matters and rejecting a fully compliant scheme; fixing the appointed date as 31.07.2018 per the applicants' consent eliminated all potential timing concerns.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, setting aside the NCLT order dated 02.03.2020, sanctioning the scheme with an appointed date of 31.07.2018, and directing NCLT Mumbai and the Regional Director to ensure immediate operationalization.
summary: RHI India Pvt. Ltd., RHI Clasil Pvt. Ltd., and Orient Refractories Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order rejecting their composite scheme of amalgamation. The NCLT rejected the scheme on grounds that the share exchange ratio disproportionately enriched holding company shareholders against public policy, and that the appointed date (01.01.2019) differed from the valuation date (31.07.2018). The NCLAT overturned the decision, holding that the NCLT exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction by interfering with shareholder commercial wisdom approved by 99.95% majority without regulatory objection. Accepting the appellants' agreement to align the appointed date to 31.07.2018, the NCLAT sanctioned the scheme.

case_title: Balaji Inimai vs. R. Srinivasan & 12 Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 182 of 2019 & No. 220 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Thangam Metal Cans Pvt. Ltd., L. Balaji (Director), and Balaji Inimai; Respondents No. 1 and 2 are minority shareholders (R. Srinivasan and S. Krishna Kumar). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Conversion of a partnership firm into a private limited company on 29.04.2004 with family shareholding across branches of Late A. Rathinasamy Nadar's family. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Challenged preferential dilution reducing Respondents 1 & 2's shareholding from 21.27% (72,500 shares) down to 9.2% through an unauthorized allotment of 4,50,000 equity shares of Rs. 10/- each. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: AGM approving authorized share capital enhancement convened on 30.09.2011; impugned share allotment carried out on 30.12.2011; company petition filed before CLB Chennai in January 2015. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Defective and irregular dispatch of notices for the AGM dated 30.09.2011; absence of any share offer to the petitioners; statutory filings made with the RoC reflecting unilateral capital increase. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents filed CP/15/2015 (TCP/159/2016) before NCLT Chennai alleging oppression; NCLT on 26.06.2019 declared the AGM and 30.12.2011 allotments null and void, restored the 3,40,000 share structure, and set aside all RoC filings since 30.09.2011.
legal_issues: Whether the complete unwinding of nine years of corporate filings and share capital expansion is the appropriate equitable remedy under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956 for unlawful share dilution, or whether parity restoration through additional issuance serves the company's best interest.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In corporate oppression proceedings, judicial remedies must prioritize the ongoing operational stability and creditworthiness of the corporate entity over rigid restitutive unwinding that disrupts long-settled commercial relations with third-party lenders. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Powers conferred under Sections 397/398 of the 1956 Act and Sections 241/242 of the 2013 Act enable tribunals to make just and equitable orders to bring an end to the matters complained of, including directing proportionate fresh share issuance rather than catastrophic balance-sheet reductions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Deprivation of statutory notice for capital expansion constitutes continuous oppression exempt from dismissal on laches, but remedial relief must balance member rights against operational disruption. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Reversing nine years of paid-up capital and cancelling RoC filings jeopardizes banking credit limits and imposes undue administrative costs; directing fresh allotment of shares to affected members at the original issuance price provides complete equitable redress.
operative_order: The NCLT order is set aside; Appellants are directed to allot additional equity shares to Respondents No. 1 & 2 within 3 months at the 2011 issue price to restore their cumulative shareholding to the original 21.27% proportion.
summary: In a family company dispute concerning Thangam Metal Cans Pvt. Ltd., the NCLT Chennai set aside an AGM resolution dated 30.09.2011 and an allotment of 4,50,000 shares dated 30.12.2011 which diluted the respondents' shareholding from 21.27% to 9.2%, additionally cancelling nine years of statutory RoC filings. On appeal, the NCLAT recognized that improper notice constituted continuing oppression not barred by limitation. However, holding that unwinding capital and cancelling years of RoC filings harmed the company's financial standing and banking covenants, the NCLAT modified the remedy by directing the appellants to issue additional shares to restore the respondents' original 21.27% shareholding at the historical issue price.

case_title: JKS The Banyaan Private Limited vs. Bank of Baroda
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: JKS The Banyaan Private Limited is the Corporate Applicant/Guarantor; Bank of Baroda is the Financial Creditor; JR Foods Ltd. is the Principal Borrower. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate guarantee extended by the Corporate Applicant to secure credit facilities availed by the principal borrower from Bank of Baroda. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by principal borrower resulting in classification of account as Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 30.03.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 issued by the Financial Creditor; Corporate Applicant's shareholders approved Section 10 CIRP initiation in an EGM on 12.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited balance sheets as on 31.03.2018, 31.03.2019, and for the period ending 15.09.2019; statutory SARFAESI notice confirming crystallized default. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Applicant filed Section 10 application in Form 6 before NCLT Division Bench-I Chennai; NCLT rejected the application on 11.02.2020 on grounds of financial statement discrepancies and suspected ulterior motives to defeat SARFAESI proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses statutory jurisdiction under Rule 7 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules to scrutinize internal balance sheet discrepancies and reject a complete Section 10 application on grounds of parallel SARFAESI proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority is statutorily mandated to admit a Section 10 application once debt and default are established, the application is procedurally complete, and the applicant does not attract disqualifications under Section 11 of the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 is purely procedural and does not confer inquisitorial power on the tribunal to assess internal balance sheet inconsistencies or probe extraneous motives. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pendency of debt recovery actions under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 or DRT Act, 1993 constitutes an extraneous consideration that cannot be utilized to impute mala fides or suppressions under Section 10. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT exceeded its limited statutory mandate by rejecting the petition based on collateral discrepancies; debt and default stood admitted, warranting remand for formal admission.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, setting aside the rejection order dated 11.02.2020 and remitting the matter to NCLT Chennai to admit the Section 10 application after affording opportunity to cure any technical defects.
summary: JKS The Banyaan Private Limited, a corporate guarantor for credit facilities extended by Bank of Baroda to JR Foods Ltd., filed a Section 10 application under the IBC following default and issuance of SARFAESI notices. The NCLT Chennai rejected the application, holding that discrepancies in the corporate debtor's balance sheets cast doubt on the bona fides of the application and indicated an attempt to frustrate SARFAESI recovery. The NCLAT reversed the order, ruling that Rule 7 provides only procedural requirements and does not empower tribunals to probe financial statements or reject complete applications on extraneous grounds like parallel SARFAESI actions.

case_title: MCC Concrete vs. Northway Spaces Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: MCC Concrete is the Operational Creditor; Northway Spaces Ltd. (formerly Mayfair Spaces Ltd.) is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of ready-mix concrete material across various construction sites of the Corporate Debtor against purchase orders between 30.09.2012 and 20.10.2014. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total invoiced value was Rs. 2,29,94,288/-; part-payments made totaled Rs. 2,09,30,948/-; unpaid operational debt claimed was Rs. 20,63,340/- outstanding as on 11.11.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued on 11.02.2017 (unreplied); Section 9 application filed before NCLT Ahmedabad on 15.01.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Stamped delivery challans; running ledger account showing part-payment of Rs. 12,00,000/- on 05.11.2015 resetting limitation; Corporate Debtor's ledger confirming Rs. 19,89,130/- due as of 31.03.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application filed on 15.01.2018; NCLT Ahmedabad rejected it on 12.02.2020 on the ground of a pre-existing dispute regarding two returned invoices from 2013 billed to Mayfair Corporate Park.
legal_issues: Whether returning two invoices outside a running account establishes a bona fide pre-existing dispute under Section 9, and whether a mutual ledger balance exceeding the threshold amount mandates admission of CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A debtor cannot defeat insolvency proceedings by isolating disputed invoices when an authenticated running ledger account acknowledges an outstanding operational liability surpassing the statutory threshold. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 9(5)(2)(d) read with Mobilox principles, a pre-existing dispute must be genuine, substantial, and supported by concrete evidence, not a feeble or spurious assertion contradicted by the debtor's own running ledger accounts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Reconciliation of internal ledger accounts demonstrating continuous credits and unliquidated debit balances constitutes conclusive proof of debt and default, rendering unproven objections irrelevant. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The running ledger maintained by the Corporate Debtor confirmed Rs. 19,89,130/- due as of 31.03.2017, well within three years of the 05.11.2015 payment; the petition was maintainable and wrongly rejected.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, setting aside the rejection order dated 12.02.2020 and remitting the case to NCLT Ahmedabad to admit the Section 9 application after issuing notice to permit settlement.
summary: MCC Concrete appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order rejecting its Section 9 IBC application against Northway Spaces Ltd. (formerly Mayfair Spaces Ltd.) for recovery of Rs. 20,63,340/- for ready-mix concrete supplies. The NCLT had rejected the petition citing a pre-existing dispute over two invoices returned in 2013 addressed to Mayfair Corporate Park. The NCLAT reconciled the running ledger accounts, found that the Corporate Debtor's own books acknowledged an unpaid balance of Rs. 19,89,130/- as of 31.03.2017, and noted that the part-payment of Rs. 12 lakhs on 05.11.2015 brought the 15.01.2018 petition within limitation. The rejection was set aside and the petition remitted for admission.

case_title: Vinod Singh Negi vs. Kiran Shah, Liquidator of ORG Informatics Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Vinod Singh Negi (ex-employee); Respondent is Kiran Shah, Liquidator of ORG Informatics Ltd. (in liquidation). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment relationship between 16.04.2007 and 31.07.2012 for which unpaid salary, gratuity, and leave encashment arrears were claimed. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed salary arrears and terminal benefits of Rs. 34,94,287/- with interest, pertaining to service terminating on 31.07.2012. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Claim submitted in Form E to the Liquidator on 07.01.2020; Liquidator rejected the claim as time-barred on 15.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant produced an unverified self-prepared calculation sheet, PAN card, appointment letters, and relieving letter, but failed to produce salary slips, bank statements showing salary credits, or any demand correspondence between 2012 and 2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IAs No. 505/2020 and 306/2020 under Section 42 of IBC before NCLT Ahmedabad seeking condonation of delay and admission of claim; NCLT rejected the applications holding the underlying claim to be barred by limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority hearing an application for condonation of delay under Section 42 of the IBC is empowered to examine the substantive limitation and maintainability of the underlying debt claim.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority adjudicating an application for delay condonation under the IBC is fully empowered to evaluate whether the underlying claim is extinguished by limitation, and cannot condone delay where the primary claim is hopelessly stale. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: By virtue of Section 238A of the IBC, the Limitation Act applies strictly to insolvency proceedings to prevent the revival of dead claims against an entity undergoing CIRP or liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unsupported self-serving calculation sheets absent corroborative bank records, employer certifications, or prior contemporaneous demand notices fail to establish a bona fide actionable debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A claim arising in 2012 filed without any demand for eight years cannot be entertained during liquidation merely by seeking condonation of filing delays; the rejection of the claim was legally sound.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order rejecting the applications for claim admission and condonation of delay.
summary: Vinod Singh Negi, a former employee of ORG Informatics Ltd., appealed the NCLT Ahmedabad order rejecting his applications under Section 42 of the IBC. Negi sought condonation of delay and admission of a claim for Rs. 34,94,287/- regarding unpaid salary and dues dating back to 2012. He submitted Form E to the liquidator in January 2020 without evidence of contemporaneous demands or supporting bank statements. The NCLAT upheld the dismissal, ruling that Section 238A bars stale, time-extinguished claims from being revived during liquidation, and held that the Adjudicating Authority acted within its jurisdiction in assessing claim maintainability when evaluating delay condonation.

case_title: Shubham Jain vs. Gagan Ferrotech Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Shubham Jain is a Director of Corporate Debtor Manju J Homes India Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Gagan Ferrotech Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is the Corporate Debtor through IRP Harish Goyal. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial operational supply of goods and materials to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding operational debt of Rs. 84,47,147/- (principal amount of Rs. 66,03,856.78/- and interest of Rs. 18,43,290.22/- at 18% per annum till 20.06.2018); default date was 02.12.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 Demand Notice dispatched and attempted on 27.06.2018; Section 9 application filed thereafter; Corporate Debtor proceeded ex-parte on 18.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Speed post receipts and tracking reports reflecting delivery remarks 'addressee moved' at registered office, 'unclaimed' at operational office, and actual personal service on the Director of the Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 CP (IB) No. 1058/ND/2018 was admitted by NCLT New Delhi (Court IV) on 02.09.2019 ex-parte against the Corporate Debtor on grounds of uncontroverted default.
legal_issues: Whether service of a Section 8 demand notice upon a Director of a Corporate Debtor constitutes valid service on the company, and whether postal endorsements of 'unclaimed' or 'addressee moved' constitute effective deemed delivery.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Service of statutory demand notice upon an officer or director of a corporate entity satisfies legal service requirements and constitutes effective notice against the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(1) mandate is harmonized with Section 2(59) and Section 20 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Section 424; since a director is an officer of the company, service on the director or postal return endorsements marked 'unclaimed' amount to legally complete deemed delivery. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Bare assertions of a disputed claim without documentary evidence demonstrating the existence of a dispute prior to issuance of the Section 8 demand notice cannot defeat an application under Section 9. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The operational debt of Rs. 84,47,147/- and default on 02.12.2016 were conclusively established, and the Corporate Debtor failed to demonstrate any pre-existing dispute or defective service.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT order admitting CIRP against the Corporate Debtor.
summary: Shubham Jain, a director of Manju J Homes India Ltd., appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Gagan Ferrotech Ltd. for an unpaid debt of Rs. 84,47,147/-. The appellant contended that the Section 8 demand notice had not been served properly because post to corporate premises was returned as 'addressee moved' and 'unclaimed', and that service on a director was legally invalid. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that a director is an officer under Section 2(59) of the Companies Act, 2013, making service on a director good service. Furthermore, postal return marked 'unclaimed' is valid service, and bald assertions of dispute unsupported by evidence cannot impede CIRP.

case_title: Sri Kaustuv Ray vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sri Kaustuv Ray (Director/Promoter); Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Corporate Debtor through its Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by State Bank of India to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred in the year 2013; Corporate Debtor's loan account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 17.06.2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 17.06.2013; Section 7 CIRP application filed on 01.04.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NPA classification date on bank record showing 17.06.2013; Section 7 petition records reflecting a time gap of nearly six years before institution of insolvency proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed by State Bank of India was admitted by NCLT Kolkata on 04.02.2020; Appellant appealed on the sole ground of limitation.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 CIRP application filed nearly six years after the date of NPA classification is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for initiation of CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, which prescribes a three-year period running from the date of default. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The three-year limitation under Article 137 runs strictly from the date of default, defined in bank debt cases as the date of NPA classification, absent acknowledged extensions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the application under Section 7 is filed beyond three years from the date of NPA without valid acknowledgment of debt in accordance with the Limitation Act, the petition is time-barred. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Default occurred when the account was classified as NPA on 17.06.2013, making the Section 7 petition filed on 01.04.2019 barred by limitation.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, setting aside the NCLT admission order dated 04.02.2020, releasing the Corporate Debtor from CIRP, relieving the IRP, and remitting determination of the IRP's fees to the Adjudicating Authority, without prejudice to other recovery remedies.
summary: Sri Kaustuv Ray appealed an NCLT Kolkata order admitting State Bank of India's Section 7 IBC application against the Corporate Debtor. The appellant asserted that the application was barred by limitation because the loan account had been declared an NPA on 17.06.2013, while the Section 7 application was filed only on 01.04.2019. Relying on established Supreme Court precedents applying Article 137 of the Limitation Act to Section 7 filings, the NCLAT held that the three-year limitation expired in 2016, rendering the 2019 petition time-barred. The NCLAT set aside the admission order and released the company from CIRP.
